addendum.file: 08 Research/Comps/ADDENDUM 05 — Conspiracy engines (what moves a conspiracy plot).md
addendum.title: Addendum 05 — Conspiracy engines (what moves a conspiracy plot)
addendum.intro:
12 Nov 2026. After Tier 2 (ten books); The Club Dumas and Six Days of the Condor (Tier 1) still not downloaded. Replaces the 11 Nov version.

Sources: the ten maps and Q&As in 08 Research/Engines/, checked against THE BOOK v8.2, the v8 brief, the v7 Part Two drafts (19, 23, 24, 27, 30, 41, 43, 45) and 01 Manuscript/v6/18 — On land.md. Where a map's claim needed it I also read v6 The vet and The gorilla mask, v7 The sheets and v8 Leave it. Everything here is a PROPOSAL. Your decisions are marked PLACEHOLDER.

The problem hasn't changed: in Part Two James receives paper. Nothing makes him prove anything before he acts, and nothing he does can go wrong except by frightening him. Tier 1 said the fix is to make the reason he can't stop into something he did. Tier 2 agrees and adds three things. The front (C) can be an engine after all, if James acts on a layer as though it were the bottom and pays for it. A canary needs no invented item; one true sentence said in public can be enough. And The Name of the Rose shows where the switch belongs: until Day 5 William is held by other people's clocks, and from Day 5 by his own mistake. Lot 49 adds the condition that makes receiving bearable: the job obliges the hero to look, so stopping would be a breach.

sections.title: a. The mechanisms, one by one

items.title: A. The gate
items.html: Supported by: King (strongly); The Name of the Rose (William sets his own gate, Day 4, Vespers, while Bernard Gui, who has none, burns the wrong people); Declare (passed by refusing, ch. 8); Libra (from outside: Oswald brings every paper to Mexico City and still gets no); Pynchon (the two columns, said by a clown and refused, ch. 6); Eco's Pendulum (inside the canary); Borges; Orwell (the dial). Weak in Gibson and Illuminatus!. Best example: King, 11/22/63, ch. 3 and 7: "ninety-five percent isn't a hundred," and knowledge loses its value once used. The calendar, not the doubt, makes the wait bearable. New: Rose's rival reader as the clock. Waiting costs because a worse reader's answer becomes the official one; in SDF the plausible endings are that answer, and every week James waits another address closes as "heart" or "sold." Fits SDF? Yes, if James sets the gate himself and a person (Frank) chooses to open it. Verdict: use it. Still the named gap, now with four more books behind it.

items.title: B. The canary
items.html: Supported by: Eco's Pendulum (central), Gibson, Orwell, Borges, Rose, Declare (both ways, ch. 7 and 9); Libra and Illuminatus! run it from the conspiracy's side. Best example: Eco, ch. 75–76: one fake sect in a real chronology; Agliè asks who mentioned it, asks again, checks his watch. Revised: the cheapest canary in ten books is Rose, Day 2, Terce. William says loudly that nobody may touch Venantius's desk, and by evening three monks have tried to steer him off it. One true public sentence about a real object. James already does this in v7 The reading room, continued ("to see which one made the woman by the window move"). Fits SDF? Yes, with invented titles only, and a true sentence wherever one will do. Verdict: keep the one invention the plan has (On land, cashed in The dinner) and give it Eco's four parts: a unique item, a hook someone can act on, a readout through a third person, a price. Add no second invention. That removes Tier 1's fake sheet in The reading room, continued.

items.title: C. The front
items.html: Supported by: Illuminatus! (deciding); Rose (each solved layer covers the next, and on Day 5 a true smaller secret closes the case officially); Libra (built by the antagonist, and by Oswald, who hides the rifle "to give them something to uncover, a layer to strip away"); Declare (Hale wears fronts and must live up to them, ch. 16); Borges, Orwell, Gibson. In Pynchon fronts run four deep but are only learned. Weak in Eco's Pendulum and King. Tier 1 said C is only ever learned, so not a Part Two engine. That holds for Tier 1 and Pynchon. Tier 2 says it works under four conditions (Illuminatus!): (1) someone acts on a layer as if it were the bottom, and pays; (2) the layer breaks from outside him, on an object or a second person, never on his deduction; (3) each layer is true at the rank of whoever hears it; (4) there is a floor, or you get Gimmel's appendices and the reader stops caring. SDF's floor is The night he stops being afraid. The map also corrects the brief: the four helper words on Kalder's phone are compartments side by side, not rungs. SDF's ladder is James's own climb, from asker (The payload) to program staff (the badge "one note up," v7 The drill), annex role, schedule, and the offer of a seat. Each promotion hands him the next layer, so C is already the shape of Part Two; condition (1) is what's missing. Best example: Illuminatus!, Trip 8: Danny takes Mama Sutra's kind counter-history, ends up defending the Illuminati, and a clearance line ("Mama isn't cleared for this") breaks it. Fits SDF? Yes, with no impersonation, no invented task, no staged ordeal. Verdict: it works when James acts on a layer and pays. Two changes below do that (The money, The math). Build no more.

items.title: D. Lock and key
items.html:
Supported by: King, Gibson, Orwell, Pynchon, Rose (doors open by choice); Libra, with a limit (a key opens talk, not choice); Declare; Illuminatus!, inverted (Joe gets every key and declines, as James declines the lower door). Best example: Gibson, ch. 29–31: the address bought with a Curta on Bigend's money, and the tie comes due. Fits SDF? Already on the page (Groningen, Els's line, Noor's shelfmark, the forum password). Verdict: nothing to build. Keep Libra's limit for The sheets: a key gets a helper talking; it doesn't decide for them.

Further mechanisms, merged, with verdicts:

  • The cost after the gate. King ch. 9, 26–29; Libra (Ferrie's exit comes with a killer at the theater). Being right doesn't make the act safe. Fits; travels with A.
  • Duty: the hero does the machine's homework. Orwell I.iv (Ogilvy); Pynchon (duty as the engine; the hero as carrier, ch. 5); Declare ch. 9. Best: Orwell I.iv. Fits; it is C's condition (1) in SDF's clothes. The money.
  • The findable trail: who handed me this? Orwell II.ix (true bait); Pynchon ch. 6 ("Every access route… traced also back to the Inverarity estate"); Libra (the Curator chooses what to send); Illuminatus! (the planted resting place, Trip 10). Best: Pynchon ch. 6. Fits; the opening already says "we leave them findable." Missing is James sorting pulled from handed. Twenty minutes, Frank, loose.
  • The side channel carries the bill. King ch. 23–25; Gibson ch. 29–31. Fits: the friendship is the channel, the dog the bill.
  • Make it useless, don't take it. Orwell III.iv (the dust put back); Rose Day 2 (the lenses stolen, the page left; "ruined by mice"); Borges (the withdrawn copy). Fits, if the thin book stays in the kitchen (d).
  • The file that discredits him. Illuminatus! Trip 4 (Saul told he is "Muldoon"); Eco ch. 108–109 (the frame); Declare ch. 3 (a file improved to discredit); Rose ("no one will believe you"). Best: Illuminatus! Trip 4. Fits exactly: Els's folder prints the rule ("reclassified") and nothing on the page uses it. Take one: Illuminatus! 5.2, Declare 5.1 and Pynchon 5.4 all want the same slot.
  • The invention that can't be taken back. Eco ch. 76, 118. The price of any invented canary, and the reason to keep to one.
  • Smaller, used as runners-up or in Part Three: the truth filed among the nonsense (Rose Day 6); evidence put up for sale (Pynchon's lot 49); the kind counter-history (Illuminatus! Trip 8); co-optation (Rose's Benno) and the slip at the middle level (Libra's Mackey); holding back as an action and the old post as tripwire (Gibson); the broken man in public (Orwell III.vi).

On lore, all ten agree: it holds when someone in the room can lose by it. Rose proves it with the same material: the Dolcino history stalls on Day 3 and runs at Remigio's trial on Day 5, where a life hangs on each answer. Your long lore scenes (Frank's kitchen, Leiden, The reading room, continued) each have someone who can lose: Frank, Noor, Anneke. Keep it so.

Does not work: Gibson's deflated conspiracy; Borges's withdrawal; Pynchon's open ending; Branch sealed in his room (Libra); the bottomless stack and Hagbard's kidnaps and drugs (Illuminatus!); the solicitor as leverage (Declare); William's stealth; Oedipa's lies for reactions.

sections.title: b. Part Two, chapter by chapter
sections.html: Every Part Two chapter in v8.2, in order. Each proposal was checked against the drafts and trimmed to what isn't already on the page. Where maps compete, the row gives one pick (or a combination that doesn't collide) and names the runner-up.

cells: Leave. The professor's letter is the spent version of Winston's diary-letter, and the whole-lot sale is already your lot 49.
Debunks three theories, asks why the documentary exists
Leave. Frank is already the clown with the sane method, and the gate needs his two columns.
Says one line to Els, gets the folder, does the arithmetic, withdraws, lies to Ana

At the end, Pieter kindly hands him a bank wellbeing referral, three sessions, reason filled in by someone else (recent bereavement in family; sleep disturbance; preoccupation with historical documents). James has just read When a Reader Notices. He signs and wears it: tells the counselor a true small story, stops asking at work, lets Ana find the appointment card and take it as the reason for four a.m. Runner-up: the Deventer neighbor who gives him the kind version of the professor's last months, so Els refuses a sentence he borrowed.
The discredit, worn as a front (C, condition 1)
Ana holds a wrong explanation he chose for her. The referral stays in his file and is read back to him later (PLACEHOLDER: Anneke in The sheets, or the old man).
Glad; best back nine of his life
Leave. The friendship must be real before it is spent. Gibson 5.2 would repeat The control case's lie about a price.
One line: the handler's "stopped asking" cites the counselor's note, settling; "out loud, which is worse," and the date moves. The verb now comes from a front James chose. PLACEHOLDER #4 stands.
The review comes closer because of his cover. He finds out in The vet.
Visits Noor; receives the template, the rule, the generals, "find the money"

After the professor's rule, James writes his own smaller one: no sheet to anyone until Frank has tried to explain one piece of paper and failed. Optional: Els's folder against Noor's 2009 photocopy, one line different (PLACEHOLDER: which). Runner-up: Declare 5.1, going loud on the forum on a timer; only instead of the referral.
Every schedule date that passes while he waits. Noor has seen Els's papers without Els's say (PLACEHOLDER: does Els find out?).
Desk forty; reads the building; the glass door won't open; copies the format; sees Kalder

Pieter, who doesn't go upstairs, asks James to carry the drill's sealed returns envelope to the archive desk. Aylin chooses to buzz him through; he signs for it in the bound book on her desk. Make this the one place the format arrives (d). Runner-up: Eco 5.5, Pieter asks whether he's come across "recall" and James, who knows rcl-agg, says no.

His name is in the visitor book in his own hand months before December; in The sheets Pieter has to say "I sent you up there." PLACEHOLDER: does the reader see him sign now, or learn it in The sheets?
Reads invoices because Saskia hands him a folder; the role added "with a sigh"

The chore becomes a task with a result: reconcile Annex C against HR records and sign it off. First he asks who granted the role: "It came through already ticked," dated his ticket week. He does the job well, corrects Pieter's three dependants to two, initials it, and only then reads companion animals are not accommodated. Runner-up: Gibson 5.4, he tells Pieter "nothing's expired" with the annex on screen (collides with the correction).
Duty; the findable trail; C, condition 1
His initials on the machine's paperwork: a helper by his own hand. The old man can thank him for the cleanest annex in years; he owes himself a sheet.
Reads 400 pages, finds page 212, emails Julian K. on Kalder's tip
The quarterly access review flags the annex role: "granted by" is blank. James writes the dull true reason for Pieter to sign and leaves the annex out. Runner-up: leave.
The cost lands on whoever opened the door
Saskia can't say who granted it, loses the right to grant roles, is moved.

rows.chapter: A room with a long table
cells: A room with a long table
Leave. "Let her" is already true bait from their side. (With Declare 5.1, Bram's "Nobody curious posts on a timer" lands here.)
Leave. Drafted and complete. See d on the nine years.
Plan only: invents a book, Kalder says he's read it

The invented book gets a hook: a printing year and a shelfmark in the depot's format, said only to Kalder and dated in his notebook. Weeks later the Groningen dealer calls James: polite people asked about that shelfmark. The gate: who else heard it? Not Ana. One more line: Kalder offers a weekend at his club, "no dogs, sorry," and James declines as a joke because of Buddy. Runner-up: Pynchon 5.3, a true professor's book back on Beard Man's stall, bought by a polite man who asks for "more from the same house" (no lie).
B with a gate; the recorded refusal
The dealer has been seen not telephoning (PLACEHOLDER: is Groningen on the schedule?). The title can't be taken back. Write On land fresh; v6 ends the friendship.
Account edited; Kalder says "Deventer"; files it

Ana still asks for the barbecue, but James agrees for a reason he keeps from her: to see what Buddy does with Kalder in the house. The four-a.m. project becomes a tell: one of Buddy's gray hairs across the thin book. Runner-up: Gibson 5.5, his old thread printed against the edited one.
The side channel; make it useless
The barbecue is where Kalder learns the back lane, the fourth gate and the water bowl.
Asks Ana to leave; reads the schedule; tells her; lets her go
(1) He reads companion and knows which sentence put it there (the club weekend). (2) He trusts the printed date and books Buddy into Frank's flat for that week. Runner-up: (1) alone.
The recorded refusal; right about the visit, wrong about the date
Buddy is poisoned before the booked week (PLACEHOLDER: how early). The date moved because he went quiet under the referral, so cover, date and dog are one chain.
Leave, though Frank's kitchen already gives the reader the 1953 panel.
Leave. It gains its cause from The gorilla mask.
Saves Buddy; Noor names Kalder; Noor gives the shelfmark; "Then nothing"

Home at six, the hair is exactly where he left it: photographed, not taken. After "Then nothing" he rings Noor's workshop; a colleague says she has stopped taking private clients and "said you'd call." (Tier 1's "he stops visiting helpers in person" is dropped.) Runner-up: the hair's payoff in Twenty minutes.
Make it useless; the cost after the gate
Noor's livelihood, heard from a person. Needs the thin book unstolen (d).
Leave. The motive, not the engine.

rows.chapter: The night he stops being afraid
cells: The night he stops being afraid
Leave. It is also the floor C needs.
Leave. An invented person next to a real event, never its cause: Declare's rule done right.
Lays every object on the cloth, labels what he can't prove

Beside each object he also writes who put it in his hands; nearly every route runs through the program or Julian. He says the hoax reading out loud before Ana can ("or they handed me all of it") and decides he needs one thing they didn't hand him. Runner-up: leave.
The strongest things on the cloth are now their paper, which the old man will use. Ana hears him doubt his own table.
Public records; the widow; tells her nothing

The records search answers Twenty minutes' question. Then the eighth address, nine days off, becomes the test he must witness before anyone gets a sheet: knock and warn them, which tells the organization he holds the schedule, or watch from a public street with Buddy. He watches. Nobody comes. Runner-up: Orwell 5, one of the quiet four met in person, cheerful, insisting nothing happened.
The test fails because he was there; a week later the address goes quiet anyway (PLACEHOLDER: quiet, moved or dead). The widow becomes his one independent source.
Reads the accounts against the years; finds the thermostat

One negative: he sees what he takes for his own invented title in the grant list, builds on it for a weekend, takes it to Frank. It is a real, unrelated film with a near title. Runner-up: Rose 5.3, a funded channelled-wisdom paperback prints the original wording of one of the forty-one entries: right in the wrong binding.
Frank finds the real film in four minutes. James has been wrong in front of the man who holds his gate.
Shows Frank the money; "I believe the invoice"

The gate opens here, as stated in Leiden: Frank tries to make the invoice boring and fails. Before Frank comes, James sorts what he holds into pulled (the invoices he queried himself) and handed (Saskia's folder, the role, Julian K.'s reply, the schedule). Frank sees only the first pile, and James says why. "I believe the invoice" now has a reason and an earned line ("you saw your own book in the accounts last month").
A (opened by a person); the findable trail
The ninth date passes while he waits (PLACEHOLDER: what happened). The annex with Pieter's children stays in the bag. "Handed" names Julian, whom Frank liked.
Lays seven true sheets; refuses five seats; passes the lower door

On the way out he stops at Aylin's desk and writes the thin book's reference on a request slip, the thing its last page and Noor told him to do. She stamps it Pending. The old man, passing, reads it upside down: "He asked too." Payoff in The final conversation: the old man marks the card "withdrawn for conservation"; when he has gone Aylin strikes it through and brings the item. Runner-up: Eco 5.2, a fake grant among the true sheets (not needed: the true ones already make Anneke move).
The ask; a status lie undone by a person
His name enters "Shelfmark requested" beside the professor's March line; Aylin overrules the old man on a card anyone can read. PLACEHOLDER: what the item is; whether the ask moves to the opening.

sections.title: c. The three changes I would make first

items.title: 1. The money: James does the machine's homework (Orwell 1 and 2)
items.html: Still first, with more support. It fixes the chapter the diagnosis names, costs one scene with Saskia, and leaves his initials on the seat annex for good. Pynchon shows paper grips when the job obliges looking; Illuminatus! shows this is also C's missing condition. Breaks: The drill (the role is granted between drill and money; with Pynchon 5.1, Pieter's errand comes first); Enjoy it while it lasts (the blank "granted by," and Saskia pays); The reading room, continued (the old man's thanks); The sheets (James's own sheet). Drop the payload line: the job is gone.

items.title: 2. James's gate: set in Leiden, given its question in Twenty minutes, tested at the eighth address, opened in Frank, loose (King 4 and 1, with Pynchon 5.2 and Libra 5.2)
items.html: Up from third. Tier 1 had the gate without a reason for The other ten's search or a rule for what Frank sees. One habit, sorting pulled from handed, supplies both, and Rose explains why waiting hurts. Breaks: Leiden (a written rule); Twenty minutes (one column, one sentence aloud); The other ten (ends on a failed watch, not on not acting); The band must precede Frank, loose; Frank, loose becomes the hinge; The sheets can't start before it; the end-of-Part-Two clock loses a week if the ninth date has passed.

items.title: 3. The math → A car park: reclassified, and he wears it (Illuminatus! 5.2)
items.html: New. It cashes a rule The math already prints, makes the switch to "he chose" in the third James chapter of Part Two, gives "stopped asking out loud" a cause he chose, and through King 2 ties his cover to the poisoning. Breaks: The math (a one-to-one at the end); A car park (one line); The schedule and The vet (the chain from cover to date to dog); Twenty minutes (the appointment card beside the cloth); The reading room, continued or The sheets (someone reads it back first); v7 Frank, loose ("Pieter thinks you're job-hunting"). It uses the one discredit slot, so Declare 5.1 and Pynchon 5.4 are out.

items.title: What moved
items.html: The On land canary falls from second to fourth. It stays in the table, but Rose shows a canary needs no invention, Pynchon offers a readout with no lie, the chapter exists only in the plan, and it hangs on two open canon questions (where "Deventer" is said; where the format arrives). The gate rises for the reasons above. The referral enters because it fixes Part Two earliest for the fewest words. Tier 1's fake sheet leaves the table. Outside the ranking because it is two lines long: James asks for the shelfmark in The reading room, continued. Every draft leaves Ask unpaid, so do it whichever three you choose.

sections.title: d. Corrections and canon conflicts
sections.html:
Carried over from Tier 1:

  • Eco 5.5 is out of order (the drill comes before the invoice); the table's runner-up uses the job name.
  • Orwell 1 is half on the page (v7 The money has "Dependants per allocation: 3. He has two children"); Orwell 2's payload cost is impossible (the job is gone).
  • King 6 and King 1 are half drafted (v6 The vet: "because I'd been to her house, with my face"; v7 The other ten and The reading room, continued: "I was there. Nobody came. Why.").
  • Gibson 5.2 repeats The control case's lie to Ana about a price.
  • The format arrives three times (Leiden; The drill, where v7 connects it despite v8.2's "doesn't connect it"; The vet). Pynchon 5.1 makes The drill the one arrival.
  • v7 Frank, loose gives Frank children against the brief, and dates the invoice step twice.
  • Borges 1 and 5 are Part One proposals. With Pynchon 5.1 and the December ask, Borges 1 would make three visitor-book entries for James; keep two.

New corrections:

  • Tier 1's King 6 went too far. "He stops visiting helpers in person" contradicts The other ten and The sheets. Dropped.
  • Tier 1's Eco 5.2 duplicated the page. v7 The reading room, continued already runs a true canary. Replaced by the ask.
  • The Libra map understates the ticket. v7 The sheets already has James open one against page 212 "as a test."

He wrote them a letter about his rights. That's not asking"), and v8.2 Deventer, March has him asking someone to come and talk, not asking for an item. Either make the March line a visit with no shelfmark, or keep the bridge. PLACEHOLDER.

items.html: v8.2 Leave it: one ticket against page 212. v8 Leave it: a decommission ticket against rcl-agg, then a low-priority one against page 212. v7 The sheets: an earlier page-212 ticket "as a test." Libra 5.4 adds another. PLACEHOLDER: which survive.

items.title: Nine years, three times
items.html: Aylin has kept the visitor book nine years (v7 The sheets); Kalder crossed nine years ago (v8.2, v7); Noor hasn't seen him in nine years (v6 The vet). Rose 5.1 uses the match. PLACEHOLDER: intended?

items.title: A dead man among the quiet four
items.html: v7 The other ten counts Henk's Zwolle address as "the first of the quiet four," but he drowned (A pension visit, Zwolle). Its first resolved address is also in Deventer, the town's third job in the book. PLACEHOLDER.

books.author: Borges
books.title: Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius
books.readfor: one copy with extra pages; dread from a variant
books.intro: Coverage: Hurley translation, Collected Fictions, read in full, 11 Nov 2026: parts I and II, the 1947 Postscript, footnotes 1–6 (about 6,000 words). Evidence: 01-the-story.md. Brief: how one variant copy (four extra pages in one encyclopedia volume) becomes dread in fifteen pages, and how the invented world it points to replaces the real one. Santi's standing ask: "really capture what made those books great and how the conspiracies actually helped progress the story." Standing-rule note: the Postscript names real people (Dalgarno, George Berkeley) as members of the society, and the invented pages sit in a reprint of the 1902 Britannica, a real work. SDF must never do either. Borges's real friends appear only as witnesses.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
Bioy Casares quotes a heresiarch from an encyclopedia article on a country called Uqbar. The narrator's copy of that volume has no such article; Bioy's copy has four extra pages. Every outside check (index, atlases, the National Library, a bookshop copy) comes back blank. Two years later a dead engineer leaves behind Volume XI of an encyclopedia of an invented planet, Tlön, stamped Orbis Tertius. A 1947 Postscript reports the rest: a letter giving the secret society's history, a Tlön compass and an impossibly heavy cone turning up in the real world, the forty volumes found in Memphis, and the world adopting Tlön while the narrator translates Browne in a hotel.

It works because every check fails in the same direction, so the dread is built from explanations he has ruled out, not from anything he is told. And each piece of evidence is heavier than the last, from four pages to a metal cone that marks his palm, while his own part in finding it shrinks.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:
Step What the narrator wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (I) The source of Bioy's epigram His Vol. XLVI has no Uqbar; Index, four spellings, an atlas: nothing He privately decides his friend made it up Bioy phones next day with the article in front of him Seeing Bioy's copy
2 (I) To see the article Same volume, same spine key, 921 pages instead of 917, no other difference Nothing; the doubt moves from Bioy to the book The variant is physical, and the spine key doesn't cover it Reading it closely
3 (I) To judge it Plausible, boring prose; borders drawn only by places inside Uqbar; one cited book is in a Quaritch catalog Nothing Half the trail touches real catalogs The National Library
4 (I) An outside record Library: nothing. Bioy's own index lacks the name. A bookshop copy: nothing Nothing He can stop, and does. Part I ends on a blank; two years pass Nothing he does; the next object comes to him
5 (II) Nothing in particular Ashe's parcel, left in a bar: Vol. XI of Tlön, stamped Orbis Tertius Dizziness; regret that he let Ashe's "Norwegian in Rio Grande do Sul" drop The volume cites other volumes and is perfectly consistent: a set means a maker A hunt on two continents; the theory of a society
6 (II) Who made Tlön Nothing; consistency itself is taken as proof the other volumes exist Nothing The author stays open The lecture on Tlön
7 (Postscript) To record what happened A letter in Ashe's Hinton gives the history; a Tlön compass in a princess's silver Nothing The fiction is now an object in a real house The second intrusion
8 (Postscript) Shelter from a flood A dead man's cone, too heavy to lift The only physical cost: the weight stays, a circle is cut in his palm, fear and revulsion He has held the proof He ends "the personal portion" by choice
9 (Postscript) Nothing; he withdraws Forty volumes in Memphis, perhaps by arrangement, strangest parts cut; schools teach Tlön His childhood's history is replaced He can stop, and does; the work goes on without him A translation he won't publish

Read the cost column honestly: he pays almost nothing. It works for fifteen pages because the evidence keeps getting heavier. Over a novel that is exactly the Part Two problem.

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
• The Uqbar article (I), about 450 words, paraphrased. No stall: it arrives inside the act of checking it, so every fact is a test result. The tell is self-reference: its "points of reference were rivers and craters and mountain chains of the region itself."
  • The Tlön volume (II), about 3,500 words, a lecture from a book. Over half the story, and nothing happens. It holds because the author is still unknown, each doctrine is a deadpan joke, and the last item (the hrönir: objects dug up because the diggers expected them) is a plant for the Postscript. It does stall for anyone not there for the philosophy; only the story's length saves it.
  • The history (Postscript), about 450 words, a letter summarized. One block, then two objects within a page. It answers a question carried since Part I, so it reads as payment.
  • The objects, about 150 and 300 words. Short scenes with a witness and a physical detail; explanation in one line at the end.
  • The takeover, about 350 words, as public record. Fast and flat; it claims nothing it has to prove.

sections.title: 4. The mechanism, writer to writer
sections.html:
Setup: a quotation over a late dinner, nothing at stake. Rule: a text can be checked against another copy of itself. First use: 917 pages against 921, and the apparatus (spine key, index) doesn't know about the extra four. Escalation: each check fails the same way and removes one dull explanation (Bioy invented it, misremembered, the index is incomplete); then the objects get heavier: pages, a book, a letter, a compass, a cone. Cost: a moment of doubting a friend, one unasked question, a palm, a childhood history. Payoff: he stops; the world doesn't.

  • A (gate): supports, inverted. He must rule out the small explanations before he allows the big one. But passing the gate never lets him do anything; it gates belief, not action.
  • B (canary): supports. The hrönir digs state its rule: the test fails if the tested know it is a test.
  • C (front): strong. Uqbar is a front for Tlön; the First Encyclopaedia a draft for Orbis Tertius; a country becomes a planet.
  • D (lock and key): adds a missed key. Ashe's Norwegian was the key, and the narrator let it drop. His one admitted cost of being wrong is a question he didn't ask.

Fifth mechanisms. Checks as the engine: the plot is a run of blank results, each ruling something out. The apparatus that wasn't updated: whoever changes a text leaves the furniture around it alone, and the furniture is the witness. The heavier object: escalate by weight and deniability, not information. The organization prunes its own lie to be believed: the Memphis copy cuts the hrönir to fit the real world. That is "given / arose" from the editor's side: an edit that makes a text more acceptable, not more false.

sections.title: 5. Transfer to SDF
sections.html: Already on the page. The sentence does copy against copy, checks the apparatus (typos, the blemish on 118, the copyright line), and gets disappointment from a trivial variant. The control case buys a third 1931 copy (the whole run) and checks nine other books (nothing). Borges adds three things: a control on the other side (is the odd copy the only one?), checks outside the book, and a price for every check.

items.title: 1. The copy that isn't there
items.html:
The control case; payoff in The night before.

  • Change: James looks for a second copy of the 1926 first impression, and the one public copy is withdrawn for conservation.
  • James does: files a library request in his own name; when it fails, finds the original wording quoted in an old dealer's catalog (invented dealer), as Borges finds Haslam in Quaritch.
  • Cost: the request has his name on it, and it is in the depot's register when he copies the visitor book. PLACEHOLDER: whether it also shows in his payload as "asked (book)". From here on he knows checking costs, and in Part Two must choose which checks are worth a line on the list. That is the missing gate.
  • Already on the page? Partly. Checked the plan's The control case (no draft exists) and v8 The sentence: both test the 1931 run; nothing tests whether another first impression exists. Entry #17 in The List already uses "withdrawn for conservation"; PLACEHOLDER: use it here or keep it there.

items.title: 2. Control the canary
items.html:
On land, then The gorilla mask; payoff in Frank, loose.

  • Change: after the invented book catches Kalder, James tries the same title on two people who can't be handlers.
  • James does: drops it on Frank ("never heard of it, sounds made up") and on Beard Man ("had a copy, sold it to a German"). Now Kalder is either a handler or a Beard Man.
  • Cost: he lies to his friend, and in Frank, loose Frank asks whether the book was a test. The result stays muddy, so he can't act on it.
  • Already on the page? Partly. Checked the plan's On land: the trap, no control.

items.title: 3. The annex the index doesn't list
items.html:
The money.

  • Change: the master agreement's list of annexes skips C, the way the spine key doesn't cover Uqbar.
  • James does: sees the gap, then asks Saskia, in writing, for a role to open a document the contract says doesn't exist.
  • Cost: Saskia's name is now on the access grant. PLACEHOLDER: whether that surfaces in The leak or The sheets, or stays a worry.
  • Already on the page? Partly. Checked v7 24 — The money: the annex needs a role and Saskia adds it "with a sigh." The gap in the index and her price are new. This is the passage the pipeline singled out.

items.title: 4. Two copies of the style guide
items.html:
The math into Leiden; cost lands in Leiden, Friday.

  • Change: Els's folder and Noor's 2009 photocopy differ by one line; the later one is shorter, cut to be believed (the Memphis rule).
  • James does: carries Els's folder to Noor's kitchen and compares it page by page.
  • Cost: he shows Els's private papers to a stranger without asking her, and Noor is now someone who has seen the newer page. PLACEHOLDER: which line, which way, and whether Els finds out.
  • Already on the page? Partly. Checked the plan's The math and Leiden (no drafts): Noor "confirms the style guide is a template"; no comparison.

items.title: 5. The index nobody reset
items.html:
The control case; across the list in Part Two.

  • Change: the 1931 index still points to page 118 under the old word (say "Transmission of traditions, 118"), because a fourth reset would show and, per Leiden, 1931, a clean plate is a confession.
  • James does: checks the back of the book. Every 1931 copy in every library carries the fossil, so the edit can be verified without a first impression. Frank-proof.
  • Cost: none for one book. Extended to the other entries, every copy he buys is a dealer inquiry, and Groningen establishes that dealers phone.
  • Already on the page? No. Checked v8 The sentence: no index.

Rejected: reading the society's history by stealth (Borges's letter simply turns up; SDF's must be handed over by a person, as Aylin hands over the visitor book). The cone is already in v7 41 — The other ten as the flask the widow presses on him; don't redo it.

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• The withdrawal ending. The narrator translates Browne, "though I never intend to publish." James publishes. The other ten already ends on James not acting; don't collect more.
  • The lecture. 3,500 words of doctrine survive in a short story on jokes and an open question. The thin book stays entries; speeches break at about 150 words.
  • The impossible object and the takeover. The cone is "a metal not of this world," and reality "caved in." SDF's reveals are paper and flasks, and it ends with a sum stepping down.

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
• "instead of 917 pages, Bioy's volume had 921." (I): the variant as a count.
  • "Naturally, he found not the slightest mention of Uqbar." (I): a movement that ends on a blank.
  • "and nothing more was said—God forgive me—of duodecimals." (II): the missed key, priced in an aside.
  • "Thus it was discovered that no witnesses who were aware of the experimental nature of the search could be allowed near the site" (II): the canary's rule.
  • "I also recall the neat circle it engraved in my flesh." (Postscript): the only cost, made physical.
  • "the cuts obey the intent to set forth a world that is not too incompatible with the real world." (Postscript): the organization edits for belief.

notes.title: the whole story (parts I, II and the Postscript)
notes.html:
Coverage: the whole story: parts I and II, the dated close (Salto Oriental, 1940), the 1947 Postscript and footnotes 1–6 (about 6,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: Andrew Hurley translation, Collected Fictions, converted text, chunk file 01. The file marks only parts I and II before the Postscript, so those three are the "chapters" cited here.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (I) To find where Bioy got the mirrors epigram The house copy of Vol. XLVI has no Uqbar; the index, four spellings and an atlas give nothing He privately decides his friend made it up Next day Bioy phones with the article open in front of him Seeing Bioy's copy
2 (I) To see the article himself Same volume, same spine key (Tor-Upps), four extra pages, no other difference The doubt moves from Bioy to the book The extra pages are physical, and the spine key does not cover them Reading the article closely
3 (I) To judge the article Dull, plausible prose whose borders are set only by places inside Uqbar; one cited book is in a Quaritch catalogue; another author is linked to the Rosy Cross Only unease Half the trail touches real catalogues The National Library, then a third copy in a bookshop: nothing
4 (II) Nothing; two years pass Ashe dies; his parcel from Brazil holds Vol. XI of an encyclopedia of Tlön, stamped Orbis Tertius A dizziness he will not describe; regret that he once let Ashe's Brazil remark drop The volume mentions other volumes and is fully consistent A library hunt; the theory of a secret society
5 (Postscript) To record what came after A letter in one of Ashe's books gives the society's history; a Tlön compass turns up in a princess's silver; a tiny cone too heavy for a man to lift The cone marks his palm and leaves fear and revulsion The fiction now has weight, and he witnessed it twice He ends the "personal portion"
6 (Postscript) Nothing; he withdraws The forty volumes found in Memphis, perhaps by arrangement, with the strangest parts cut; the world adopts Tlön The history of his childhood is replaced in schools The work continues; he predicts a second encyclopedia He translates Browne in a hotel and will not publish

Why it grips

  • The checks make the dread. Part I is a run of controls, and each fails: the index, the spellings, two atlases, the volumes side by side, the National Library, Mastronardi's bookshop copy. Each blank removes a dull explanation until only one is left: this copy is different. Part I ends on the third copy's absence, not on a find.
  • The fake gives itself away by what it points to. The Uqbar article is plausible and even boring; the tell is that its borders are drawn by rivers and mountains inside Uqbar, and its few real names are put in loosely (I). An invention can only refer to itself, and the narrator tests for that.
  • Each find is more physical than the last. Four pages, a 1001-page book, a letter, a compass, then a cone that marks his flesh. The narrator does almost nothing: Bioy brings the volume, Ashe leaves the book in a bar, the compass arrives in someone else's silver. He is as passive as James, and it works for fifteen pages because the evidence gets heavier while his part shrinks. (My judgement: over a novel it would need a cost he chooses.)
  • The Postscript turns the story into a document. Parts I and II, the narrator says, are reprinted from a 1940 anthology, so what we just read becomes one more object in the case. Then he hands the rest to the reader's own memory.
  • Funny throughout. Englishmen afflicted with unreality, a friendship that soon eliminates conversation, and an ending about translating Browne while the world dissolves.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The conspiracy moves the story by sending objects, never people. Nobody threatens or blocks the narrator; Orbis Tertius never notices him. It puts things in his path, and each forces the next search: the variant sends him to the library, Vol. XI sends scholars after its companions, the letter answers what Vol. XI raised.

The society is revealed in three steps, each an object inside another object: a stamp on a page (a name only), a theory drawn from the book's coherence (a plan too vast for one inventor, II), then a letter in a Hinton book with an Ouro Preto postmark (the history). The organisation never appears in person.

The Postscript's turn is that the conspiracy edits its own text to be believed. The Memphis copy has cut or muted the hrönir, and its discovery may have been guided; the narrator thinks so. Part II's lore then becomes the plot: hrönir are objects produced by expectation, and the whole Tlön project works like one, on a world that, he says, wanted to cave in.

How the lore gets in

  • The Uqbar article (I), about 450 words, a document paraphrased. Wrapped in the act of checking it, so the lore is evidence; no stall.
  • Tlön's languages, philosophy, nine coins, geometry and hrönir (II), about 3,500 words, a lecture from a book. More than half the story, and nothing happens. It holds because who invented Tlön stays open until the Postscript's letter, each doctrine is a straight-faced joke, and the last item, the hrönir (prison and school digs that produce what the diggers expect), sets up the Postscript.
  • The society's history (Postscript), about 450 words, a letter summarised. One block, followed at once by two objects.
  • The takeover (Postscript), about 350 words, told as public record.

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate), inverted. He rules out the smaller explanations first: Bioy invented it, Bioy misremembered, the index is incomplete. Only control copies settle it, and Borges uses two (his own, Mastronardi's). For SDF: the "given/arose" first impression should be checked against a third copy before James may believe anything, and that copy should come back blank or ambiguous.
  • B (canary), from the other side. Tlön is a planted invention, and the hrönir digs state the canary's rule: the test fails if the tested know it is a test, and hope and greed spoil it (II). Andrea's imaginary Rosy Cross, later founded by imitators (I), is the same idea.
  • C (front), strong. Uqbar is a front for Tlön (its literature refers to Tlön); the First Encyclopaedia is a draft for Orbis Tertius; the society meant to invent a country until Buckley said a planet (Postscript).
  • D (lock and key), as a missed key. Ashe's Norwegian in Rio Grande do Sul was the key, and the narrator let it drop (II). His one admitted cost of being wrong is a question he did not ask.
  • Fifth: the organisation revises its own book to be believed. The Memphis copy differs from Vol. XI because strange parts were cut to fit the real world. That matches "given/arose": an edit that makes a text more acceptable, not more false.

Quotes

  • "instead of 917 pages, Bioy's volume had 921." (I): the variant stated as a count.
  • "Naturally, he found not the slightest mention of Uqbar." (I): part I ends on an absence.
  • "Thus it was discovered that no witnesses who were aware of the experimental nature of the search could be allowed near the site" (II): the canary's rule.
  • "the cuts obey the intent to set forth a world that is not too incompatible with the real world" (Postscript): the conspiracy edits for belief.

Flags

  • Real people named as members of the secret society: Dalgarno and George Berkeley (Postscript). Borges's real friends (Bioy Casares, Mastronardi, Reyes, Martínez Estrada, Amorim) are witnesses, not conspirators. SDF must not name real people as complicit.
  • The invented pages sit in one copy of an encyclopedia the text calls a reprint of the 1902 Britannica, a real work. Whether the Anglo-American Cyclopaedia existed I cannot confirm [from memory, not from the text]. SDF must not attach an invented edit to a real book.

books.qa:
Pointers: 00-map.md (the map), 01-the-story.md (the section note), and the story's parts (I, II, Postscript). v8.2 chapters are named by title from 02 Structure/THE BOOK v8 — every chapter explained.md.

1. What is the story, in two lines? One copy of an encyclopedia volume has four extra pages on a country called Uqbar, and every other check comes back blank (I). Later a whole volume about an invented planet turns up, a secret society is revealed by letter, Tlön objects enter the world, and the world adopts Tlön (II, Postscript). See 00-map.md §1.

2. Why read it for SDF at all? It is the shortest model there is of a textual variant turning into dread, and its variant is as trivial as "transmitted to / arisen among." It also shows a conspiracy that edits its own text to be believed (Postscript), which is the organization's method in The sentence seen from the editor's side. See 00-map.md §4.

3. How does Borges make a trivial variant frightening? Through checks, not through a find. Index, spellings, two atlases, the National Library, Bioy's own index and a bookshop copy all come back blank, and each removes a dull explanation (I). The dread is the narrowing. See 01-the-story.md "Why it grips" and 00-map.md §2, rows 1–4.

4. Doesn't The sentence already do this? Yes, copy against copy and the apparatus check (typos, blemish, copyright line) are on the page, and the disappointment at a trivial variant is already better than Borges's. What Borges adds is a control on the other side (is the odd copy the only one?), checks outside the book, and nothing more. See 00-map.md §5 opening.

5. And The control case? The plan has a third 1931 copy (whole run) and nine other books (nothing). Both test the second impression. Nobody tests whether another first impression survives, which is Borges's whole Part I. Proposal 1 in 00-map.md §5.

6. What exactly is "the apparatus that wasn't updated"? Bioy's volume has 921 pages but the same spine key, Tor-Upps, which doesn't cover Uqbar, and his own index lacks the name (I). Whoever inserted the pages left the furniture alone, and the furniture gives it away. In SDF the copyright line already does this; proposal 5 adds the 1931 index.

7. Is the index idea consistent with the plan? Yes. Leiden, 1931 has the printer reset three lines and leave the misprints, because a clean plate is a confession; resetting the index would be a fourth visible change. The index entry is a fossil in every 1931 copy. It is a proposal, not canon (00-map.md §5, proposal 5).

8. What does the narrator lose? Almost nothing: a private doubt about Bioy (I), regret over a question he didn't ask Ashe (II), a circle cut in his palm by the cone, and the history of his childhood (Postscript). The map says so plainly in §2. Don't cite this story as a model for cost.

9. Then why doesn't the passivity kill it? Because the evidence gets heavier as his part shrinks: four pages, a 1,001-page book, a letter, a compass, a cone. Fifteen pages can run on that. A novel can't, which is why every SDF proposal attaches a cost (00-map.md §5).

10. Where can the narrator stop, and does he? After Mastronardi's blank, end of Part I: he stops for two years and something comes to him. And at the end, by choice: "Here I end the personal portion." See 00-map.md §2, rows 4 and 8–9.

11. How does a 3,500-word lecture not stall? The inventor is still unknown, each doctrine is a deadpan joke, and the last item, the hrönir, is set up for the Postscript (II). It still stalls for a reader not there for philosophy. SDF's brief breaks speeches at about 150 words, so don't take it (00-map.md §3, §6).

12. What are hrönir and why do they matter? Objects produced by expectation: prisoners and schoolchildren dig up what they were shown or hoped for (II). They state the canary's rule (the tested must not know it is a test), and they model the Tlön project itself. See 01-the-story.md "Mechanism notes".

13. Which of A–D does the story support most? C (front) most strongly: Uqbar is a front for Tlön, the First Encyclopaedia a draft for Orbis Tertius, a country becomes a planet (Postscript). B and an inverted A also hold; D appears as a missed key. See 00-map.md §4.

14. What is the fifth mechanism? Four candidates: checks as the engine; the apparatus that wasn't updated; the heavier object; and the organization pruning its own lie to be believed (the Memphis copy cuts the hrönir). The last matches "given / arose" most closely. See 00-map.md §4.

15. How does the conspiracy move the plot if it never meets the narrator? By sending objects. Bioy brings a volume, Ashe leaves a book in a bar, a compass arrives in someone's silver, a cone falls from a dead man's belt. Orbis Tertius never notices him. See 01-the-story.md "How the conspiracy moves the story here".

16. Is there a canary in the story? Yes, twice: the hrönir rule (II) and Andrea's imaginary Rosy Cross, "which other men later founded, in imitation" (I). For SDF, On land already runs the invented-book trap once; proposal 2 adds controls (Frank, Beard Man) so the result means something.

17. What does proposal 2 cost James? A lie to Frank, which Frank raises in Frank, loose, and a muddier result: Beard Man claims to know the invented book too, so Kalder could be a Beard Man. James can't act on it, which matches the plan's "passing without knowing if he's passing." See 00-map.md §5.

18. How does Borges fix The money? Through the spine key: in proposal 3 the contract's list of annexes skips C. James must ask Saskia, in writing, for a role to open a document the contract says doesn't exist, and her name is now on the grant. Proposal 3; checked against v7 24 — The money.

19. Is the style-guide comparison (proposal 4) safe under the rules? Yes: both copies are given to James by people who chose to (Els, Noor), and he compares them in Noor's kitchen. The cost is a breach of Els's trust and Noor's exposure, which points at Leiden, Friday. Which line differs is PLACEHOLDER.

20. Does SDF already have Borges's heavy object? Yes. The flask in v7 41 — The other ten, which the widow presses on James ("take it, I don't want it in the house now"), is the cone: a small object a witness hands over that carries the weight of the case. Don't redo it.

21. Does SDF already have the guided discovery? Yes. The Memphis find may have been "consented to and guided" (Postscript); the old man in The reading room says "We leave them findable" about the seats. Same move, already placed.

22. What about the real people in the society? Dalgarno and Berkeley are named as members (Postscript). SDF forbids real people as complicit; real names may appear only as the old man's unconfirmed claims in The final conversation. See 00-map.md standing-rule note and 01-the-story.md "Flags".

23. Is the Anglo-American Cyclopaedia real? The story calls it a reprint of the 1902 Britannica, which is real; the section note could not confirm the Cyclopaedia from the text [from memory, not from the text]. Either way the lesson is the rule: never an invented edit on a real book. Waters Before Memory is invented, so proposals 1 and 5 are safe.

24. Should SDF end like Borges? No. The narrator withdraws to translate Browne, "though I never intend to publish" (Postscript). James is allowed to publish in Leave it. The other ten already ends on James choosing not to tell the widow; one Adrogué ending is plenty (00-map.md §6).

25. What makes the Postscript work as a device? It reframes parts I and II as a reprinted 1940 article with "editorial cuts," so what you just read becomes evidence, and the narrator is quietly doing what the society does: trimming his text for a new reader. Then it hands the rest to "every reader's memory." See 00-map.md §3.

26. Is the story funny, and does that matter for SDF? Yes: Englishmen "afflicted with unreality," a friendship that soon eliminates conversation, Reyes tired of "subordinate drudgeries of a detective nature," an ending about a translation. The deadpan carries the doctrine, which is why SDF's rule "funny to the end" is compatible with dread. See 01-the-story.md "Why it grips".

27. Best single line to quote to Santi? "instead of 917 pages, Bioy's volume had 921." (I). It is the variant stated as a count, which is how James would log it. Others in 00-map.md §7.

28. Which proposal should be built first? Proposal 1 (the copy that isn't there), because it gives Part Two its missing gate: from The control case on, every check has a price and James has to choose. Then 3 (The money) and 2 (On land). See 00-map.md §5.

books.author: Crouch
books.title: Recursion
books.readfor: the leak: dead memories a character must act on; resets
books.intro: Coverage: converted English text with no edition data in the file. Read in full through three section notes (01-book-one.md, 02-middle.md, 03-books-three-to-five.md, about 90,000 words), 15 Nov 2026. The text has no chapter numbers, so cites are by Book, date or loop, and note file. Tier 3, so shorter than the Tier 1 maps. Brief: the leak. You have proposed that fragments of past lives, or of the world before a reset, leak into this one. This is the novel that builds a whole plot on a leaked memory, so it is read for how a leak becomes something a character must act on, how one device grows for 300 pages, and where it goes wrong. Standing-rule note: real organizations and people are named (DARPA, RAND, WikiLeaks, the Guardian, Trump Tower; 02). The heroes raid a building with guns and kidnap Slade (02, 03). Suicides, a child murder and mass shootings are shown, and the middle is not funny (02). The cause of everything is a machine. Take the handling of the leak, none of that.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
A New York detective, Barry, fails to stop a woman jumping; she says she remembers a whole life that never happened. Checking her story leads him to a hotel where a chair sends a dying person back into an old memory to live on from there. He takes the offer and saves his daughter. Every use leaves the abandoned timeline behind as "dead" memories, which arrive in everyone on a fixed date. Helena, who built the chair, and Barry try to destroy it; the state takes it; the design gets out; the world remembers and fires its missiles. Helena restarts the same twenty-nine years again and again until Barry goes back to the first timeline and stops the invention.

What makes it work: the leak has one tell, one rule and a date, so a character can predict it, share it and check it. And the same device is shown at a larger scale each time, so the reader never gets the same scene twice until the last third.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:
Step What the protagonist wants right now What he/she finds What it costs Why he/she cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Barry, Nov 2018, 01) To talk Ann off a ledge, then to settle her story Her second life in small gray details; a police report that contradicts her Ann dies in front of him A report and a witness disagree, and a detective can check that in an afternoon Montauk, to find Joe
2 (Barry, 5 Nov, 01) To hear Joe's side In a diner his own last three days are replaced by a gray set His belief that the past is fixed It has now happened to him, and it matches what Ann said The address Joe gives him
3 (Helena, 2007–09, 01, 02) Money to build a chair for her mother's memory Slade's foreknowledge; a test subject killed on purpose; a "dead" memory of a morning that never happened Her team, her project, Reed's life She is on a rig 173 miles out, and her own head now holds the proof She maps a memory in secret and dies to escape into it
4 (Barry, 6 Nov 2018 to 2007, 01) To get out of the chair He wakes in his own body on the night Meghan died His wish to expose the hotel: he is now its client A two-minute head start and his daughter ahead of him on the street He saves her and is told to tell no one
5 (Barry, 2007–18, 02) To live the second chance well Eleven years on, on the date, the first life arrives in him, Julia and Meghan Meghan cannot hold both lives and dies the same day His family has it too; then a building appears and a whole city has it He stands outside the hotel with a gun
6 (Book Three, 02) To destroy the chair Helena has already lived this; she proves it with facts only he knows Barry dies twice; Slade dies; a masked team takes the lab The raid made the chair someone else's property Helena is taken
7 (Book Four, 02) To stop the people who hold it Five ground rules, each broken; averted massacres arrive as memories in a nation; the design leaks Her freedom, then her sense of which day is real Each use saves lives, so refusing looks like harm; then the next change is an hour away She gets into the chair herself
8 (loops 1–4, 03) One calm life before the date Every restart ends on 16 April 2019 with the world remembering and the missiles Each loop takes more: her mother's last day, his skin, the marriage, then Helena herself The date is fixed and each loop's research failed A phone call: Slade once undid a timeline
9 (loops 5–7, 03) The method from Slade Slade, bargaining while a city burns: go back to the original timeline What he learned is lost at each restart; Helena dies; he lies down in his own grave A half-remembered sentence comes back as he lies there He maps a dead memory and goes in
10 (last chapter, Epilogue, 03) To reach the first timeline and stay A gray field of every memory he has; the temptation to live in the best one Helena becomes a memory only he holds He must choose to live forward He stops Slade and sits down next to a stranger

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
• Ann on the ledge (about 700 words, 01): a confession that ends in her death. It gives the feel of a leak before any rule.
  • The CDC briefing in a bar (about 600 words, 01): numbers and the spread between people, carried by Gwen's jokes and her doubt, set between a death and a blackout.
  • The police report (about 300 words, 01): the shortest piece and the one that makes Barry move.
  • Joe's call (about 600 words, 01): one rule, an address, and a hang-up before "they" are named.
  • Barry's bathroom (about 1,200 words, 02): a family explains the rule to itself at three in the morning. The crisis carries it.
  • Helena's kitchen (about 2,500 words, 02): the future told over a meal she cooks from his own memories.
  • The five ground rules (02): a list, each item broken in turn.
  • Where it runs: Slade through the cell glass in loop six (about 900 words, 03). Barry has to unlock the door to get the answer, and the clock is visible.
  • Where it stalls: Slade's first long explanation (about 2,000 words, 01) and the neutrino and wormhole pages (03). In both, nobody in the room can lose anything by what is said, and the physics in 03 pays off nothing, because the answer turns out to be a human act.

This confirms ADDENDUM 05's rule on lore: it holds when someone in the room can lose by it.

sections.title: 4. The leak
sections.html:
The rule in one line. When someone restarts time, the abandoned stretch comes back to everyone who lived it as a second, gray set of memories, on the date the restart happened (01, 02).

How a leak becomes something a character must act on. Five devices, and the book uses all five in its first eighty pages.

  1. The tell. A nosebleed and a stab of pain behind the eyes, every time (01, 03). Because it is bodily and always the same, a character can recognize it in someone else across a room, and the reader learns to fear a tissue.
  2. The fixed date. The leak arrives at the moment the other self died. Helena calls it a timeline anniversary (02). So people can say "tonight," wait up for it, and be wrong about how bad it will be.
  3. The second witness. Barry cannot treat it as his own illness, because Meghan and Julia have the same memories on the same night (02). The CDC's detail that it spreads between people who know each other does the same job earlier (01).
  4. The checkable contradiction. Ann says Franny jumped. The report says Joe saved her. That is a train ride and an interview (01). The leak is given to a man whose job is to settle exactly this kind of disagreement.
  5. Evidence inside the leak. Dead memories hold a route, a gun position, a door code (02). Helena opens Barry with things only he knows: his eclipse, his orchard, his father (02). The leak is treated as a document that can be read for facts.

Add a sixth that is easy to miss: the leak hurts in its small details. A birthmark, a cake fight, morning breath (01). Crouch never gives a leaked life in summary.

Escalation without repeating. Scale changes every time: one woman, one detective, a family, a city (a building nobody built), a nation (news coverage of shootings that never happened), the world in one gulp, one morning rewritten four times, and last a reversal, where an older mind arrives in a younger body (02). Then the device turns into a tool: Helena cuts her arm to leave herself a vivid memory to return to (02). Then it costs its user: Slade has lived so many lives he gets only flashes (02).

Rules under pressure. Each rule arrives when someone needs it to decide something in the next minute. Nobody asks how it works until the reader has seen it work (01).

Payoff. The first timeline is the one place with no earlier leaks. Barry reaches it by refusing the perfect memory. The leaks stop, and he alone keeps them (03).

What goes wrong.

  • The physics lectures. See section 3.
  • The villain hands over the fix. Slade tells Barry what to do. The scene survives only because he withheld it for a stated reason and because Barry must free him to hear it (03).
  • The loops numb. Two of the seven anniversaries are nearly the same nuclear strike (03). The notes say the characters name their own fatigue, which helps a little.
  • The cause is a chair. Once the leak has a machine behind it, the last third is about the machine.

Against A–D. A: weak (Shaw's five rules, a synaptic number; 02, 03). B: one small use (the killer left under the window so a rumor starts; 02). C: present but only learned (hotel, chair, timeline; 01), which agrees with the Tier 1 verdict. D: strong, in a new form: a private memory is the key (02).

Further mechanisms, checked against ADDENDUM 05's list. Two are new. The dated arrival: a hidden thing that surfaces by itself on a known day. The perishable finding: what the hero learns is lost at the next restart and survives only if a person carries it (03). A third, the gift as a lock (the detective is given what he wants and told to keep quiet; 01), is the addendum's co-optation with a better price.

sections.title: 5. Transfer to SDF
sections.html:
Where you already are. SDF has a leak, and it is of one kind: what a person carries across a death. The funeral gives the flash (cold mud, a cracked hand). The night he stops being afraid pays it: the hand seen all his life, lives cut off by somebody's administration. v6 The floor already lists remembered → imagined beside transmitted → arisen. The organization's own word for what it counts is "recall" (Utrecht, 1993; rcl-agg in Leave it; the invoice in The money). The final conversation says the remembering is the one thing they took out of every book and kept. So the obvious reading you describe is already latent: the edits remove the paper trace of anything crossing, and the count finds the people it crosses in.

What SDF lacks is Crouch's kit. James's flash has no tell, no second witness, nothing checkable and nothing usable in it, so for forty chapters he can only file it. The four proposals below add those, in order of scale: two people, two sentences, one table, one room.

items.title: 5.1 The widow is the second witness
items.html:
The other ten.

  • Change: Henk's "strange things about his father" get one small physical detail and the same bodily sign James had at the funeral (PLACEHOLDER: the sign; make it small and a little ridiculous, never a nosebleed).
  • James does: he asks Marijke the dull question, what exactly did Henk say, and writes it down in her words. Then he tells her his own, the first person he tells after Ana and the dog. She adds that the pension man asked Henk whether he "recalled anything else."
  • Cost: she asks whether Henk is somewhere, and James is back at the grave being asked for the sentence. He says he doesn't know. He leaves her with a matched pair and no comfort, and she is now someone who has talked (PLACEHOLDER: is she visited again).
  • On the page? Partly. v8.2 and v7 The other ten have the flask and "he tells her nothing yet." Nothing says what Henk said.
  • Already proposed? No. King 1 (the eighth address) uses the same chapter and does not collide.

items.title: 5.2 The line to Els is a leaked sentence, and James tries to kill it
items.html:
The math, The control case, The sheets.

  • Change: PLACEHOLDER 5 becomes a sentence James has always said and never read. Els's father said it too.
  • James does: when Els rings, he runs the control he ran on the 1931 printing. He searches his shelves, his forum export and the forty books for a source. He asks Ana whether he has said it before ("You say it to the dog"). He asks Els whether her father wrote it down, and she chooses to hand him a dated page.
  • Cost: he cannot find a source, which for James is worse than finding one. Els gives up the one private thing she had of her father's, and it becomes a specimen. He has also said it out loud in a shop where every visitor is reported.
  • On the page? Partly. v8.2 has "why did you say that, my father said that," and The sheets already reaches the quiet ones by "the deleted phrasing." Nothing connects the two or tests the line.
  • Already proposed? No. It sits beside the addendum's referral in The math: the referral is how the organization answers a man who recalls.

items.title: 5.3 The flash log on the tablecloth
items.html:
Twenty minutes.

  • Change: one more object on the cloth: every flash James can date, written out the way he would write an incident log.
  • James does: he builds it from his notebook and puts it down labeled "can't prove."
  • Cost: Ana reads the dates. One is her grandmother's funeral, the minute she needed him and he said yes without believing it. She learns where he was.
  • On the page? Partly. v6 The floor says "waiting rooms and on trains and once in the middle of a presentation"; there is no list and Ana never sees one.
  • Already proposed? No. Pynchon 5.2 adds a "who handed me this" column to the same cloth; both fit, but that is two additions to a 1,900-word chapter.

items.title: 5.4 The sentence on the old man's table, and one word corrected
items.html:
The reading room, continued.

  • Change: James's last item is the sentence from 5.2, written on a slip. The old man, who refuses every specific, reads it and changes one word.
  • James does: he puts it down and watches, as he already does with the true sheets. Then he asks nothing.
  • Cost: they now know he recalls, which is worse than reading. The five seats that follow stop being a bribe and become what Kalder got: recruitment. On the second of December the object on the tray carries the old man's word, so James's memory was wrong by one word and theirs was exact.
  • On the page? Partly. v7 has seven true sheets and "to see which one made the woman by the window move." PLACEHOLDER 7 asks whether the remembering line is planted here.
  • Already proposed? No. The addendum's request slip at Aylin's desk can stay.

Where the leak idea breaks the plan or a rule. Say no to these.

  • More than one kind of leak. You listed other realities, past lives and earlier societies. Crouch has one kind and one tell. Take past lives only. The world before the reset reaches the book through people who carried it, which is who the givers were.
  • Leaked objects. Crouch's building that appears (02) would wreck SDF. If things can change by themselves, a sentence that differs between two printings stops being evidence of an editor, and Leiden, 1931 becomes unnecessary. 01 flags that Crouch uses the Mandela Effect exactly this way. Nobody in SDF may offer a leak as the reason a book changed.
  • A new right column. Bram defines it as people whose fear is leaving. Keep that. The leak is the sign a handler looks for, as in 5.1.
  • James as the chosen one. The sentence must be common: the professor, Henk and the quiet ones all have it.
  • A public leak on a date. Leave it says nothing loud happens. The dates stay private and small (02:14, the log).

REVIEW 01, findings 1.1 to 1.3.

  • 1.1 (the edits mean three things): yes, if you take one kind of leak. What was given was the method of carrying across, the givers were the people who carried it, and "the thing that passes" is the carrying. That is the review's own cheapest join, and 5.2 gives it a visible form before Part Three.
  • 1.2 (the hidden thing is in every bookshop): partly. A leak is the one thing a bookshop cannot sell, because it is yours, ordinary and unasked for. That supports the review's reading (they remove the ordinary versions and make the rest exotic), but Noor still has to say it.
  • 1.3 (no motive): mostly. A person who recalls is a witness to the world before the record was arranged, so the paper is corrected and the witness is found. That is self-interest in one sentence. It must arrive on paper before Part Three (the folder's When a Reader Notices is the place), or the old man becomes Slade. Kalder still needs his line.

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• A machine behind the leak, or any physics. SDF's leak has no cause the book can name.
  • The villain as the source of the fix. The final conversation already risks this.
  • Restarts. A book about resets must not reset on the page, must not make one free, and must not show the same catastrophe twice. SDF's reset stays offstage and in the past.

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
1. "You’ll have two sets of memories—one live, one dead." (Book Two, 01) The whole rule in one line.
  2. "FMS isn’t what people think it is." (Joe's call, 01) An illness turned into a choice, then the call is cut.
  3. "Would you like a do-over?" (Joe's call, 01) Recruitment as a small ad.
  4. "I think of it as a timeline anniversary." (Book Three, 02) A name that makes the leak predictable.
  5. "Healthy minds are being made unwell; unwell minds are being driven over the edge." (Barry, 2018, 02) The cost to people who did not choose it.
  6. "Cause and effect are still alive and well." (Book Three, 02) Nothing is undone for free.
  7. "Using the discovery to erase itself." (Slade, 03) The antagonist's motive in six words.
  8. "Life with a cheat code isn’t life." (last Barry chapter, 03) The climax is a refusal.

notes.title: section 01 (Book One, plus the opening of Book Two)
notes.html:
Coverage: Book One in full and the first three chapters of Book Two (Helena's explanation, Barry's first morning back), about 31,300 words, read in full, 15 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 01; no edition data in the file. The chunk ends at Barry in 2007 drinking coffee on his porch.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Barry, 2–5 Nov 2018) Barry, a detective, wants to stop a stranger jumping, then to settle a contradiction (Ann says Franny jumped; the report says Joe saved her) Ann's false life; the CDC picture of FMS; a Montauk diner where his own memory of the last three days is replaced by a grey one in which none of it happened Ann dies in front of him; his sense that the past is fixed The contradiction is "whispering" to him, and now the same thing has happened to him, so it is no longer someone else's case He goes to the address Joe gives him and walks into the hotel
2 (Helena, 2007–09, interleaved) Helena wants unlimited funding to build a chair that saves her mother's memories Slade's money, his strange foreknowledge, and a test in which a subject is killed on purpose Her team, her control of the project, her mother's care Slade holds her on a rig 173 miles out and her mother's clock is running The test succeeds only by being invisible: she is hit by a "dead" memory of a morning that never happened
3 (Barry, 6 Nov 2018 to 2007) Barry wants to get out of the chair He is killed in a tank and wakes in his own body on the night Meghan died His belief that the past is closed A two-minute head start and a daughter ahead of him on the street He saves her; Vince hands him three rules and leaves

Why it grips

  • Two clocks that meet. Barry's chapters run forward through 2018; Helena's run forward through 2007–09. They touch in the chair. The reveal is staged in Helena's room: Slade at the door is played twice, first as the "dead" version, then with champagne, and the repeat is how reader and Helena learn what happened.
  • A hook that costs a life at once. Barry's failure on the ledge sends him to Montauk, so his curiosity has grief behind it.
  • The best single scene is Barry's first memory (6 Nov). The reader waits through the straps and the questions about Meghan, then the tank. Crouch builds the memory by sense, in order: smell of the house, taste of the beer, the screen, then touch, then her voice. The pain of dying fades as the memory sharpens. When his finger moves, the reader learns before Barry does that this is not a recording.
  • The comic edge is thin. Gwen's bar banter is the only relief.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The hidden thing is two layers deep. On the surface it is a hotel that invites the dying and the desperate; underneath it is a man who changed history and has left the world's memory in a mess. In this section it works in three ways:

  1. It blocks nothing, it invites. Joe gives Barry the address and the garage door opens by itself.
  2. It threatens once. Vince tails and drugs Barry, then the hotel switches to rewarding.
  3. It makes the detective a client. The cost of the secret is that Barry is given what he wanted most. By the end of the section he has more reason to protect the conspiracy than to expose it, and he has been told to tell no one.

How the lore gets in

  • Ann's account (1, about 700 words), a spoken confession on a ledge. It gives the emotional rule of FMS (grey, small details hurt most) and ends in her death, so no stall.
  • Gwen's CDC briefing (about 600 words), dialogue in a bar. Barry reports the state of knowledge: 64 cases, 10 percent suicide, social spread, the Mandela Effect. Gwen's jokes and her doubt (maybe Ann was just unwell) dress it; it sits between a death and a blackout, so it does not stall.
  • The police report (about 300 words), a document. It contradicts Ann and is the object that makes Barry act.
  • Joe's phone call (about 600 words), on a train. One rule, an address, then a hang-up before he says who "they" are.
  • Slade's explanation (Book Two, about 2,000 words), a conversation. The only true lecture: time as illusion, then the first timeline, Jon Jordan, Slade's own death. The fish and sensory-volume passage slows it, but it ends on a threat and a question, and the next chapter returns to Barry.

Mechanism notes

How each leak is delivered.

  • Ann (Ch. 1). A whole second life, grey and in small physical detail (Sam's birthmark, the cake fight, her husband's morning breath), arrives after a nosebleed and a stabbing headache. She acts: she tracks down Joe, tells him her plan, and goes to the ledge hoping he will come. It costs her the life she is in.
  • Barry (diner, 5 Nov). A nosebleed and glint of pain; three days of memory replaced with a grey set where he sat watching the Knicks. He cannot dismiss it, because it matches what Ann said, and it pushes him to the hotel (he says he is more afraid than ever).
  • Helena (Book Two). A grey, haunted memory of the previous half hour, in which a man died in the tank and she tried to throw a chair. It arrives at the exact moment the original event would have happened, which is how Slade proves it.

What the leaks share. Sensory, grey, small, with a nosebleed, at a fixed moment. Each is also proof: Slade uses Helena's as evidence, Barry uses his as a reason to move.

How a leak becomes something a character must act on. Three devices:

  1. Someone else has a stake in the contradiction. Ann's claim that Franny jumped and the report that she lived are checkable by a detective in an afternoon. The leak becomes a puzzle with a train timetable.
  2. The leak is shared. Gwen's social-spread detail means Barry cannot treat it as a private illness.
  3. The leak carries an instruction. The man in the chair tells Barry to change what happened, and Vince adds rules.

How the book explains its rules without stalling. Each rule is delivered exactly when a character is under pressure. The CDC facts come over whisky; Joe's explanation is cut off by a hang-up; Slade's physics comes while Helena is angry and wants to know what he did to her. Nobody asks "how does it work" until the reader already has the evidence.

Fixes.

  • A (gate). Absent. Barry proves nothing before acting; he is just curious.
  • B (canary). Weak: Slade's planted fact ("my mother's name is Susan") proves a mechanism, not a believer.
  • C (front). Present: hotel hides chair, chair hides the timeline change.
  • D (lock and key). Present: Joe opens only because Barry already knows Ann's name and the Poe Building ledge. Barry's private fact (the last night with Meghan) is the key the hotel then uses on him.
  • Fifth: the gift as a lock. Vince's rules make the rescued man a silent helper, close to SDF's helpers who know one task and the word "continuity".

Quotes

  • "FMS isn’t what people think it is." (Barry, Joe's call): one line that turns an epidemic into a choice, then the call is cut.
  • "Would you like a do-over?" (Barry, Joe's call): the recruitment is a classified ad, small and banal.
  • "Don’t try to game the larger system with your knowledge of what’s to come." (Barry, 2007): the rule is given as a courtesy, not a threat.
  • "You’ll have two sets of memories—one live, one dead." (Helena, Book Two): the whole leak mechanism in eight words.

Flags

  • Real things named in a non-conspiratorial way: Mandela Effect, Berenstain Bears, D-Wave, the Challenger launch, the 2007 World Series. None is made complicit. SDF should keep any such nod short and harmless.
  • No invented edits on real books.

notes.title: section 02 (Helena's July 2009 chapter, Barry's second life, Book Three, first third of Book Four)
notes.html:
Coverage: from "Helena, July 5, 2009, Day 613" to the sixteen-year-old girl in the Silverado (about 33,000 words), read in full, 15 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 02. The chunk has no chapter numbers, so cites are by heading and date. The opening third was not read.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Helena 2009 to 2018; Barry 2007 to 2018) Helena: out from under Slade. Barry: to live his second chance well A death in the tank returns the dead timeline as "false" memories on a fixed date Reed hangs himself; Helena hides for nine years; Meghan remembers her own death, then dies anyway The Big Bend appears and the leak now reaches a whole city; the hotel is still running Barry stands outside the hotel with a gun; Helena stops him
