2 (Book Three) Destroy the chair before anyone else has it A future Helena has already lived, and a "save point" cut into her own arm Barry dies twice; Slade dies in the dark; a masked team takes the lab The raid made the chair someone else's property Barry shouts for her to run; she is taken
3 (Book Four, days 8 to 160) Stop the people who now hold the chair DARPA uses it to undo disasters, the rules slip, the design leaks, a stranger rewrites New York every few minutes Her freedom, then her sense of which day is real If she waits, the next change arrives within the hour She climbs into the chair herself

Why it grips

  • Dying is a chapter break. When a viewpoint character dies, the next section starts in a changed timeline with a nosebleed and a clean memory of a different route. Barry's death in the corridor is written in full, then replaced by a run where he does not die: the reader gets the death and the retry.
  • A calm stretch the reader knows is borrowed. Barry's second life is summarised in a few lines per year (graduation, divorce, his mother's death exactly as remembered). Then Ann Voss Peters lands on a car, and the pleasant years become what the cost is measured against.
  • Exposition at a table or in a car, never in gunfire. Helena cooks Barry's favourite meal while telling him what has not happened yet.
  • Cuts on action. Helena's 2018 chapter ends on her cutting her arm; the next opens on Barry watching.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

Hotel Memory turns Barry's grief into a plan, then a raid. DARPA replaces it as the thing Helena must stop, and holds her in an apartment with cameras, a contract and a pitch. Shaw's argument drives Book Four: each use saves lives, so refusing looks like harm. Then the design leaks and the choice disappears, because the thing is now everyone's.

How the lore gets in

  • Slade's test (July 2009), about 900 words. A conference room: Slade says the experiment already happened, and the reader feels the rule before it is explained.
  • Barry's bathroom (2018), about 1,200 words. A family explains the rule to itself, so an emotional crisis carries the exposition.
  • Helena's kitchen (Book Three), about 2,500 words. Future events told over a meal; eating gives the telling a pause.
  • Dead-memory Q&A in the car, about 400 words. Barry's questions ("couldn't you have gone back?") do the lecturing.
  • DARPA ground rules (Day 17), a five-item list. Each rule is broken in turn.

Mechanism notes

How each leak is delivered, what the character does, what it costs:

  1. Slade's test. To Helena and Reed, minutes later, as a nosebleed and a replay of the failed experiment. Helena acts: she secretly maps the memory of Jee-woon's first visit and dies on purpose to return to it. Cost: nine years in hiding. Reed's own leak is a memory of a beach at age two, and he wishes he had not been revived; he hangs himself.
  2. Barry's anniversary. The first life arrives eleven years late. Julia knocks at three in the morning; Barry works out that Meghan has it too and races to her flat. Cost: in the new timeline Meghan cannot hold both lives and dies the same day.
  3. The Big Bend. A building, delivered to a whole city with memories of having eaten in it. Barry acts by reading a news caption and going to the hotel. Cost: three more dead in Meghan's building and more suicides.
  4. Helena's future memory. She remembers a goodbye with a Barry four months ahead and uses it as proof: his eclipse, his orchard, his father.
  5. The save point. She cuts her arm to leave herself a vivid short memory. A leak turned into a tool; she replays the ambush with Barry's wound in mind.
  6. Slade's own mind. He has lived too many lives to map a new memory and gets only flashes of lifetimes. The leak costs its user.
  7. School shooting (Day 8 to 11). Delivered to a nation as coverage of events that never happened; Helena sees a "murdered" student recounting being gunned down, a little unhinged. It gives Shaw his best argument.
  8. Day 136. The same device with the timing changed: every averted massacre since January arrives in one gulp.
  9. Tunnel, bridge, Grand Central, Trump Tower (Day 160). Four timelines in minutes. Helena dies in a flood, wakes, watches the bridge burn, shifts again. She keeps the physical feeling of impacts that never happened.
  10. The girl in the Silverado. The direction reverses: Helena's older mind takes over a sixteen-year-old's hands. Planted earlier by a photograph of her in the same truck in her mother's care-home room.

How a leak becomes a thing to act on:

  • A tell and a clock. A nosebleed signals arrival; the date is fixed by when the other self died, so characters can predict it ("tonight is the night").
  • A second person holds it too. Barry cannot sit on it, because Meghan has it.
  • Evidence, not feeling. The dead memory holds a route, a gun position, a code.
  • A price paid by the one who acts. Barry is shot twice; Helena dies again and again.

How it escalates without repeating: one man, a family, a city, a nation, the world on one morning, a stranger rewriting the same morning four times, then one person taken over from the inside.

For the four fixes:

  • A (gate). Shaw's five rules and a vote; orders from above break it.
  • B (canary). Helena asks that the killer be left under the window with his tools so the group becomes a rumour; a newspaper profiles it at three months.
  • C (front). Shaw offers a false-front program for his superiors; the real one is later exposed.
  • D (lock and key). Helena's private facts open Barry. The strongest scene in the section.
  • Fifth: a scheduled leak. A known date on which the hidden memory arrives for everyone present. For SDF, past lives could surface on the anniversary of a reset.

Quotes

  • "Every time Reed dies in the tank, he orphans a string of memories that become dead in our minds after we shift." (Helena, July 2009): the rule, stated by the person exploiting it.
  • "I think of it as a timeline anniversary." (Book Three): a name that makes the leak predictable.
  • "Healthy minds are being made unwell; unwell minds are being driven over the edge." (Barry, 2018): the cost to people who did not choose it.
  • "Cause and effect are still alive and well." (Helena, Book Three): why nothing is undone for free.

Flags

  • Real people and organisations are named: Greenwald and the Guardian, WikiLeaks, Trump Tower, Turing, Hitler, Franz Ferdinand, DARPA, RAND. SDF must not do this.
  • Suicides, a child murder and mass shootings are shown. The book is not funny in this stretch.

notes.title: Helena (end of Book Four) to Barry (Books Five and Epilogue)
notes.html:
Coverage: the last Helena chapter, Book Five ("Barry"), the Epilogue, and the back matter, to the last page (about 25,800 words), read in full, 15 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 03; no edition data in the file. I did not read the first two thirds, so earlier setup is only what this section restates.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Helena, then Barry, anniversaries 1 to 4) To live one calm day with Helena before the world remembers Each fresh loop ends the same way: on 16 April 2019 every living person receives the memories of the previous timeline, and the world panics, then fires missiles Helena resets by dying in a tank, each time killing her own sixteen-year-old self. Barry's death in the first life is the reason the loop exists Every loop's research failed, and the date is fixed In loop four he is a New York cop with no Helena; he phones Jee-woon, who says Slade once reset a timeline
2 (anniversaries 5 to 7) To get the method out of Slade A jailed Slade, once he remembers, says to go back to the original timeline, which exists only as a dead memory, and stop his killing of Helena Barry sees San Francisco burn; Helena dies of dementia in Antarctica; he swallows pills and lies in his own grave A half-remembered sentence from the last loop surfaces as he lies there He maps a dead memory (his daughter's birthday eve) and goes into the tank
3 (the last Barry chapter, Epilogue) To get back to the original timeline and stay there The original is a gray, frozen field of every memory he has; he must refuse the perfect first memory Everything: Helena becomes a dead memory he alone has He has to choose forward living over nostalgia, then use what he knows He reconciles with Julia, stops Slade, and sits down beside a stranger Helena

Why it grips

  • The same day, escalated. Anniversary one is a quiet desert morning with a mild sedative on the table. Anniversary two is a nuclear strike on Denver written second by second, with the hero's skin coming off. Anniversary three is the same date but with only a short window before the missiles. Four shows a precinct whose cops shoot themselves; five is a vaporised Central Park; six is a captive Slade; seven is a grave. Each is a different genre, place and horror, so the reader never gets the same scene twice.
  • The couple is the engine, not the apocalypse. Helena has lived about eighty-seven years of the same twenty-nine, while Barry gets each loop as new. The talk on the mountain (the hike, "I will leave you!" and the offer to walk it again) puts the relationship inside the loop. The reader waits for Barry to learn enough to catch up with her.
  • A countdown is always running. Pain, a short battery, a pill clock, a soldier at the door. Each chapter ends with a hand-off to the next reality (a flash of white, a world bleeding of colour, a dawn).
  • The short sentence as a trap. Single-line paragraphs ("Slowing." three times) push the reader fast through each disaster.
  • The best scene: Barry in the gray frozen field of his own memories (ch. "Barry", Book Five). It is built as a catalogue of small, specific moments (the Christmas-lights drive, a bike crash, a mother singing) that ends in a temptation, to live in the first memory forever. The climax is a refusal, not a fight.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The "secret" is the chair itself, plus Slade's known workaround. It is not a hidden organisation. Its use here: each time a hidden fact is learned, Barry loses it at the next reset and has to carry it as a rumor. The fact that Slade once reset a timeline (the Jee-woon call, loop four) is forgotten in loop five until the new anniversary returns it. The fact that Slade needs to be kidnapped is Helena's loop-five plan. The fact that the answer lies in the original timeline arrives in loop six and is forgotten until Barry is dying in a grave. The conspiracy therefore does one job: it makes knowledge expensive, perishable and passed by a person. Slade is the keeper of the key, and his motive for withholding it (using the discovery to erase itself) is the best single device in the section.

How the lore gets in

  • Barry's memory flood (anniversary one), about 1,000 words. The reader gets a decade of backstory as a "tsunami of memories", with a bar scene, prophecies Helena told him in advance, then a short list of lifetimes. Then the news turns on and it is over; no stall.
  • Slade's answer (loop six), about 900 words. A confrontation through glass, with missile blasts going off in the background. He makes Barry unlock the cell, and the information comes out on the hill while San Francisco burns. The talk is delivered as bargaining, with the clock visible.
  • Helena's video (loop seven), about 900 words. An object in Barry's hands: a DVD, paused, with a message that asks him to pause it. It is the long emotional centre. The physics here (Einstein's line about the "persistent illusion", Augustine's question) is spoken as grief, not lecture.
  • The blackboard in Maine, about 500 words. The equations are explained as something Barry knows because he wrote them, in the five minutes after his memories arrive.
  • The neutrino detector, about 300 words, paragraphs of physics ending in "They got nowhere", so even the failure is brief.

Mechanism notes

How each leak is delivered. The rule: at 16 April 2019 in each timeline, everyone is hit with a nosebleed, a headache behind the eyes and the previous timeline's memories ("dead memories"). Barry notes that they come late and slowly in later loops, and that "sometimes you miss entire lifetimes." Delivery is physical first (blood, pain), then an image (a "super-cooled drop of rain", then a storm), then a list of specific scenes, then a decision.

The leaks are shared and individual at once. A population leak (mass suicides, jets crashing, the precinct shooting) is public, and a private leak (Barry's memory of the Antarctic years) is separate. The public one carries the plot's consequence; the private one carries the character.

What each loop costs. Loop 1: Helena's mother's last day, the 29-year project, a life without kids. Loop 2: his hair, hands and skin, and Helena's hardening. Loop 3: Helena's suicide attempt and a ruined marriage. Loop 4: Helena herself; Barry is alone. Loop 5: a kidnapping he is uneasy about. Loop 6: the research years, Helena's mind, and ten extra deaths. Costs are mostly bodily and relational, not abstract.

How the resets stay gripping. (1) The setting, genre and companions change every time. (2) The hero's information is deliberately uneven, so the reader learns something he will lose. (3) Costs deepen rather than repeat: the couple degrades, the world nears extinction. (4) The reset is rendered once in full detail (Helena's tank in Tucson), then compressed by a fade or a sentence. (5) The characters themselves name the fatigue ("Rinse, repeat", "The thirtieth?"), which lets the reader feel it without being bored by it.

Does the ending pay the device off? Yes, in two ways. The mechanics pay off: the original timeline is the only place with no earlier leaks, because nothing predates it, and Barry's refusal to nest in a "perfect memory" is the key. The emotional payoff is that leaks end, and Barry alone keeps them. The Epilogue is quiet: a brunch, a made peace, and a last "You look like you want to buy me a drink" turned around so he is the one waiting. The last sentence cuts off, and the reader supplies the answer. The ending takes the leak, which was a burden, and makes it a private gift.

What a book about resets must not do (from where this section drags).

  • Do not let the explaining go on for more than a page without a scene break. The neutrino and wormhole paragraphs here are the slowest in the section, and they pay off nothing (the experiments fail and the answer is a human act).
  • Do not make a reset free for the hero. The best reset is the one where the hero loses a person or a skill.
  • Do not make the fix a piece of tech; the fix is a decision. Crouch's own best material is the refusal, not the physics.
  • Do not repeat the same apocalypse twice without changing its kind; anniversaries two and five are almost the same nuke, and 5 is stronger only because the call with Jee-woon is happening during it.
  • Do not give the solution to the villain. Slade handing over the fix is convenient and rescued only by his stated motive.

For SDF's four fixes. A (gate): weakly. Barry must map a dead memory with a "synaptic number" (121, "just barely in the safe zone") and cannot reset otherwise; a number as a gate is cheap and clear. B (canary): none. C (front): each loop's answer is the cover for the next (more physics, then Slade, then the original timeline). D (lock and key): Slade's key is held back until Barry unlocks his cell and gives him a view of the burning city. A fifth: knowledge decays across the reset, so what James learns must be written down or told to a person, and a lost note is a cost.

Quotes

  • "Stop thinking linearly." (Slade, Book Four to Five): the key to the whole plot in three words.
  • "Using the discovery to erase itself." (Slade): the antagonist's motive, as a tidy joke.
  • "Only now, in this brief moment, are they equals." (anniversary three): the rare moment the loop produces for the couple.
  • "Life with a cheat code isn’t life." (last Barry chapter): the thematic refusal, the climax's actual turn.

Flags

  • Real figures: Einstein, Augustine and Kierkegaard are quoted. The Acknowledgments name real writers as namesakes and two real MIT neuroscientists, with thanks, not as complicit in anything. Nothing for SDF to avoid, but the back matter should not be copied as a pattern.
  • Real cities (Denver, New York, San Francisco, Glasgow, London) are destroyed in missile strikes; nothing is attributed to real organisations beyond "Russia and China" as unnamed governments.
  • No invented edits on real books in this section.

books.qa:
Answers point to the section notes in this folder (01-book-one.md, 02-middle.md, 03-books-three-to-five.md) and, where relevant, to a v8.2 chapter by title. The map is 00-map.md. The text has no chapter numbers, so cites are by Book, date or loop. Everything about SDF here is a PROPOSAL; Santi's decisions are PLACEHOLDER.

The leak itself

1. What is a leak in this novel, in one sentence? When someone restarts time from an old memory, the stretch they abandoned comes back to everyone who lived it as a second, gray set of memories. Helena is told she will have one live set and one dead (01-book-one.md, Mechanism notes and Quotes).

2. What is the tell? A nosebleed and a stab of pain, then the memories (01-book-one.md; 03-books-three-to-five.md adds the headache behind the eyes). It is the same every time, so characters and the reader can recognize it in someone else. For SDF see map 5.1: the flash in The funeral has no repeatable sign yet.

3. How does the fixed date work? The dead memories arrive at the moment the earlier self died or left, which Helena names a timeline anniversary (02-middle.md). In Book Five the date is 16 April 2019 for everyone alive (03-books-three-to-five.md). The date lets characters wait for the leak and prepare, and lets Crouch write the dread before the event.

4. Who is the second witness, and why does it matter? Barry's first life arrives in Julia and Meghan on the same night, so he cannot file it as his own illness (02-middle.md, leak 2). Earlier, Gwen's CDC detail that the syndrome spreads between acquaintances does the same job (01-book-one.md). In SDF the candidate is the widow in The other ten (map 5.1).

5. What is the checkable contradiction? Ann says Franny jumped; the police report says Joe saved her. A detective can settle that with a train ride (01-book-one.md, Movements step 1 and the lore list). The leak is handed to someone whose job is to settle that kind of disagreement, which is also James's job at the bank.

6. How does a leak carry usable evidence? Dead memories hold a route, a gun position and a code, and Helena proves herself to Barry with his eclipse, his orchard and his father (02-middle.md, leaks 4 and 5 and "Evidence, not feeling"). The memory is read like a document. Map 5.2 gives James the SDF version: a sentence he can test for a source.

7. Why do the leaked lives feel real? They come in small physical details: a birthmark, a cake fight, morning breath (01-book-one.md, Ann). Barry's own first memory is built sense by sense, smell first (01-book-one.md, Why it grips). v6 The floor already agrees: the lives are short, ordinary and "boring."

8. Does a leak always cost the person who has it? Yes. Ann dies, Reed hangs himself, Meghan cannot hold two lives, and Slade ends with only flashes (02-middle.md). 03-books-three-to-five.md notes that the costs are bodily and relational, never abstract.

Escalation

9. How does Crouch use one device for a whole book? He changes the scale each time: one person, a family, a city, a nation, the world at once, one morning rewritten four times, and last an older mind arriving in a younger body (02-middle.md, "How it escalates without repeating").

10. What is the SDF ladder, and how much exists? Most of it. The funeral (one man), The math (the professor said the same line), The other ten (a dead stranger), Leiden, nine years ago (the handler, seen only by the reader), The sheets (the quiet ones, by password), The final conversation (remembering as policy), and the Epilogue (Ida at the stairs). The missing rungs are the second and third, which map 5.1 and 5.2 supply.

11. What is the "save point," and can SDF use it? Helena cuts her arm to make a short vivid memory she can return to (02-middle.md, leak 5). No. It needs the chair, and it turns the leak into a tool the hero controls. Rule 9 of the v8 brief says insights happen to James.

12. Where does the escalation fail? In the last third. 03-books-three-to-five.md says anniversaries two and five are almost the same nuclear strike. Each loop changes place and genre, but the reader has learned the pattern.

13. How do the loops stay readable at all? Five ways, listed in 03-books-three-to-five.md: new setting and companions each time, uneven knowledge between the couple, costs that deepen, one restart shown in full and the rest compressed, and characters who name their own fatigue.

Lore and rules

14. How does Crouch explain the rules without stalling? Each rule arrives when a character needs it to act in the next minute: whisky after a death, a phone call cut off, a family in a bathroom at three in the morning (01-book-one.md, 02-middle.md). Nobody asks how it works before the reader has seen it work.

15. Where does the lore stall? Slade's first long explanation to Helena, about 2,000 words (01-book-one.md), and the neutrino and wormhole pages (03-books-three-to-five.md). The second pays off nothing, since the answer is a decision. ADDENDUM 05's rule holds: nobody in the room can lose by what is being said.

16. Which lore scene should I study for Frank's kitchen or Leiden? Helena's kitchen in Book Three (02-middle.md, about 2,500 words): the future is told over a meal she cooks from his own memories, so every fact is also proof. Then Slade through the glass in loop six (03-books-three-to-five.md), where the listener must unlock a door to hear the rest.

17. Is there a document that works as a reveal? The police report, about 300 words (01-book-one.md), and Helena's DVD in loop seven (03-books-three-to-five.md), an object in Barry's hands that asks him to pause it. Both fit SDF's rule that reveals are objects.

The conspiracy

18. Is there an organization at all? Barely. First a hotel that invites the desperate, then a state program, then nobody, once the design is public (01-book-one.md, 02-middle.md). 03-books-three-to-five.md says the secret by then is only the chair and Slade's workaround. It is a poor model for SDF's helpers and a good one for a single device.

19. How does the conspiracy treat the investigator? It invites him, threatens once, then gives him what he wants most and asks him to keep quiet (01-book-one.md, "It makes the detective a client"). SDF has the same move in the five seats of The reading room, continued, which James refuses.

20. What is Shaw's argument, and does SDF have it? Each use of the chair saves lives, so refusing looks like harm (02-middle.md). SDF has it in Anneke's reason in The final conversation: the truth would collapse the world. No change proposed.

21. What does the book say about A, B, C and D? A is weak (five rules, a synaptic number). B appears once. C is three layers that are only learned. D is the strongest: private facts open Barry, and Slade's key is held until his cell is unlocked (all three notes, "Fixes"). See map section 4.

22. Are there mechanisms not in ADDENDUM 05? Two. The dated arrival, a hidden thing that surfaces by itself on a known day (02-middle.md). And the perishable finding: what the hero learns is lost at each restart and survives only through a person (03-books-three-to-five.md). The gift as a lock is the addendum's co-optation with a clearer price.

The leak in SDF

23. Does SDF already have a leak? Yes, of one kind. The funeral has the flash of cold mud and a cracked hand, The night he stops being afraid pays it, v6 The floor lists remembered → imagined among the edits, and the old man says in The final conversation that some of them remember across lives. What is missing is anything James can do with it before the floor.

24. Does the organization already have a word for it? "Recall." The foundation man uses it in Utrecht, 1993, the nightly job is rcl-agg in Leave it, and the invoice in The money bills a "recall index." No change is needed to make the count a count of people who recall; someone only has to say the word in front of James (map 5.1).

25. Should the right column change to "people who are leaking"? No. A room with a long table defines it as people whose fear is leaving, judged by handlers who have crossed. Keep that and make the leak the sign a handler looks for. Changing the definition would touch Bram's scenes, The long table, again and the opening.

26. What leaks, to whom, in the proposals? A memory with a bodily sign, to Henk and to James (map 5.1, The other ten). A sentence, to James and the professor (5.2, The math). Dated flashes, laid out for Ana (5.3, Twenty minutes). The same sentence, corrected by the old man (5.4, The reading room, continued). No object leaks.

27. Why may an object not leak? Because SDF's proof is two printings compared. If things can change by themselves, a changed sentence no longer needs an editor, and Leiden, 1931 loses its point. 01-book-one.md flags that Crouch uses the Mandela Effect this way; 02-middle.md has a building that appears in a city.

28. Should SDF use other realities as well as past lives? No. Crouch has one kind of leak and one tell, and it is the reason the reader can follow. The earlier world reaches SDF through people who carried it, which is who the givers were.

29. How does the organization answer a leak? It discredits. When a Reader Notices in The math already says agree and reclassify, and ADDENDUM 05's change 3 gives James a wellbeing referral. The thermostat in The band already funds the exotic version, so the ordinary one sounds like it. Nothing new needs building.

30. Does the leak repair REVIEW 01 finding 1.1? Yes, if it is one kind. What was given was the method of carrying across, the givers were the ones who carried it, and "the thing that passes" is the carrying. Map 5.2 puts that in James's hands as a sentence before Part Three.

31. Does it repair 1.2? Partly. A leak is ordinary, personal and unasked for, which no published book of the dead is. That supports the review's reading that the edits remove the ordinary versions. Noor still has to say so in Leiden.

32. Does it repair 1.3? Mostly. A person who recalls is a witness to the world before the record was arranged, which gives the organization a selfish reason to find them. It has to arrive on paper before Part Three, or the old man hands over the answer the way Slade does (03-books-three-to-five.md). Kalder's line is still missing.

33. What must a book about resets not do? Explain for more than a page without a scene break, make a restart free, make the fix a piece of technology, show the same catastrophe twice, or give the solution to the villain (03-books-three-to-five.md, the list in Mechanism notes). For SDF add: never show the reset.

34. Would a public leak on a date work in SDF? No. Leave it promises that the date passes and nothing loud happens, and the machine counts people one at a time. Keep dates private: 02:14 on the oven clock, and the log in map 5.3.

35. Does the leak make James special? It must not. In Crouch everyone gets it. In SDF the professor, Henk and the quiet ones in The sheets share the sentence, and the password scene depends on that.

Rules and limits

36. What in the book breaks SDF's rules? Real organizations and people named (02-middle.md, Flags), an armed raid and a kidnapping (02-middle.md, 03-books-three-to-five.md), a machine as the cause, and a middle with no comedy. 01-book-one.md notes that Gwen's banter is the only relief.

37. Is there anything for the dog? No dog in the notes. The nearest thing is the ending: Barry keeps the memory of someone who does not know him and sits down beside her (03-books-three-to-five.md). The Epilogue's Ida at the stairs is SDF's version, already planned.

38. Do the three notes disagree anywhere? In one place. 03-books-three-to-five.md puts the phone call with Jee-woon in loop four in its Movements table and in loop five in its "do not" list. Also, Slade dies in Book Three (02-middle.md) and is alive in a cell in loop six (03-books-three-to-five.md); that is a new timeline, though the note does not say so. 03 was written without the first two thirds.

books.author: DeLillo
books.title: Libra
books.readfor: compartments; a plot smaller than it looks; the archivist drowning in paper
books.intro: Coverage: English, converted text with no edition data in the files (note 04 has running heads to p. 456). The conversion repeated the last quarter of the book; it was cut to one copy, so the whole novel to the Author's Note is covered by four section notes (01–04, about 153,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Anything from outside the notes is marked [from memory, not from the text]. Brief: compartments; a plot that is smaller than it looks (Everett's staged miss, which gets away from him); and Nicholas Branch, the archivist drowning in paper, who is SDF's Part Two problem made into a character. Set against SDF's "few hundred professionals on millions of one-task helpers." Standing-rule note: real people are made complicit (Ferrie, Banister, Ruby, de Mohrenschildt, Clay Shaw, Roselli, the mob with "people... in the police"; 01–04). Branch's lists put invented men (Vasquez, Latta) beside the real dead (02, 03). Everett's fakes are pinned on real CIA units, and Alpha 66 is said to be CIA-run (02, 03). Mackey breaks into Oswald's flat (02). Take the shapes, none of that.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
Two lines that do not know they are converging. In chapters named by date, Win Everett, a CIA man pushed out after the Bay of Pigs, designs a fake attempt on Kennedy: shots that miss, and a paper trail to Cuban intelligence. In chapters named by place, Lee Oswald makes himself into exactly that man, years earlier: the Marines, Minsk, a rifle, an alias. The plotters find him. Their compartments let one middle man turn the miss into a kill, the designer loses touch, and chance does the rest. Between them, an archivist, Branch, reads the whole record decades later and cannot stop.

What makes it work: the reader brings the date, so every safeguard Everett builds reads as a crack. And no one inside the plot can see more than his own piece, so the reader is the only person who holds the whole thing.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:
Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 ("17 April", 01) Everett: his career back A staged miss, traced to Havana Two colleagues' careers The plan is all that keeps him an officer He needs a man
2 ("26 April"–"20 May", 01) Parmenter, Mackey: a gunman to fit De Mohrenschildt offers a defector who shot at Walker A written "expedite" memo The real man has already done what they meant to invent Shooters recruited; the miss withheld
3 ("In the Bronx"–"In Atsugi", 01) Oswald: a cell that gives him tasks People who want his U-2 knowledge, not him Courts-martial, his clearance Being used is his own fantasy He walks into 544 Camp Street
4 ("19 June"–"2 July", 02) Everett: handwriting to forge a gunman Oswald already has Hidell, the rifle, two draft cards His invention is pointless He arranged to hear only at second hand He steps further back
5 ("In Moscow", "In Minsk", 02) Oswald: to matter Every office files him and sends him on A suicide attempt Everyone has a file on him he can't read He writes his own and brings paper home
6 ("15 July"–"12 August", 02) Mackey: a sealed team Alone in a car, he chooses a kill Everett loses track of him No one above him knows Dallas; Ruby's debt planted
7 ("In Dallas", 03) Oswald: shoot Walker, be noticed He misses; the radio is silent Job, Marina, his mentor The act made him no one New Orleans
8 ("In New Orleans", 03) Oswald: a dossier for Havana Ferrie and Banister take him in; they know about Walker Arrest, "intense scrutiny" The plotters keep handing him things Mexico City
9 ("In Mexico City", 03) Oswald: a visa Full papers, and each embassy sends him to the other "A zero in the system" Family and rifle are in Dallas Texas, as Mackey bet
10 ("6 September"–"4 October", 03) Everett: to know if his plan lives Three lines in a local paper His authorship Sealed compartments; nobody can stop it, its designer included Miami shrinks to a small Dallas killing
11 (first "In Dallas", 04) Oswald: job, flat, Marina The route passes his building; Ferrie calls it a sign and offers an exit Marina's no; his ring A way out, and nowhere else The window
12 ("22 November", 04) Oswald: get out, tell it his way He fires early; Raymo kills; the theater pickup is a killer Tippit, arrest Every story needs him alive Ruby, through a new compartment
13 (Branch, 01–04) Branch: to master the data The Curator chooses, holds back, then sends novels His old age He reaches a verdict (chance) and still can't stop The book ends with him in the room

The pattern: every row's "cannot stop" is a compartment. Each man stops seeing at the edge of his own task, so nobody can call it off.

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
• Everett's pitch (17 April, about 800 words, a monologue in a parked car; 01). The lore is the plot. It ends on a turn ("We miss him"), and a phone call follows.
  • Backstory as motive, inside a scene: Mackey's Bay of Pigs in broken stills while he waits; Parmenter's Guatemala inside a marriage argument (01).
  • Lore as the terms of a deal: Bateman's Alpha 66 briefing is a job offer (03); Karlinsky's 1,800 words to Ruby end in instructions for the alley and the door, and the next scene is the act (04).
  • Lists: Mackey's inventory of the flat, read through Everett's panic (02); Branch's lists of deaths, each closed by a verdict ("No arrests in the case"; 02, 04).
  • Where it stalls: Branch on 2 July (02), about 900 words of the Warren Report and later deaths, placed right after Everett learns Oswald is real. The stall is deliberate, it is the subject, and it is short.
  • Where it doesn't: Walker's 1,200-word John Birch-style monologue ("In Dallas", 03) holds because the reader has already watched the car turn into his street.

sections.title: 4. The mechanism we came for: the compartment that breaks its own plan
sections.html:
Setup ("17 April", 01): "Each level of the committee was designed to protect a higher level." Compartments are presented as protection. Rule: one task, one reason per man. "He has his work, we have ours" (02); "You don't tell Frank or Wayne" (03). First use ("20 May", 01): Mackey briefs the shooters without target, city, or "that they were supposed to miss." The only safeguard sits in the only compartment with no rifle in it. Escalation (02–03): Everett reaches Mackey only through Parmenter. Mackey, alone in a car, decides on a kill (15 July). Parmenter can't find him (12 August). Mackey cuts them off (6 September). Everett learns of the Texas trip from a newspaper (4 October). The plan gets smaller as it gets deadlier, from Miami's wall of shooters to "an everyday Texas homicide." Cost: the designer is cut out of his own plot, and he knows plots "move toward death" (15 July). Payoff (04): Oswald fires before the oak tree, against orders. The staged miss happens inside the hit. The police beat Wayne to the theater, so the silencing passes to a fresh compartment: Ruby, a debt and an unlocked door. Branch's verdict: "due mainly to chance."

For a writer: compartments make a plot strong against outsiders and blind from inside. SDF's Compartments chapter has the first half. Libra adds the second: a failure inside the organization that nobody above the middle can see.

Against A–D. A supported, and seen from outside: Oswald brings every paper to Mexico City and the clerk still won't say yes (03). Ruby's self-set gate ("if I'm late, it wasn't meant") is no gate (04). B run by the conspiracy (Mackey leaks Miami on purpose, 03), and as farce: Ruby's box numbers "didn't match" and he shrugs (04). C contradicts ADDENDUM 05, which says C is only ever learned. Here it is built, by the antagonist (Everett's second layer, "the little surprise he was keeping for the end", 01) and by the patsy, who hides the rifle "to give them something to uncover, a layer to strip away" (04). See 5.4. D supported, with a limit: a key opens talk, not choice (Oswald "says no", 03).

New mechanisms (not in ADDENDUM 05): the slip at the middle level (lethal one level down, unseen above, 02); the originator cut out (03); the archive as containment, where the Curator chooses, holds back and floods (03, 04), extending Orwell's "why could I find it?" from one piece of bait to a whole supply; the decoy task (the Oswald doubles as busywork, 04); the found man, already scripting himself (01).

sections.title: 5. Transfer to SDF
sections.html:
Branch, precisely. DeLillo keeps a pure receiver from stalling the book in six ways. (1) Short slices, 700 to 1,000 words, at chapter edges (01). (2) Branch is never the engine. The clock runs in the dated chapters, against a date the reader brings. (3) His material comes as lists closed by verdicts, so the form sets the pace (02, 04). (4) His reading tells the reader the future ("No arrests in the case" for a man we have just met), so receiving builds suspense in the other line (02). (5) He reads the sending: why these objects, why now, and later what is held back (03, 04). (6) He pays only in years, and the book uses him as the warning.

James can't have (1) or (2), because Part Two is his. SDF already has (2) by other means: the villain-alone chapters run the clock, and the opening gives the reader the date. It has (3) in v7 The other ten. It also has Branch's temperament: "What I do is read everything in the order it comes, at the same speed" (v7 The money). So James must do what Branch never does: ask by name for what he wasn't sent; sort what he was sent by who sent it; spend a conclusion on a person. The thin book already says Ask, and Part Two never has him do it.

Already on the page, so not proposed: one task per helper (v7 Compartments); the hunter's trace (The payload); bait set from their side ("Let her," A room with a long table); helpers' self-stories as doors (Aylin in v7 The sheets). The gate, the homework and the canary are in ADDENDUM 05.

items.title: 5.1 Ask anyway
items.html:
The reading room (the opening); The reading room, continued; The sheets.

  • Change: the tray is set before he arrives, so the archive answers before he asks. He asks anyway.
  • James does: at Aylin's desk he writes the thin book's reference on a request slip. "It's already up." He hands it over; she stamps it. Two lines.
  • Cost: his hand now sits in the visitor book's "Shelfmark requested" column, with the same number as the professor's March line, marked Deceased. "Counted the night you asked" becomes an object he made, and the old man can read it back to him ("He asked too").
  • Already on the page? No. v7 The sheets: "No shelfmark; I hadn't asked for one."
  • Already proposed? No. The King map counts Ask as a theme, not an act.
  • PLACEHOLDER: is the tray's ledger the item the reference names? Noor's "nobody has ever simply asked" (v8.2 The vet) conflicts with the professor asking in March.

items.title: 5.2 Pulled, not handed
items.html:
Frank, loose.

  • Change: before Frank comes, James sorts everything he holds by how it reached him.
  • James does: two piles on the table. Pulled: the thirty-one years of invoices he queried himself (v7 The money). Handed: Saskia's folder, the annex role, Julian K.'s eleven-minute reply after Kalder's tip, the schedule. Frank sees only the first pile, and James tells him why.
  • Cost: the annex with Pieter's children, the piece most likely to move Frank, stays in the bag, so Frank's belief stops at the invoice. Saying "handed" aloud names Julian, whom Frank liked at the barbecue, as the hand behind two of the items.
  • Already on the page? Partly. v7 Frank, loose picks "one thing he couldn't argue with" but has no rule for picking it.
  • Already proposed? It adds to ADDENDUM 05's Frank gate and Orwell 2. New is the sort, which is the habit Branch never forms. It also explains "I believe the invoice": it is the one paper nobody gave him.

items.title: 5.3 One code, all the deaths
items.html:
What was on the phone → The night before → A market, Sunday.

  • Change: on Kalder's phone, the handler codes set against this quarter's outcomes put every death under one code, his. The other codes' visits ended in sales, moves and quiet. This is Mackey: the method said "visit," a man in the middle made it "kill," and nobody above checked, because each ending was plausible.
  • James does: he makes one extra sheet (address, date, outcome, code) and puts it only in Anneke's envelope.
  • Cost: he hands the organization its cover story (one handler went too far), and he knows what they do with a man who embarrasses them. A market, Sunday becomes his act, and "I wanted it to be me" carries it.
  • Already on the page? Partly. v7 What was on the phone has codes, statuses and one personal note against Kalder's. v8 A market, Sunday leaves how he was found unexplained.
  • Already proposed? No. PLACEHOLDER: do Zwolle and Deventer fall under his code? It keeps the rules: killing is rare and a failure, and James kills no one.

items.title: 5.4 A layer to strip
items.html:
The sheets → The leak → Leave it.

  • Change: while the envelopes go out by hand, James gives the count something to read. A car park says silence is worse, so he asks out loud again, about something true, dull and findable: Oswald's rifle, hidden "to do the expected thing."
  • James does: he raises page 212 in stand-up, files a ticket, and asks Frank to co-sign. The organization does what it always does: the ticket is closed as a duplicate, and a forum thread laughs at "the blind spot."
  • Cost: Frank, "never in it," goes on the nightly list for the first time. The decoy buys days, not safety, because the brewery man still leaks (PLACEHOLDER: how many days).
  • Already on the page? Partly. v8 Leave it files a ticket against rcl-agg, and v8.2 one against page 212. That filing becomes their second.
  • Already proposed? No. It answers ADDENDUM 05's question of whether C can be an act. Risk: James as manipulator (compare Orwell 6), though the ticket is true.

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• Real people as plotters, and invented men listed beside the real dead (01–04).
  • Branch's ending: the reader who never stops, sealed in the room. James publishes, and the final conversation must not become Branch's room.
  • Killing as the plot's success. Libra's plot works because someone dies. In SDF a death is one man's failure, and the organization prefers a sale, a move, quiet.

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
1. "Each level of the committee was designed to protect a higher level." ("17 April") Compartments, stated as safety.
  2. "The other thing he did not say was that they were supposed to miss." ("20 May") The safeguard in the wrong compartment.
  3. "It was no longer possible to hide from the fact that Lee Oswald existed independent of the plot." ("2 July") The found man.
  4. "Plots carry their own logic. There is a tendency of plots to move toward death." ("15 July") The designer afraid of his design.
  5. "Branch must study everything. He is in too deep to be selective." ("26 April") The receiver's disease.
  6. "The notes are becoming an end in themselves." ("6 September") The stall, named.
  7. "He wanted to give them something to uncover, a layer to strip away." ("22 November") The front as an act.
  8. "We didn't arrange your job in that building or set up the motorcade route." (first "In Dallas", 04) The plot admits its size.

notes.title: section 01 ("In the Bronx" to "20 May")
notes.html:
Coverage: Part One from the epigraph through "In the Bronx", "17 April", "In New Orleans", "26 April", "In Atsugi" and "20 May" (about 43,000 words; printed pages 3–131), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 01; no edition data in the file. The chunk runs past "In Atsugi" and ends with "20 May".

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 ("17 April") Win Everett, pushed out after a failed polygraph, wants Cuba back and his own life back An idea: stage an attempt on Kennedy that misses, with a paper trail pointing to Cuban intelligence Two colleagues risk their careers by sitting in his car. The plan has a gunman-shaped hole in it The outlawed group's only secret is now the group itself. The plan is all that keeps him an officer He needs a man: name, face, fingerprints, handwriting
2 ("26 April" to "20 May") Parmenter and Mackey want a gunman to fit Win's script Over lunch, de Mohrenschildt offers a real ex-Marine defector who he thinks shot at General Walker Parmenter writes an "expedite check" memo, which is a written trace. Then the kid vanishes from Dallas, and his rifle scores contradict themselves The real man fits too well: he has already done what they meant to invent Mackey recruits Raymo and Frank but holds back the target, the place and the miss
3 ("In the Bronx" to "In Atsugi"; end of "20 May") Oswald wants a cell that will give him tasks and a secret name Konno and Dr. Braunfels want his U-2 knowledge ("She talked about his job, not his life") A self-inflicted gunshot, two courts-martial, the brig, his clearance Being used as one piece is his own fantasy, so he keeps offering himself He walks into 544 Camp Street, unasked, to apply as an undercover agent

Why it grips

  • The reader knows the ending; the plotters don't. All the tension sits between Win's "We miss him" (17 April) and the November date every reader brings along. Each safeguard Win designs reads as a crack. By 20 May the brief is "Hit, don't kill" a Secret Service man, and Mackey answers, "This isn't a controlled experiment."
  • Two lines that do not know they are converging. The Oswald chapters are titled by place and the plot chapters by date. The plotters hunt for a man while we watch him, years earlier, making himself into one: Hidell, the derringer, the U-2 talk. The section ends where they meet. Ferrie hears the young man's voice through a wall and cannot see his face.
  • The plot is small. Five men, a paint scraper from the hardware store, a briefing in a parked car with the windows up against a pickup's dust. Nobody big needs to be behind it, and that makes it frightening.
  • The scene that does the most work is the de Mohrenschildt lunch (26 April): wine talk and an ambassador saying hello, then one remark ("I think I know who tried to kill him") turns the fiction into a person. Parmenter laughs at the "daisy chain of rumor" and then goes back and writes a memo. The scene is light first, then ends in an act on paper.
  • Funny under dread: "Texas Woman's University. Savor the name."; the college's old initials spelled CIA; Ferrie's pasted eyebrows.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The committee lecture (17 April) sets the rule: men leave the room and others enter, and the President is "the summit of unknowing". Every later scene repeats it on a smaller scale. Win does not know Mackey's real name. Parmenter hides his interest from de Mohrenschildt. Banister is asked to hold rifles without being told why ("You do know. Take my word"). Mackey tells Raymo and Frank there will be a shooting but not the target, the city or the miss. Oswald hides his lost clearance from Braunfels while she hides her purpose from him.

The result: the one man who knows the whole plan cannot control the shooters. Win designs a miss, and the men holding the rifles have not been told it is one. The compartments that protect the plan are what will let it get away from him. The section plants this and never states it. The plan also pulls in a network that already existed: Ferrie met the teenage Oswald back in "In New Orleans" over a broken .22.

How the lore gets in

  • The committee structure (17 April), about 600 words of Win's thoughts between two lines of office dialogue. Its comedy keeps it moving (poison cigars, the coughing monkey). No stall.
  • Win's pitch (17 April), about 800 words, a monologue in a parked car. A pickup's dust interrupts it, it ends on a turn ("We miss him"), and the next scene is a phone call. The lore is the plot itself, so it cannot stall.
  • Mackey's Bay of Pigs (26 April), about 1,200 words of broken stills while he waits in a hot room. It gives his motive: "a clear and simple reading".
  • Parmenter's Guatemala and front companies (20 May), about 1,000 words set inside a marriage argument. Beryl's needling carries it, and it reveals his motive: Cuban oil.
  • Branch (17 April, end of 26 April), 700 to 900 words each. These are the only real stalls, and they are short and placed at chapter edges.
  • A document: the Navy medical record of the gunshot (In Atsugi), set as a typed form. It is the first page of Oswald's paper trail, and it reaches the reader as an object.

Mechanism notes

  • Branch is SDF's Part Two problem, made into a character. He receives documents: the Curator sends "precisely the right document". He is never blocked and pays only in years ("becoming bodiless"). He has written "precious little" because "It is impossible to stop assembling data." DeLillo keeps him in short slices and runs the clock in other people's scenes. For SDF: if James mostly receives, the momentum must come from someone acting on a deadline in the next scene, or James must stop receiving. Branch is James if he reads everything and never has to decide.
  • C (front), designed by the antagonist. Win's trail has two layers on purpose. The first points to Cuban intelligence. The second, "even more unclear", points to the CIA's own plots against Castro, "the little surprise he was keeping for the end" (26 April). SDF's "findable" seat list could be built the same way, so that each layer James solves is the cover story the next one needs.
  • A (gate), held by the hunters. Oswald's scorebook disagrees with itself ("either the number is wrong or the designation is wrong"). The plotters do not resolve this; they widen the search, and widening is how a plot leaks.
  • B (canary), at small scale. Oswald feeds Konno and Braunfels technical terms, "studying her reaction to the terms". It is a canary done only by talking, which suits James, who reads pauses.
  • D (lock and key). Each recruit opens to one thing: Raymo and Frank to Cuba plus $500 a month, Banister to his hatred of Kennedy, Oswald to being given a task.
  • Fifth: the found man. Win wants to "script a person or persons out of ordinary pocket litter" and finds a man already scripting himself. The cost is that the found man brings his own plot. An SDF helper may already be telling himself a story about his one task, and that story is the door.
  • Fifth: the hunter's trace. Parmenter's memo records his interest, much like SDF's nightly count of who asks. Asking leaves paper.

Quotes

  • "Each level of the committee was designed to protect a higher level." (17 April): compartments as a rule.
  • "We do the whole thing with paper." (17 April): a plot built as a trail meant to be found.
  • "Branch must study everything. He is in too deep to be selective." (26 April): the reader of everything, stuck.
  • "The other thing he did not say was that they were supposed to miss." (20 May): the compartment that will break the plan.

Flags

  • Real people are made complicit: de Mohrenschildt as an Agency asset who thinks he pushed Oswald toward Walker; Banister with a CIA weapons cache; Ferrie carrying money from "Carmine Latta" (a stand-in name [from memory, not from the text]); Branch's list of real deaths; Kennedy wanting Castro dead. SDF must not do this.
  • The useful structure: the planners (Everett, Parmenter, Mackey, Raymo, Vasquez, Branch) are invented and placed among real people. SDF's rule that people and companies are invented goes further and makes nothing real guilty.
  • No invented edits on real books. Oswald's library Das Kapital has "weird notes in an obsessive hand", which is texture only.

notes.title: section 02 ("In Fort Worth" [Marguerite, the freighter] to "12 August")
notes.html:
Coverage: In Fort Worth, 19 June, In Moscow, 2 July (with the first Nicholas Branch passage), In Minsk, Part Two, 15 July, In Fort Worth (second), 12 August (about 43,900 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 02, page headers 132–265.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (19 June, 2 July: Everett) A sample of Oswald's handwriting, so he can forge a gunman out of paper who leads investigators to Cuba Mackey breaks into Oswald's flat. Oswald already has the rifle, the leaflets and forged papers in two names (Hidell) The gunman he was inventing is already alive in the world, and his basement forgery is pointless Oswald is real and acts on his own. Everett set things up so he only hears at second hand He keeps further away while the plot goes on without him
2 (In Moscow, In Minsk: Oswald) To matter in history: citizenship, study, writing Every office files him and sends him on. The KGB finds him unfit to be an agent. The Red Cross money stops when he asks to go home A suicide attempt, Minsk instead of Moscow, silence from Alek Everyone has a file on him he cannot read, so he writes his own (the Historic Diary, "The Kollective") He comes home with pages stuffed in his clothes. Paper becomes what he has to trade
3 (15 July to 12 August: Mackey, Oswald) Mackey: a sealed team. Oswald: a job Mackey decides to turn the miss into a kill. The FBI, then de Mohrenschildt, then Collings, each want one piece of information from Oswald Everett loses track of Mackey. Oswald's notes go to the CIA No one above Mackey knows the plan has changed The Dallas job; Ruby's debt to the mob is planted

Why it grips

  • The planner learns his invention exists. On 19 June Everett is at his worktable flattening a Diners Club card and looking forward to choosing his gunman's names. On 2 July Mackey's inventory arrives as a list: two draft cards, Hidell as chapter president, signatures in different hands, a Minox at the back of a closet. Everett feels displaced and panics, and the reader does too. There is no longer any gap between the man he made up and the real one.
  • Each conspirator has his own chapter, and none has the whole plot. Banister drinking at the bar, Elko on a bench in Denver, Ferrie at Carmine's lodge, Raymo and Frank at an old men's softball game. Each scene is complete and often funny, and each holds one piece. The reader puts together what the men cannot. Elko guesses the job is serious from how little Raymo and Frank say.
  • Both sides are guessing. Kirilenko (In Moscow) suspects the KGB knows less about the boy than the boy knows about them, and he has a recruitment quota to meet. The U-2 altitude dispute turns Oswald's possible mistakes into intelligence. The enemy service is as baffled as the reader.
  • It stays funny: Banister's fifteen Kennedy doubles, Oswald writing to Connally because he thinks Connally runs the Navy, the State Department getting rid of Marguerite with a snow forecast, the Weird Beard on the radio.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The plot is small by design. Everett wants a miss: a Secret Service man winged so the attempt looks real, and a trail of papers to Cuban intelligence, half fabricated and half real. It gets away from him through the compartments he built himself. He reaches Mackey only through Parmenter, and Camp Street only through Mackey. Driving alone, Mackey decides to take it all the way. He picks each recruit for a single job (Elko kept short-range, nowhere near the President). He thinks about inventing a target for Banister so Banister never learns the real one. Banister has already stated the rule: "He has his work, we have ours." By 12 August Parmenter cannot find Mackey, and Everett lets himself be reassured. So nobody owns how this ends. Everett's own theory (15 July) is that plots move towards death, and the rules he built to keep his plot contained are what let it get there.

How the lore gets in

  • Everett's planted documents (19 June), about 450 words, told as he walks to his car. A fake DDP memo, a news item planted in an exile magazine, phone doodles on TSD stationery. It does not stall, because each item is something he is making.
  • Mackey's inventory of the flat (2 July), about 500 words, a list. It comes through Everett's panic, so it lands as a shock.
  • Branch (2 July), about 900 words. The Warren Report's contents, one FBI memo given verbatim, the photographs, then three later deaths (Banister, Vasquez, Roselli), each closed with "No arrests in the case." It sits straight after Everett learns Oswald is real. Records of what happened later arrive as flat entries in a file, and they tell us ahead of time that Frank, whom we have only just met, will be shot. It stalls on purpose: Branch believes every item belongs, the Agency paid to fireproof his room, and he bills them for less than he spent.
  • Kirilenko's thinking (In Moscow), about 1,200 words, interior. It gives the KGB's procedure through one tired man's doubts, broken up by the polygraph and Powers scenes.
  • Marguerite's monologues addressed to "your honor", and Postcards 3 to 5. She is the first to say conspiracy, and sounds unhinged saying it.

Mechanism notes

  • C (front) is Everett's whole design. The Cuban trail is a layer meant to be solved, and he leaves it imperfect on purpose so that it reads as real. That is SDF's deliberate typos and the seat list left "findable". What Libra adds is a way for the front to fail: the real man turns out stranger than the cover. SDF's cover stories could be outrun by a real helper who goes further than he was asked.
  • The plan slips at a middle level (15 July, 12 August). It turns deadly one level down, with one man in a car going one step further, not at the top. That is a ready-made way for SDF's one-task helpers to fail, and it fits the rule that killing is a failure. PROPOSAL: in The other ten, one of the deaths turns out to be a helper who acted on his own, and the organisation is as alarmed about it as James is.
  • D (lock and key) (In Fort Worth). Collings's price is one specific truth, how the KGB handled Oswald, and he pays with a job. Each SDF helper could likewise be opened by the one question only his own task can answer.
  • B (canary), turned round (In Moscow). Oswald signs up for a Russian exam to see whether Naval Intelligence notices him, and scores "poor" all the way down.
  • Branch is the warning for James. Branch has every document and no nose for which one matters, and the people paying for his room are the people he studies. PROPOSAL: in The reading room continued, someone points out that James's reading is supplied by the organisation, and the order of what he was handed shows what they wanted him to read first. That gives him a cost of being wrong.
  • Fifth: everyone makes paper. Banister opens an empty file and says material will come to it. Oswald writes down the FBI agent's licence plate "to build up the record". Beryl writes to her friends in newspaper clippings. In this section the conspiracy runs on documents, SDF's own medium.

Quotes

  • "It was no longer possible to hide from the fact that Lee Oswald existed independent of the plot." (2 July): the turn, as a single realisation.
  • "Once you start a file, Delphine, it's just a matter of time before the material comes pouring in." (19 June): the file pulls in material.
  • "A fact is innocent until someone wants it. Then it becomes intelligence." (In Fort Worth): the rule for the documents James receives.
  • "Plots carry their own logic. There is a tendency of plots to move toward death." (15 July): the planner is afraid of his own plot.

Flags

  • Real people are shown as complicit or connected: Banister, Ferrie, Ruby, de Mohrenschildt (passing Oswald's work to the CIA) and Roselli. The invented planners (Everett, Parmenter, Mackey), mob boss (Carmine Latta) and CIA man (Collings) are mixed in with them, and Branch's list puts the invented Vasquez beside the real dead. SDF must not do this.
  • Everett's fakes are pinned on real CIA units and on real attempts on Castro.
  • No invented edits on real books.

notes.title: section 03 ("In Dallas" to "4 October")
notes.html:
Coverage: "In Dallas", "6 September" (with a Nicholas Branch passage), "In New Orleans", "25 September", "In Mexico City", "4 October" (about 32,000 words, printed pages 269–366), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 03; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 ("In Dallas") To shoot General Walker and have the news reach Havana He misses. The radio says nothing. De Mohrenschildt jokes about the miss and leaves for Haiti His job, Marina's trust, his only mentor Nobody noticed. The act was meant to make him someone and it made him no one New Orleans, and a plan to reach Cuba
2 ("In New Orleans") A dossier proving to the Cubans he is a friend of the revolution Bateman makes him an FBI informant. Ferrie and Banister take him in, and they know about Walker Arrest, mug shots, his flat searched, "the object of some intense scrutiny" The dossier only counts once he shows it. Meanwhile the plotters keep handing him things Mexico City, with the rifle sent on to Dallas with Marina
3 ("In Mexico City") A Cuban transit visa Each embassy sends him to the other. His papers move nobody His money and his picture of himself ("a zero in the system") Every other door is shut, and his family and rifle are in Dallas Back to Texas, which is what Mackey is counting on

Why it grips

  • The reader knows more than anyone in the scene. Walker's monologue about the invisible Control Apparatus ("In Dallas") comes after the reader has watched the car turn onto Avondale, so the rant holds because a bullet is on its way. The miss arrives as a hole the size of a half-dollar and Walker picking metal out of his arm with tweezers.
  • Dark comedy built into the plotting. Oswald gets the date wrong (the 17th, it is the 10th). Dupard comes dusted in bakery flour. Oswald forgets to visit Trotsky's house. The book stays funny while it walks toward a killing.
  • The hand that steers him stays out of sight. "In New Orleans" is told from inside Oswald, so the plotters show up only as feelings: things moved in his spare room, people at 544 Camp looking at him differently. Then Ferrie says it in the Habana Bar ("You're the night-rider"). The scene that does the most work is the Trailways terminal: Lee asks what they want, Ferrie will not say, and Lee answers "You know. I don't." The man at the centre of the plot knows least about it.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The plot gets smaller and loses touch with the man who started it. Mackey stops contact with Everett and Parmenter, "leaving them to their hieroglyphics" (6 September). In "4 October" Everett does not know whether his plan is still alive. He learns the President is coming to Texas from three or four lines buried in a local paper, and he daydreams about a polygraph as his way out. [From memory, not from the text: his original design was a staged miss to be blamed on Castro.] The escalation is on the page. Mackey tells Frank that even if "all the gears don't mesh... Someone has to die" (6 September). The wall of shooters planned for Miami (25 September) shrinks to a small Dallas killing (4 October), and a plot that small needs Oswald more.

The conspiracy moves Oswald in two ways, and neither is force. It shuts doors somewhere else: Banister says Mackey "can fix it so the Cubans won't take him" (25 September), and in Mexico City Oswald blames bureaucracy. It also gives him things: ammunition he could not find, a place at the camp, an office at 544. Mackey bets on where Oswald will go instead of ordering it.

Compartments everywhere. Alpha 66's CIA mentors deal with only one or two men, under false names. Wayne picks up Leon's role only from "sideline dialogue". Mackey tells Raymo "You don't tell Frank or Wayne". Banister "doesn't know the exact nature of the role". Bateman insists no other agency share his informant, while Oswald works out of Banister's office. Tony Astorina's job for Carmine is to tie him into his body armour each morning. Each man knows one task, close to SDF's helper structure. DeLillo's twist: with the compartments sealed, nobody can stop the operation, its designer included.

Branch drowning in paper (6 September). The Curator sends autopsy photos, goat skulls and a test bullet. Branch cannot tell why these, why now, and decides the choice is itself a message, a mocking one. His notes stop leading anywhere, and the record gives Oswald's eye colour, height and handedness three ways each.

How the lore gets in

  • Walker's monologue (about 1,200 words, inside his head): Birch-style lore. It does not stall, because the reader is waiting for the shot.
  • Frank's Cuba backstory (6 September, about 900 words, memory during a drive): ends in his deduction that Kennedy is Alpha's target.
  • Branch and the Curator's objects (about 1,000 words, a list): stalls on purpose, and the stall is what the passage is about.
  • Bateman in the diner (about 1,200 words): Alpha 66, the crackdown, Banister. It comes as a job offer, so every fact sets terms for Oswald.
  • Ferrie on the CIA and the Mafia plotting against Castro (about 200 words). The next morning's Times-Picayune confirms it. The gossip comes first and the newspaper confirms it next day.
  • Tony on Kennedy and Giancana's mistress (25 September, about 400 words): blocks Ruby's loan request, so the scene keeps moving.
  • Banister and Ferrie's briefing (25 September, about 900 words): the shooting gallery and "Oswalds all over Texas".

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate), inverted. In Mexico City Oswald brings every document and the gate still holds, because a person chooses ("She does not say si. She does not say no."). SDF could refuse James once with full paperwork in hand. That is a cost of being wrong about what papers can do, and it fits the rule that doors open only by choice.
  • B (canary), run by the conspiracy. Mackey leaks Miami on purpose ("Let everyone know", 6 September) and welcomes the Chicago leak (4 October). Bateman will feed Banister selective information. SDF's organisation could bait James the same way.
  • C (front). Miami fronts for Dallas. 544 Camp has two entrances: "One for who you are, one for who you say you are." The made-up Oswalds cover the real one.
  • D (lock and key) that fails. Ferrie uses his key, the private knowledge of Walker, and Oswald still does not turn: "He says no" (25 September). A key gets someone talking. It does not make the choice for him.
  • Fifth: read why the documents were sent. Branch treats the Curator's choice of material as the clue. This is the strongest fix for James's passive Part Two: every document that reaches him raises the questions of who sent it and why now, and he can get that wrong (PLACEHOLDER).
  • Sixth: the originator cut out. Everett learns of his own plot from a newspaper: a model for an SDF character who designed part of the method and lost track of it.

Quotes

  • "Stamp some numbers and letters. This makes it true." ("In New Orleans"): self-made documents as identity.
  • "The notes are becoming an end in themselves." (6 September, Branch): the man who reads everything goes under.
  • "We create our own Oswald. A second, a third, a fourth." (25 September): a made-up trail that discredits instead of preventing.
  • "Small, spur-of-the-moment, that's what we want. An everyday Texas homicide." (4 October): the plot shrinks and gets harder to stop.

Flags

  • Real people shown as complicit: David Ferrie, Guy Banister, Clay Shaw (with Ferrie and Oswald), Jack Ruby (seeking money from the invented Carmine Latta). The Giancana and Kennedy affair comes as gossip. The CIA is said to run Alpha 66, a real group. SDF must not do this.
  • Branch's list of aliases puts real names (Ruby, de Mohrenschildt) beside invented ones (Everett, Mackey, Latta) as if they were the same kind of fact. It works, and it is exactly the mixing SDF forbids.
  • No invented edits on real books in this section.

notes.title: section 04 ("In Dallas", "22 November", "In Dallas", "25 November", Author's Note)
notes.html:
Coverage: the second-to-last "In Dallas" chapter through "25 November" and the Author's Note, i.e. to the end of the novel, plus a stray fragment (pp. 344–354) appended to the chunk file (about 34,300 words in all), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text with running heads "LIBRA • 367" to "456"; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 ("In Dallas", to Thursday night) Oswald: a job, an apartment, Marina back; out from under the FBI The motorcade route runs past the building where he happens to work. Ferrie and then Mackey give him the timing, four cartridges and an escape route to the Texas Theater Marina says no three times; he leaves her $170 and his wedding ring Ferrie tells him the coincidence is a sign, and the plan includes a way out (Galveston, Havana). He has nowhere else to go The window on 22 November
2 ("22 November" to the second "In Dallas") Oswald: get out, then tell the story his way He fires before the oak tree, ignoring Mackey's order. His shots wound, miss and hit Connally, and Raymo's shot from the fence kills Kennedy. The pickup at the theater is really Wayne waiting to kill him Tippit, arrest, and then Ruby Every story he tries (framed, partly guilty, lone gunman) needs him alive and believed. In the cell he decides he has found his life's work: reading everything about the case Ruby in the basement
3 (Branch passages, both "In Dallas" chapters) Branch: to master the data More paper, a list of deaths that looks like a pattern, the Curator holding back, and then the Curator sending novels His old age. The room becomes "the room of growing old" He has reached his conclusion (chance, a rambling affair) and still cannot stop reading The book ends on him trapped in the room, and on Marguerite promising to research the case herself

Why it grips

  • Suspense moves from what happens to who knows what. The reader already knows the outcome. The tension is in the gaps between compartments. Oswald thinks the theater is his pickup. Ferrie suspects they will both be killed in Yucatán. Wayne sits two rows behind Oswald with a silenced pistol. Mackey's private checklist ends with Ferrie spending a lonely night in Galveston, which is exactly what Ferrie does later. Each man plays his part inside a frame he cannot see, and the reader can see all of the frames.
  • The shooting is built from a dozen partial views ("22 November"): Oswald, Raymo, Hargis, Nellie Connally, Agent Hill, the woman with the camera, Mackey across the plaza, and teletype fragments. No viewpoint holds the whole event. Oswald thinks he missed with his last shot, and Raymo thinks Oswald is "picking them off". The form itself is compartmented.
  • Small things keep interrupting the plot. The washing machine Oswald promises Marina, Ruby wiring $25 to a stripper (receipt stamped 11:17) and opening Alpo for his dog before he walks into the garage, Wayne joining the cry of "Lights, lights" so the film starts again. These are the jokes and they are also the timing. Ruby is late enough that the timing works by accident.
  • It stays funny. Ruby asks a DJ who Earl Warren is. Ruby boasts that he learned to vomit out of a moving car as a boy in Chicago. Mackey calls a fire truck coming down Main Street the dumbest thing he has seen in twenty years.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The plot turns out to be smaller than it looks, and the section shows how. Ferrie says outright that they did not arrange Oswald's job or the motorcade route; the coincidence, not the plot, puts Oswald in the window. Mackey thinks his own plan has one thing Win Everett's careful design lacked: luck. Mackey treats Oswald as "redundant, strictly backup", useful mainly for leaving a traceable trail. The staged miss Everett planned [from memory, not from the text: Everett wanted a spectacular miss that would be blamed on Castro] does happen, inside the hit: Oswald's shots wound and miss, and by his own account he killed no one. The plot then breaks down in steps. The police reach the theater before Wayne can shoot, and the job of silencing Oswald passes to a new compartment: Karlinsky recruits Ruby over loan forgiveness and a door left unlocked. Branch states the conclusion in the second "In Dallas": the whole thing worked through chance.

The compartments drive every scene, because every handoff is a person told only his own task and lied to about the rest. Branch's theory adds a twist: the Oswald doubles were busywork to keep Alpha 66 stuck in "countdown" while Mackey's own team was "sitting on go". In other words, the job a helper is given can be a decoy to keep him occupied.

How the lore gets in

  • Milteer tape (first "In Dallas"), about 600 words: a transcript, then two numbered theories, then the doubles. It is a document in Branch's hands, so it is an object. It ends on a riddle (the Mexico City photograph matches descriptions of Mackey) and cuts straight to Branch buried in paper. No stall, because each fact ends in a question.
  • Two lists of deaths (Branch passages), about 300 and 400 words. Short dated entries, each with its verdict ("Ruled a heart attack"; "No arrests in the case"). The pace comes from the list form. They end on Branch suspecting that someone wants him to believe in coincidences.
  • Karlinsky–Ruby (second "In Dallas"), about 1,800 words of conversation. The mob's logic arrives as an appeal to Ruby's Jewishness, his debts and his wish to be somebody, and it ends with operating instructions (the alley, the unlocked annex door, the fire stairs). The next scene is the act. No stall.
  • Marguerite's monologue ("25 November"), about 2,200 words, addressed to an unnamed judge. It is cut in with the burial scene, so the account and the scene take turns. It is the theorist's voice: real anomalies (three yearbook photos of a boy who attended one month) beside nonsense (Marina is "trained").
  • Weird Beard on the radio, teletype, police radio: atmosphere carried by broadcast fragments, under 400 words each.

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate), ignored. Mackey gives Oswald a strict gate: wait until the car clears the oak tree. Oswald fires early ("Leon fired too soon"). Ruby's gate is the reverse: he lets the clock decide (if he is too late, he was not meant to do it). For SDF: a gate a man sets himself can be fake, a way of handing the decision to chance. James's gate should be one he can fail.
  • B (canary), done cheaply and wrong. Ruby tests a theory with physical evidence, comparing the box number on the ad with the one on the billboard: "The numbers didn't match." He shrugs it off. That is the cost of being wrong that SDF lacks, shown as farce. The Miami leak (Milteer) also worked as an accidental canary, and it cancelled the Miami operation.
  • C (front), stated by the patsy. Oswald hides the rifle "just to do the expected thing", giving investigators a layer to strip away. Hidell is "a dozen layers", and Mackey's design means for Oswald's leftism to point to Castro. Each layer exposed is the cover story for the next.
  • D (lock and key), a door literally unlocked for one man. Karlinsky's key is Ruby's need to make a name. Ruby walks in and thinks that if it is this easy, they must want him to do it. Marina is the counter-example: the door she keeps shut.
  • Fifth: the archive as containment (strongest for SDF). The Curator floods Branch, holds some things back, then sends fiction and a 400-page study of Lincoln–Kennedy parallels. Branch suspects someone wants him to believe in coincidences, and decides the room was built to hold him. Proposal: SDF's diagnosis (James mostly receives documents) could become the plot. James, who reads everything, slowly sees that the documents arrive to keep him reading, the way SDF's organisation funds nonsense so every real question has a clown beside it. Receiving becomes the trap he has to notice. Not on the page in v8.2 as far as this reader knows (PLACEHOLDER).
  • The reader becomes the researcher. Oswald in his cell plans to read every book about his own case, and Marguerite vows to time his movements. Three people end up reading the same case: the killer, his mother and the archivist.

Quotes

  • "We didn't arrange your job in that building or set up the motorcade route." (first "In Dallas"): the plot admits how small it is.
  • "He wanted to give them something to uncover, a layer to strip away." ("22 November"): the front, planned by the patsy.
  • "the conspiracy against the President was a rambling affair that succeeded in the short term due mainly to chance." (second "In Dallas"): Branch's verdict.
  • "Branch wonders if there is some limit inherent in the yielding of information gathered in secret." (second "In Dallas"): the archive holds things back from its own reader.

Flags

  • Real people shown as complicit: Banister and Ferrie as plotters; the mob recruiting Ruby with police help inside ("They have people they render assistance in the police"); Milteer on tape. Carmine Latta is a stand-in name, but the deaths list names real people (Giancana, Powers, Veciana). The Author's Note says DeLillo extended real people into imagined events. SDF must not do this.
  • No invented edits on real books.
  • Pipeline: the chunk file ends with a stray fragment, pp. 344–354 (Ruby with Tony Astorina; Banister and Ferrie plan Oswald doubles: "We create our own Oswald"). It belongs earlier in the book (it also appears in chunk 03). The chunk's filename says "in-dallas-to-in-dallas", but the real range runs to "25 November" and the end of the book, so chunk 05 ("in-mexico-city-to-in-dal-as") may duplicate or misorder material. The coordinator should check.

books.qa:
Answers point at the section notes (01–04 in this folder) and at the map (00-map.md). v8.2 chapters are named by title. Everything about SDF is a PROPOSAL; Santi's decisions are PLACEHOLDER.

1. What is Libra in one line, for our purposes? A conspiracy that is small, compartmented and run on paper, which gets away from its own designer because nobody inside can see more than his own task. The reader, who knows the date, is the only one who holds the whole thing. See 00-map.md §1 and 01, "Why it grips."

2. Who is the protagonist? There are three lines. Everett and his men (chapters named by date), Oswald (chapters named by place), and Branch the archivist (short passages inside both). The engine table follows whichever man is pushing at that moment. See map §2.
