3. What was Everett's original plan? A staged attempt that misses on purpose: "We miss him" (17 April), a Secret Service man winged ("Hit, don't kill," 20 May), and a paper trail to Cuban intelligence, with a second layer pointing at the CIA's own plots against Castro. See 01, Movements and Mechanism notes; 02, "How the conspiracy moves the story." Notes 03 and 04 mark this as from memory, but 01 and 02 have it from the text.

4. How exactly does the miss become a kill? At the middle level. Everett reaches Mackey only through Parmenter. Mackey never tells the shooters it is a miss (20 May), decides on a kill alone in a car (15 July), and cuts off contact (6 September). See 01, 02, 03. Nobody above him knows.

5. Is the plot big or small? Small, and it gets smaller: five men, a paint scraper, a parked car (01). Miami's wall of shooters becomes "an everyday Texas homicide" (03). Ferrie admits they didn't arrange Oswald's job or the route (04). Branch's verdict is that it worked "due mainly to chance."

6. Why does the small plot frighten more than a big one would? Because nobody big is needed for it to work, and nobody can stop it, its designer included. See 01, "Why it grips," and 03, "How the conspiracy moves the story." For SDF, v7 Compartments already reaches "a few dozen men with codes... that's a club." Libra says a club is enough to kill.

7. What is Branch's role, in a sentence? A CIA-commissioned archivist who reads the whole record decades later, is sent material by a "Curator," never acts, and ages in the room. See 01, Mechanism notes; 02, How the lore gets in; 03 and 04, Branch passages.

8. Exactly how does DeLillo keep Branch from stalling the book? In six ways: short slices at chapter edges; the clock running in other men's dated chapters; lists closed by verdicts; reading that tells the reader the future; reading the sending as evidence; and paying only in years while the book uses him as the warning. See map §5 "Branch, precisely," and 01–04.

9. What must James do that Branch doesn't? Ask by name for what he wasn't sent, sort what he was sent by who sent it, and spend a conclusion on a person. Branch reaches his verdict and keeps reading (04). James is the narrator, so he can't be kept short and offstage the way Branch is. See map §5.

10. Is James already Branch on the page? In temperament, yes. v7 The money: "What I do is read everything in the order it comes, at the same speed." v8.2 Enjoy it while it lasts has him read all four hundred pages. The difference must come from acts, not from a change in temperament.

11. Where does Branch stall on purpose, and why does it work? 2 July (02): about 900 words of the Warren Report and later deaths, right after Everett learns Oswald is real. It works because it is short, because it is placed after a turn, and because it tells us that one of the shooters, whom we have only just met, will be shot. The stall is the point, and the next chapter moves.

12. What does the Curator do that matters for SDF? He chooses what Branch gets (autopsy photos, goat skulls), then holds things back ("some limit inherent in the yielding..."), then sends novels and a Lincoln–Kennedy study. Branch suspects the room was built to hold him (03, 04). That is SDF's thermostat aimed at one reader, and it is why the v8.2 opening's tray, already set, matters (map 5.1).

13. How is that different from Orwell's "why could I find it?" Orwell's is one piece of bait (the book). Libra's is a supply regime: an order, a withholding, a flood. ADDENDUM 05 places Orwell's at The money. Map 5.2 sorts all of James's material by how it arrived, in Frank, loose.

14. Does Libra support mechanism A, the gate? Yes, from new angles. Seen from outside, Oswald has every paper in Mexico City and a clerk still won't say yes (03). Mackey's oak-tree gate is ignored when Oswald fires early (04). Ruby's gate ("if I'm late, it wasn't meant") hands the choice to chance (04). For SDF, a gate James can't fail is no gate.

15. Mechanism B, the canary? Run by the conspiracy. Mackey leaks Miami on purpose ("Let everyone know," 03), and the Milteer leak cancels Miami (04). Small versions: Oswald feeds technical terms and watches reactions (01), and signs up for an exam to see whether Naval Intelligence notices (02). Ruby's box-number test is the cost of being wrong played as farce (04).

16. Mechanism C, the front? ADDENDUM 05 says it never becomes an act. Libra contradicts that. Everett builds a two-layer trail (01), and Oswald himself hides the rifle "to give them something to uncover, a layer to strip away" (04). Map 5.4 turns this into James's act in The sheets: a true, dull ticket for the count to read.

17. Mechanism D, lock and key? Supported, with a limit: a key gets talk, not a choice. Ferrie uses the Walker secret and Oswald "says no" (03). Karlinsky's key to Ruby is his need to be somebody, plus an unlocked door (04). SDF's keys are already on the page (Groningen, Els, Noor's shelfmark), so nothing to build.

18. What mechanisms are genuinely new here? The slip at the middle level; the originator cut out; the archive as containment; the decoy task; the found man. See map §4, last paragraph.

19. How does "the slip at the middle level" map onto SDF? SDF's handlers are Libra's middle. If the method's word is visit and one handler made it kill, the deaths are his failure, not the method. Map 5.3 puts that on a sheet in What was on the phone and The night before, paid off in A market, Sunday. It fits "killing is rare and a failure."

20. Doesn't 5.3 contradict Monday's "they have killed before, and it was cheap"? Not necessarily. The organization still owns the killing; the sheet shows how it happened in this quarter. PLACEHOLDER: whether Zwolle (A pension visit, Zwolle) and Deventer, March fall under Kalder's code. Leiden, nine years ago, with Kalder asking "Who else?", supports it.

21. Who in SDF is Everett, the originator cut out? Possibly Bram: sincere, believes the story, never had the experience he counts (v8.2 Part 0). Libra suggests he might learn from paper what his count became. No proposal is made, because James never meets Bram on the page. PLACEHOLDER if you want it for The leak.

22. Is any SDF helper's task a decoy, like the Oswald doubles? Pieter's "security test" (the honeypot tier in What was on the phone) is the closest: a task that keeps a helper busy and reassured. Libra's version (04) suggests the tier list could include one task that exists only to occupy. Already partly on the page through the tiers.

23. What is "the found man," and does SDF have one? Everett looks to script a gunman and finds one already scripting himself (01, 02). In SDF the brewery man ("I'm in," The sheets) and James's own twelve-year forum persona are the nearest. Gibson 5.5 covers the persona, so no new proposal.

24. How does Libra handle documents as objects? The Navy medical form is set as a typed form (01), Mackey's inventory is a list (02), Oswald's Historic Diary is paper he smuggles home (02), and the Milteer tape is a transcript (04). Each reaches the reader as a thing. That fits SDF's "reveals are objects."

25. "A fact is innocent until someone wants it." Where, and how to use it? "In Fort Worth" (02), on Collings's price for a job. It is the rule for James's received documents: each one becomes intelligence only because someone wanted him to have it. It sits under map 5.2.

26. How does DeLillo keep it funny? Comedy is built into the plotting: Oswald gets the Walker date wrong, Dupard is dusted in flour, Banister has fifteen Kennedy doubles, Ruby asks who Earl Warren is (02, 03, 04). The jokes are also the timing: Ruby is late for reasons that make it work (04). That fits SDF's "funny to the end."

27. What does the 22 November chapter teach about form? The shooting is built from a dozen partial views, and nobody holds the whole event (04). The form is compartmented. For SDF, The night before, with twelve doors and twelve partial views, could borrow that shape. It is not proposed, because the chapter is drafted (v8).

28. What is the pattern of "why he cannot stop"? Every row's reason is a compartment. Each man stops seeing at the edge of his own task, so none can call it off (map §2). SDF's "nobody who matters knows anything" is the same fact, used by James as a weakness (Compartments).

29. Could James's own sheets leak the way Everett's plan did? Yes, and Libra warns that the designer of a compartmented operation can't control each piece. In The sheets each recipient knows only his own page, so one may act beyond "Nothing. That's the point." The v8.2 leak is the brewery man's refusal, and Orwell 6 makes it James's choice. Keep it to one leak.

30. What does Libra contradict in ADDENDUM 05? The C verdict (see Q16). It also qualifies D: keys open talk, not choice (Q17). It confirms A and the "cost after the gate" (Ferrie's exit plan comes with a killer at the theater, 04).

31. Which real-world items must SDF not copy? Real people as complicit (Ferrie, Banister, Ruby, de Mohrenschildt, Shaw); invented men listed beside the real dead in Branch's lists; fakes pinned on real CIA units; Mackey's break-in. See every note's Flags and the map's standing-rule note.

32. Does Libra put invented edits on real books? No. Oswald's library Das Kapital with "weird notes" is texture only (01). Nothing to flag for SDF's book rule.

33. Is there an equivalent of SDF's count, the nightly list of who asked? The hunter's trace: Parmenter's memo records his own interest (01), and Oswald writes down the FBI agent's plate "to build up the record" (02). Asking leaves paper on both sides. SDF already has this in The payload.

34. What did the reading notes flag about the source text? Note 04's chunk ends with a stray fragment (pp. 344–354, Ruby and Tony; "We create our own Oswald") that belongs earlier and also appears in 03. The duplicated last quarter was cut before splitting (PIPELINE stage 1). Notes 01, 02 and 04 disagree on whether Carmine Latta is an invented or stand-in name.

35. If Santi takes only one thing from Libra, what should it be? Map 5.1 or 5.2. Both turn James from Branch into a man who asks and sorts, at almost no cost in words. 5.3 is the strongest for Part Three, but it is also the riskiest for tone.

books.author: Dick
books.title: The Man in the High Castle
books.folder: 08 Research/Engines/Dick — The Man in the High Castle
books.readfor: the leak: fragments of another reality as objects in hands
books.intro: Coverage: converted English text with no edition data in the file. Read in full through three section notes (01 chapters 1–6, 02 chapters 7–12, 03 chapters 13–15; about 79,600 words), 15 Nov 2026. Tier 3. Anything from outside the notes is marked [from memory, not from the text]. Brief: the leak. You have proposed that fragments of other realities, past lives or an earlier version of society reach into SDF's world. This novel is built on five such fragments. The map says how each one is delivered, which of them move the plot, and what the idea does to THE BOOK v8.2. Standing-rule note: real people are named as rulers and perpetrators in an invented history (01–03). An invented novel rewrites real history. A man travels under a false identity to kill; another under a cover name to warn. The police get a signed statement from a shopkeeper by pressure (02, ch. 7). Two men are shot and one has his neck cut (02, 03). Characters think and speak in slurs. Take the shapes, none of that.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
Germany and Japan won the war. In Japanese-run San Francisco an antiques dealer (Childan) learns his stock may be forged; a fired metalworker (Frink) starts making new jewelry; a trade official (Tagomi) hosts a "Swedish" visitor who carries a warning about a German first strike. In the Rockies, Juliana takes up with a truck driver who is reading a banned novel in which the Allies won. She works out he was sent to kill its author, stops him, and drives to the author's house to ask how the book was written. He says the oracle chose everything and will not say what that means.

What makes it work: every thread is stopped on a fact that someone has already acted on and cannot check. And the other world never arrives as an explanation; it arrives as a thing in the hands of a person who has something else to lose that day.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:
There is no single protagonist. Each row names who is being pushed.

Step What they want right now What they find What it costs Why they cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 1–2, 4; 01) Frink: his job back. Tagomi: to know what his visitor Baynes is Oracle readings with no clean answer; a coded cable; an offer of a jewelry shop Frink's pride and place Each has staked something on a reading he cannot check The shop; Childan's big sale
2 (ch. 4; 01) Childan: an Admiral's fifteen-thousand-dollar order A caller says a Colt in his shop is fake; a lab agrees; a newspaper desk says the Admiral's ship sank in 1945 His stock may be worthless The tip is true and the tipper is false; he can let neither lie He goes to his supplier
3 (ch. 5–6; 01) Wyndam-Matson, the forger: to end a blackmail he has only inferred He blames Frink and his partner, who did nothing, and pays them two thousand dollars Money he need not have paid He acted on the wrong culprit, and it is done A jewelry firm funded by a misreading
4 (ch. 5–6; 01) Juliana: company. Baynes: to deliver a message The banned novel in Joe's hands, with the author's address; the Chancellor's death Owning the book could get Joe shot; Tagomi collapses at a briefing She has a name; Baynes's errand now waits on one old man from Tokyo The drive; the wait
5 (ch. 7–8; 02) Childan: acceptance. Reiss, the consul: not to be blamed Childan signs a police statement against "Frank Frink." Reiss reads the novel, drafts an order to kill its author, burns it Childan's pride; Reiss's nerve The paper "ends your involvement"; Reiss fears the men above him Frink is on file; the hunt goes on without Reiss
6 (ch. 9, 12; 02) Frink: to sell the first batch Consignment only, nothing sold, then arrest on Childan's complaint His money; held for the Germans as a Jew The file already says what he is Handed over
7 (ch. 11; 02) Childan: to rescue his business A client says the plain pin has worth with no history, then offers a charms deal He cannot tell praise from insult He is "sole agent" of a thing he can neither sell nor throw away He sells the new work as new (ch. 14)
8 (ch. 10–12; 02) Baynes: to be heard The old man is a general; the plan is a nuclear strike on Japan; the SD arrive; Tagomi shoots two Two lives; Tagomi's calm The faction that opposed the plan must be persuaded again Tagomi back to the oracle
9 (ch. 13; 03) Juliana: a good time, then not to go at all Small slips (an ironed shirt, dyed hair) add up to an assassin; she cuts him and runs She leaves a man bleeding and tells no one The oracle tells her to warn the author whatever it costs Cheyenne
10 (ch. 14; 03) Tagomi: a life that means something again He stares at a silver piece, gives up, and is for a few minutes in another city Fear, lost time, later his heart The consul puts a form in front of him the same day He signs Frink's release instead
11 (ch. 15; 03) Juliana: did the oracle write the book? The author admits it, then refuses what follows; her own throw says the book is true The room cools She cannot go home not knowing; he cannot say it in full She leaves, unexplained

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
• Childan's ride to a meeting (ch. 2, about 1,100 words; 01). The state of the world as one man's self-justifying chatter, two minutes before a client.
  • The succession briefing (ch. 6, about 900 words; 01). The one true lecture. Dick cuts it with Tagomi's collapse and gives the rest in a phone call.
  • The banned novel, retold (ch. 5 and ch. 10, 700 to 900 words, both in cars; 01, 02). Each retelling is an argument: the forger disputes every point, the driver is angry at the praise of the New Deal. You learn the listener, and the plot comes with him.
  • The first-strike plan (ch. 12, about 800 words; 02). A negotiation between three men who are each hiding something; the general supplies the missing parts, so the plan arrives as a test of the speaker.
  • The author on his method (ch. 15, about 2,400 words; 03). Held up by a party going silent and a coin toss done in public.

Where it stalls: the novel read aloud in ch. 8 and 10, a page or two at a time. The note calls the stall deliberate; the interruptions are the relief (02). Where it doesn't: the first-strike plan, because the SD are one phone call behind and a man who may not believe it is weighing every sentence. This confirms ADDENDUM 05 on lore (someone in the room can lose by it) and adds that a retelling holds when the listener disagrees.

sections.title: 4. The leak
sections.html:
Five fragments of a world that isn't this one. They do different work.

The book within the book. It is never shown whole, and each time it is in the hands of someone with a reason of his own. A secretary takes it off the forger's shelf (ch. 5). A truck driver reads it aloud, furious at its version of Italy (ch. 6). Childan hears of it at dinner and decides to buy it as a duty (ch. 7). The German consul reads it in a locked office, is moved, and nearly orders a murder (ch. 8). What each scene gives you is the reader. It pushes twice: the consul's order, drafted and burned, and the plan to visit the author (ch. 10, paid in ch. 13). Elsewhere it colors. It never touches the German plot (03).

The forged Colt. The gun is fake, the lab proves it, and the man who said so is a fake too. This is the hardest push in the book and nothing in it is mystical: Childan goes to his supplier, the supplier calls the forger, the forger pays the wrong men (ch. 4–6). The lesson is about paper. The forger puts two lighters on a table, one of which was in Roosevelt's pocket, and says only the certificate tells them apart (ch. 5). History lives in the document.

The pin with no historicity. Made by two men who are not artists. Childan's client says it has a worth that owes nothing to any past (ch. 11). It pushes: Childan is responsible for an object he cannot price. It is the Colt reversed, a thing with no paper at all, which paper therefore cannot expose.

The oracle. Quoted line by line in the hands of whoever throws. It colors: it never tells anyone what he could not reach by judgment, and the reader cannot check it (01). Frink's reading says the money will not come, and it comes. It pushes once, when it sends Juliana to Cheyenne (ch. 13).

Tagomi's glimpse. He has killed two men and wants the silver piece to tell him something. He shakes it, curses it, tastes it. Nothing. When he has given up he is in another San Francisco for a few minutes (ch. 14). Nobody else sees it, and his own explanation is that his senses slipped. It pushes one decision: back at his desk, asked to hand Frink over, he signs the release. [From memory, not from the text: the piece is Frink's work, and neither man learns what he did for the other.]

The rule under all five. A leak here is never information the plot needs. It pushes when it changes what one person will sign, pay, drive to or burn, and colors when it only tells him something. And the discredit comes from the receiver: Tagomi blames his senses, the consul calls it cheap popular fiction, the author will not stand behind his own book. Nobody has to suppress anything.

Why the ending stays open. Juliana gets a yes from the oracle in front of witnesses, and the one man with the standing to accept it says he is not sure of anything (ch. 15). The reader holds a proof no character will take. The note names the price: it keeps the dread and loses a payoff, because nothing in the German plot depended on the answer (03). ADDENDUM 05 lists the open ending under "does not work," and this book agrees. What transfers is the refusal by the person in authority. v8.2 has it in The final conversation, after a win that happened on paper.

Against A–D. A: supported in small. Childan must know whether the gun is real before he acts; he passes, and it gets worse (ch. 4), which is ADDENDUM 05's "cost after the gate." B: inverted; the caller plants a false story and is never explained (ch. 4). C: the forgery trade inside an iron foundry; a cover identity that exists, the general says, to force the other side through formalities (ch. 12). D: Juliana gets past the author's deflection with a hexagram they both know without the chart (ch. 15); Baynes reaches his contact with a clerk's name (ch. 10).

New, not in ADDENDUM 05's list:

  • Paper against object. The certificate makes the antique. A thing that arrives with no paper cannot be reclassified; only its holder can be.
  • The wrong payee. A true fact, the wrong culprit, and money moves on the mistake (ch. 5–6). Near King's "right in its claim, wrong in a detail," but here a third party acts on the error and an innocent man collects.
  • The enemy as reader. The man whose job is to remove the fragment reads it, and it works on him (ch. 8).

The note's "object that works only when you stop pushing" is already yours: the fourth night of The night he stops being afraid.

sections.title: 5. Transfer to SDF
sections.html:
What the leak idea already has on the page. More than you may think. The funeral gives James cold mud and a cracked hand. v6 The floor says he has seen that hand all his life and filed it, and that the lives were cut off "by a man with a list." The job is called rcl-agg and the invoice line is "recall index." Utrecht's foundation man calls the two-rooms paper "recall." Henk Boersma dies after he "started saying strange things about his father." In v6 Coda, Ana wakes having dreamed James's hands cracked at the knuckles. And PLACEHOLDER #5, the line James says to Els, is already a leak slot: "why did you say that, my father said that."

Does it repair REVIEW 01, findings 1.1 to 1.3?

  • 1.1 (the edits mean three things): yes. Read given as "received from before" and arose as "you made it up yourself." Then the edit is the discredit, done to a sentence: it reclassifies a leak as an invention. Transmitted to arisen, shared to coincident, remembered to imagined (v6 The floor) are one move. History, instruction and "the passing" become one thing without a new speech.
  • 1.2 (the hidden thing is on sale): mostly. A leak happens in people, so it cannot be deleted from the world, only refiled. That fits the review's own fix (they make it exotic or funny) and gives the forty-one a plain job: the dry, sober books where an author reported a leak as received.
  • 1.3 (the motive): only if you decide what the leaks contain. A leak by itself gives the organization no reason to care. It gets one if what people recall includes the organization: the man with a list. Then every leak is a witness statement and the motive is self-interest. PLACEHOLDER: yours. Kalder still needs his line.

Where it breaks the plan or a rule.

  1. A third leak to James makes him a seer. The brief forbids him out-deducing the book. He has two (the funeral, the floor). Any more must land in other people and reach him as their words or paper.
  2. An object from before a reset breaks three things: the real-world rule (Urfa: "the book never says he found it"), the book that claims nothing, and REVIEW 01 1.4, which found the reset already cut. Past societies can leak only as invented sentences in invented books, which is what the forty-one are.
  3. "All forty-one are one edit" does not survive The List as written. Entries 3, 7 and 17 soften a date or an uncertainty; they are not verbs of receiving. Rewrite them or narrow the claim.
  4. The count counts words said, per v7 The payload. A leak is counted only when someone says it. Keep that and "counted the night you asked" stands.
  5. The win is paper. Sheets are diffs. A leak may not appear on a sheet as a claim.
  6. This book's own flaw. If nothing in Part Three depends on the leak, you have Dick's ending. Proposals 1 and 3 are there to prevent that.

Proposals. Your decisions are PLACEHOLDER.

items.title: 1. The payload → The gorilla mask (a memory, into James's hands, sent out on purpose)
items.html: Change: after he finds asked (job) beside his number, James tests what else the job reads by posting one true thing nobody has heard, the hand in the mud, on the forum; the next night he has a second row with a verb he has not seen in the other 112: recalled (forum). James does: sends a known input and watches the output, as he would at work. Cost: strangers and a bank job know about the hand before Ana does, and he has to say so in Twenty minutes. The organization's answer is already planned: his forum account is edited "with bloodlines." That edit now has a cause he chose, and the reader watches an edit remove a leak. "James has hands" (The long table, again) gets a paper origin. Already on the page? Partly: v7 The payload has the reason column and no recall verb; the forum edit is in the plan. Already proposed? No. REVIEW 01 2.2 asks for two rows, for a different reason. Depends on the lurker-or-poster conflict in ADDENDUM 05 d.

items.title: 2. The math (a sentence, said to Els)
items.html: Change: decide PLACEHOLDER #5 as a leak: a dull household sentence the professor said at home and never wrote. James does: when Els calls, he goes through the forty-odd books and the thin book for his own line, the control case run on himself, finds nothing, and tells her "I don't know where I got it." Cost: that is the worst answer for a woman tired of polite men, and she hands over the folder to someone she has reason to fear. The folder then answers him in print: a correct reader is agreed with and reclassified. Already on the page? Partly: the slot is in v8.2; the line is undecided. Already proposed? No. This is break 1. If you want the key without the leak, let him have read it in a margin; then it is D and nothing more.

items.title: 3. The sheets → The night before (a memory, in Anneke's hands)
items.html: Change: Anneke's sheet shows what "per flagged person" buys: one week of the reason column with the employee numbers removed, including the recall rows. James does: strips the numbers himself, which protects 113 people and means he cannot prove the page is real. Cost: at six in the morning she tells him which row is hers. The head of risk has been approving a line that went up by one because of something she once said aloud. Her refusal to sign on Monday is then hers, as Tagomi's is (ch. 14). It also gives REVIEW 01 2.1 a reason she was not turned in December: nothing on that table was about her. Already on the page? Partly: v7 The sheets has the thirty approvals and her seat; "flagged" is not shown. Already proposed? No.

items.title: 4. The final conversation (an object with no paper)
items.html: Change: ADDENDUM 05 has Aylin bring the item James asked for and leaves "what the item is" open. Make it the pin: an invented, plain thing whose catalogue card has a shelfmark and every other field blank. The old man tells him what it is. James does: does not try to make it speak; he asks Aylin to write the card truthfully (description, "source unknown," seen by, date) so the next person can request it. Cost: Aylin's hand is on a card that has been kept empty since 1931; and James gives up the one thing he could have carried out. Already on the page? No; v8 The final conversation has nothing on the table, which is REVIEW 01 5.2. Already proposed? The ask is (ADDENDUM 05, from Libra and Rose); the item is new. Holds only if the narration never says where the thing is from (break 2).

items.title: 5. Epilogue (a memory, in Ana's hands)
items.html: Change: restore the v6 Coda beat that v8 dropped: Ana, half asleep, says his hands were cracked at the knuckles and that she knew them. James does: says nothing to her and enters it in the thin book in a third hand, in the professor's format, with no "before" and no "after." Cost: the book began with a small lie to Ana and ends with something kept from her; and he holds the only two-copy check of a leak in the book under a deal that lets him claim nothing. Already on the page? Yes in v6 Coda (without the entry); no in v8 Epilogue. Already proposed? No.

items.title: 6. Enjoy it while it lasts (no leak; the Colt call)
items.html: Change: Kalder's tip works in eleven minutes, as the caller's tip about the gun was true. James then checks the tipper. James does: rings the switchboard number under Julian K.'s signature, gives his own name, and asks to be put through. Cost: one more asked row, and on the next round Julian knows he rang. Leave the answer as two facts that do not resolve. This turns one "filed" into an act (REVIEW 01 2.5). Already on the page? Partly: the tip and the reply are in v8.2. Already proposed? No; ADDENDUM 05's row for this chapter was dropped by REVIEW 02.

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• The open ending. A proof nobody accepts, with no thread depending on it. Keep the refusal; keep your vote.
  • The oracle as a steering device. A text that tells characters what to do and that the reader cannot check. James checks things.
  • Real people in an invented history, and a fragment that works as a vision on demand. The first breaks your rule. The second fails inside the novel itself until Tagomi stops trying.

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
1. "the carrier Syokaku is at the bottom of the Philippine Sea. It was sunk by an American submarine in 1945." (ch. 4): one phone call makes a true tip come from a false man.
  2. "The paper proves its worth, not the object itself!" (ch. 5): the rule of provenance, said by the man who profits from it.
  3. "Amazing, the power of fiction, even cheap popular fiction, to evoke." (ch. 8): the fragment's effect, in its enemy's mouth, with the discredit built in.
  4. "Bit of knowledge like that goes a long way." (ch. 9): one fact about a fake changes a man's relation to everything he owns.
  5. "To have no historicity, and also no artistic, esthetic worth, and yet to partake of some ethereal value—that is a marvel." (ch. 11): value stated by a person, with no paper behind it.
  6. "That book will help him, for it provides an external frame of reference." (ch. 12): the only stated use for a leak: somewhere to stand.
  7. "I am a mask, concealing the real. Behind me, hidden, actuality goes on, safe from prying eyes." (ch. 14): a character works out he was the front.
  8. "Germany and Japan lost the war." (ch. 15): the whole payoff as an angry question, and refused.

notes.title: section 01 (chapters 1–6)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 1–6 (about 31,500 words), read in full, 15 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 01; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 1–2, first half of 4) Childan wants a gift for Tagomi's client and the Kasouras' money; Frink wants his job back and a decision from the oracle; Tagomi wants to know what Baynes really is Oracle readings that give no clean answer (Frink's Peace with a doom line, ch. 4); a coded cable that makes Tagomi suspect Baynes; an offer from McCarthy to start a jewelry shop Frink's pride and his place; Tagomi's confidence in his own reading of people Each man has already staked something on a reading he cannot check (Frink goes ahead on half an answer, ch. 4) Frink agrees to the shop; Childan gets the sale he cannot miss
2 (ch. 4 second half to ch. 5) Childan wants the Admiral's fifteen-thousand-dollar order A caller who spots a fake Colt in his own shop, a lab that confirms it, and a newspaper desk that says the Admiral's carrier sank in 1945 His main stock may be fake; he may be ruined; the stranger's motive stays unknown The gun is a fake and the buyer is an impostor, and both facts are true; he cannot let it lie, so he goes to Ray Calvin (ch. 4) Calvin calls Wyndam-Matson that night; W-M wrongly blames Frink and McCarthy and pays them two thousand dollars (ch. 5–6)
3 (ch. 5–6) Juliana wants company; Tagomi wants a working day A banned novel in a truck driver's hands; Bormann's death Juliana's unease about Joe; Tagomi's collapse at the lecture Bormann's death breaks every plan, and Baynes drops the molds to wait for Yatabe (ch. 6) Everyone now waits on one old man

Why it grips

  • Four threads, each stopped on a question. Childan does not know why the buyer lied; W-M thinks Frink did something he did not do; Tagomi thinks Baynes is a spy but not for whom; Juliana senses something wrong in Joe (ch. 6).
  • Dramatic irony runs on a misreading. The strongest chain is ch. 4 to 5. Childan's catastrophe is a stranger's lie. W-M, hearing about it, makes the wrong inference about who is blackmailing him, and the money flows to Frink and McCarthy by accident. Frink's oracle said the money would not come, and it did.
  • The most efficient scene is the Syokaku phone call (ch. 4). One call to a newspaper reference desk turns a fifteen-thousand-dollar sale into an unexplained impostor in three lines. The facts do not resolve.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The secret machinery (Baynes's cover, Yatabe's trip, the cipher) is only a pressure in the background: it makes Tagomi waste a morning and makes Baynes stop talking about the molds (ch. 6). The thing that actually shoves people is the forgery trade, a secret everyone knows and no one says. It makes Childan nearly end his life (ch. 4), makes W-M pay two thousand dollars he need not pay (ch. 5), and starts Edfrank (ch. 6). The conspiracy here is a market that survives because nobody tests it ("everyone was happy", ch. 4). Closer to SDF's funded nonsense than to its nightly count.

How the lore gets in

  • Childan's pedecab ride (ch. 2), about 1,100 words, inner monologue. Africa, the Mediterranean project and the Slavs, as his self-justifying chatter. It does not stall, because he has a meeting in two minutes.
  • Frank's morning (ch. 1) and Juliana's evening (ch. 3, 6). Backstory as dread, small talk and a radio broadcast.
  • The Foreign Office lecture (ch. 6), about 900 words. Five portraits of the Nazi contenders, cut by Tagomi's collapse and followed by a phone call that summarises the rest. The one real lecture, broken by a body reaction.

Mechanism notes

How each leak is delivered, in this section:

  1. The Grasshopper Lies Heavy, a book within the book. It reaches the reader twice, each time in the hands of someone who does not own it for the reason the reader expects. First as an item on W-M's bookshelf, taken down by a secretary, Rita, who tells him to read it, and whom he dismisses (ch. 5). She retells the plot in a car for about 900 words, with Churchill, Rommel, Stalingrad, Tugwell and no Pearl Harbor, and W-M argues with each point. Then it appears as Joe's thumbed, greasy copy, read to Juliana in her apartment (ch. 6), with one quoted passage of an empire that never fell. Joe is enraged by its version of Italy. What each character does because of it: Rita leaves W-M in disgust; Joe is shown to be tense and defensive; Juliana picks up the author's name and the address "The High Castle" (ch. 6) and says he is brave. Cost: the book is forbidden to everyone on the East Coast, and Juliana fears Joe could be shot for owning it. Pushes or colors? Weakly pushes: it gives Juliana a name to find and a reason for tension with Joe.

  2. Historicity (objects with or without it). W-M's two Zippo lighters, one of which was in Roosevelt's pocket, and the Smithsonian certificate (ch. 5). The delivery is a demonstration on a coffee table by a man who wants to prove it is a swindle, and the scene turns when the young woman asks to see the paper. The object that carries history is indistinguishable from the one that does not, and only the document separates them. Cost: the evening ends, because the girl is saddened (ch. 5). The lighters only color; the Colt forgery (ch. 4) pushes hard, since the whole chain starts from whether Childan believes the stranger.

  3. The oracle. Frink in ch. 1 (Hexagrams 15 and 44), ch. 4 (11 changing to 26, with a doom line), ch. 6 (47, line nine in the fifth place); Tagomi in ch. 2 and 6. Delivered as a book in the hands of the one who casts, with the text quoted line by line, then interpreted at length. What the character does: Frink takes McCarthy's offer after reading a doom line as a general warning and the judgment as personal (ch. 4); Tagomi reads a Hexagram 46 comment on a strong, brusque man as confirming his doubt about Baynes (ch. 2). Cost: Frink spends half an hour on one line (ch. 6) and still reads it wrong when the check arrives. It colors choices rather than forcing them. The point that matters: the oracle never tells anyone anything they could not reach by judgment, and the reader cannot check it.

  4. A glimpse of another world. None as an object in this section. Tagomi's attack at the embassy (ch. 6) is the nearest, but it is a collapse into dread, with no vision.

A (gate). Childan's ch. 4 gate is internal: he must find out whether the gun is real before he can decide whether to ruin himself or Calvin. He passes it, learns the answer, and it makes things worse.

B (canary). The Syokaku stranger (ch. 4) acts like an inverted canary: he plants a false story (a ship sunk in 1945) and watches how Childan responds. Whether he was a rival, a trap or a prank is never settled here, which is the useful part.

C (front). The forgery trade hides inside W-M's iron foundry (ch. 4).

Fifth: a clue that is both right and a lie. The caller is right about the gun and wrong about everything else. For SDF: let a source be accurate and fraudulent at the same time.

Quotes

  • "the carrier Syokaku is at the bottom of the Philippine Sea. It was sunk by an American submarine in 1945." (ch. 4): the stranger's identity collapses in one phone call.
  • "The paper proves its worth, not the object itself!" (ch. 5): the historicity argument, said by the man who profits from it.
  • "There is evil! It’s actual like cement." (ch. 6): a lecture is cut by a body's reaction.
  • "The Grasshopper was not merely classified; it was forbidden, and to everyone." (ch. 6): the cost of owning the book.

Flags

  • Real people appear in an alternate history as perpetrators (Goring, Goebbels, Heydrich, Rommel, Speer, Bormann and others, ch. 5–6). SDF must not do this; keep to invented people.
  • The Grasshopper rewrites real history inside the fiction (Churchill, Roosevelt, Stalingrad, ch. 5). That is a novel inside a novel, not an invented edit of a real book; SDF's rule still forbids an invented edit on a real book.

notes.title: section 02 (chapters 7–12)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 7–12 (about 29,700 words), read in full, 15 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 02; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 7–8, 11) Childan; Reiss Childan: be accepted by the Kasouras, then rescue his business. Reiss: avoid being blamed by Berlin or the SD Childan: the Kasouras are reading the banned novel. A Kempeitai man gets him to sign a statement against "Frank Frink". The Edfrank pin is judged to have "wu" and then turned into a charms deal. Reiss: the book moves him, and he nearly orders a killing Childan: his pride, and (ch. 11) a duty he cannot hand back. Reiss: he burns his own note, afraid of the people above him Childan is now the "sole agent" of an object he cannot sell or throw away (ch. 11). Reiss wants the author dead and fears the order Childan faces the importer. The SD hunt for Wegener moves ahead anyway
2 (ch. 9, 12b) Frink and Ed Sell the first batch, then stay in business Consignment only, five stores with nothing sold, and then a "bunco" arrest on Childan's complaint His half of the money. In ch. 12 he is held for the German consul as a Jew The police have the name Fink on file. He cannot argue his way out because the file already says what he is He is handed over as a prisoner
3 (ch. 10, 12a) Baynes and Tagomi Get Yatabe to hear the Dandelion warning Yatabe is really General Tedeki. Dandelion is a nuclear first strike on Japan. The SD come for Baynes; Tagomi shoots two of them with a collector's Colt Tagomi's calm, and two lives. Baynes has already exposed himself by contacting the agent in the department store Goebbels now backs Dandelion, so the faction that opposed it has to be persuaded again A siege at the Trade Mission, and Tagomi's turn to the oracle

Why it grips

  • Several clocks run together and share one fear. The SD are one phone call behind Baynes (ch. 11); Frink's money is leaking out; Joe's talk makes Juliana more uneasy each mile. Chapter 11 ends the Reiss scene on a joke: the second phone call is a teacher asking for scenic posters.
  • Dramatic irony does the work. The reader knows Frank Frink and the Jew in the Kempeitai photo are one man (ch. 7). Childan signs a paper that leaves him pleased about "law and order", and Dick lets him think it all through.
  • Each important scene is a trade of face. In the Kasoura dinner (ch. 7) and the office scene (ch. 11), each man offers something and the other decides what it means. Childan reads Paul's praise of the pin as a cold insult, and the reader cannot be sure whether Childan or Paul understood it right.
  • Violence is quick and comic first. The Colt scene (ch. 12) turns from a siege of phone calls (including Tagomi's stage-rage at the SD) into a jaw shot away in two sentences, followed by Tagomi saying "Sickening".

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The conspiracy is in the foreground and it drives events. Dandelion (the plan to destroy Japan) is told to Tedeki in about 800 words (ch. 12). It gives the five-way scene its reason: the SD must catch Baynes before the message reaches Tokyo. Goebbels' call to Reiss (ch. 11) is the proof that the SD can use the Chancery's name, and the attempted snatch follows from it. The conspiracy also fills the background in smaller ways: Reiss's habit of covering himself with timestamped replies (ch. 8), and Kempeitai's paper that "ends your involvement" (ch. 7), which is how the state gets signed statements from ordinary people. It costs the people on the edge: Frink is arrested for something real (the Navy-officer pose) that the state then upgrades into something larger.

How the lore gets in

  • The Grasshopper, read aloud by Reiss and then by Juliana (ch. 8, 10). Excerpts of a page or two each, set in the middle of scenes where someone else interrupts: Pferdehuf cuts in again and again in ch. 8, Joe interrupts Juliana in ch. 10. The reading stalls on purpose and the interruption relieves it.
  • Joe's summary of the book's plot (ch. 10, about 700 words). This is a debate inside a moving car, and Joe's reaction to the book (he is angry at the praise for the New Deal) shows his character more than it shows the book. The story keeps moving because a man is driving.
  • Dandelion (ch. 12, about 800 words). A conversation between three men who each have something to hide. The lecture is given as a negotiation: Tedeki fills in the missing parts ("The date, sir") so the reader hears the plan as a test of the speaker.
  • Paul on wu (ch. 11, about 700 words). A monologue, but the listener is wrecked by it, so the scene is about Childan's reaction.

Mechanism notes

How each leak of another world is delivered in this section:

  • Leak 1: the novel (ch. 7, 8, 10). In Childan's hands it is an object he picks up as small talk, and his reading changes nothing; he decides to buy it as "patriotic duty". In Reiss's hands it is contraband in a briefcase; he reads it in a locked office, resents its grandeur, and almost writes a murder order (ch. 8). In Juliana's hands it is a book in a car; she asks to hear the plot and Joe gives away the ending. Cost: Reiss's anger, and Childan's shame in front of the Kasouras. It pushes the plot twice (Reiss's note to Skorzeny, burned; Joe's plan to visit the author, ch. 10) and colors it elsewhere.
  • Leak 2: the pin and its "historicity" (ch. 9, 11). The piece is made by two men who are not artists. Childan sees it as a hedge ("no historicity either real or imagined"). Paul says it has wu. Cost: Childan's obligation. It pushes: Childan must now deal with the importer, and Frink and Ed's venture changes.
  • Leak 3: the oracle (ch. 9, 12). Tagomi gets "Shock" at 7 a.m. (ch. 10) and the telephone rings at once with Yatabe's arrival. Frink avoids asking (ch. 9) and later says he needs no oracle to know defeat (ch. 12). The oracle is a coloring device that nudges Tagomi to act, but it never tells him anything he did not already half know.
  • Leak 4: "an external frame of reference" (ch. 12, Tedeki). Tedeki says the book will help Tagomi recover. That is the section's only direct claim that a leaked fragment of another world has a use: it gives a man something to stand on after an act with no meaning.
  • A gate / lock-and-key. Dandelion needs Baynes to pass his information on to the Japanese, and the SD must stop him. Baynes uses a department-store clerk and a code phrase, a named clerk ("Larry") (ch. 10), and the Japanese agent answers within six minutes. This is a lock-and-key door that opens by recognition, not force.
  • Front. The "Swedish industrialist" cover is a front, but Tedeki says it exists "to require the formalities in case of exposure". A cover story exists to make the other side prove its case in law.
  • No canary here. Nothing is planted to see who believes it. Joe steering Juliana toward visiting the author (ch. 10) is the nearest thing, and it is his own aim, not a test.

Quotes

  • "Amazing, the power of fiction, even cheap popular fiction, to evoke." (ch. 8): Reiss's reaction to a leaked world, in the mouth of its enemy.
  • "To have no historicity, and also no artistic, esthetic worth, and yet to partake of some ethereal value—that is a marvel." (ch. 11): the section's description of an object with value but no history.
  • "That book will help him, for it provides an external frame of reference." (ch. 12): the book as a tool for a character in trouble.
  • "Bit of knowledge like that goes a long way." (ch. 9): knowing a thing is fake changes a man's whole relation to his stock.

Flags

  • Slurs and antisemitism appear in the characters' heads and mouths (ch. 7, 8, 12). They are the characters' views and Dick treats them as such, but SDF must not copy the voice.
  • Real people named in the fiction as complicit in alternate-history crimes (Goebbels, Heydrich, Bormann, Skorzeny, Ohlendorf). SDF must not do this with real people.
  • The Grasshopper is an invented book with invented events about real history. SDF's rule bans an invented edit on a real book; this novel does something else (a whole invented book), so nothing here transfers directly.
  • Outside knowledge was not used.

notes.title: section 03 (chapters 13–15, the end)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 13–15 (about 18,400 words, including the acknowledgments), read in full, 15 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 03; no edition data in the file. I have not read chapters 1–12, so earlier setup is not described.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 13) Juliana A good time in Denver, then not to go to Abendsen's at all Joe has dyed his hair, tells her to wear the blue dress, and has a radio hidden in a pen; she works out he is a German assassin. She cuts his neck and flees Her fear, her own panic and a spell of confusion; she leaves a man bleeding and does not report it The oracle (hexagrams 42 to 43) tells her to warn Abendsen "at the court of the king", whatever it costs Greeley by night, a phone call to Mrs. Abendsen, then Cheyenne
2 (ch. 14–15, Tagomi, Frank, Wegener) Tagomi wants a way back to a life that has meaning; Frank wants his old bench; Wegener wants to get home alive Tagomi gets a silver piece of jewelry, stares at it and is thrown into a different San Francisco; back in his own, the German consul comes, he signs Frank's release, and his heart gives out His career, his health, his calm The consul's form hands him a choice; the other San Francisco gives him no peace Frank walks free by luck. Wegener lands in Berlin, in SS custody
3 (ch. 15) Juliana Truth from Abendsen: did the oracle write the book? A party in a plain house. He answers "no" about the oracle at first, then admits it chose everything. Her own throw gives Inner Truth Abendsen's goodwill; the room cools She cannot go home not knowing; he cannot say it in full She leaves, alive and unexplained, toward Frank

Why it grips

  • A comic sequence turns into a thriller in one line. Chapter 13 opens with a shopping trip told lightly, but every purchase is a detail Joe handles badly (he pays in notes, forgets nightgowns, will not have the suit altered). The reader waits for the point where she sees it. The turn arrives as a threat said in the same flat voice he used for shirts.
  • Reader and hero find the answer by the same clue. Juliana works out Joe is a German assassin from small slips: he knew a new shirt needed ironing, and the hotel had valet service. This is a fairer reveal than any file or confession.
  • Two scenes show the mind failing. Juliana's blade work and her scrambled words in 13, and Tagomi's attempt to force a charm to speak in 14, are both told close to the character's thoughts, so the reader loses footing with them. The Tagomi scene is the hinge: he shakes it, curses it, tastes it, then gets what he wanted when he has stopped asking.
  • Parallel endings. Four people end on a small physical act (a buffing wheel, a taxi, a blackshirt's lap, a hand reaching for fresh ice). Nothing is solved; each gets only a next step.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The German plot (Operation Dandelion, the factions around Goebbels and Heydrich) is not delivered by revelation in these chapters; it is spent. It shapes what each person does and then lets them go. Joe is an SD man sent to kill Abendsen, and Juliana ends the threat by instinct, then fails to tell anyone. Tagomi has already shot two men; here he turns down the German request to take Frank and signs his release, which is the one act in the section where a document changes a life. Wegener lands among men who may be taking him to safety or to a cell, and he reasons that it is a choice at each step. The hidden order is thus a pressure on four lives rather than a puzzle for any of them to solve. The mystery that matters (who wrote the book) is carried by Juliana and Abendsen alone.

How the lore gets in

  • The shopping trip and the hotel scene (ch. 13), about 4,000 words, a long scene whose dread is carried by detail. Lore is nil; the story moves because she confronts him, and the reveal is a conversation under threat.
  • The oracle readings (ch. 13), about 700 words, set out as hexagram text in her hands. The reading both tells her what to do and reminds the reader that this book's world is steered by a text.
  • Tagomi and the silver piece (ch. 14), about 2,500 words, one long interior scene. It sits between two action scenes and does not stall because he is trying something with his hands.
  • The ending conversation (ch. 15), about 2,400 words, a scene where Abendsen explains his method. It is the nearest thing to a lecture and is made dramatic by the room going silent and by a coin toss done in public.

Mechanism notes

Each leak, and how it arrives

  1. The oracle (ch. 13 and 15). In Juliana's own hands, in two black volumes she carries; she throws coins. It costs her time, and each time it tells her to take a risk. In 13 it pushes the plot: it sends her to Cheyenne at once. In 15 she asks it a question and the answer, Inner Truth, is her proof, though Abendsen refuses to accept it.
  2. The silver piece of jewelry (ch. 14). Sold by Childan as "the new" and pressed on Tagomi, who holds it in a park bench and, after he has given up, is dropped into a world with a freeway, cars, and white men who call him by a slur. The cost is fear and a stretch of lost time; the piece was left on the grass, and the other San Francisco lasts a few minutes. It pushes his decision rather than the plot: he comes back to sign the release for Frank. Nobody else sees it, and a policeman reads him as someone with a puzzle.
  3. The book within the book (ch. 15). Juliana buys a copy in a Denver hotel bookshop and finishes it in a Cheyenne motel, deciding nobody else really understands it. It sends her to the house, but she gets there by the oracle. It costs Abendsen his peace. It does not move the German plot at all.
  4. Historicity (ch. 14). Tagomi decides the gun carries a bad past and tries to trade it, and Childan will not take it. The idea is used as a motive: Tagomi wants rid of the gun, is refused, and the same weapon saves him from nothing. It only colors the plot.

Ending: leaves it open. Abendsen says the oracle did the choosing and then refuses to say whether it knows the world is true. Juliana's hexagram answers yes, and he answers "I'm not sure of anything." The reader is left with a proof that the character will not take. Tagomi's glimpse is likewise unexplained; his explanation is that his own senses slipped, and the boys' count of pedecabs seems to settle it. This keeps the dread but loses a payoff: nothing in the German plot depends on it.

For SDF

  • B (canary), loosely. Abendsen's book is an invented "other world" that a reader takes as true; what matters is who believes it. Juliana does, Abendsen will not say, and the reader watches a person choose.
  • D (lock and key). Juliana opens Abendsen's door with one thing: the hexagram that she and he both know without the chart. A shared private fact is what makes him stop deflecting.
  • Fifth: the object that works only when you stop pushing. Tagomi's attempt shows that a leak delivered on demand fails; it arrives after he lets go. Useful if James tries to force a document to give up its secret.

Quotes

  • "Germany and Japan lost the war." (ch. 15): the whole payoff stated as an angry question, and refused.
  • "was sound asleep all through the writing of the book. Sound asleep in the corner of the office." (ch. 15): the author withholds credit for the source and the reader gets a joke instead of an answer.
  • "I am a mask, concealing the real. Behind me, hidden, actuality goes on, safe from prying eyes." (ch. 14): a character who works out he was a front.
  • "Thank you for what you did in Denver" (ch. 15): the act is acknowledged in one polite line, with no discussion.

Flags

  • Real people named in the alternate history: Goebbels, Heydrich, Bormann, Dietrich appear as rulers in this invented Nazi-world. SDF must not do this.
  • Joe is called a "wop" and Tagomi is called "Tojo"; the book uses slurs in character.
  • No invented edits on real books.

books.qa:
Answers point to the section notes in this folder (01-chapters-1-to-6.md, 02-chapters-7-to-12.md, 03-chapters-13-to-15.md) and, where relevant, to a v8.2 chapter by title. The map is 00-map.md. Everything about SDF here is a PROPOSAL; Santi's decisions are PLACEHOLDER.

The leak, in the novel

1. What counts as a leak in this book? Five things: a banned novel in which the Allies won, a forged Colt, a plain pin with no past, the oracle, and a few minutes Tagomi spends in a different San Francisco. The first three are objects, the fourth is a text consulted by hand, and the fifth is an experience nobody else witnesses. See map section 4 and the "Mechanism notes" in all three section notes.

2. Which leaks move the plot and which only color it? The Colt moves it hardest (ch. 4–6, 01-chapters-1-to-6.md). The pin moves Childan and later Tagomi (ch. 11, 14). The banned novel moves it twice: the consul's burned order (ch. 8) and the trip to the author (ch. 10, 13; 02-chapters-7-to-12.md). The oracle moves it once, in ch. 13 (03-chapters-13-to-15.md). Everything else colors.

3. What separates a leak that pushes from one that colors? Whether it changes what someone signs, pays, drives to or burns. Tagomi's glimpse tells him nothing useful, but he signs a release because of it. The oracle tells Frink a lot and changes little. Map section 4, "The rule under all five."

4. How is the banned novel delivered without stopping the story? It is retold in cars by people who disagree with it (ch. 5, about 900 words; ch. 10, about 700 words) and read in short excerpts that someone interrupts (ch. 8, ch. 10). Each scene is about the reader's reaction. The straight excerpts do stall, on purpose (02-chapters-7-to-12.md, "How the lore gets in").

5. What does the forged Colt teach that the mystical leaks don't? That a fact can be true while its source is a fraud, and that acting on it can still ruin the wrong person. The caller is right about the gun and lying about himself; the forger then pays two innocent men (01-chapters-1-to-6.md, movement 2 and "Why it grips"). In SDF, Kalder's tip in Enjoy it while it lasts is already this: a true tip from a false friend. Map proposal 6.

6. What is "historicity" and why does it matter to SDF? The idea that an object's history lives in its paperwork. The forger shows two identical lighters and says only the certificate separates them (ch. 5, 01-chapters-1-to-6.md). SDF's organization works the same way: it controls catalogue cards, "withdrawn for conservation," the Outcome column in the visitor book. A thing with no paper is the one thing it cannot refile. Map section 4, "Paper against object."

7. How does Tagomi's glimpse arrive? After he stops trying. He shakes the piece, curses it, tastes it, and gets nothing; the other city comes when he has given up (ch. 14, 03-chapters-13-to-15.md). It lasts minutes, costs him fear and lost time, and nobody else sees it. SDF has the same rule in The night he stops being afraid (the fourth night).

8. Who discredits the leaks? The people who receive them. Tagomi decides his senses slipped. The consul calls the novel cheap popular fiction while it is working on him (ch. 8). The author will not stand behind his book (ch. 15). The state bans the novel in one zone, but nobody in the book has to argue against it. SDF's James does the same at the funeral: "filed it under lack of sleep."

9. Does the oracle ever tell anyone something they could not have reached alone? No, according to 01-chapters-1-to-6.md, and the reader has no means to check a reading. Frink's reading says the money will not come and it does. This is why the map puts the oracle under "Do not take": James's method is checking.

10. Why does the ending stay open? Juliana's throw says the book is true and the author answers that he is not sure of anything (ch. 15). The proof is given and refused. 03-chapters-13-to-15.md says this keeps the dread and loses a payoff, because nothing in the German plot depends on it. ADDENDUM 05 already lists open endings under "does not work."

11. What is the one direct claim that a leak is useful? The general says the banned novel will help Tagomi recover because it gives an outside frame of reference (ch. 12, 02-chapters-7-to-12.md). That is the only time a character states what a fragment of another world is for.

12. What happens when the enemy reads the leak? The consul is moved, resents it, writes an order to have the author killed, and burns the order out of fear of his superiors (ch. 8, 02-chapters-7-to-12.md). For SDF this is a possible beat for Bram, who counts an experience he has never had (A room with a long table). The map names it and does not propose it, because James is not in that room.

The engine

13. Why can no character stop? Each has acted on something uncheckable before the chapter starts: Frink on half an oracle answer, Childan on a stranger's tip, the forger on a guess about who is blackmailing him. See the engine table in the map and the "Movements" tables in each note.

14. What is the most efficient scene? The phone call to the newspaper desk in ch. 4. Three lines turn a large sale into an impostor nobody can explain (01-chapters-1-to-6.md). The facts do not resolve, and Childan has to act anyway.

15. How does the conspiracy proper (the first-strike plan) move things? It is background pressure in chapters 1–6, the driver of chapters 7–12 (the SD must reach Baynes before his message reaches Tokyo), and in 13–15 it is spent: it shapes each life and lets it go (01, 02, 03, "How the conspiracy moves the story here"). The mystery that carries the ending is a different one: who wrote the book.

16. How does the reader learn the assassin's identity? By the same small slips the heroine sees: he knew a new shirt needed ironing, the hotel had valet service, he dyed his hair (ch. 13, 03-chapters-13-to-15.md). The note calls this fairer than any file or confession. It matches the brief's rule that James gets there by dumb small questions.

17. How does a document change a life in this book? Twice. Childan signs a police statement that "ends your involvement" and puts Frink on file (ch. 7, 02-chapters-7-to-12.md). Tagomi signs Frink's release when asked to hand him over (ch. 14, 03-chapters-13-to-15.md). Both men sign without knowing who Frink is to them. Compare Anneke's signature in Monday.

18. Is there a gate (A)? A small one. Childan has to know whether the gun is real before he can decide whom to ruin; the lab answers, and the answer makes things worse (ch. 4, 01-chapters-1-to-6.md). This supports ADDENDUM 05's "cost after the gate."

19. Is there a canary (B)? Only inverted: the caller plants a false story about himself and watches (ch. 4). 02-chapters-7-to-12.md says there is none in chapters 7–12. The map does not build on it.

20. Is there a front (C) and a key (D)? Fronts: the forgery business inside a foundry (01), and a cover identity whose stated purpose is to make the other side go through formalities (ch. 12, 02). Keys: a clerk's name that reaches a contact in six minutes (ch. 10, 02), and the hexagram Juliana and the author both know without the chart (ch. 15, 03). The second is the model for PLACEHOLDER #5 in The math.

The leak, tested against SDF

21. What in SDF already reads as a leak? The flash in The funeral (cold mud, a cracked hand). The hand seen "all my life" and the lives cut off "by a man with a list" in v6 The floor. The job name rcl-agg, the invoice's "recall index," and "recall" in Utrecht, 1993. Henk Boersma's "strange things about his father" (A pension visit, Zwolle). Ana's dream of cracked hands in v6 Coda, which v8 Epilogue dropped. And the line James says to Els in The math.

22. Would a leak mechanism repair REVIEW 01 finding 1.1? Yes. If given means "received from before" and arose means "you made it up," the edit is a discredit applied to a sentence. History, instruction and "the passing" become the same thing. Map section 5.

23. Would it repair 1.2 (the hidden thing is on sale)? Mostly. Leaks happen in people and cannot be deleted, only refiled, which fits the review's own fix (make it exotic or funny). The forty-one then are the dry books where an author reported a leak plainly.

24. Would it repair 1.3 (the motive)? Only with one more decision. A leak gives the organization a reason to care if what people recall includes the organization, "a man with a list" in v6 The floor. Then every leak is testimony against it. That decision is Santi's, PLACEHOLDER, and Kalder still needs a line.

25. Where does the leak idea break a rule? Five places, listed in map section 5: a third leak to James makes him a seer; an object from before a reset breaks the real-world rule and the book that claims nothing; "all forty-one are one edit" does not fit entries 3, 7 and 17 of The List; the count registers only what is said (v7 The payload); and a leak cannot go on a sheet as a claim.

26. Can James have more leaks than the funeral and the floor? The map says no. The brief forbids him out-deducing the book, and insights are meant to happen to him slowly. Further leaks should land in Els, Anneke, Ana or the widow and reach him as their words. Proposal 2 is flagged as the exception and the risk.

27. Can a physical object leak from an earlier world? Not as a confirmed thing. Urfa, 1994 is careful ("the book never says he found it"), and REVIEW 01 1.4 found the reset already cut from the plan. Proposal 4 puts an invented plain object on the table in The final conversation and requires that only the old man says what it is.

28. How would the organization respond to a leak? As it does now: agree, then reclassify (Els's folder in The math). Under proposal 1 the forum edit in The gorilla mask becomes that response to a leak James sent out on purpose. The 1931 method was to edit books; the present method is to count and refile people. Killing stays rare.

29. How does a leak join the nightly count? v7 The payload lists verbs of asking (posted, wrote, asked, searched, requested, enquired, raised). Proposal 1 adds one verb, recalled, which James produces by posting the hand and reading the next night's file. The opening's "counted the night you asked" stays true.

30. How does a leak join the win? Through paper only. Proposal 3 puts a week of the reason column, numbers removed, on Anneke's sheet in The sheets, so "per flagged person" has content, and she finds her own row. That keeps the sheets as diffs and gives her refusal to sign in Monday a cause of her own. It also answers REVIEW 01 2.1.

31. What is the check for a leak, given James's method is two copies? Two people with the same thing and no route between them. The plan already says "the reports rhyme" (Reading with a pen). Proposal 5 gives the book one such pair, James and Ana, and has him enter it in the thin book and say nothing.

32. Does this map confirm or contradict ADDENDUM 05? It confirms the rule on lore, the cost after the gate, and the verdict on open endings. It adds three mechanisms (paper against object, the wrong payee, the enemy as reader). It contradicts nothing, but it puts a limit on "reveals are objects": in this novel the object alone proves nothing, and a person or a paper has to vouch.

Practical

33. What must not be copied? Real people as perpetrators in an invented history; slurs in the characters' heads; a cover identity used to kill; a statement signed under police pressure; the shooting and the cut neck. See the Flags in all three notes and the map's standing-rule note.

34. Do the section notes disagree anywhere? On small things. 01 says the novel "weakly pushes," 02 counts two pushes, 03 says it does not move the German plot; these fit together but read differently. 02 heads its oracle paragraph "ch. 9, 12" and then cites ch. 10. 03 has Tagomi holding the piece on a bench and also says it was left on the grass. 03 does not say who speaks the "sound asleep" line, and its reader had not read chapters 1–12.

35. What did the map add from memory? One thing, marked: that the silver piece Tagomi holds is Frink's work and neither man learns of the link. The notes give both halves (the Edfrank pin in 02, the signed release in 03) and do not join them.

36. Which proposal should be tried first? Proposal 1 (The payload → The gorilla mask). It is one posted sentence and one new row, it makes an existing plan beat (the forum edit) into a consequence of something James did, and it shows the reader an edit removing a leak without anyone explaining it.

books.author: Eco
books.title: Foucault's Pendulum
books.readfor: B: the canary; the clowns beside the question
books.intro: Coverage: English translation (William Weaver), read in full via seven section notes (01–07 in this folder), 11 Nov 2026. Chapter cites come from those notes. Brief: mechanism B, the canary. How the invented Plan leaks, who believes it first, how heavy lore is carried without stalling, and how the Diabolicals work as the clowns beside the real question. Standing-rule note: Eco names real people, orders and bookshops as plotters (Bacon, Rachkovsky, Hitler, the Golden Dawn, the OTO, the Jesuits), reads codes into real books (Shakespeare, Verne), has a character insert a line into the sonnets (ch. 73), and turns the Holocaust into a map hunt (ch. 100). Our rules forbid all of it. Take the mechanics, never the roll-call.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
Three Milan editors at a vanity press read occult manuscripts by cranks they call the Diabolicals. As a joke they invent "the Plan," a Templar conspiracy that explains everything, built with a computer, bar talk and stolen crank material. Agliè, a believer who consults for the press, takes it seriously. Belbo, the editor who wrote most of it, uses it to get revenge on Agliè and sends him after a map that does not exist. The believers come for him. The book opens with Casaubon hiding in a Paris museum on the night they hang Belbo from the Pendulum, and it ends with him waiting for them to come for him too.

What makes it work: the reader knows from chapter 3 that the joke kills someone, so every funny lecture after that reads as a fuse. And the conspiracy never arrives as information. The heroes make it, and every piece they make gets a reaction from a real person.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:
Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 1–6, frame) To find Belbo, open his files "They found me," a sound like a shot, the password "NO" His doubt: he reasons "just like the Plan" (ch. 5) Belbo is missing; only midnight shows if the Plan is real Hide in the Conservatoire; the files become the flashback
2 (ch. 7–20) Young Casaubon wants facts and an audience Garamond Press; Colonel Ardenti's "Provins message," published as bait Nothing yet; the photocopy stays with them (ch. 19) Ardenti says the last man who knew was killed Next day the colonel is gone
3 (ch. 21–27) To stay out of it A body that vanished, a false "Rakosky," Inspector De Angelis He and Belbo lie to the police; the friendship ends for years (ch. 22) They hold what the police lack; a psychic repeats the private phrases (ch. 24) Brazil, and Agliè
4 (ch. 28–45) Amparo, then a trade The Rosicrucian hoax; Project Hermes pulls in cranks by the hundred Amparo leaves; Camestres threatens (ch. 44) In Brazil he does stop; only the frame pulls (ch. 29, 34). In Milan it is his living He phones Agliè
5 (ch. 46–63) A sharp reader for the slush pile Agliè hired; Salon the informer; De Angelis tests him with "Tres" (ch. 53) Belbo loses Lorenza (ch. 50); Casaubon lies to a policeman Agliè is in the author file (ch. 54); Lia is pregnant (ch. 63) The game
6 (ch. 64–76) Material for a book, and a joke Tomar fits (ch. 67); a fake sect planted in a real list; Agliè asks "Which manuscript?" (ch. 76) They stop laughing; they have lied to a believer about a source Every answer leaves a named hole, with whisky bet on it (ch. 68) Find the Templars' secret
7 (ch. 77–97) Be with Lia; finish the parody Every crank source fits He misses the birth (ch. 80); "addicted," "converted" (ch. 87) The Plan always has an empty slot, and it asks to be filled Hitler and the hollow earth
8 (ch. 98–107) Belbo wants a win over Agliè Diotallevi falls ill (ch. 100); Lia proves the source is a delivery list (ch. 106) Guilt; Belbo needs it true A gambler shown the cards (ch. 102); a dead dog and Lorenza leaving tip him (ch. 107) Belbo uses the Plan as a weapon
9 (ch. 108–109) Revenge: send Agliè after a map A suitcase bomb; his train jokes become witness testimony; Garamond is in it Wanted for terrorism; two Libyans detained He cannot prove the Plan false (ch. 109) Paris, 20 June
10 (ch. 110–114) Casaubon wants to know if it is real Belbo confessed and was not believed; the rite stages the editors' Plan He watches two killings and does nothing He has been seen; he is the last man who "knows" (ch. 111) The sewers
11 (ch. 115–120) Someone to tell him he is mad The museum spotless; Diotallevi dead; a key, Belbo's trumpet story He waits, with Lia and the baby in mind Denying the map makes Them want it more (ch. 118) Nothing. He waits

Sources: rows 1–2 01/02, 3 02, 4 03, 5 04, 6–7 05, 7–9 06, 10–11 07.

Read down the fifth column. From step 6 on, the reason he cannot stop is something he made: a lie about a source, a hole in the Plan, a bait already taken. Before that the reasons are borrowed, and in Brazil the engine idles under the frame's dread. SDF's Part Two idles the same way with nothing over it.

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
• Templar history (ch. 13–14), about 8,500 words, two bar nights. A lecture the listeners keep interrupting, the trial set out as numbered "enigmas" that Ardenti will answer wrongly when he walks in two chapters later. (01, 02)
  • The Rosicrucian hoax (ch. 29–30), about 4,500 words. Pillow talk, with Amparo heckling and doing the best reasoning. Never stalls. (03)
  • Agliè's talk (ch. 28 to 76), 700 to 2,500 words a time. A performance with a turn: the pyramid book recited, then demolished with a lottery kiosk; a slip into the first person; the Masonry talk ends on "Which manuscript?" (03–05)
  • The Plan sessions (ch. 64–104). Three voices, one a heckler ("Make beer?"). Each objection forces the next invention, so lore arrives as a solved problem. (05, 06)
  • The rite (ch. 113), about 700 words of titles read while Lorenza stands drugged: joke and countdown at once. (07)

Where it stalls: ch. 84–96, about 12,000 words of Plan history. Eco knows (the narrator calls it a Keystone Kops film, ch. 85), ends each run on a punchline, and lets Diotallevi's yellow skin keep time underneath. It is still the slowest stretch. Where it doesn't: the list of sects (ch. 75), 1,700 words of dead catalogue that pays off within a chapter because the trap is hidden in it. A list stalls only if nothing is hidden in it. (05, 06)

sections.title: 4. The mechanism we came for: the canary
sections.html:
Setup. Before any bait, Eco builds the channels: a consultant in the author file (Agliè, ch. 54), an informer (Salon, ch. 57), a policeman who drops names (De Angelis, ch. 53). The antagonist states the rule from his side: believers are detectors (ch. 33). (03, 04)

Rule. Put one invented thing where a believer will find it. The tell is what he does, not what he says.

The progression:

  1. Ardenti's bait (ch. 20–22). A believer publishes so that whoever knows must show himself. Something bites within hours; the believer pays, and the doubters' lie to the police is their price. (02)
  2. The psychic (ch. 24–25). A private phrase surfaces and its carrier vanishes. Then the result is taken back: her magazines had already printed it. A gate inside the canary: the bait proves something only if nobody else could have printed it. (02)
  3. Project Hermes (ch. 42–45). Invented inquiries in the right channel. Clowns bite first; the first threat comes from a crank, not the order. (03)
  4. The Tres dropped on the hero (ch. 53). De Angelis tests Casaubon with a name; Casaubon lies. The hero is the bird. (04)
  5. The Tres hidden in a list (ch. 75–76). One fake sect in a real chronology, credited to someone else's manuscripts. Agliè does not claim to know it. He asks who mentioned it, asks again, says it does not matter, checks his watch. The tell is the second question and the quick exit. The lie about the source is now a debt. (05)
  6. Belbo's test of Agliè (ch. 108). The Plan passed off as authentic, with actionable hooks: a map "in full view," papers destroyed so the map is only in his head, a trip "around the summer solstice." Within a day the believer acts on the hooks, and Belbo learns what the canary shows from what is done to him. (06)
  7. The denial that proves more (ch. 110, 118). Belbo confesses there is no secret; refusal makes it bigger. (07)

Escalation: the setter moves closer (a crank, the boss, the police, the heroes) and the hook gets more specific (a theory, a phrase, a name, a date and a place). Cost climbs with it, from a lie to the police to two deaths. Payoff: "if you invent a plan and others carry it out, it’s as if the Plan exists" (ch. 118). Who believes first: the inventors (ch. 63, 67–69, 87).

Against the four fixes. B is supported and sharpened: Eco aims it at his heroes, SDF wants it as James's instrument, and what transfers is the anatomy (a unique item, an actionable hook, a readout through a third party, a price). A is added inside B: the psychic (ch. 25) and Lia's source test (ch. 106) are the gates the editors never pass. C is weak (Garamond/Manutius, ch. 38; synarchy as fronts with nothing at the bottom, ch. 53). D is small (the password, ch. 6; Agliè's one peek, ch. 61; the key, ch. 118). A fifth: the frame. The order never stops Belbo talking. It makes his own words and habits the evidence against him (the train, ch. 108; "Why, it sounds like a novel," ch. 109). That is SDF's "discredit, not prevent," working on one man in one day.

sections.title: 5. Transfer to SDF
sections.html: Checked against the v8.2 plan, 01 Manuscript/v6/18 — On land.md and the v7 Part Two drafts. On land, as planned, has the invented-book test (Kalder: "Oh, that one. Yes."), and The dinner cashes it ("the book you said you'd read"). No draft contains it; v6 On land is the older Deventer-slip version.

items.title: 5.1 Give the On land book a hook, and read it back through the Groningen dealer
items.html:
• Chapters: On land; The schedule; The sheets.
  • Change: the invented book carries one checkable detail, and James learns the bait was taken because someone acted on it.
  • James does: he gives the title a printing year and a shelfmark in the depot's format (copied in The drill), says it only to Kalder, and dates it in his notebook. Weeks later the Groningen dealer, who said he would make no more calls, calls James instead: polite people asked whether anyone had come in for that shelfmark. Before believing it James runs the gate (ch. 25): who else heard the title? Not Ana; she was laughing at something else (already in v8.2). So it came from Kalder.
  • Cost: the dealer has now been seen not to telephone. PLACEHOLDER: is Groningen one of the addresses in The other ten? Echo in The sheets: Aylin's visitor book has a "shelfmark requested" column (v7 draft), and the bait is in it.
  • Already on the page? Partly (On land and The dinner, plan only). Eco adds the actionable hook (ch. 108), a readout through someone who chooses to talk, and the gate. Without them the test proves only that Kalder is vain.

items.title: 5.2 Bury one fake among the seven sheets
items.html:
• Chapters: The reading room, continued; The sheets.
  • Change: one of James's findings is invented: a grant to an invented documentary company in a year that fits the pattern.
  • James does: he lays it fifth, credits it to "the published accounts," and watches. The old man waves off six. On the fake he asks one extra question: which year? That is Agliè's second question (ch. 76). By refusing everything except the one he did not recognize, he has confirmed the other six.
  • Cost: Anneke saw him lie about a source. In The sheets she will not act until he walks her through the source of every line, and that delay lets the leak outrun the envelopes (The leak).
  • Already on the page? No. v7 has seven true sheets and a flat refusal. It does already have the unreadable result ("Did it occur to you that nobody came because you'd gone?"), which is ch. 25.
