items.title: 5.3 A second bait in the forum, and a stranger who gets counted
items.html:
• Chapters: The gorilla mask; The vet; The sheets.
  • Change: James answers the edit to his forum account with a different invented title, so a reaction tells him its channel.
  • James does: he posts the title once, as a question. The first to bite is a clown: the forum man from the barbecue claims to have seen it (ch. 19, the believer who thanks you for the addition) and starts asking libraries. James posts that he made it up; the man believes it more (ch. 118).
  • Cost: the stranger is counted for asking. He posts that he got a very polite correction in wording James knows from When a Reader Notices. James owes him a sheet (The sheets, the quiet ones by forum).
  • Already on the page? No. The gorilla mask (v6) has the edited account and eleven readers; nobody plants anything. Gate: this title must differ from 5.1's, or neither can be read.

items.title: 5.4 One negative, and it costs him with Frank
items.html:
• Chapters: The band; Frank, loose.
  • Change: James sees one of his own invented titles in the grant list and builds on it for a weekend. It is a real, unrelated film with a near title.
  • James does: he takes it to Frank as proof. Frank finds the real film in four minutes.
  • Cost: in Frank, loose, "I believe the invoice" now carries a line Frank has earned: you saw your own book in the accounts last month. It lands harder because Frank has watched him be wrong (the inventor believes first, ch. 87; the investigator infected, ch. 115–116).
  • Already on the page? No. In The money, The band and Frank, loose (v7) James is right every time; the SYNTHESIS asked for one costly negative per act.

items.title: 5.5 James as the bird: Pieter drops a word, James lies
items.html:
• Chapters: The drill; The sheets.
  • Change: De Angelis's test (ch. 53), run on James by a helper who thinks it is part of the security test.
  • James does: at desk forty Pieter asks, lightly, whether he has come across the word "recall." James says no. It is on the invoice he has read.
  • Cost: in The sheets Pieter says: you told me at the drill you'd never heard it. James has to own the lie before Pieter reads on.
  • Already on the page? No. In v7 Pieter hovers and "the sentence isn't in the building."

items.title: 5.6 The uncontaminated witness
items.html:
(Gudrun, ch. 118): the widow in Zwolle. Already on the page: yes (The other ten, v7). Eco adds only: in The sheets, show her the photograph without a question.

Rejected: a bait passed off as a genuine document (Belbo's ch. 108 move would make James a fraud toward the people he must later turn); any bait set in a real book; any readout that needs someone's account or mail.

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• The roll-call: real people, orders and bookshops as plotters; the Holocaust as a riff (ch. 73, 100, 113, 115).
  • The 12,000-word stall (ch. 84–96). Eco can afford it because the frame has promised a hanging. SDF's Part Two has no such promise to carry it.
  • The passive ending: a hero who watches the killing and waits. James acts, and wins small.

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
• "I’m casting the bait. We’ll see if anyone bites." (ch. 20): the canary stated by its setter.
  • "The fact that they didn’t answer was taken as proof of their existence." (ch. 30): silence as fuel.
  • "The mystic is useful, because he is conspicuous. He broadcasts himself." (ch. 33): believers as the other side's detectors.
  • "Let’s add a sect that doesn’t exist. Founded recently." (ch. 75): one fake in a real list.
  • "It’s just that I never heard of it before. You really can’t tell me who mentioned it?" (ch. 76): the second question is the tell.
  • "His reticence about the final truth guaranteed the truth of its premises." (ch. 108): how to make bait believable.
  • "The drawing didn’t resemble Belbo, but Belbo resembled the drawing." (ch. 108): the frame.
  • "the more he vowed he didn’t possess it, the more convinced They were that he did possess it" (ch. 118): denial as fuel.

notes.title: section 01 (front matter, chapters 1–13)
notes.html:
Coverage: front matter (contents, epigraphs) and chapters 1–13, Keter, Hokhmah and the start of Binah (about 31,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: William Weaver's English translation, converted text with OCR errors (the title page reads "Foucalt’s"); no publisher data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 1–2) To hide in the Conservatoire before it closes at 5.30 and see what happens at midnight Every exhibit reads to him as a coded message (Lavoisier's mirrors, the glass lion and serpent, the periscope) His doubt. He watches himself slide into "the same game that had driven Jacopo Belbo out of his mind" Belbo is missing, and only midnight will show whether the Plan is real Two hours standing in a periscope, filled by remembering
2 (ch. 3–6) To find Belbo, then to open Belbo's files A phone call ("They found me"), a sound like a shot, two keys, a password prompt A day and a bottle of whiskey; he catches his own reasoning working "just like the Plan" (ch. 5) Belbo said everything is on the disks and that he would call The files, read in Belbo's apartment, become the story told in flashback
3 (ch. 7–13, the past) Young Casaubon wants documented facts for his Templar thesis Belbo, the lunatic typology, Garamond Press, a crank's Templar manuscript He is recruited as the expert, and at Pilade's he tells the Templar story "with feeling" (ch. 13) Belbo trusts "curiosity" and wants the trial next: "Who, what, when, and why" The trial lecture, and the start of the partnership that will build the Plan

Why it grips

  • The ending comes first. By chapter 3 the reader knows the Plan was invented, that Belbo now thinks it is real, and that someone has taken him. Everything from chapter 7 on is a comedy in a bar, read under that phone call. The School of Comparative Irrelevance (ch. 12) and the Templar routine (ch. 13) are funny, and each joke is also evidence of how the disaster was built.
  • Three time layers, each with a clock. The hill "now" (dogs, the moon, "Was that really the end", ch. 2 and 6), the periscope two nights ago, and the Milan years. The periscope makes remembering plausible and puts a deadline (midnight) on the flashback.
  • The password scene (ch. 4–6) is the best-built sequence. It is a lock with a timer of its own (two thousand years by brute force, ch. 4). Casaubon tries the Sefirot, 36, 666, the 720 names of God, the list read backwards, SOPHIA. Every guess is lore used as a tool, and all of it fails. The answer, typed in anger, is "NO" (ch. 6), and the narrator withholds why: "Now I know."
  • The reader is infected first. Chapter 1 is written from inside the delusion ("the Only Fixed Point"); the deflation comes later.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

Here we see only what the Plan has done, never how: it has leaked, been believed, and come for its makers. Belbo, its author, believes it first: Casaubon says Belbo was obsessed "beyond the confines of the game" (ch. 3). Then "They" believe it, and think the inventors hold what the invention describes: "They think I have the map, they tricked me, made me come to Paris" (ch. 3). The invented conspiracy produces an appointment (the Conservatoire, midnight, Saint John's Eve). The believers set a time and place; the inventors must turn up. That turns a game into a plot.

Casaubon takes the blame early, in an aside to Lia (ch. 7): the inventors supplied a depth that others wanted. That is the canary's cost from the other side: the stranger who believes is not the only one counted, because the person who planted the false thing gets counted as well.

The Diabolicals are not on stage yet. Their place is prepared in two ways. First, Belbo's typology (ch. 10): cretins, fools, morons, lunatics, and the lunatic "sooner or later" brings up the Templars. Second, the cranks come in as manuscripts left at a publisher's door (ch. 10, 12): "A lunatic, but with a human face." Casaubon dismisses the crank's logic in one line (the Puss in Boots argument, ch. 12). So the clowns are first a professional joke, a category editors sort, and that joke is what the Plan will later be built from. In chapter 12 Casaubon names the risk himself.

How the lore gets in

  • The Conservatoire as occult text (ch. 1–2), about 6,000 words, a walk through a museum. Carried by a practical task: each car or case is judged first as a hiding place, then read as a symbol. It does not stall, because the clock ("they closed at five-thirty") and the guards keep pressing.
  • Cabala and permutation (ch. 5), about 2,000 words, a remembered office argument with the BASIC program printed in full. It is set inside the password hunt, so the lore marks out the search space and the reader uses it at once. It stalls only for as long as one argument lasts.
  • Credulity versus incredulity (ch. 7), about 1,500 words, an essay. Slow, but it holds the thesis and the guilty aside to Lia.
  • Belbo's files (ch. 3, 8, 11): "Abu", "A bevy of fair women", "Seven Seas Jim". Documents that carry character, not conspiracy; on plot terms they stall, kept alive only because they are the evidence the narrator broke into.
  • Templar history (ch. 13), about 5,000 words, a barroom lecture. It is interrupted by jokes, a petition girl, and Dolores joining the table. The key move is that Belbo and Diotallevi turn the Templar prohibitions into an invented scandal ("From prohibitions you can tell what people normally do"): the method of the Plan, tried as a game. It slows the story, and the narrator admits he was "dreaming aloud". It works as seduction: Dolores is won over, and the reader with her.

Mechanism notes

  • B (canary), seen from the receiving end. Eco shows the canary coming back to bite. The invented Plan does not just catch a believer. It names its inventors as the people who know. For SDF: if James plants an invented title or edit (On land already has the invented book Kalder claims to have read), the cost could be that the plant comes back to him. Someone, or the organisation, now takes James for a man who knows what he made up. The cost is also a door: people come to him.
  • Who believes first. The inventor, not the mark. A risk for James: after enough plants, he is no longer sure which edits are his.
  • Clown beside the question. The publisher's slush pile (ch. 10, 12) is the place where cranks gather and can be sorted. Close to SDF's organisation, which funds the nonsense the real question must be picked out of.
  • D (lock and key). The password opens by understanding the person, not the lore (ch. 6).
  • Fifth: open with the cost. The bill is shown before the game, so every later joke reads as a fuse.

Quotes

  • "The Plan. The Plan is real. I know, don’t say it. They’re after me." (ch. 3): the inventor is the first believer, and the first hunted.
  • "If two things don’t fit, but you believe both of them, thinking that somewhere, hidden, there must be a third thing that connects them" (ch. 7): Eco's definition of credulity, close to SDF's title.
  • "I made Them believe there was a depth, a depth that They, in their weakness, desired." (ch. 7): the cost of the canary falls on the person who planted it.
  • "If the public gets wind of this, people will show up with manuscripts." (ch. 12): an invented scheme draws cranks, shown as a joke.

Flags

  • Belbo's "Seven Seas Jim" file (ch. 11) has an editor fantasising that he rewrote Hamlet ("William S."). It is plainly a comic daydream, but SDF must not borrow it as an invented edit on a real book.
  • In chapter 1, the narrator in his delusion suggests that Lavoisier was "killed to silence what his fraud revealed" and reads the Convention's plan as Bacon's House of Solomon. Real people in a conspiracy reading, framed as illness; SDF should not do this.

notes.title: section 02 (chapters 14–27)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 14–27 (about 31,400 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: English translation, converted text, chunk file 02; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 14–20) Casaubon, a thesis student, wants to show off his Templar learning and help Belbo get rid of a crank author Colonel Ardenti and his decoded "Provins message" (36 invisibles, six seals, a 600-year relay to a Stone), which he says he is publishing as bait Nothing yet. The colonel's photocopy ends up with them; Casaubon still has it "among my papers" (ch. 19) Ardenti says the last man who knew this was killed, and he wants readers to come forward The next day the colonel is gone from his room
2 (ch. 21–22) To stay out of it A strangled colonel whose body vanished, a "Rakosky" on a stolen passport, an inspector from the political squad He and Belbo lie to the police about Ingolf and the message, and the shared lie ends the friendship for years They now hold something the police lack He leaves for Brazil
3 (ch. 24–27) Love and Brazil, and to forget the Templars Belbo's letter: a psychic in a trance repeats the six seals and the 36 invisibles, then disappears. Then Aglie, who seems to know too much A taste for "resemblance" that he will later turn into a machine (ch. 23) The coincidences keep finding him; Aglie now has him marked as "a young Templar" Aglie becomes the way back to Milan

Why it grips

  • The narrator is already in the trap. Casaubon tells all this from the periscope in the museum on the Saturday night, so every scene carries a line looking back from the disaster: "the first drops of the poison" (ch. 21), "This was our first, remote contact with the Plan" (ch. 19). The reader knows the game will kill before it is invented, so every crank detail in ch. 17–20 could be a fuse.
  • The crank lecture is a comedy scene with three straight men. Ardenti talks for four chapters. Casaubon corrects his facts, Belbo deadpans ("Your reasoning is flawless", "O basta la"), and Diotallevi joins in with numerology, which the colonel takes as proof. The method failing is the lesson (Belbo on the stars, ch. 20).
  • The disappearance stays open. Only a drunk old porter saw the body (ch. 21), and the sober inspector half suspects he dreamed it. Every event gets a sensible reading (fraud, a drug debt) and a plotted one, never settled. In ch. 25 De Angelis's explanation "seemed the most economical", and the periscope narrator then gives the sinister one.
  • A character test under the lore. Ch. 15–16 (the riot; Belbo's "Canal" file) set up his shame about running away; ch. 22 pays it off when he lies to the police and expects to be called a runaway again.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The editors' Plan does not exist yet; this section plants it. Ardenti's theory moves the plot three ways.

  1. The theory pulls in a believer, and the believer pays. Ardenti calls his book a fishing expedition: once two thousand readers know, killing him is pointless. Something bites within hours (ch. 20–21). This is mechanism B run by the wrong man. The cost falls on the one who believes, not on the doubters.
  2. The disappearance makes the bystanders complicit. Belbo and Casaubon never believed the colonel, but they lie anyway, on Belbo's Piedmont rule that you never give away a name (ch. 21). The lie is the cost. A silly theory becomes real guilt between them.
  3. A detail leaks, and the leak can be traced. The psychic (ch. 24) speaks the Provins phrases in a trance. Belbo moves toward her and she vanishes; De Angelis says either the police watch or Belbo's approach was seen. A private phrase surfaces in public, and whoever carried it is taken. That is a canary. Then ch. 25 takes it back: her magazines had already printed "the thirty-six invisibles" in a Rosicrucian article. Eco shows a canary result that cannot be read. You cannot tell whether the bird died because of you.

Ch. 25 states the book's rule (quoted below): the editors invented the Plan and reality ran ahead of it. Ch. 23 gives the inventor's motive to believe it: if the Plan is real, he is not to blame.

How the lore gets in

  • The Templar trial (ch. 14), about 3,500 words, a lecture. The narrator tells it over drinks at Pilade's, broken by Belbo's jokes and Diotallevi's cabala, and builds it as numbered "enigmas" (no resistance, matching confessions, the retracted retractions). Each fact becomes a question the colonel later answers wrongly. No stall: it is a performance with an audience, ending on doom.
  • Ardenti's theory (ch. 17–20), about 9,000 words, a conversation with documents. It is long, but it is broken into objects: the 1894 newspaper, the Ingolf ledger, the sheet that falls out of a book, the cipher page, the Trithemius wheel, the decoding printed in capitals, a drawn rune. Each gets a listener's reaction, and the planted danger ("There are secrets that kill") pays off one chapter later.
  • Brazilian syncretism and Saint-Germain (ch. 23–27), about 8,000 words, travel scenes and a dealer's patter. The slowest stretch, carried by the love story and Aglie's charm; ch. 26 stalls. It trains Casaubon in resemblance and brings Aglie in.

Mechanism notes

  • B, canary. Ardenti's book is a canary set by the believer, and it works: Rakosky comes, and Rakosky turns out not to exist (ch. 22). For SDF: the stranger who believes James's invented title and goes out with it is the one who gets counted, the cost Santi names. Eco puts it on a crank the reader half laughs at, which keeps it funny. The ch. 25 lesson is that any result can be explained away. So the canary only tells James something if he planted a detail nobody else could have printed. That is a gate (A) inside the canary.
  • Already on the page in SDF. James's invented book that Kalder says he has read (On land) is Diotallevi's numerology in ch. 19: the believer takes in any addition and thanks you for it ("You’ve given me the courage to go on"). Eco plays it as comedy, not as a probe; SDF can have both.
  • The clowns. Ardenti (a collaborator with the SS and a treasure fraudster, per De Angelis, ch. 22), the Picatrix séance with Radio Moscow on the speakers (ch. 24), Aglie playing Saint-Germain. Each crank stands beside something unexplained: the vanished body, the trance, what Aglie knows. That is SDF's every real question has a clown beside it, except that here nobody can tell whether anyone paid the clowns.
  • D, lock and key. Ingolf's daughter gives the colonel the attic because he promises to honour her father (ch. 18), and he steals from her. The door opens by her choice, and what it costs the visitor is moral.
  • Copies. In ch. 18 the colonel argues that Ingolf's copy is the original (quoted below). The crank's version of SDF's printings problem.

Quotes

  • "I’m casting the bait. We’ll see if anyone bites." (ch. 20): the believer as canary, stated by the believer.
  • "You just have to decide which stars to omit" (ch. 20): every crank's method in one line, played as a joke.
  • "Casaubon, when originals no longer exist, the last copy is the original." (ch. 18): how a copy nobody can check becomes scripture.
  • "Since we invented “the Plan” ourselves, and only much later was it possible for reality not only to catch up with fiction" (ch. 25): the book's mechanism, said plainly while the evidence is still ambiguous.

Flags

  • Real people pulled into the occult plot by a crank: Otto Rahn, Hitler's "secret weapon", Saint Bernard as a Druid (ch. 20). A discredited speaker covers Eco; SDF should not allow even that.
  • Real books appear only as crank evidence; none is said to be edited.

notes.title: section 03 (chapters 28–45)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 28–45 (about 30,500 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted English text, chunk file 03; no edition data in the file (William Weaver's translation [from memory, not from the text]).

The Plan does not exist yet. This section plants its machinery: the channel that will spread it (Project Hermes, the Diabolicals), the man who will believe it (Aglie), and a full model of an invented society taking hold (the Rosicrucian manifestoes, ch. 29–30).

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 28–33, Brazil) Amparo, and an amused hobby (Templars, then Rosicrucians) The Rosicrucian hoax; Bramanti the crank; Aglie's theory of initiates; Amparo, the materialist, possessed at the gira Amparo leaves (ch. 33) He does stop: a year on the beach flying kites. The pull comes only from the frame (the narrator waiting in the periscope, ch. 29, 34; "the fear that They will find me", ch. 39) Nothing in the story; Aglie hands over his Milan address
2 (ch. 34–40, Milan) A trade He invents one ("private eye of learning", ch. 34) and a card file; Belbo hires him; he sees Manutius, the vanity press behind Garamond Complicity: he enjoys the swindle (ch. 40) It is his living, and the card-file habit has no off switch The metals book sends him to Paris for pictures
3 (ch. 41–45) Good illustrations for the metals book Garamond turns his magic-and-science pictures into Project Hermes; the cranks arrive in hundreds Camestres leaves threatening "means, out of the ordinary" (ch. 44); the slush pile needs an expert The boss orders it, and the editors cannot tell the obvious from the new Casaubon phones Aglie. Last line: he is "as much of a bee" as the ones they lured (ch. 45)

Why it grips

  • The frame does the work the plot cannot. Brazil (ch. 28–33) has no forward plot. The narrator writes from hiding after the catastrophe, and every few chapters reminds us these are "the stages of my undoing" (ch. 35). Each episode reads as evidence for a disaster not yet shown.
  • The skeptic's body betrays her. Amparo mocks every lecture, then is taken by Pomba Gira at the rite (ch. 33). Drums and smell build, then a cut ("It was then that I saw Amparo."), a Sefirot aside, the possession. The section's one real reversal, and it proves Aglie's point before he makes it.
  • The cranks are introduced as comedy and leave as danger. Bramanti is a tapir in Rio (ch. 31), then sits in Garamond's Milan office (ch. 41), unexplained. Camestres is funny for two pages, then threatens (ch. 44). The laughs stay; a pattern starts to show.
  • The scene doing the most work: Garamond's office (ch. 38). A fake phone call, set off by a button under the desk, shows in one page that this firm makes belief for money. Project Hermes is the same trick, larger.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

No conspiracy acts on the heroes yet. Two things push them anyway.

First, money. Project Hermes exists because occult books sell and occult authors pay (ch. 42): a respectable series (Hermetica, at Garamond) as a lure, and a crank series (Isis Unveiled, at Manutius) the cranks are steered to. The editors do not invent a secret yet. They build a place where secrets are delivered to them.

Second, the leak is planned from the start. Garamond writes letters to occult reviews under false names asking about the new series. The editors phone Manutius, and he "acted mysterious, saying he could not yet reveal the first ten titles" (ch. 43). A flier is mailed to every group in a directory of secret societies, and Lorenza hands them out in occult bookshops. Withholding draws people in, as with the Rosicrucians (ch. 30). The Diabolicals arrive within months. Camestres takes his dismissal as an insult and threatens them (ch. 44). The volume then forces the step that matters, a consultant, and that is Aglie (ch. 45).

How the lore gets in

  • Aglie at the terreiro (ch. 28), about 1,000 words, a lecture. Broken by Amparo's jabs; ends in a palm reading.
  • The Rosicrucian manifestoes (ch. 29–30), about 4,500 words, pillow talk. The heaviest lore in the section, and it never stalls. Casaubon reads from a book in bed while Amparo heckles, passes a joint and asks for the fan; it ends in sex, with the book titles as endearments. The skeptic does the analysis: her riff on Rosicrucians who deny it ("He’d say he was, to make them think he wasn’t") is the section's sharpest reasoning.
  • Bramanti's lecture (ch. 31), about 900 words, reported speech with Amparo's asides in parentheses: crank and mockery at once.
  • Aglie's Tradition (ch. 32–33), two bar talks, about 1,500 words, each ending on a turn ("The secret lies beyond.").
  • Bramanti's syllabus (ch. 41) and the society directory (ch. 43), one paragraph each. Lists run on until they are funny, then cut off by an interruption ("Templar phenomenology," Belbo slipped in).
  • The slush pile (ch. 45), about 1,500 words. The editors trade crank theses (Mu, Columbus the Templar, the electric Ark) and knock each down with one fact. Lore as a sorting job, so it moves.

Mechanism notes

  • B (canary), the antagonist's own version. Aglie tells Casaubon how initiates use believers: "The mystic is useful, because he is conspicuous. He broadcasts himself." (ch. 33). He also calls the mystic litmus paper. This is the canary from the hidden side. For SDF: the clowns the organisation funds are also its detectors, so James's planted title has a second edge; the organisation may be watching the same believers he is.
  • B, the template in miniature: the Rosicrucian hoax (ch. 30). A prank text, real people who answer it, silence read as proof, and the author's denials useless. The cost falls on the inventor (Andreae's reputation) and on a bystander (Descartes, suspected, clears himself only by being seen). That is SDF's wanted cost: a stranger believes and gets counted.
  • B in practice: Garamond's fake inquiries (ch. 43). An invented question in the right channel, and real people respond: close to James posting an invented title in a forum. The first to respond are professional believers (Bramanti, Camestres), not the hidden order. The canary catches clowns first.
  • The clown beside the real, built on purpose. Belbo's Encyclopedia of Illustrious Italians places an invented paying author next to a famous one "in alphabetical proximity" (Lampedusa / Lampustri, ch. 39). Garamond pairs Hermetica with Isis Unveiled (ch. 42). Kiesewetter's citation of a page in the Theatrum Chemicum, repeated by hordes of Rosicrucians, is not on that page, as Aglie can show from his own copy (ch. 32). A found object for James could take this form: a citation everyone repeats and nobody checked.
  • C (front). Garamond and Manutius are two doors three steps apart (ch. 38). The respectable firm covers the predatory one, which feeds it. Garamond's rule that crank books must repeat each other (ch. 45) is how a front stays believable.
  • What this section has that SDF lacks. The first threat comes from a crank, not from the order (Camestres, ch. 44). Misjudging a believer costs something before any real conspiracy arrives.

Quotes

  • "The fact that they didn’t answer was taken as proof of their existence." (ch. 30): silence as the engine of an invented order.
  • "The mystic is useful, because he is conspicuous. He broadcasts himself." (ch. 33): the canary, stated by the hidden side.
  • "We disguise ourselves as a flower" (ch. 43): Garamond on bait. The section's last paragraph turns it on the narrator.
  • "They confirm one another; therefore they’re true. Never trust originality." (ch. 45): how cranks make each other credible.

Flags

  • Real organisations named in a crank directory, among them the Jesuits, Opus Dei, the Mormons, Rotary and the OTO (ch. 43, 44). Satire, but SDF must not list real groups in any hidden order.
  • A false claim about a page of a real book (Theatrum Chemicum, ch. 32). A crank's error, disproved, not an edit; still, any SDF equivalent should use an invented book.
  • A real murder (Moro, ch. 34) as background only; no real person named as complicit.

notes.title: section 04 (chapters 46–63)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 46 to 63, up to the TIFERET part heading (about 31,300 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: English translation, converted text, chunk file 04; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 46–52) Casaubon and Belbo want a sharp reader to sort the Manutius manuscripts Agliè, who recites the pyramid book from memory and then takes it apart (47–48); Lorenza walks in and calls him Simon (48) Belbo loses Lorenza to Agliè's game, publicly, at Riccardo's show (50) Agliè is now on the firm's payroll, and Salon, the taxidermist next door, knows about Colonel Ardenti, a case Casaubon thought was buried (51) Casaubon goes to the library to look up Saint-Yves and Agarttha
2 (ch. 53–54) To read one book quietly Inspector De Angelis has just returned it. Over coffee he lays out synarchy and asks about an organisation called the Tres Casaubon is now an informal source for the police and has lied to a policeman (he denies Ardenti mentioned Agarttha) The police are still circling Ardenti, and Agliè has been seen going through the Manutius author file (54) The trip to Piedmont: the castle and the druids
3 (ch. 57–63) To see the Diabolicals' world from the inside, as a tourist A staged alchemical wedding, homunculi in jars, a Rosicrucian initiation seen through a window, a druid rite cut short. Salon, now named as a police informer, pressing Pierre about the Paris sewers (60) His own scepticism. Back home he reads every object as a sign (63) The narrator says the Plan first stirred that evening (57). Lia warns him, then tells him she is pregnant (63) The next part, where the game begins [from memory, not from the text]

Why it grips

  • Everything is set-up, and the narrator tells you so. Visits, parties and talk; little happens. The narrator, writing after the disaster, plants regret in advance (the Plan stirred on the castle night, 57; he should have listened to Lia, 63), so every comic crank is read knowing someone will take him seriously.
  • Lore comes in already doubted. Agliè recites the pyramid numerology (47), then knocks it down with the lottery kiosk outside his window (48). The reader gets the lore and the joke together, and Agliè comes out stronger: he despises the cranks and still believes. Casaubon notices him reading the ceiling while pretending to remember (47), which plants doubt.
  • Each lore scene is broken by a personal sting. The pyramid lecture ends with Lorenza at the door (48). The Gnostic Sophia myth arrives as Lorenza's drunk flirting, with Belbo jealous in front of his rival (50). The alchemical wedding is felt through what Casaubon thinks is Lorenza's hand, and she was never there (58–59).
  • Belbo's memories hold up the real question. Uncle Carlo and Mongo saluting as veterans (49), the bullet in the corridor (55) and the bombardon (56) give Belbo a time when things were clear and a time he did not choose. Eco ties them to the conspiracy once, in the druids' trumpet (62), so the occult gets a private hook in him.
  • The rites are cut off just as they get real. Agliè allows one peek and lowers the curtain (61). At the druid rite he says it is over just as the pigs appear and the knife comes out (62). Played as comedy, it still works as a hook.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

There is no Plan yet. What this section builds is the network the Plan will later leak into. Agliè gets inside Garamond as a consultant (47), learns the Manutius trick (52), goes through the author file and proposes writing to every Manutius author of twenty years (54): a mailing list of people who want to believe. Salon and De Angelis show the firm is already watched because of Ardenti, the one real disappearance (51, 53). Agliè tells Casaubon that Salon is an informer, and that to an informer a secret is worth having whether or not it is true (57). That is the leak rule the plot will run on.

The first believer in this section is the narrator. In chapter 63 Casaubon catches himself reading shop signs and clouds for hidden stories, and Lia names the cost. The canary dies in the miner's own lungs first.

How the lore gets in

  • Pierre's sorcery quarrel with Bramanti (46), about 1,500 words, overheard through a curtain. Farce (a plaster Baphomet, a sorcery death that was cirrhosis); the eavesdropping keeps it moving.
  • Pyramid and kiosk numerology (47–48), about 2,500 words, a performance. No stall: the scene is a hiring and ends in a rivalry.
  • Agarttha and Saint-Yves (52), about 700 words, office conversation. Agliè slips into the first person, as if he had been there, so the lore carries the question of whether he is Saint-Germain. Ends on a punchline.
  • Synarchy (53), about 1,800 words, a café interview with a policeman. Played as a card game (who learns more), with a bomb on a train as stakes; ends with the Tres, a named unknown. No stall.
  • The Chymical Wedding (58), about 1,500 words, a projected spectacle, told through drink, incense and desire. The plot does not move, and the night is where the Plan is born (57).
  • Lia's lecture on the body (63), about 1,800 words. She explains the symbols away through the body; the antidote, from the person with most to lose, ending with her pregnancy.

Mechanism notes

  • B (canary), what is planted. Three leak channels are built before anything is invented: the consultant who reads the files (Agliè, 52, 54), the informer who repeats whatever he hears (Salon, 51, 57, 60), and the policeman who asks about names (De Angelis, 53). De Angelis drops the Tres to see whether Casaubon reacts: a canary aimed at the hero, answered with a lie. For SDF: On land already has James test Kalder with an invented book; the reverse, James tested and lying back, would give him a cost.
  • The clown beside the question. Agliè states SDF's organisation logic outright (61): the real Templars would hide in the crowd of their caricatures. Casaubon's joke to De Angelis (53) is the same idea turned round. A possible insider explains how cover works while seeming to side with the cranks.
  • C (front). Synarchy (53) is a chain of fronts with nothing at the bottom: each public pact is denounced as cover for a secret pact, which turns out to be the same public pact. A model for making any SDF leak look like one more version.
  • D (lock and key). Agliè decides how much the editors may see, one peek and then the curtain (61, 62). Doors open because a person chooses to open them, which matches SDF's rule.
  • Fifth: the counter-voice who pays. Lia (63) is the one who sees it clearly, and she has the most at stake. The narrator's later regret at not listening to her turns her into the measure of what he loses.

Quotes

  • "it was definitely on that evening that the Plan first stirred in our minds" (ch. 57): the narrator dates the start before anything happens.
  • "There exists a secret society with branches throughout the world, and its plot is to spread the rumor that a universal plot exists." (ch. 53): the joke that is SDF's premise.
  • "What better hiding place for the true Templar than in the crowd of his caricatures?" (ch. 61): the clown as cover, said by a man who may be inside.
  • "now I came to distrust the very masters who had taught me to doubt" (ch. 63): the first believer is the narrator.

Flags

  • Real people and groups appear as cranks or accused plotters: Crowley and the Golden Dawn (47), Saint-Yves d'Alveydre (51–52), and in De Angelis's synarchy history real people and groups (Navachine, La Cagoule, Du Mas and Canudo, Husson) (53). SDF must invent its cranks and accused.
  • No invented edits on real books. Agliè claims to own a third copy of Khunrath's 1595 first edition (47). That is a claim about a copy, not an edit.

notes.title: section 05 (chapters 64–83)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 64 to 83 (about 30,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: English translation, converted text, chunk file 05; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 64–68) Material for Garamond's history of magic, and a joke on the Diabolicals Abulafia's random output (ch. 65); Tomar, a real castle that fits the Provins message (ch. 67) Casaubon stops laughing. Belbo forgets the Plan is fake (ch. 68–69) Every answer leaves a named hole (the Refuge, the Popelicans, the break in 1824), with a bottle of whisky bet on one (ch. 68) Read the Rosicrucian manifestoes
2 (ch. 70–76) Explain the break and bring it up to modern times The 1584 calendar error (ch. 71); Saint-Martin, which holds the Pendulum, as the Refuge (ch. 74); a list of sects (ch. 75) They plant a fake sect, "Tres". Aglie catches it, presses for its source, and leaves (ch. 76). They have lied to a believer "We still haven't decided what this secret is all about" (ch. 76) Find the Templars' secret
3 (ch. 77–83) Be with Lia for the birth Salon's den, the Protocols, a father in the Okhrana under Rachkovski (ch. 78–79) He cannot be reached when her waters break. "I had to count all by myself" (ch. 80) Even in the den, "new, malicious ideas for the Plan whirled in my head" (ch. 79) The telluric secret, the Pendulum as pointer, which map (ch. 82–83)

Why it grips

  • Three voices, one of them a heckler. Each lump of lore answers an objection: "honey and pepper" (ch. 68), "Make beer?" (ch. 82), "But suppose it's overcast?" (ch. 82). The objection forces the next invention, so the lore arrives as a solved problem, never as a lecture.
  • Puzzles with a deadline and a stake. "I'll give you two weeks" (ch. 68); "It took seven days to make the world" (ch. 81). Each lore chapter is framed as a delivery.
  • The narrator keeps telling us it went wrong. "If I had only stopped there" (ch. 77) and the line about waiting under the Pendulum turn the game into a countdown toward something we know is bad but cannot name.
  • A real life alongside. The scene that does the most work is ch. 78–80. Casaubon has a presentiment, Lia sends him to work, and Salon pulls him into the den. While Salon talks about tunnels, Casaubon invents new lies, then gets home to a note on the kitchen table. The Plan's first cost is a missed hour, and it is a private one.
  • Still funny. The car as the Tree of the Sefirot (ch. 66), Minnie Mouse as an axiom (ch. 65).

How the conspiracy moves the story here

Here the Plan mostly acts on its makers. It takes their attention: Casaubon at Tomar, Belbo forgetting it is fake, Casaubon plotting while his son is born.

The leak starts at one point, the Tres test (ch. 75–76). They doubt Aglie knows every sect, so they add a fake one and say it came from the Diabolicals' manuscripts. But the name is not wholly theirs. Casaubon takes it from a question the inspector De Angelis once asked him (ch. 75). So the bait is half-real, and Aglie's reaction reads two ways: either he has caught an invention or he has recognised a real word. He is the first outsider to touch the Plan, and he does it calmly. He asks which manuscript, asks again, says it does not matter, and checks his watch. The three lie about the source and can no longer take it back.

Salon (ch. 78–79) is the clown beside it. He believes his own anti-Semitic tunnel plot. But his father worked for the tsarist secret police under a man whose name echoes the colonel's visitor Rakosky. Casaubon refuses the link: "No more coincidences." The clown and the possible real danger are the same man, and the hero chooses not to see it.

How the lore gets in

  • Abulafia printouts (ch. 65, 71, 82), a few lines each, objects. Read like a dice roll, so the next idea seems to come from outside.
  • Provins message (ch. 67), about 800 words, document plus dialogue. A real place has already done the persuading, and Lia is on the phone looking up bannock cakes.
  • Popelicans (ch. 68), about 1,200 words, monologue with interruptions. It is told to win a bet and gets a laugh every few lines.
  • Rosicrucian manifestoes (ch. 70), about 1,500 words, close reading. The nearest it comes to stalling, since Casaubon reads alone with no one to object. It is saved by ending on a deduction.
  • "The Cabinet of Dr. Dee" (ch. 73), about 3,000 words, a pastiche inside the novel. Lore turned into melodrama, and it shows Belbo writing his own story inside the Plan.
  • Chronology of sects (ch. 75), about 1,700 words, a list. A dead stop on purpose, and it pays off at once as the vehicle for the trap.
  • Aglie on Masonry (ch. 76), about 2,500 words, conversation. He slides into the first person, as if he had been there. It ends on "Which manuscript?"
  • Telluric secret and map (ch. 81–83), about 3,000 words. Built through objections: which Pendulum, which hour, which map.

Mechanism notes

  • B (canary), clearest case so far (ch. 75–76). How it works: hide one invented item among many real ones, credit it to someone else's material, and watch who asks about the source. The tell is not belief. It is a second question and a quick exit. The price is not paid in this section; the frame only announces it (ch. 77). For SDF: James's invented book for Kalder in On land is the same move, already on the page. Eco adds three things. (1) Bury the item in a long, genuine list, such as a catalogue or bibliography, so that noticing it is itself the tell. (2) Lie about the source, so James cannot withdraw it without exposing himself. (3) Build the bait from a word James once overheard, so he cannot tell whether a reaction means his invention was caught or the real word was recognised. Cost: the lie about the source becomes his debt.
  • The inventor believes first (Casaubon ch. 67, Belbo ch. 68–69). An SDF canary could catch James himself, if he starts to treat his own planted edit as evidence.
  • The clown holds one real thread (Salon, ch. 79). One of SDF's funded cranks could carry a true connection, so that James's habit of dismissing them costs him.
  • C (front), weakly. Masonry is "A facade. The secret is elsewhere" (ch. 76).
  • Fifth: the job supplies the fuel. Garamond's commission (ch. 64) is why they read the Diabolicals at all. Like James, they receive documents through work, but they turn them into something they make, and the making is what exposes them.

Quotes

  • "the idea is not to discover the Templars’ secret, but to construct it." (ch. 67): the game said out loud, just as he stops laughing.
  • "Let’s add a sect that doesn’t exist. Founded recently." (ch. 75): the canary planted as a test of one man.
  • "It’s just that I never heard of it before. You really can’t tell me who mentioned it?" (ch. 76): the tell is the second question.
  • "Serves you right, I said to myself that other evening. Now here you are, waiting for what will happen under Foucault’s Pendulum." (ch. 77): the cost announced before it is paid.

Flags

  • Real people named as complicit: Dee plans murders and Bacon has Dee killed (ch. 73); Postel and Fludd as grand masters; Galileo's cardinals as Templar adepts (ch. 82).
  • Real texts read as coded (the Fama, Shakespeare), and Bacon inserts a line into the sonnets (ch. 73). That is an invented edit on a real book.
  • Salon voices the Protocols (ch. 79). The book frames this as a believer's hatred, but no SDF clown should borrow it.

notes.title: section 06 (chapters 84–109)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 84 to 109 (about 31,900 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: English translation, converted text, chunk file 06; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 84–97) The three editors want to finish the Plan as a parody of their Diabolicals Every crank source fits: pendulums, Eiffel Tower, Jesuits, Protocols, Saint-Germain Their judgement: "addicted", "corrupted", "converted" (ch. 87) The Plan always has an empty slot (where do the Paulicians go?), and an empty slot asks to be filled Hitler and the hollow earth (ch. 98–100)
2 (ch. 98–105) Belbo wants a win over Aglie, who is taking Lorenza and the office Diotallevi falls ill in the middle of the Hitler riff; they stop for a month (ch. 101); Casaubon's Alamut idea restarts it Guilt. Belbo starts to need the Plan to be true (ch. 105) Belbo is a gambler who has been shown the cards (ch. 102) Belbo uses the Plan as a weapon
3 (ch. 106–109) Belbo wants revenge, sending Aglie after a map that does not exist Lia proves the source is a merchant's delivery list (ch. 106), but Belbo has already told Aglie he holds the map (ch. 108). He is handed a suitcase bomb, sketched by the police, blackmailed Freedom: wanted for terrorism, the policeman scared off, his boss in on it He cannot prove the Plan false; he alone knows he does not know Paris, Librairie Sloane, 20 June

Why it grips

  • The reader learns it is false before the believers act. Lia's laundry list (ch. 106) comes just before chapters 107–109. Straight after, the invented Plan produces a real bomb. The dread now comes from the Plan not being true. Her answer to the coded half is cut off at the part break.
  • Pace is set by the joke. Chapters 84–96 hold about 12,000 words of pseudo-history, and Casaubon tells us how to hear them: a Keystone Kops film (ch. 85). Every chapter opens with a real crank's epigraph. Each lore run ends on a laugh ("Templars of the world, unite!", ch. 87).
  • A body under the game. Diotallevi's yellow skin is mentioned in passing (ch. 87). His "gastritis" arrives during the Holocaust riff (ch. 100), then come the hospital (ch. 101) and the unnamed "bisyllable" (ch. 107). The illness keeps time for the Plan,.
  • The scene that does the most work is the train (ch. 108). Each of Belbo's small rudenesses on the train comes back as evidence: the Burberry blazer, the maroon tie, a seat booked to Rome with a ticket only to Bologna, and his joke about "Arab metaphysics", told to scare off a chatty neighbour. By evening they are witness testimony on the news.
  • A comic defeat turns him. A run-over dog and Lorenza leaving by train make one humiliating farce (ch. 107); that night he decides to put Aglie into the Plan.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

This section is where mechanism B fires, in this order:

  1. The inventors believe first (ch. 87, the spy and the man who lives with a dog). By ch. 98 they keep their talk from Aglie with "the natural reserve of those who possess a secret". The first leak is inward.
  2. Leakage is ambient before it is deliberate. Aglie spends "hours and hours on the Manutius address file" (ch. 98), Salon is seen coming out of Manutius (ch. 102), and the editors steal from the Diabolicals' manuscripts (ch. 85). Nobody tracks what moves through the house.
  3. The deliberate plant is a canary test (ch. 108). Belbo passes the Plan off as Ardenti's ten authentic pages and adds three baits. The map is "in full view". The papers are destroyed, so the map now exists only in his head. He will travel "around the summer solstice". He holds back the final truth, and the holding back is what makes him believable (quote 2). Within a day Aglie hands him the suitcase.
  4. What the canary shows. It shows that Aglie believes, that Rakosky, Ragotgky and Aglie are one name, that Garamond is in the same "spiritual knighthood" (ch. 109, overheard on his line), and that the Tres exists. He learns it all from what is done to him.
  5. The cost lands on him. The organisation does not kill him and does not lock him out. It frames him: a police sketch, his own words, a threat to name seat 45. De Angelis's car bomb is "hardly more than a firecracker" (ch. 109), just enough to make him ask for a transfer. Strangers get counted too: "Two Libyan citizens had been detained in Bologna" (ch. 108).

How the lore gets in

  • Ch. 84–96, the Plan's history (about 12,000 words), carried as a three-way game. Short chapters, turn-taking, punchlines. It stalls on purpose, to show the habit taking hold.
  • "The Return of Saint-Germain" (ch. 97, about 4,000 words), Belbo's file. All the lore is retold as pulp melodrama: a trapdoor, a knife, each group's envoy drowned in turn.
  • Hitler and the hollow earth (ch. 99–100, about 2,000 words), a rant. Diotallevi's collapse cuts it off, so something happens in the room straight away.
  • Alamut (ch. 103–104, about 2,500 words), proofs at Pilade's bar, broken up by Belbo's refills; it ends on Casaubon's verdict that Belbo is now "an adept".
  • Lia's laundry list (ch. 106, about 2,500 words), a lecture with the document on the table. This is anti-lore, sourced from a tourist booklet.

Mechanism notes

  • B (canary), in full and with its price (ch. 108–109). Belbo's test is SDF's On land move (James invents a book; Kalder says he has read it). Eco does not drop it after the reaction: the reaction becomes the trap. The believer acts on the bait's actionable details (a date, a place, a map kept only in his head), not on its lore. For SDF, James's invented title or edit should carry one checkable hook (a printing, a shelfmark, a forum date), and whoever touches it should act on that hook. The brief's cost is in the text twice. Strangers are counted (the Libyans). The inventor becomes the keeper of a secret "that did not exist" (ch. 109).
  • Discredit, not prevent. The Tres never stop Belbo from talking. They make what he says unbelievable: to the police his story would need a second, more outlandish story behind it (ch. 109). Garamond does the same thing gently ("Why, it sounds like a novel").
  • The clown's book holds the true clue (ch. 109). A hack manuscript, The True Story of the Comte de Saint-Germain, arrives among the day's submissions and names "Marquis of Aglie" as Saint-Germain's real name. A reveal as an object, from the nonsense pile.
  • A (gate), as an absence. Lia's test (is the source real?) is the gate the editors never passed, and Belbo plants without asking it.
  • Fifth: the frame made from the hero's habits. Belbo's jokes become the witness description. James's dry asides could be used against him the same way.

Quotes

  • "there is no longer any difference between developing the habit of pretending to believe and developing the habit of believing" (ch. 87): the inventors are the first believers.
  • "His reticence about the final truth guaranteed the truth of its premises." (ch. 108): how to plant a canary.
  • "The drawing didn’t resemble Belbo, but Belbo resembled the drawing." (ch. 108): the frame in one line.
  • "So Garamond, too, was part of the secret. What secret? The one that only he, Belbo, could reveal. The one that did not exist." (ch. 109): the canary's price.

Flags

  • Real people are named as complicit throughout the Plan (Rachkovsky, Nilus, Napoleon, Hess, Hitler). SDF must not do this.
  • Ch. 100 turns the Holocaust into a search for the map inside the parody, and the characters themselves recoil. Do not borrow.
  • Hidden codes are read into real books (Verne, ch. 84–85). These are readings, not invented edits, but SDF should keep any canary titles or edits off real books.

notes.title: section 07 (chapters 110–120, the end)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 110 to 120 (Nezah to Malkhut, the end of the novel), about 25,900 words, read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: English translation, converted text, chunk file 07; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 110–111) Casaubon, having finished Belbo's files, wants to know if any of it is real Diotallevi, dying, says the game wrote itself into his cells; Belbo went to Paris to confess there was no secret and was not believed Nothing yet Belbo phoned for help, the rite is tonight, no one else knows. Eco asks it openly: "Why... didn’t you pretend nothing had happened?" (ch. 111) The occult bookshop, where asking for Aglie by name gets him noticed; hiding in the museum
2 (ch. 112–114) To see the rite, maybe save Belbo Every crank from earlier in the book, assembled as one order, acting out the Plan the editors invented He watches Lorenza stabbed and Belbo hanged from the Pendulum, and does nothing He has been seen ("now they know that you’re here, too", ch. 111) and is the last man who "knows" Escape through the sewers
3 (ch. 115–120) Someone to tell him he is mad The museum spotless; Dr Wagner's whole diagnosis, "Monsieur, vous etes fou" (ch. 117); Diotallevi dead; a house key in his pocket, and in that house Belbo's trumpet story Lia and the baby: he waits for Them to come Denying the Map makes Them want it more (ch. 120) Nothing. The book ends with him waiting

Why it grips

  • The reader is ahead of the hero's hope. Belbo's file (ch. 110) already says They caught him. Paris is the reader waiting to see how. Eco withholds the method, not the outcome.
  • The rite is a farce that turns lethal halfway (ch. 113). The cast are the clowns from earlier chapters, in titles a paragraph long. They fight among themselves: Olcott outvotes Aglie, Aglie exposes a "spirit" as quoting a book "I wrote it myself; anyone can read it for sixty francs!", Pierre takes the throne, the mediums die of their own ectoplasm. Then, with no change of tone, the knife comes out. These people are ridiculous and they kill, and that is what frightens.
  • The victim wins by the sense of the ridiculous. With the wire round his neck, Belbo relaxes once he sees how silly the room is; his last words are a Piedmontese obscenity. Garamond, mid-stampede: "Gentlemen, please! Manners!" The book stays funny through its worst scene.
  • The investigator catches the disease (ch. 115–116). Casaubon walks Paris reading every shop window, street name and the Eiffel Tower as proof of the Plan. The reader sees he is wrong and sees why. The cost of belief is shown on the page as a mind that no longer works.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

This is mechanism B's payoff: the editors invented the Plan as a game, others believed it, and the believers come for the inventors. Three things happen.

  1. Denial becomes proof. Belbo goes to Paris to confess; "His words were too undramatic, too simple" (ch. 110). Chapter 118 spells out why: refusal makes the secret look bigger. Once a canary is believed, its author cannot take it back. This is the strongest engine in the section.
  2. The fake Plan gives the believers an identity. Aglie tells the assembly the prisoner knows who they are better than they do (ch. 113). Ardenti, whose "message" started everything, kneels and admits he never understood it: the original source has been overtaken by the version built on top of it.
  3. It puts the wrong people in the room. Garamond, whose vanity press fed on cranks, is now a robed dignitary.

On whether anything was real, Eco closes every door but one. The Provins message was a laundry list (Lia, recalled in ch. 118); the museum shows no trace. But two people are dead, Garamond is missing from Milan, and Casaubon concludes "something did happen", like Amparo, who knew something possessed her even if not the god (ch. 118). His rule for trust: Gudrun, who never understood the game, is the only reliable witness. The Plan is false; the believers are real, and he waits for them.

How the lore gets in

  • Diotallevi's deathbed lecture (ch. 110), about 1,500 words, conversation. Torah as body, metathesis as metastasis. No stall: the speaker is dying as he talks, so the lecture is the cost scene.
  • The museum walk (ch. 112), about 1,800 words, interior monologue. Each machine read as a Templar instrument. It moves because he must cross dark rooms before midnight.
  • Anathemas and titles (ch. 113), about 700 words, ceremony. A catalogue of orders read out while Lorenza stands drugged and Belbo has not yet appeared. A joke and a countdown at once.
  • The three rules of the game and the empty secret (ch. 118), about 2,500 words, notes on a plane. The thesis arrives only after the climax, as a man explaining to himself what he saw. It stalls on purpose; the action is over.
  • Belbo's juvenilia (ch. 119), about 3,000 words, a found manuscript. The last reveal is an object, and it is not about the conspiracy: a boy holding one trumpet note at a partisan funeral, the one real moment of Belbo's life, which he never recognised.

Mechanism notes

  • B (canary): the cost. Eco's canary works too well. Believers adopt the planted material and act on it, and the inventor's denial counts as confirmation (ch. 110, 118). For SDF: if a stranger believes James's invented title, James telling him "I made it up" should deepen the belief. The cost falls on James's honesty, not only his safety. Place: after On land, where the invented book exists and Kalder says he has read it. PROPOSAL.
  • B and the clowns. Eco's clowns self-organise; an invented Plan is enough to gather them. SDF's organisation funds its clowns. A twist to test: James's canary is picked up first by a funded clown, so he cannot tell whether the bite came from the organisation or its decoy. PROPOSAL.
  • The outsider as witness (ch. 118). Someone who has never heard the theory (the widow in Zwolle in The other ten) is reliable because she cannot be contaminated.
  • D (lock and key), literally. A house key in a pocket (ch. 118) opens the cupboard with the final text. It opens a private memory, not the secret, and it is an object in the hero's hands.
  • Fifth: the investigator infected (ch. 115–116). James, a monitoring engineer, could misread an ordinary alert as a signal: a cheap, funny, visible cost of being wrong.
  • A and C: no gate here; the front shows only weakly (the Tres calls every other order fake, ch. 113).

Quotes

  • "But if you invent a plan and others carry it out, it’s as if the Plan exists. At that point it does exist." (ch. 118): the canary's payoff.
  • "the more he vowed he didn’t possess it, the more convinced They were that he did possess it" (ch. 118): denial as fuel.
  • "He knows even who we are; in fact, we learned who we are through him." (ch. 113): the invented plot gives the believers their identity.
  • "Gudrun was never part of our story—she wouldn’t have understood it—so she is the only one left who tells the truth." (ch. 118): the uncontaminated witness.

Flags

  • Real organisations (Golden Dawn, Ordo Templi Orientis, the Priory of Sion) are named in the anathema (ch. 113) as rivals, not killers; Kelley, Khunrath and Saint-Germain are summoned as spirits. SDF should not borrow the naming.
  • Real Paris bookshops (Editions Rosicruciennes, Librairie la Vouivre, Arcane 22) are read as parts of the Plan (ch. 115). SDF keeps companies invented.
  • A fictional character claims authorship of a real text, the Très Sainte Trinosophie (ch. 113): close to the forbidden invented edit on a real book.
  • The ch. 111 epigraph cites Cazotte "from a page suppressed in later editions": a real-book variant, on-theme for SDF, but SDF must not invent such variants for real books.

books.qa:
Answers point to the section notes in this folder (01–07) and, where relevant, to a v8.2 chapter by title. The map is 00-map.md. Everything about SDF here is a PROPOSAL; Santi's decisions are PLACEHOLDER.

The canary itself

1. What is the canary in this book, in one sentence? An invented thing placed where a believer will find it, so that what he does with it shows who he is and what he serves. Eco runs it seven times, from Ardenti's published theory (ch. 20) to Belbo's fake map (ch. 108). See map section 4 and 05-chapters-64-to-83.md, 06-chapters-84-to-109.md.

2. What is the tell, exactly? Belief? No. In the clearest case Agliè doesn't claim to know the fake sect; he asks who mentioned it, asks again, says it does not matter, and checks his watch (ch. 76). The tell is the second question and the quick exit. In the later case (ch. 108) the tell is action on a concrete hook: a date, a place, a map (05, 06).

3. Kalder in On land says he has read James's invented book. Is that Eco's tell? It is a weaker one. It is closer to Diotallevi feeding numerology to Ardenti (ch. 19): a believer, or a pretender, takes in any addition and thanks you for it (02-chapters-14-to-27.md). It proves vanity or bluff, not who Kalder reports to. Map proposal 5.1 adds the step that does prove it: the hook gets acted on and the action comes back through a third party.

4. Is the On land canary already written? Only in the plan. v8.2 On land has the invented book and Kalder's "Oh, that one. Yes," and The dinner calls it back ("the book you said you'd read"). The only draft, 01 Manuscript/v6/18 — On land.md, is the older version built on the Deventer slip, with no invented book. No v7 or v8 draft of On land exists.

5. Does the pipeline's claim that On land "drops" the canary hold? Half. Nothing in Part Two follows it up, but in the plan The dinner cashes it in Part Three as James's stated reason for doubt. What's missing is anything between the pub and the dinner that the canary does. See map 5.1.

6. What is the gate inside the canary? The psychic case (ch. 24–25): a private phrase surfaces in public and its carrier vanishes, then it turns out her magazines had already printed the phrase. Once that is known, nobody can say what the canary showed (02). The rule for SDF: a bait tells James something only if nobody else could have printed or heard it. In On land, Ana laughing at something else (v8.2) is what lets the gate pass.

7. Why plant a fake inside a list rather than say it alone? Because then noticing the fake is itself the tell (ch. 75–76, 05). Someone who refuses everything in the same tone has told you nothing. Someone who asks about the one item he didn't recognize has confirmed the rest. Map 5.2 puts this in The reading room, continued.

8. What does the canary cost the person who plants it? First a lie about the source, which can't be taken back without exposing the planter (ch. 76). In the end it costs him his credibility: Belbo's denial reads as proof (ch. 110, 118, 07-chapters-110-to-120.md). The notes also find strangers counted: two Libyans detained after Belbo's train joke (ch. 108, 06).

9. Who believes the invention first? The inventors. Casaubon at Tomar (ch. 67), Belbo forgetting it is fake (ch. 68–69), all three "addicted," "converted" (ch. 87). Casaubon reads shop signs as signs as early as ch. 63 (04-chapters-46-to-63.md, 05, 06). For SDF that suggests a cheap negative: James seeing his own invented title out in the world (map 5.4, The band).

10. Does the canary ever work for the hero? Never. Every canary in the book ends up turned on the people who planted it. SDF wants it reversed: James's instrument, with a price. What carries over is how it is built (a unique item, an actionable hook, a readout through a third party, a cost), not where it ends (map section 4).

11. Is there a canary aimed at the hero? Yes. De Angelis says "Tres" to see whether Casaubon reacts, and Casaubon lies (ch. 53, 04). Map 5.5 gives James the same test, set by Pieter in The drill, so that the lie costs him in The sheets.

The clowns

12. How do the Diabolicals work as clowns beside the real question? They come in as manuscripts at a publisher's door, sorted by a typology (ch. 10, 12), and they stay funny while a pattern forms (Bramanti in Rio, then in Milan; Camestres funny for two pages, then threatening, ch. 31, 41, 44). At the rite the same clowns kill (ch. 113). See 01-chapters-1-to-13.md, 03-chapters-28-to-45.md, 07.

13. Who bites a canary first? Clowns. Project Hermes's fake inquiries draw Bramanti and Camestres before any hidden order shows (ch. 43–44, 03). Map 5.3 lets the forum man from The gorilla mask bite James's forum bait first, so James can't tell decoy from organization.

14. Does any clown hold a true thread? Salon. He believes his own tunnel plot, but his father served the tsarist secret police under a man whose name echoes "Rakosky," and Casaubon refuses the link (ch. 78–79, 05). Also the hack manuscript on Saint-Germain that arrives in the slush pile and gives his real name as "Marquis of Aglie" (ch. 109, 06). SDF's Beard Man already plays this part (the bucket theory).

15. How does the hidden side use its clowns? As cover and as detectors. "What better hiding place for the true Templar than in the crowd of his caricatures?" (ch. 61, 04); "The mystic is useful, because he is conspicuous" (ch. 33, 03). That matches SDF's thermostat, and it warns that any believer James watches is being watched as well.

16. Is there anything like SDF's farmed forums? Garamond/Manutius: a respectable imprint that steers cranks to the paying one, and Garamond's rule that crank books must repeat each other (ch. 38, 42, 45, 03). The gorilla mask's edited forum account is already SDF's version.

Lore

17. How does Eco keep 12,000 words of Plan history moving? He mostly doesn't, and the notes say so. Ch. 84–96 stall on purpose to show the habit setting in, held up by punchlines, crank epigraphs and Diotallevi's yellow skin (06). Don't copy this. SDF has no hanging promised in the frame to carry it.

18. What is the best-carried piece of lore? The Rosicrucian manifestoes as pillow talk (ch. 29–30, about 4,500 words): Amparo heckles, the skeptic does the best reasoning, and it ends in sex (03). The other is the list of sects (ch. 75), a dead catalogue that pays off in the next chapter because the trap is inside it (05).

19. How does the heckler work? Each lump of lore answers an objection ("Make beer?", "But suppose it's overcast?", ch. 82), so the objection forces the next invention and the lore arrives as a solved problem (05). For SDF: Frank in Frank's kitchen and Frank, loose, and Ana in Twenty minutes, already do this job.

20. How does Agliè deliver lore without it reading as a lecture? He performs it and then turns it: the pyramid numerology recited, then knocked down by the lottery kiosk outside (ch. 47–48). He slips into the first person as if he had been there (ch. 52, 76), and the talk ends on an act ("Which manuscript?") (04, 05). The old man in The reading room, continued and The final conversation can borrow the turn.

21. Where is the thesis stated, and does it hurt? Ch. 118, about 2,500 words of notes on a plane after the climax. It stalls on purpose, because the action is over (07). Ch. 7's essay on credulity states it early and is slow too (01).

22. Is any lore delivered as an object? Ardenti's theory comes as a stack of objects: a newspaper, a ledger, a sheet that falls out of a book, a cipher wheel (ch. 17–20, 02). Lia's laundry list is a document on the table (ch. 106, 06). The last reveal is Belbo's juvenilia behind a key (ch. 119, 07). All of these fit SDF's rule that reveals are objects.

Structure and cost

23. Why can't Casaubon stop? Is it the same reason throughout? No. Early on the reasons are borrowed: a missing friend, a dead colonel, a phrase from a psychic. From ch. 75 on, each reason is something the heroes made, a lie or a gap or a bait already taken (map section 2). SDF's Part Two needs the same switch.

24. Does the engine ever idle? Yes. In Brazil (ch. 28–33) Casaubon simply stops, flying kites for a year, and only the frame keeps the pull (03). That is the honest equivalent of James receiving documents in The drill and The money.

25. What is the most effective cost scene? Ch. 78–80. While Salon talks tunnels, Casaubon plots, and he gets home to a note on the kitchen table: Lia gave birth without him. The Plan's first cost is private and an hour long (05). It is the model for costing James time with Ana rather than putting him in danger.

26. How does the order handle Belbo once he has baited them? It frames him. His own train jokes and clothes become witness evidence, a police sketch is made, a firecracker of a car bomb scares off the inspector, and Garamond proves to be inside (ch. 108–109, 06). They never stop him talking. They make his story unbelievable, and that is SDF's "discredit, not prevent."

27. Who is the reliable witness? Gudrun, "never part of our story" (ch. 118, 07). For SDF: the widow in Zwolle in The other ten, already on the page in v7.

28. Does Eco ever confirm the conspiracy is real? No. The Provins message is a laundry list (ch. 106) and the museum shows no trace, but two people are dead and Garamond is missing (ch. 118, 07). The Plan is false and the believers are real. SDF is different, because its organization is real, so take the ambiguity only for individual results (the psychic, ch. 25).

Transfer specifics

29. Which proposal is strongest, and why? 5.1 (On land → The schedule): it fixes the exact gap the pipeline names (no gate, no cost of being wrong) on a scene that is already planned. The hook is a shelfmark in the depot's format, the readout is the Groningen dealer choosing to call James, and the cost lands on the dealer (06 for the hook; 02 for the gate).

30. Does 5.1 break the rule that doors open only when a person chooses? No. The dealer chooses to call; James asks nobody for anything and reads nothing he isn't given. Aylin's visitor book in The sheets is shown to him by Aylin (v7 draft).

31. Can James plant a fake edit to catch someone? Only in an invented book. Never in a real one (v8.2 Part 0). Every bait in map section 5 is an invented title, an invented company or a word.

32. Why does 5.2's cost fall on Anneke's trust? Because Eco's cost for a canary is the lie about the source (ch. 76), and the person who watched James tell it is the one he most needs to believe his paper. Her delay in The sheets feeds The leak, so the cost moves the plot.

33. Doesn't 5.3 hand James too many baits? Two at most, and they must differ, or neither can be read (the psychic problem, ch. 25). If Santi keeps only one, keep 5.1. PLACEHOLDER.

34. Where does Part Two still lack a negative result? In The money, The band and Frank, loose (v7), James is right every time. Map 5.4 gives him one wrong weekend in The band that costs him in front of Frank. That answers Rule 2 of the SYNTHESIS (08 Research/Comps/00 — SYNTHESIS…).

35. Is there a fifth mechanism here worth testing? The frame (ch. 108–109, 06): the organization answers a probe by turning the prober's own habits into evidence against him. For SDF the material is already lying around: James's dry asides, the edited forum account, the tinfoil hat. PLACEHOLDER: whether Part Three uses it.

36. What should never be borrowed? Real people and orders as plotters, codes read into real books, Bacon's inserted line (ch. 73), and the Holocaust riff (ch. 100). The notes flag each one under "Flags" in 01–07.

books.author: Eco
books.title: The Name of the Rose
books.folder: 08 Research/Engines/Eco — The Name of the Rose
books.readfor: an archive that kills to keep a book unread
books.intro: Coverage: William Weaver's English translation (note 06 names the Warner Books 1984 printing; the others give no edition data). Read in full through six section notes (01–06, about 184,000 words), 11 Nov 2026; map written 12 Nov 2026. Anything from outside the notes is marked [from memory, not from the text]. Brief: an archive that kills to keep one book unread: how the library guards itself, who holds which part of the secret, and how a beaten guardian talks. Compared with SDF's foundation archive on top of the recovery site, its catalog and visitor book, Aylin, the one thing taken out of every book, and the final conversation. Standing-rule note: real popes and inquisitors are plotters (01–05). Eco invents the surviving text of a real lost work, Aristotle on comedy (02, 06): not an edit to a real book, but next door to SDF's line. William enters by stealth (02–04), plans leverage (03), and lets Berengar fear torture (02). Take none of it.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
In 1327 the Franciscan William of Baskerville and his novice Adso reach a rich abbey to prepare a meeting between pope and emperor. A monk has fallen from a wall, and over seven days more die, each tied to the library, which only the librarian and his assistant may enter. William works around the ban, maps the labyrinth from outside, gets in at night, and loses his glasses, a book, and the case to an inquisitor who burns the wrong people. On the last night he finds the hidden room and the blind monk Jorge, who has poisoned the one book he cannot bear to have read. Jorge eats it, and the library burns.

What makes it work: the archive's defense is a set of ordinary arrangements (a ban, a catalog that tells you nothing, two keepers who each know half), so every step William takes is a step around a person. And whenever William gets close, someone else pays first, so the clock is kept in bodies, not hours.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:
Step What William wants right now What he finds What it costs Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Day 1, Prime–Terce, 01) To do his errand A death half-told under the seal of confession; everything open but the library He is hired to uncover and, "if necessary," to cover He has accepted powers in public; the abbot's "And if that were all" Work around the ban
2 (Day 1, Sext–Vespers, 01) To see the library from the one room he may enter A chained catalog in order of arrival; shelfmarks only the librarian reads; a quarrel about laughter Jorge "does not remember" Malachi watches him The room reacted: blushes, a push, a blind man shouting A tidy answer (suicide); a watch on Berengar
3 (Day 2, Matins–Sext, 02) How Venantius died Tracks from the library; "finis Africae"; books called "lost" Only "act quickly" The body was carried out of the library, and every monk steers him off the desk Get in at night
4 (Day 2, Nones–Night, 02) A door A deadline (the legation); a heretic cellarer offered as a lead; a key by choice; a cipher, a stolen book, mirrors, drugged smoke Lenses stolen, Adso drugged, the abbot's trust The cipher is half-read; Berengar is missing New lenses; a method for the maze
5 (Day 3, 03) The abbot's leave Refusal; Bernard Gui is coming; the lenses break A lost day Unsolved by tomorrow, the abbey goes to a man who burns people Map the library from outside
6 (Day 3, Night, 03) Who walks at night The cellarer's trade; Berengar drowned A third death; the pattern looks real It predicts a fourth Question the cellarer
7 (Day 4, Lauds–Terce, 04) How Berengar died A poison swallowed on purpose They eat only from the common plate "After Berengar we are the ones who know most" Rebuild the book from other books
8 (Day 4, Compline–Day 5, Prime, 04) Into the hidden room Deduced from the plan; the mirror won't open; Bernard arrests the girl; Malachi hands him papers William does not defend her Bernard's story stands unless William solves it The trial
9 (Day 5, Terce–Sext, 05) The "strange book" Severinus dead. William held the book and set it aside: he wanted Greek, its first pages were Arabic Benno walks off with it It exists, and kills Chase it through people
10 (Day 5, Nones–Vespers, 05) What the trial gives up A false confession; Benno made assistant librarian, hands the book back Mission failed; the girl will burn The case is closed wrong and he knows it Everything onto the book
11 (Day 6, Matins–Prime, 05) Who holds it now Malachi dead; Jorge, not Malachi, knew what the books meant The official answer collapses The last man who knows is the abbot Back to the catalog
12 (Day 6, Sext–Nones, 06) Which book, who guarded it Handwriting changes date the librarians; the text filed among disreputable titles Expelled at dawn One night left; the abbot is next In tonight
13 (Day 6–Day 7, Night 1, 06) To get in A key from Adso's joke; Jorge waiting; William's pattern was false and Jorge used it The abbot dies in the wall as they talk The book is in his hands and offered A duel of explanations
14 (Day 7, Night 2–Last Page, 06) The book Jorge eats it; the lamp burns the library Everything; "my method failed" Nothing left Adso's "lesser library" of scraps

Read down "cannot stop." Until Day 5 it is held by other people's clocks (legation, inquisitor, expulsion). From Day 5 it is held by William's own mistake (step 9) and a false solution he can see through (step 10). That switch, from other people's clocks to the hero's error, is what the ADDENDUM wants for Part Two.

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
• The abbot on the library (Day 1, about 900 words, 01): a speech in a negotiation that ends in "no."
  • The catalog (Day 1; Day 6, about 900 words, 01, 06): an object on a chain. The second reading uses a method (hands, dates, paper) and ends in a name.
  • The labyrinth (Day 2, Night, about 4,000 words; Day 4, about 3,500, 02, 04): walked, a shock a page; the second tour ends at a wall. The best delivery in the book.
  • Jorge's reasons (Day 7, about 1,700 words, 06): pure argument, held up by an open poisoned book on the table.

Where it stalls: the John XXII table talk (Day 4, Sext, 04); Adso admits it "does not add much." Where it doesn't: Remigio's trial (Day 5, Nones, about 5,500 words, 05), which is the same Dolcino history that stalled on Day 3, now with a life at stake in every answer. The same material moves when someone in the room can lose by it.

sections.title: 4. The mechanism we came for: an archive guarding one book
sections.html:
Setup (Day 1, Terce, 01). No door divides scriptorium from library; the ban must be stronger than a lock ("The library defends itself"). The catalog is public and useless without the room. Rule (03, 05). The keeper's creed: learning stays unsullied "only if it prevents its reaching anyone at all." After Malachi, monks "may consult the catalogue. Nothing else." Access is controlled at the catalog. First use (Day 2, 02). Soft before hard. The catalog lies about status, not existence ("ruined by mice"). Herbs and mirrors send intruders back with ghost stories. A body is moved to point away. Escalation (04, 05). Split custody: Malachi keeps the catalog without knowing what he guards; Jorge knows. The keepers hold everyone's secrets. The questioner is recruited (Benno). The book kills only those who want to read it. A true smaller secret (Remigio's letters, from the same vault) closes the case officially. Cost. The archive "now lives to bury" its books (Day 5, Vespers); Malachi dies by his own guard. Payoff (Day 7, 06). Jorge chose the room and hour. William explains; Jorge confirms, then offers the book as "your prize," poisoned. He picked William out by the question William never asked, and fed William's wrong pattern to Malachi so the deaths fit it. He fears not laughter or heretics ("their presence is precious to us") but one respectable text that turns the act into a plan. He destroys the book rather than lose it.

Against A–D.

  • A, the gate: supported. William sets his own (Day 4, Vespers); Bernard, with none, burns the wrong people. Every clock is a third party's. New: the rival investigator as the clock: waiting costs because a worse reader's answer becomes the official one.
  • B, the canary: supported, and it corrects the ADDENDUM's assumption that B needs an invented item. William announces loudly that nobody may touch Venantius's desk (Day 2, Terce) and by evening three monks have tried to steer him off it. One public sentence about a real object.
  • C, the front: stronger than in any Tier 1 book. Each solved layer covers the next (02, 03, 05), and the catalog files the forbidden text fourth in a binding, between jokes and an alchemist's ravings (06).
