It partly answers the ADDENDUM's verdict that C is only learned. It drives the plot when the official side accepts the smaller secret as the end and a death reopens it.
  • D, lock and key: steady; doors open by choice (02, 03). The final lock is a mechanism; in SDF it must be a person.

New mechanisms, checked against the ADDENDUM: split custody (05); the status lie (02); co-optation of the questioner (05); disable the reader, not the text, the glasses taken and the page left (02); the guard wears the hunter's theory (06); the truth filed among the nonsense (06).

sections.title: 5. Transfer to SDF
sections.html: Checked against v8.2, the v8 brief, the v7 Part Two and Three drafts, and v8 The night before and The final conversation. Already on the page, so not proposed: split custody (Aylin "never told what the last column means," v7 The sheets, is Malachi); a keeper who believes the creed ("heritage… somebody has to," same draft); "no one will believe you" ("what they are in a room is nothing," v7 The reading room, continued); the public sentence that makes a watcher move (James lays the sheets "to see which one made the woman by the window move," same draft); co-opting James (Leave it; the five seats); laughter against the beaten head ("Walt fucking Disney," v8 The final conversation). Most of the section notes' own proposals fail canon: James cannot ask Aylin for anything before 2 December (02), and the lower floor is not hidden from him (04).

items.title: 1. Thursdays at the card index
items.html:
The reading room, continued → The sheets → The night before.

  • Change: the "Same time Thursday?" James says yes to (v7) gets a purpose: he reads the one thing any reader may consult, the card index, and dates it as William dates the librarians (Day 6, Sext, 06).
  • James does: across Part Three's Thursdays he reads drawers, not books. Five or six hands since 1931; "withdrawn for conservation" in later hands, clustered in review quarters; the first card in Aylin's hand dated nine years ago, the season of Kalder's library transfer (v7 gives her nine years at the desk; PLACEHOLDER whether the match is meant). Her own withdrawals, dated, go on her sheet.
  • Cost: Aylin. v7 says hers was the thinnest sheet, one James "couldn't make… say anything that would hurt her." Now it does, in her hand, and she watched him read it. Showing him the visitor book becomes the harder choice.
  • Already on the page? Partly: the Thursday and the card index (v7); "the cards squared to the edge of the desk" (v8 The night before). Nobody reads them.
  • Already proposed? No. Borges 1 and Orwell 4 use "withdrawn for conservation" on outside copies, not the depot's catalog.

items.title: 2. The man at Pieter's door brings a better seat
items.html:
The leak → The night before.

  • Change: the visit after the brewery man's report carries an offer: an amended allocation, a fourth place, for Pieter's mother. Benno's promotion (05), and an echo of Utrecht, 1993 ("not his mother; it's a budgeting thing").
  • James does: tells Pieter on the phone to sign it, keep the copy, say nothing. The signed form, dated the night of the leak, goes into Anneke's envelope as the organization's own reply to the sheets.
  • Cost: Pieter signs his mother onto a list he now understands, at his kitchen table, with Marieke watching, on James's advice. PLACEHOLDER: does Pieter forgive it.
  • Already on the page? Partly. v7 The leak has the visit, the tea, "likes lists," a card. No offer, no paper.
  • Already proposed? No. Pairs with Orwell 6. Risk: James as manipulator; Pieter must be free to refuse.

items.title: 3. What they kept, filed in the nonsense they fund
items.html:
The band → The reading room, continued → The final conversation.

  • Change: one cold-year grantee, an invented press of channelled-wisdom paperbacks, prints in a book's middle the original wording of one of the forty-one entries, credited to a spirit guide. Filed like Jorge's book, among company nobody hears (06).
  • James does: buys the back list because he reads middles, finds the sentence, and lays the paperback at the reading-room table as an eighth item. It is the only one the old man picks up; he reads the cover copy aloud, and Anneke smiles.
  • Cost: being right in the wrong binding. He has handed Anneke a reason to put him with the clowns. In The sheets her "the rest of it" leaves the paperback out. PLACEHOLDER: kept there on purpose ("took out of every book and kept"), or a crank owned a first impression.
  • Already on the page? Partly: "Nobody reads the middle." / "I read the middle" (v8 The final conversation), with no object behind it.
  • Already proposed? No, but it competes with Foucault 5.2 (a fake among the sheets) and 5.4 (a negative in the grants). Take one. This is the one where he is right and still pays.

items.title: 4. The beaten head's last act is a status line, and James finally asks
items.html:
The vet → The final conversation.

  • Change: James never asks for the shelfmark. The ledger is on the tray before he can, and v7 The sheets says of his line: "No shelfmark; I hadn't asked for one." Noor's "nobody has ever simply asked" and the thin book's Ask are never paid. Jorge destroys rather than lose; the SDF-sized version: on his last day with keys the old man marks that shelfmark's card "withdrawn for conservation," in his own hand.
  • James does: when the old man has gone, asks Aylin for the item by number. She strikes the status through, initials it, and brings it to a table that was empty all scene.
  • Cost: his name enters the "shelfmark requested" column beside the professor's March line, in a book that will outlast Anneke's eighteen months; Aylin has overruled the old man on a card anyone can read. PLACEHOLDER: what the item is and whether he opens it. Keep v8's last line ("Pending" struck, nothing beside it).
  • Already on the page? Partly: Aylin books the room and writes in the book (v8); the column exists (v7 The sheets). The request does not.
  • Already proposed? No. Borges 1 and Foucault 5.1 use the same column for other moments.

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• William's methods: stealth entries, leverage on the cellarer and Salvatore, the torture he lets Berengar fear (02, 03).
  • A real lost book with invented contents, and real churchmen as plotters (01–06). Invent the hidden document outright.
  • The stalls Eco can afford: the Day 3 heresy block, the table talk, the dream (03–05). SDF's lore must reach someone who can lose by it within a page or two.

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
1. "No one should. No one can. No one, even if he wished, would succeed. The library defends itself" (Day 1, Terce) Guarded by belief.
  2. "though it did indeed exist in the catalogue, it had been ruined by mice fifty years earlier" (Day 2, Terce) The status lie.
  3. "not only committed Malachi to keep watch over the monks, but also set the monks themselves to keep watch over Malachi" (Day 2, Terce) A canary from one sentence.
  4. "Over the centuries it is no use at all. In a space of years or days it has some use." (Day 4, Terce) Hiding delays.
  5. "Now he is the guardian of those secrets he wanted to know" (Day 5, Vespers) Co-optation.
  6. "Malachi kept the catalogue and went up into the library, but Jorge knew what each title meant." (Day 6, Prime) Split custody.
  7. "Speak of it, if you wish: no one will believe you." (Day 6, Nones) Discredit, not prevent.
  8. "I conceived a false pattern to interpret the moves of the guilty man, and the guilty man fell in with it." (Day 7, Night 1) The guard wears the hunter's theory.

notes.title: section 01 (Prologue and First Day, Prime to Vespers)
notes.html:
Coverage: Prologue, then First Day from Prime to Vespers (about 32,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: William Weaver translation, converted text, chunk file 01; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Prime to Terce) To arrive with a reputation, then do his imperial errand Adelmo's death, which the abbot half-tells (he is bound by a confession), and a ban: the whole abbey is open to him except the library He is hired to uncover and also, if needed, to cover up. The one room where the death may have started is closed to him by a person, not a lock He has asked for and been given powers in front of the monks, and the abbot has said something he will not explain ("And if that were all") He works around the ban: Ubertino, then Severinus, then the scriptorium
2 (Sext to After Nones) To see the library through the only door he is allowed: the scriptorium A chained catalogue that lists every book but in order of arrival, shelfmarks that only the librarian can read, and a quarrel among the monks about a debate on Aristotle and laughter that Jorge says he "does not remember" He has shown his hand, and Malachi now watches him with suspicion The room has reacted. Berengar blushes, Venantius pushes, Malachi ends the scene, and a blind man shouts that the Antichrist is coming He walks the grounds instead of going to vespers
3 (Vespers) An explanation that needs as little as possible A glazier's rumours of a monk who saw serpents in the library at night, and lamps that cause visions. Then William's own answer: Adelmo jumped from the wall, and a landslide moved the body Being wrong. Adso has already warned that "the next morning" will undo the abbot (Terce) William's conclusion stands: they want nobody in the library at night, and many keep trying to get in Keep watch on Berengar. The library becomes the target

Why it grips

  • The detective proves himself before the case begins. Brunellus (Prime) is a small closed case: hoofprints, twigs broken at five feet, black hairs on a bramble. The best part is invented. He describes the head and eyes from Isidore, because monks see a fine horse the way the authorities describe one. William reads the world and how this community reads. He also slows his mule so the story reaches the gate first, so the method is a performance too.
  • The abbot's scene is built on what he will not say. William gets the closed windows from one fact, the burial in consecrated ground (Terce), then hits a wall: the abbot knows something under the seal of confession. The reader gets the outline of the secret and none of its contents.
  • The forbidden room is withheld all day. The reader gets its outside, the floor below and the rules, and nothing more. The waiting is built from a refusal.
  • A crowd gives itself away (After Nones): laughter at the marginalia, Jorge's rebuke, Venantius's "It is strange you should not remember", the word "dear" said to Berengar. Each reacts to one remark, and nobody explains any of it. William only reads the room.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

Section 01 is all setup, but it sets up exactly how the archive guards itself. The guard has layers, and only one of them is a lock:

  1. A prohibition, not a door. No door separates the scriptorium from the library; the abbot's ban must be stronger than any door (Vespers).
  2. An open but useless catalogue. Any monk may read it, but it runs by date of arrival, and its shelfmarks mean nothing without the room. The librarian decides who gets what (Terce, After Nones).
  3. Knowledge held by one living person. The plan goes from librarian to assistant only, which makes Berengar the weak point. William marks him by Vespers.
  4. Fear for the simple, rumour for everyone. Servants are kept out by hints of supernatural punishment (Terce). Nicholas reports a monk who came out of the labyrinth half mad, and night lights taken for dead librarians (Vespers). The secret is surrounded by stories that make anyone who looks for it seem gullible, which is SDF's method of discrediting instead of preventing.
  5. The confessor. Jorge hears many monks' confessions (After Nones) and is the one who "forgets" the Aristotle debate. The text does not link the two. [from memory, not from the text: Jorge is the guardian and the killer, and the book is Aristotle's lost second book of the Poetics, on comedy.] In this section the forbidden book is present only as a subject (laughter, Aristotle, "metaphors and puns and riddles") and as Jorge's anger.

Compare SDF. Aylin's archive already has layers 1 and 2: a public reading room, and a reference format James notes and does not connect (The drill). Layer 3 is the one to borrow: a keeper who knows what the catalogue cannot say. The reading room also sits on top of what it hides, as in Eco.

William and James. William states his method: signs, then the fewest causes ("less costly for our minds", Vespers). Ubertino gives James's advice: "question faces, do not listen to tongues" (Sext). Eco gives William both. He notices Severinus's "naturally" and lets it go, and he probes Salvatore with one word. For SDF: the method can be wrong where the nose was right. William's tidy suicide theory comes just after a room full of faces said otherwise.

How the lore gets in

  • Prologue politics (about 1,500 words, summary): stalls, held only by the promise of terrible events.
  • The abbot on the library (about 900 words, speech in a negotiation): no stall. William wants entry and the speech ends in a refusal, so the lore is the obstacle.
  • The portal (about 2,000 words, ekphrasis): a deliberate stall that pays off when Adso reads the abbey into the carvings and Salvatore breaks in.
  • History of the Spirituals (about 2,500 words, Adso's thoughts): the longest stall, held because Ubertino stands waiting.
  • The catalogue (about 500 words, an object chained to a desk): read in William's hands through his lenses.
  • Nicholas's rumours (about 600 words, gossip): rules arrive as hearsay that the speaker doubts.

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate), in reverse. William rules out the bigger explanation (murder) before acting (Vespers), and Adso has warned it will cost him. For SDF: a gate convinces more if James once passes it wrongly.
  • B (canary), near version. "Apostles" makes Salvatore flee (Sext); "visions" makes Severinus stiffen (Toward Nones). One word is dropped to see who reacts. No invented item is needed, and James can do this without pressuring anyone.
  • D (lock and key). Malachi will not decode the shelfmarks (After Nones). In SDF, Aylin's one truth could be a location rather than a document.
  • C (front), weak. The abbot's request to cover things up makes the inquiry itself a cover.
  • Fifth: rumour as a guard. The keepers let the library be haunted instead of denying its secrets. That is close to SDF's funded nonsense.

Quotes

  • "Acute in uncovering, and prudent (if necessary) in covering." (Day 1, Terce): the investigator is hired by the institution under investigation.
  • "But a list of titles often tells very little; only the librarian knows, from the collocation of the volume, from its degree of inaccessibility" (Day 1, Terce): a public catalogue and a private key.
  • "No one should. No one can. No one, even if he wished, would succeed. The library defends itself" (Day 1, Terce): the archive guarded by belief.
  • "Often the learned man must make seem magic certain books that are not magic, but simply good science, in order to protect them from indiscreet eyes." (Day 1, Vespers): hiding a secret by making it look absurd.

Flags

  • Real historical people speak and are spoken of as plotters: John XXII, the curia trying to assassinate Ubertino (his claim, Sext), and Ubertino's later murder "by a murderer never discovered". SDF must not name real people as complicit.
  • The library list mixes real and invented titles. William's doubts about De plantis and De causis are real scholarship. No invented edits on real books in this section.

notes.title: section 02 (First Day, Compline, to Second Day, Night)
notes.html:
Coverage: First Day, Compline, through Second Day, Night (about 31,300 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: William Weaver translation, converted text, chunk file 02; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Day 2, Matins to Sext) To know how Venantius died A body in the pig's blood, dragged tracks from the Aedificium, Berengar's "ghost" story, Benno's "finis Africae" (a catalogue mark for books Malachi calls "lost") Nothing yet except the abbot's "act quickly" The body was carried out of the library, and every monk tries to keep him from Venantius's desk He has to get into the library at night, and needs a lamp and a way in
2 (Day 2, Nones to After Vespers) Permission, or at least a door The abbot sets a deadline (the papal legation) and offers the cellarer's heretic past as a lead; Alinardo, treated as senile, gives the ossarium key The investigation now risks the meeting he came to arrange; the abbot may lose his sovereignty to French archers William reads the heresy lead as a cover for the library, and the abbot's ban as proof there is something there He enters through the ossarium after Compline
3 (Day 2, Compline and Night) To read Venantius's papers and see the library A page in invisible ink with a zodiac cipher; a book stolen from under him; mirrors, drugged smoke, wind that moans; a maze he cannot map His lenses are stolen, Adso is drugged, they are almost trapped, and the abbot catches them coming back The cipher is half-read ("Secretum finis Africae"), and Berengar is missing at Matins A third death is coming; he needs new lenses and a method for the maze

Why it grips

  • The clock is the liturgy. Each chapter is an hour of the office, and the legation's deadline (Nones) sits on top of it.
  • Every witness steers. Benno points to the library to keep William from the desk; the abbot points to heresy to keep him from the library; a thrown book pulls him away from the desk (Compline). William says each steer out loud, so the reader follows both what is said and why.
  • The best scene, built in three beats (Compline): William finds a page; Adso's clumsiness with the lamp brings out hidden writing (an accident does the revealing, no genius needed); the intruder takes the glasses, not the page. He leaves the document in William's hand and takes away his ability to read it.
  • Fear, then a laugh. Each horror in the library ends with William explaining it ("A mirror!", the wind slits), except the drugged vision, which is the one that hurts Adso.
  • Method admitted to fail. Asked if his maze rule works, William says "Almost never" (Night); they find the stairs by luck.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The hidden order is the library's self-defence, and here it acts in layers, from soft to hard:

  1. The catalogue lies about status, not existence. Entries are real, in marks "that only the librarian understands" (Prime); asking gets "lost", or Jorge's "ruined by mice" (Terce). The record is findable; the shelf is closed.
  2. The building discourages. The east tower corner of the scriptorium is the coldest, so nobody sits near the only stair up (Terce, Adso's guess).
  3. Stagecraft that turns witnesses into madmen. Herbs, mirrors, moaning wind, a lit thurible to suggest the dead walk. Aymaro says it outright: the powers of hell are used "to derange the minds of the curious" (Terce). Whoever gets in comes back with a ghost story, like Berengar. The archive discredits visitors rather than stopping them: SDF's organisation in miniature.
  4. The body points away. William reads the dragged trail: the killer "does not want attention to be concentrated on the library" (Matins). The death is staged to point away.
  5. Power offers a front. The abbot ties the murders to the Franciscans' politics and hands William a heretic cellarer. William: "So he offers me the suggestion of the cellarer, to distract my attention from the Aedificium" (Nones).

It makes William break the abbot's ban, and it makes him pay: the lenses, Adso's health, the abbot's trust.

How the lore gets in

  • Benno's account of the laughter quarrel (Prime, about 1,200 words, conversation). The lost Poetics book arrives as gossip and ends on "finis Africae" and a librarian's lie. No stall.
  • Aymaro on abbey politics (Terce, about 800 words, spite in the kitchen). It slows a little, then ends on a warning ("be careful at night").
  • The Avignon negotiation (Nones, about 2,500 words, summary plus debate). The longest still stretch, and it stalls for a page or two. It earns its place by ending in a deadline, and because the heresy argument is also the abbot steering.
  • The library's layout (Night, about 4,000 words, walked). The lore comes as rooms crossed, with a shock about every page. No stall.
  • Cryptography (Compline, about 600 words, lecture). The page is in his hand and the lenses are gone, so the lecture is the only way forward.

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate), present as a deadline plus a ban. William must rule out the abbot's alternative (the heretic cellarer) before the legation arrives; if he is wrong, the abbey goes under French control. For SDF: a gate gets weight from a third party's deadline that James does not control.
  • B (canary), a clean, legal version. In Terce William says loudly that nobody may touch Venantius's desk. It "set the monks themselves to keep watch over Malachi", and by After Vespers Malachi, Benno and Berengar have each tried to steer him away, so they have shown themselves. PROPOSAL for The reading room, continued (/home/santi/somethingdoesntfit/01 Manuscript/v7/45 — The reading room, continued.md; no v8 draft yet): James asks Aylin, in front of others, for a record the catalogue marks as damaged; who answers, how fast and with which excuse is the find. No forbidden act. Cost: he has shown his hand, and the next document arrives already arranged.
  • C (front), three times. Benno's library tip covers his desire for the desk; the abbot's heresy lead covers the library; the thrown book covers the theft. Each cover is true enough to follow.
  • D (lock and key). Alinardo gives the key because William sits with him (price: chickpeas); Nicholas will make lenses because he wants to try something new. Each door opens by choice.
  • Fifth: disable the reader, not the text. The thief leaves the page and takes the glasses. SDF's organisation could leave James the document and take his access, his credibility, or the one colleague who reads the format.
  • Method vs nose. William's method is real (snow tracks, drowned faces), but his best moves are nose: the abbot's glare means "another door does exist" (First Day, Compline); Severinus pauses "too long" (Matins); the cipher starts from a guess. That is James's skill. But William also presses: he lets Berengar fear torture (Prime). James may not.

Quotes

  • "not only committed Malachi to keep watch over the monks, but also set the monks themselves to keep watch over Malachi" (Day 2, Terce): a canary made by one public sentence.
  • "though it did indeed exist in the catalogue, it had been ruined by mice fifty years earlier" (Day 2, Terce): the catalogue lies about status, not existence.
  • "the first rule in deciphering a message is to guess what it means." (Day 2, Compline): the method starts from the nose.
  • "Knowledge is used to conceal, rather than to enlighten." (Day 2, Night): the archive's whole way of defending itself.

Flags

  • Real people. Pope John XXII is called a necromancer who feeds hosts to his morays (Alinardo, After Vespers), and real churchmen and princes (Michael of Cesena, Louis, Arnald Amalric and Béziers) are written into the plot. SDF must not do this.
  • Real book, invented copy. The lost second book of the Poetics is a real gap; the plot hints a copy survives here. Not an edit to a real book, but close to SDF's line.
  • Pressure. William gets Berengar's confession by letting him fear torture (Prime). This is forbidden for James.

notes.title: section 03 (Third Day, Lauds to Night)
notes.html:
Coverage: the whole Third Day, from "From Lauds to Prime" to "Night" (about 30,300 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: William Weaver translation, converted text, chunk file 03; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Lauds to Vespers) William wants new lenses to read Venantius's Greek notes, and the abbot's leave to enter the library The cipher opens onto a riddle. The abbot refuses the library and announces the inquisitor Bernard Gui is coming. The lenses break A lost day, and an investigation now held "within the limits I have established" If the killer is not found by tomorrow, the abbey passes to Gui, who will burn people William maps the library from outside, counting windows, so he can go in without permission
2 (After Compline) Adso wants to know who Dolcino was, then to enter the library alone Dolcino's story and burning, his memory of a friar burned in Florence, then a village girl in the kitchen and a bundle with a heart in it His vows; he faints He now knows that someone uses the abbey at night and trades food for sex He confesses to William, which turns his sin into evidence
3 (Night) William wants to know who the girl was meeting By reasoning he names the cellarer or Salvatore. Alinardo's trumpet prophecy leads them to the baths, where Berengar lies drowned A third death; the apocalypse pattern now looks real The pattern says a fourth death is due, and the cellarer's secret gives William a handle on him Questioning the cellarer; following the trumpets

Why it grips

  • The stall is named, then paid for. The first hour's title ends "and that is all". Eco tells the reader nothing happens, and Berengar's absence then hangs over a whole day of lectures. The open question is answered on the last page, so the lore never quite reads as dead time.
  • A clock and a worse detective. The abbot's letter (Vespers) makes the case urgent: solve it by tomorrow or the inquisitor takes over. Gui wants a confession, not the truth. Losing to a rival investigator means people burn.
  • Small payoffs inside long talk. The heresy lecture (Nones) ends with William saying, "By the way", that he has cracked the cipher. The decoded line is itself a riddle. Each gain comes with a new lock.
  • Method and nose, side by side. William works from the outside: windows counted, "first let us find the rule, then we will try to explain the exceptions", fifty-six rooms on a tablet. Adso works by drift: he goes in with no plan, gets lost, and stumbles on the night traffic the method could not have predicted. His throwaway "There are only the baths" finds the body. The nose supplies the stray fact and the method places it; SDF could split James's two sides between James and whoever reasons beside him.
  • One scene does the most work. The kitchen at night (After Compline) gathers everything Adso heard that day and ends on an object, the heart. William's laugh ("what man could have such a big heart?") turns horror into a clue about the abbey's economy.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The hidden order in this section is the library's withholding, and on the Third Day it acts through access, not violence. The catalogue is open: Adso leafs through it "after obtaining Malachi’s permission". The shelves are not. The abbot denies the library has anything to do with the murders. The building is designed to lose people ("The maximum of confusion achieved with the maximum of order"). Adso's Terce meditation gives the archive its justification: knowledge wears out with use, so keeping it means keeping it from everyone. A foundation reading room that sits on a bank's recovery site could claim the same thing ("we keep it safe; safe means unread"), and Aylin could believe it sincerely.

It forces William round the gatekeeper (the outside map) and sets the clock, because the abbot hides the case to keep his power and so rations William. Berengar's body is hidden rather than displayed, and William's comment that the searchers "were looking for a corpse lying somewhere theatrically" says outright that this order hides some deaths and displays others.

A second order sits on top: the inquisition, which discredits rather than refutes. William explains (Nones) that the inquisitors "attribute to one the errors of the other", so every reform movement is made to look like the most violent one. That is SDF's clown beside every real question, practised as policy.

How the lore gets in

  • Adso's scriptorium meditation (Terce), about 1,200 words, interior. The story stops, but this is the archive's thesis, tied to watching hands at work.
  • Salvatore's life (Sext), about 3,500 words, reported speech. Mostly texture. It ends on a hook: at Dolcino's name he crosses himself and leaves.
  • William's heresy lecture (Nones), about 4,000 words, dialogue at a workbench. It stalls, broken up by lens-grinding and Adso pushing back, and ends with the cipher reveal.
  • The abbot's letter (Vespers), about 1,000 words. An object that turns politics into a deadline. No stall.
  • The library geometry (Vespers), about 1,500 words, a walk with a tablet. The lore is a task: Adso draws as he is told. It ends with a plan for tonight.
  • Ubertino on Dolcino, the written history, and Michael's burning (After Compline), about 8,000 words together. A conversation, a document found on a desk, and a memory. The longest stall so far, held up by Ubertino's unsettling closeness and by Adso climbing the stairs as he remembers. It pays off when the same words for flame return in the sex scene: the lore causes the act.

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate), inverted. The abbot's gate is a permission: show the library connects or stay out. William goes in by stealth instead, which SDF forbids. Usable version: Aylin opens a shelf only when James can show the connection.
  • B (canary), seed. Alinardo's apocalypse pattern is a story an old man believes, and William half-adopts it ("whether there were not some element of truth"). It finds the body. [from memory, not from the text: later the killer follows the pattern because William believes it, a canary that works backwards on the detective.] For SDF: the organisation may plant a pattern for James to "discover".
  • C (front), clear here. The cellarer's night trade (sex for offal) and his possible Dolcinian past are a real secret that explains strange movement at night but not the murders. One solved layer is the cover story for the next. The abbot's fear of Gui is another: political scandal covers the book.
  • D (lock and key). Salvatore hands Adso a lamp unasked ("Peut-être your magister wants to go in dark place"): a helper opens a door by choice, which fits SDF. William's leverage plan does not.
  • Fifth: the edited record. Brother Michael protests that his written confession has been altered by the notary. William tells Adso that the story of Francis preaching to sweet birds is one "the order has revised today", when the original audience was carrion birds. Two institutional edits of the record in one day: SDF's "given" into "arose", already a background fact.

Quotes

  • "can maintain this learning unsullied only if it prevents its reaching anyone at all, even the monks themselves" (Third Day, Terce): the keeper's creed, preservation as withholding.
  • "The maximum of confusion achieved with the maximum of order: it seems a sublime calculation." (Third Day, Vespers): the archive's defence is its design.
  • "Michael protested that the notary had now added “many false consequences”" (Third Day, After Compline): an edited record as a weapon.
  • "if there is need, the cellarer and Salvatore are ours" (Third Day, Night): the detective's leverage, which James may not use.

Flags

  • Real historical figures appear as persecutors (John XXII, Bernard Gui, Clement V). That is recorded history, not complicity in the fictional murders.
  • William's stealth entry and his leverage plan break SDF's rules against breaking in and pressure.
  • No invented edits on real books.

notes.title: section 04 (Fourth Day, Lauds, to Fifth Day, Prime)
notes.html:
Coverage: Fourth Day, Lauds, to Fifth Day, Prime, ending mid-debate (about 34,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: William Weaver translation, converted text, chunk file 04; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Day 4, Lauds–Prime) How Berengar died Black fingers and tongue: a poison swallowed on purpose. A poison vanished from Severinus's shelves years ago; Severinus asked Malachi about it in the secret books He and Adso become targets and eat only from the common plate The killer kills whoever knows, and "After Berengar we are the ones who know most" He questions everyone who walks at night
2 (Day 4, Prime–Terce) Who walks at night Salvatore and Remigio are ex-Dolcinians; Venantius died in the kitchen and was moved; Berengar had the lenses; Venantius's notes, decoded, stay obscure He swears silence to two heretics on the eve of the Inquisition The motive is a book he doesn't have; he must reconstruct it from other books Reading at Venantius's desk, then the library at night
3 (Day 4, After Compline, to Day 5, Prime) Into the finis Africae The library is a map of the world; the walled room is deduced from the plan. Bernard arrests Salvatore and the girl; at dawn Malachi hands Bernard papers The door won't open. Adso loses the girl; William does not defend her Bernard now has a necromancy story to use against the Minorites. If William doesn't solve it, Bernard's version stands The debate, then Bernard's inquiry

Why it grips

  • The door is found before it can be opened. The night tour is about 3,500 words of shelf-reading, carried by its purpose. It ends when mirror room S proves to be the tower with no heptagon. William argues from space (without the room the others would be larger), so the hidden room arrives as a deduction. Then the mirror won't move. The reader knows where the secret is and cannot reach it.
  • Questioning a man with numbers. William lets Remigio reel off measures of land, oil and wine, then asks again, "How much did you say a square trabucco was?" (Prime). Each time the dull question comes back, it carries the Inquisition's threat.
  • Two investigators side by side. Bernard questions only servants and lay brothers and uses "the fear of others" (Nones). William admits at Vespers that he beat Brunellus by luck. Adso, tired of not knowing, thinks "Good thing the inquisitor has come." Bernard's certainty condemns the girl that night.
  • Funny throughout. Salvatore's black-cat spell, two bishops brawling over Christ's purse.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The hidden order is the library and whoever controls who reads what.

  1. It explains why hiding works only for a while. Adso asks why anyone hides books when the open ones lead to the hidden ones. William answers that hiding is useless over centuries and useful over days, and agrees the library exists to delay the truth (Terce). An archive that delays the truth instead of destroying it is SDF's foundation. It also explains SDF's premise: if open books lead to the hidden one, the open books have to be edited.
  2. It puts the keeper in league with the inquisitor. Malachi holds Remigio's secret ("Does he know something about you?" "Yes."), cannot refuse William a reading, and at Fifth Day Prime hands Bernard papers in the fog. His power is knowing everyone's secrets and deciding who reads, which is what Aylin's visitor book could hold.
  3. It discredits rather than prevents. Bernard doesn't stop the meeting. He turns an innocent bundle (cat, eggs, a cockerel that looks black at night) into witchcraft with a lecture on sources, and William expects him to hold it back to wreck the talks later. The debate also wrecks itself: Jerome repeats a rumour he admits he hasn't seen, and a brawl breaks out while Bernard smiles. This is SDF's clown beside the real question, shown working.

How the lore gets in

  • Severinus on poisons (Lauds), about 900 words, talk over the body. It ends in the black tongue and a missing jar. No stall.
  • Remigio's Dolcino story (Prime), about 700 words, a confession under pressure. It ends in a fact: Venantius dead by the sink. No stall.
  • Venantius's notes (Terce), about 100 words, a document. The lore comes in fragments. William's point that the nature of the stolen object shows the nature of the killer turns them into a motive.
  • Adso's love meditation (Terce), about 3,000 words. A deliberate stall while William reads; the weakest stretch.
  • The John XXII table talk (Sext), about 4,000 words. Adso admits it "does not add much". Its one plant is John's doctrine that the dead won't see God before the Judgment, which pays off at Night when William jokes that Saint Francis may be "waiting for judgment day". Its subject is what happens after death, as in SDF, but it comes as gossip.
  • The library walk (After Compline), about 3,500 words, a tour with a map. The lore comes as walking and reading the letters over the doors, and it ends at the walled room. The best delivery in the section.
  • The poverty debate (Day 5, Prime), about 3,500 words. Argument that turns into a brawl.

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate). William sets his own gate: "rather than appear foolish afterward, I renounce seeming clever now" (Vespers). Bernard shows what acting without one costs: he takes the obvious explanation, and the girl pays. PLACEHOLDER for SDF: James reads a pause as guilt and someone else pays, before he learns to rule out the bigger explanation. Part Two currently has no cost for being wrong.
  • D (lock and key), literally. The finis Africae opens only to one correct reading of one text (idolum as the image in the mirror). William has half of it. In SDF the lock can be a person who opens it when James reads a document correctly.
  • C (front). Venantius's notes first read as Dolcinian instructions, which is the cover story tied to Remigio. The figs, stone and cicadas don't fit that reading, which points to a different book underneath.
  • B (canary). William doesn't use one. Bernard does the reverse: he dresses a harmless object up as evil and watches who flinches.
  • Fifth: finding the absence in a plan. The hidden room is found from the building's symmetry. PROPOSAL for "The reading room" or "The sheets": Aylin's catalogue skips a run of shelfmarks, and the lower floor James knows from The drill appears nowhere in it. He reads the gap himself. The door opens only when Aylin decides to show him the visitor book. Not on the page yet.
  • Method against nose. Here the reader of faces is the inquisitor, whose weapon is the fear he sees. James's nose is nearer Bernard's skill than William's method, so his gift can do harm.

Quotes

  • "Over the centuries it is no use at all. In a space of years or days it has some use." (Day 4, Terce): the archive delays the truth.
  • "The room exists, but cannot be reached." (Day 4, After Compline): the hidden room deduced from the plan.
  • "But instead of conceiving only one, I imagine many, so I become the slave of none." (Day 4, Vespers): William's method.
  • "He will keep it in reserve: it will be of use later, to upset the progress of the discussions" (Day 4, Night): discredit, don't prevent.

Flags

  • Real historical people get invented speech and charges: John XXII (perjury, greed, the penance tariff Jerome repeats), Bernard Gui, Michael of Cesena, Bertrand del Poggetto. The deaths of Clement V and Philip the Fair are treated as suspicious (Sext). SDF must not name real people as complicit.
  • The library shelves Virgil of Toulouse under Hibernia ("They corrected the errors of nature."). That is a misfiling, not an edit to a text, so there is no invented edit on a real book here.

notes.title: section 05 (Fifth Day, Terce, to Sixth Day, Terce)
notes.html:
Coverage: Fifth Day, Terce, to Sixth Day, Terce (about 33,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: William Weaver translation, converted text, chunk file 05. The file gives no other edition data.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Day 5, Terce–Sext) The "strange book" Severinus has found Severinus killed. The book was in the room, but William set it aside: he wanted Greek, and its first pages were Arabic His shout across the narthex sent the cellarer running. Benno takes the book He held the book. He now knows it exists and must be handled with gloves He chases the book through people (Benno, Malachi), not through rooms
2 (Day 5, Nones–Vespers) To see what the trial gives up Bernard gets Remigio to confess to murders he did not commit. Benno takes the assistant librarian's post and hands the book to Malachi His mission fails, Ubertino flees, the girl will burn, his ally switches sides The case is officially closed with the wrong answer, and William knows it ("he isn't, not at all") He moves everything onto the "forbidden book"
3 (Day 6, Matins–Prime) To know who holds the book now Malachi dies at matins with black fingers ("a thousand scorpions"). Nicholas: librarians become abbots, and Jorge, not Malachi, knew what the books meant The false solution falls apart. Greek readers are targets, "Including me" A next victim is predicted, and the only living person who holds the library's secrets is the abbot Back to the scriptorium to re-read Venantius's books

Why it grips

  • The detective's mistake is the engine. The book is lost because of William's method, not bad luck. He was filtering for Greek and threw out a bound volume of several texts whose first pages were Arabic. He corrects himself by recalling Severinus's exact word, "strange" (Day 5, Sext), so the method is rescued by remembering what someone actually said. That is close to James's nose. The error has a price: the book moves on, and in the next section the man holding it dies. SDF lacks exactly this, a hero whose mistake gets someone hurt.
  • A false answer arrives before the true one. Bernard's trial (Day 5, Nones) gives the abbey a guilty man, a confession and an end. The reader knows it is wrong because William says so. Malachi's death at matins (Day 6) then breaks the official story in front of everyone. A closed case that reopens is a stronger turn than an open case that stays open.
  • Still funny: "No, that's Arabic, idiot!"; the John the Baptist skull "at the age of twelve"; William's whisper that Jorge's Antichrist "seems his own portrait".

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The archive protects its book three ways, and this section shows all of them working.

  1. The book defends itself. Readers die with black fingers. Severinus put on gloves; Malachi held the book and did not. Nobody has to be present for the guarding to work, and that is how the library can kill so rarely in person.
  2. It recruits the curious. Malachi does not threaten Benno. He makes him assistant librarian, and Benno hands the book back. William: "Now he is the guardian of those secrets he wanted to know." The person who asked questions becomes a keeper. Malachi also sets two keepers watching each other, and William copies the move by sending Benno to watch Malachi.
  3. It divides knowledge. Malachi keeps the catalogue but cannot read what it lists ("a guard dog ... with no knowledge of what he was guarding", Day 6, Prime). Jorge, who is blind, knows what each title means. The abbot orders that monks "may consult the catalogue. Nothing else." The catalogue is where access is controlled.

The secret is also tied to power: by tradition the librarian becomes abbot. Nicholas's gossip that they died "so that they would not become abbot" is a wrong explanation the reader cannot yet rule out.

Bernard models SDF's discrediting. Indifferent to who killed, he uses one confessed murderer to tie respected theologians to Dolcino's ravings (his "sixth sign" condemns "the authors of those books" heretics used). Every serious argument gets a madman beside it: SDF's clown beside every real question.

For Aylin (proposal). Which keeper is she, Malachi or Jorge? Eco's split suggests the reading room should have both: a visible keeper who runs the catalogue, and someone behind her who knows what the entries mean. James's nose would catch the keeper deferring. The treasure crypt under the church matches the reading room on the bank's recovery site: the relics are mostly fakes ("an entire forest") yet real wealth, so the foundation's worth need not depend on its holdings being true.

How the lore gets in

  • William's political speech (Day 5, Terce), about 2,000 words. Played as comedy and cut off by the archers' news.
  • Remigio's trial (Day 5, Nones), about 5,500 words, a scene. The Dolcino history comes in as a forced confession, with a life at stake in every answer. No stall: an oath counts as proof of guilt, and so does refusing one.
  • Jorge's sermon (Day 5, Compline), about 3,000 words, a public speech. It sets out the archive's ideology ("Preservation ... not search") and doubles as a warning to whoever is still reading. It stalls, but the reader knows it is a threat.
  • Nicholas in the crypt (Day 6, Prime), about 1,500 words, gossip during a tour. The succession history comes while he polishes glass cases, and the objects carry the scene.
  • Adso's dream (Day 6, Terce), about 3,500 words. A recap and the biggest stall, but it plants clues: "a book shaped like a scorpion", Jesus with black fingers handing out pages, and William's "You have already seen it!" [from memory, not from the text: the dream follows the Coena Cypriani, which later helps William].

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate), shown by its absence. William will not warn the abbot without "convincing evidence" (Day 6, Lauds). Bernard rules nothing out and burns the wrong man: what James becomes if he skips the gate.
  • C (front), strong. Remigio's Dolcino letters, hidden by Malachi "in the most inaccessible of the secret rooms of the library", are a real secret found in the same vault, and finding them closes the inquiry. A true but smaller secret serves as the cover story. Compare SDF's "findable" seat list: finding it should feel like the end of the hunt.
  • D (lock and key). Benno's key is the job. Nicholas talks because he has just been promoted and is proud. Remigio breaks when Bernard gives him a past he can own. Each door opens because the person chooses to open it.
  • B (canary), weak. William plants a fear of the book in Benno and watches who acts on it.
  • Fifth: co-optation. The organisation answers a questioner by giving him the job, not by killing him. Proposal for The reading room continued: Aylin offers James a small real role in the catalogue. Taking it gives him access but costs him the right to tell anyone, and refusing it marks him. Either way he pays.

Quotes

  • "This library was perhaps born to save the books it houses, but now it lives to bury them." (Day 5, Vespers): the archive's purpose turned upside down, in one line.
  • "Now he is the guardian of those secrets he wanted to know" (Day 5, Vespers): the questioner co-opted.
  • "Malachi kept the catalogue and went up into the library, but Jorge knew what each title meant." (Day 6, Prime): split custody.
  • "We looked, but did not see. Or else saw, but did not recognize." (Day 5, Sext): the method's blind spot.

Flags

  • Real people shown as complicit: Bernard Gui forces a false confession for political ends; Cardinal Bertrand del Poggetto, John XXII and Jacques Fournier are named as plotting and burning people; Adso says Ubertino was "mysteriously killed" two years later. SDF must not do this.
  • No invented edits on real books in this section.

notes.title: section 06 (Sixth Day after Terce to the Last Page)
notes.html:
Coverage: Sixth Day (After Terce, Sext, Nones, Between Vespers and Compline, After Compline), Seventh Day (both Night chapters) and the Last Page (about 23,700 words of story; the rest of the file is publisher matter), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: Warner Books, Weaver translation, 1984 printing.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Day 6, Sext to Nones) To confirm which book it is and who has guarded it The catalogue entry, a ten-year gap in the librarians' handwriting, Benno's "linen paper" The abbot will not listen, lectures on his ring, and expels him: leave at dawn A deadline, and William's warning that the last person who knows (the abbot) is the next victim He has one night to get into the finis Africae
2 (Day 6, After Compline, to Day 7, Night 1) To get in, and save "someone who does not deserve it" The key comes by accident from Adso's joke about a horse; Jorge is sitting there waiting with the book His apocalyptic pattern turns out to be false; the abbot dies in the wall while he listens The book is in his hands and Jorge is talking A duel of explanations, which Jorge has set up as a second trap
3 (Day 7, Night 2, to Last Page) The book itself Jorge eats it; in the struggle he flings the lamp and the library burns The library, the abbey, Benno and Alinardo; William cries and says his method failed Nothing left to chase Adso spends his life rebuilding a "lesser library" from scraps

Why it grips

  • A clock set by the wrong man. The abbot's dismissal (Day 6, Nones) gives the last act its deadline. William's fury on the stairs ("that inflated wineskin") keeps it funny while the stakes go up.
  • The withheld key comes from the sidekick, twice. Adso's dream points to the Coena Cypriani (After Terce). Adso's "tertius equi" gives away the mirror lock (After Compline). In both scenes the master's method only becomes useful once someone else blurts something out.
  • The confession scene is a seduction. Adso says outright that the two men admire each other (Day 7, Night 1). William does most of the explaining. The villain's speech comes only after the hero has earned it, and it is offered as a prize, "Here is your prize", in the form of a poisoned book. So the explanation is a weapon too: will William lick his finger?
  • The win becomes a loss on the page. The book is eaten in the dark, and the fire starts from a lamp knocked over in a scuffle.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The conspiracy here is one blind keeper and the people he controls through who holds each post: an abbot he got elected, two librarians he ran (Day 7, Night 1). Abo protects the abbey's honour and Jorge protects a book, and that clash is what kills the abbot. The abbot's reflex is SDF's organisation in one line: he does not deny the story, he tells William it will not be believed. Jorge's reasons go further than the abbot's. He does not fear laughter, heresy or rebels; he says "we know how to destroy them" and that "their presence is precious to us". He fears one respectable text that would turn what common people do into a learned doctrine ("Provided the act is not transformed into plan"). That is SDF's clown beside every real question, with the reason spelled out: the noise is useful; the danger is one document with authority.

The defence in this archive is reading. The poison only gets the people who want to read. Jorge picked out William by the question he never asked ("you never asked questions about the library"). SDF's nightly count of askers, turned around: Jorge counts the missing question.

How the lore gets in

  • The catalogue (Day 6, Sext), about 900 words, an object read with a method. Changes of handwriting and dated papal bulls set the order of the librarians. It ends in "Only some premises", and the linen-paper clue follows at once. No stall: a date points to a person.
  • The abbot's numerology and gems (Day 6, Nones), about 1,000 words, a speech as a power move. He dazzles Adso with the ring and orders him to "Swear"; William breaks in.
  • William's reconstruction (Day 7, Night 1), about 2,000 words, the hero's own explanation. The detective explains the deaths, the villain confirms; the open poisoned book keeps the pace.
  • Jorge's reasons (Day 7, Night 1), about 1,700 words, one monologue. It is the only long stretch of pure argument. Carried by six days of waiting and the threat on the table; William answers with insults and friar jokes.
  • The fire (Day 7, Night 2), about 3,500 words, a scene. Why the archive dies is physical: few entrances, untidy rooms, wind.
  • Last Page, about 2,000 words. History in a few paragraphs, then Adso's fragments: a deliberate, elegiac slowdown.

Mechanism notes

  • C (front), already in the catalogue. The forbidden text is the fourth item in a bound volume, between an Arab book of jokes, an alchemist's "ravings" and a Coena gloss, and it is listed as a book about virgins and prostitutes (Day 6, Sext). The disreputable company is the hiding place: "No one would lend an ear" (Day 7, Night 1). For SDF: what Aylin's catalogue hides could be filed inside the nonsense the organisation pays for, the entry true but unappealing.
  • Fifth: the guardian uses the investigator's theory. Jorge heard William believed in the seven trumpets and fed it to Malachi ("the power of a thousand scorpions"), so the deaths fit the pattern and the wrong theory became cover. The reverse of B. For SDF, a wrong theory of James's could come back to him as confirmation, and he pays for believing it: the missing cost of being wrong.
  • A (gate), as a clock. The expulsion forces a decision by morning, but no gate checks whether William is right. Eco then shows what that costs: William reaches the right man by a false route and says so himself ("I discovered it by mistake", Day 7, Night 2).
  • D (lock and key). The mirror opens with one exact truth ("quatuor"), but it is a mechanism; in SDF the lock must be a person.
  • The defeated head talks: a contrast with SDF. Jorge is not defeated when he talks. He chose the room and hour and talks to stall and tempt, and "wins" only by destroying the book and himself. SDF's old head, talking in defeat, still needs something on the table: an offer, a test, a thing he can destroy.
  • Method against nose. William's method works on objects (handwriting, dated bulls, paper). His nose (the right questions, listening for what people avoid) is what Jorge noticed. Breakthroughs come from another's chance remark. James, a nose, not a method, fits this ending better than William does. William's ladder you climb and throw away lets James be wrong and still arrive.

Quotes

  • "Speak of it, if you wish: no one will believe you." (Day 6, Nones): the guardian discredits instead of preventing.
  • "the victim poisoned himself when he was alone, and only to the extent that he wanted to read" (Day 7, Night 1): the defence works through reading.
  • "I conceived a false pattern to interpret the moves of the guilty man, and the guilty man fell in with it." (Day 7, Night 1): the hunter's theory turned into cover.
  • "The library had been doomed by its own impenetrability, by the mystery that protected it, by its few entrances." (Day 7, Night 2): how the archive ends.

Flags

  • Real historical figures (Louis the Bavarian, John XXII, Bernard Gui) are background only; none is complicit in the murders.
  • Eco makes up the surviving contents of a real lost book (the second book of Aristotle's Poetics) and has it destroyed. Not an invented edit, but close to SDF's rule: invent the hidden document outright, not as a real lost work.

books.qa:
Answers point to the section notes in this folder: 01-prologue-and-first-day.md, 02-second-day.md, 03-third-day.md, 04-fourth-day.md, 05-fifth-to-sixth-day.md, 06-sixth-day-to-last-page.md, and, where relevant, to a v8.2 chapter by title. The map is 00-map.md. Everything about SDF here is a PROPOSAL; Santi's decisions are PLACEHOLDER.

The archive and how it guards itself

1. How does Eco's library actually keep people out? Mostly not with locks. There is no door between the scriptorium and the library, so the abbot's ban has to be stronger than any door (01). Then come layers: a public catalog that is useless without the room, a plan known only to librarian and assistant, rumors of ghosts for the simple, stagecraft (herbs, mirrors, moaning wind) for the bold (01, 02), and finally a poisoned book (05, 06). SDF's reading room, a public catalog plus a keeper, already has the first two.

2. What is "the status lie," and does SDF have it? The catalog admits a book exists and lies about its state: "lost," or "ruined by mice fifty years earlier" (Day 2, Terce, 02). The record is findable; the shelf is closed. SDF has the phrase ("withdrawn for conservation," List #17; "records moved for conservation," The schedule) but nobody reads the depot's own catalog as a record of when it was used. Map proposal 1 does.

3. Who knows what in Eco's library? Custody is split. Malachi keeps the catalog and goes up into the library but does not know what he guards; Jorge, blind, knows what each title means (Day 6, Prime, 05). The abbot's order after Malachi's death: monks "may consult the catalogue. Nothing else." So access is controlled at the catalog. Nicholas adds that librarians become abbots, which ties the secret to power (05).

4. Is Aylin Malachi or Jorge? Malachi. v7 The sheets has her say she has kept the visitor book nine years and "never been told what the last column means." The old man is a partial Jorge: he knows the method but "doesn't read manuals" (v7 The reading room, continued). In SDF nobody holds the whole meaning, which is the Compartments point. Note 05 raised the question; the drafts had already answered it.

5. Does the archive kill in person? Rarely, and that is the useful part. The poisoned book does the guarding when nobody is in the room, and it gets only those who want to read (05, 06: "only to the extent that he wanted to read"). SDF's equivalent is the count: asking is what puts you on the list (The payload). Both make the victim's own curiosity the trigger.

6. How does the archive treat people who get in? It makes them sound mad. Berengar comes back with a ghost story; Aymaro says the powers of hell are used "to derange the minds of the curious" (Day 2, Terce, 02). This is SDF's discredit-not-prevent, at the scale of one building. The forum edit in The gorilla mask is the same move.

7. What does the keeper believe he is doing? Preserving. Adso's Day 3 meditation states the creed: learning stays unsullied "only if it prevents its reaching anyone at all" (03). William later turns it over: the library "now lives to bury" its books (Day 5, Vespers, 05). Aylin's "heritage… somebody has to" (v7 The sheets) is the sincere version; keep her believing it until the sheet.

8. Why does hiding work at all if the open books lead to the hidden one? William's answer (Day 4, Terce, 04): over centuries it is useless, over years or days it has some use. The archive delays the truth. That matches Monday's "you've bought time, a generation" and explains SDF's premise: if open books lead to the hidden thing, the open books have to be edited.

9. Is the reading room on top of the recovery site like anything in Eco? The treasure crypt under the church is the nearest match (05): mostly fake relics, yet real wealth, so the institution's worth doesn't depend on its holdings being true. The library itself is a front for one room (the finis Africae). In SDF the structure is already there, the archive on top of the seats. The ADDENDUM's verdict on C stands: the building is something James learns, not an engine.

10. How does Eco's archive end, and is that useful? By its own design: few entrances, untidy rooms, wind, a thrown lamp (Day 7, Night 2, 06). Don't take the fire. Take the small echo already in v8 The night before: Aylin propping the outer door with a fire extinguisher, "the loudest thing she ever said."

The engine

11. Why can't William stop? Until Day 5, because of other people's clocks: the legation (Day 2), Gui's arrival (Day 3), the abbot's dawn expulsion (Day 6) (02, 03, 06). From Day 5, because of his own mistake (he set the book aside) and because the official answer is wrong and he knows it (05). See the map's engine table.

12. Where is William's mistake, and what does it cost? Day 5, Sext (05). Filtering for Greek, he set aside a bound volume whose first pages were Arabic; it was the book. Severinus was already dead; Benno walks off with it, and the next man who holds it dies. He recovers by remembering Severinus's exact word, "strange." SDF lacks a mistake of James's that someone else pays for; the King and Foucault maps propose versions.

13. What is the "false solution" and why is it strong? Bernard's trial gives the abbey a guilty man, a confession and an end (Day 5, Nones, 05). The reader knows it is wrong because William says so, and Malachi's death that night breaks it in public. A closed case that reopens turns harder than an open case that stays open. In SDF the seat list in The money is the smaller true secret, and James's freezing theory is the case closed wrongly; the reopening is spread across Part Three.

14. Does Eco use a rival investigator? Yes. Bernard questions only servants, uses fear, and condemns the girl the night he arrives (04). He is the clock: if William doesn't solve it, Bernard's story becomes the official one. SDF has no rival reader. The handlers (Kalder, Bram) judge the right column, but they are not racing James to an answer.

15. How do the deaths keep the pace? Each death removes the person who knew most, so "who knows" is the threat: "After Berengar we are the ones who know most" (Day 4, Lauds, 04). In SDF the professor, Noor and the Zwolle engineer play this role off-page. James is never told, in so many words, that he is now the one who knows most.

The mechanisms

16. What's the cleanest canary in the book, and can James use it? William announces loudly that nobody may touch Venantius's desk (Day 2, Terce, 02), which sets the monks to watch Malachi, and by evening three have steered him away. One true public sentence, no invented item. James already does this in v7 The reading room, continued (he orders the sheets to see what moves Anneke). Don't add another.

17. Does this book support the gate? Yes. William sets his own ("rather than appear foolish afterward, I renounce seeming clever now," Day 4, Vespers, 04), and Bernard shows the cost of having none. All the clocks belong to third parties, as the ADDENDUM says they should. Note 04 suggests a PLACEHOLDER: James reads a pause as guilt and someone else pays, before he learns the gate.

18. Is the front (C) any better here than in Tier 1? Yes, partly. Layers cover layers: the cellarer's night trade covers the murders (03), the heresy lead covers the library (02), Remigio's letters close the inquiry (05), and the forbidden text sits fourth in a binding of disreputable texts (06). It drives the plot when officials accept the smaller secret as the end. Map proposal 3 uses the binding.

19. What is "the guard wears the hunter's theory"? Jorge heard that William believed the deaths followed the seven trumpets and fed the next sign to Malachi, so the deaths fit the pattern (Day 7, Night 1, 06). William: "I conceived a false pattern… and the guilty man fell in with it." For SDF: the organization could let James's freezing theory stand as cover. The old man's "No dogs; I'm told it's a question of air" (v7 The reading room, continued) already half does it.

20. What does "disable the reader, not the text" mean for SDF? The thief leaves William the page and takes his glasses (Day 2, Compline, 02). For SDF, the organization leaves James the document and narrows his access, as Enjoy it while it lasts already does with page 212. Already on the page; not proposed.

21. Co-optation: is it new for SDF? The move is: answer a questioner by giving him the job (Benno, Day 5, Vespers, 05). SDF already does it to James ("Continuity want you," Leave it; the five seats). What is new is doing it to a helper who has already turned. Map proposal 2 does that at Pieter's door in The leak.

The final conversation

22. How does Jorge's talk compare with the old man's in The final conversation? Jorge is not beaten when he talks: he chose the room and the hour, talks to stall and tempt, and offers the book as "your prize," poisoned (06). SDF's old man is retired and talks because it no longer matters (v8 The final conversation). Note 06 says the beaten head still needs something on the table: an offer, a test, or a thing to destroy. Map proposal 4 gives him a status line on a card.

23. Who explains in Eco's last scene, the hero or the villain? The hero. William reconstructs the deaths and Jorge confirms (Day 7, Night 1, 06), then Jorge gives his reasons. In v8 The final conversation the old man does almost all of it. If Santi wants James to earn the talk, one option is for James to say his own reconstruction first and be corrected on freezing. PLACEHOLDER.

24. What does Jorge fear, and does it match the old man? Not laughter or heresy, which "we know how to destroy" and whose "presence is precious to us," but one respectable text that turns what common people do into doctrine: "Provided the act is not transformed into plan" (06). That is the old man's "it comes out all the time… we're there first" (v8 The final conversation). It also explains why the sheets work where forums didn't: they are the bank's own paperwork.

25. How did Jorge pick William out? By a question William never asked: "you never asked questions about the library" (06). SDF already has the reversed form: "stopped asking out loud, which is worse" (A car park). Not proposed.

26. Does James laughing in the final conversation have a source here? It has a match. The forbidden book is about laughter, and William answers Jorge's speech with insults and friar jokes (06). v8 The final conversation already has James laugh at "Walt." Keep it; it's the right weapon against a man who needs to be believed.

27. Should the old man destroy something at the end, like Jorge? Not a fire, and not violence. SDF's organization discredits rather than prevents. The scaled-down version is a status change, "withdrawn for conservation," written in his hand on his last day, which Aylin overrules when James asks (map proposal 4).

Transfer specifics

28. Which of the map's proposals is cheapest to write? Proposal 2 (Pieter's door). It adds one object to a scene that already exists in v7 The leak and one line to the twelfth envelope in The night before. Proposal 1 needs Thursday beats across Part Three that v8.2 does not list.

29. Does proposal 1 break the opening? No. James reads the card index only after 2 December, on the Thursdays v7 already gives him ("Same time Thursday?" in The reading room, continued; "the appointment she'd booked me into" in The sheets). It changes Aylin's sheet in The sheets and adds weight to her midnight in The night before.

30. Is Aylin's nine years matching Kalder's transfer nine years ago canon? The numbers are both in the drafts (v7 The sheets for Aylin; v8.2 Leiden, nine years ago for Kalder) but nothing connects them. Proposal 1 uses the match. PLACEHOLDER: intended or coincidence.

31. Which proposal conflicts with other maps? Proposal 3 (the paperback) competes with Foucault 5.2 (a fake sheet on the reading-room table, cost with Anneke) and 5.4 (a negative in the grants, cost with Frank). Take one of the three. Proposal 3 is the only one where James is right and still pays.

32. Does proposal 3 break the real-book rule? Not if both books are invented: the forty-one entries and the channelled paperback. Never put an original wording into a real crank book, and never claim a real publisher was funded.

33. Which section-note proposals did the map drop, and why? Note 02's "ask Aylin publicly for a damaged record" in The reading room, continued: James has no visit before 2 December and the public canary is already in that draft. Note 04's "a catalog that skips the lower floor": canon puts James on that floor at The drill. Note 05's "Aylin offers James a role": already done by Leave it and the five seats.

34. What should never be borrowed from this book? William's stealth, his leverage plan, the fear of torture he uses (02, 03); real popes and inquisitors as plotters (01–05); and inventing the contents of a real lost book (02, 06). See map section 6.

35. Where is the best single scene to study for craft? Day 2, Compline (02): William finds a page, Adso's lamp reveals the hidden writing by accident, and the intruder takes the glasses, not the page. Three beats, and the document is in the hero's hand at the moment he loses the ability to read it. Day 5, Nones (05), the trial, is the best lesson in lore that doesn't stall.

books.author: Gibson
books.title: Pattern Recognition
books.readfor: a nose, not a method; a forum as a place; clues as objects
books.intro: Coverage: English, read in full via three section notes (01-chapters-1-to-11.md, 02-chapters-12-to-26.md, 03-chapters-27-to-43.md), 11 Nov 2026. Plot facts and chapter numbers are the notes'. Brief: read for a protagonist with a nose, not a method; a forum as a real place; clues as physical objects. Question: how does the hidden thing make Cayce act, and what would James do if we borrowed it. Standing-rule note: real brands as triggers (Bibendum, Tommy Hilfiger), Kevin Bacon's dog in passing, real institutions as background (Echelon, an NSA pension, "ex-KGB"), 9/11 as the private wound. None is complicit, but SDF wants invented companies. Take the mechanics, not the brands.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
Cayce Pollard, a logo consultant whose body reacts to brands, is hired in London by the ad man Bigend to find whoever makes anonymous film fragments that a web forum, F:F:F, obsesses over. Her flat is entered, a rival (Dorotea) attacks her through her phobia, and a forum friend's invented Japanese girl gets her a watermark number in Tokyo. The number leads to a map, to a Russian apparatus that has been watching the forum, to an ex-NSA man who trades an address for an antique calculator, and to the maker: Nora, whose footage is the shape of the shrapnel in her brain. Cayce is drugged and held, refuses to name her source, and is paid off with a file on her missing father.

What makes it work: every step is an object someone hands her, and every handover costs her something personal (shame, privacy, a lie told in person). Her gift is also the hole in her armor, so the same nose that finds things is what her enemies use to steer her.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:
