7 (ch. 27–31) The address behind the watermark "Mama Anarchia" knows she is in Tokyo; a clean rectangle in the dust where her mail lay (ch. 27); Baranov will trade the address for a Curta A gun to her forehead; £4,500 of Bigend's money that ties her to him They are already in her flat and her keystrokes, so waiting is not safe An email address on a curry-house card
8 (ch. 32–35) To know who the maker is Her unsent letter sends itself; Stella replies; the T matches a Claymore part (ch. 33) She lies to Boone Stella's story ends with men in leather coats (ch. 35) She goes to see Nora
9 (ch. 36–37) To see the work being made Nora editing; the city in the footage is the shape of the shrapnel (ch. 37) She breaks with Bigend in her head She has promised to protect Nora from the man paying her She refuses to name her source
10 (ch. 38–41) To get home quietly Dorotea drugs her; a private prison; the full explanation: her old forum post put her on their list (ch. 41) Kidnapped, the skin off her feet They want Baranov's name; she won't give it Payment: cash and a file on her father
11 (ch. 42–43) To close her father's case Three blue sheets on Win's last morning (ch. 42) The allergy itself is gone (ch. 43) — (the engine stops when the private wound is closed by a document) She gives the money away; Paris

The "cannot stop" column runs on two motors: competition early (CNN, a rival finding the maker), then, from ch. 24, the fact that stopping gives the enemy what it paid for. Nobody threatens her into going on; Bigend lets every no stand and changes what she knows instead (01).

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
• The footage stays an object: fragments watched (ch. 1–2), then data (a number, a T, a 75% shape match, ch. 33), then meaning, by watching one edit (ch. 37).
  • The forum: factions in about 700 words, read behind a barricaded door (ch. 6); Parkaboy's emails, 300–900 words, each ending in a question or an instruction (ch. 8, 14, 16, 19).
  • Bigend's theories (about 1,000 words, ch. 6–7) are always a pitch, so we watch him work on her.
  • The watermark: short Q&As with people who argue back (Voytek, ch. 9; Boone over noodles, ch. 11; Ngemi on Echelon, to justify a price, ch. 30).
  • The Russians: a hostile confession (about 900 words, ch. 24) and a 2,000-word explanation placed after the climax (ch. 41), where each item explains a weirdness already shown.

Where it stalls: Win's 9/11 disappearance (ch. 15), about 1,000 words of memory held up by one falling rose petal. Deliberate, and still the one place the plot stops: nothing in it changes what she does next. Where it doesn't: Dorotea's confession (ch. 24). Cayce interrupts, Dorotea needles, every exchange lands a fact, and we wait to see if Cayce walks out. The rule: a lore scene holds if someone in it wants something from the listener now.

sections.title: 4. The mechanism we came for
sections.html:
Setup. The nose is defined by its price before it is used: a yes/no instrument with no reasons ("either blue or it's not," ch. 2), then the Hilfiger collapse in Harvey Nichols (ch. 3). Gibson spends as long on the damage as on the gift.

Rule. The nose reads surfaces, not people working against her. It misses the scooter rider who is tailing her (ch. 16); Boone, who has a method, spots him. And it comes with a built-in check, her father's rule on paranoia (ch. 13, ch. 36). Labor is split: nose (Cayce), method (Boone), reach (the forum); she never cracks anything herself (02).

First use, against her. Dorotea's "wrong envelope" with Bibendum gets a verdict out of her through her trigger; then the doll hangs outside her rekeyed door (ch. 10). The locks hold and don't help.

Escalation. The forum goes from refuge to fishbowl (ch. 7, 9) to people ("everting," ch. 23). Every clue is a copy that can be lost or taken: napkin, palm, notepad, laptop (ch. 17–19).

Cost. Shame and privacy: catfishing Taki (ch. 17), the therapist's notes (ch. 24).

Payoff. The allergy becomes the alarm: the hallucinated Michelin Man with her father's voice, "She's drugged the water. Scream." (ch. 38). And the tripwire is revealed: one throwaway post guessing at a Russian patron put her on their list (ch. 41). She had reread it twice (ch. 33, 36) without knowing.

Against A–D.

  • A (gate): weak. Only social tests (Taki checks "Keiko" with Anne of Green Gables, ch. 17). Nothing must be proved before she acts; Gibson does not fix SDF's missing gate.
  • B (canary): central, and it bites back. Keiko is invented to see who bites (ch. 8); Judy, the real model, finds out and threatens a journalist (ch. 23). Reversed: Mama Anarchia gives herself away by knowing Tokyo, and a friend notices (ch. 27).
  • C (front): layered, then deflated. Franco → Dorotea → a Russian "if indeed he was from Cyprus" → "them" (ch. 24), and the top is small and protective (ch. 41).
  • D (lock and key): with a price. Baranov trades the address for a Curta bought on Bigend's money, and the tie comes due (ch. 29–31). Forum trivia works as a password (ch. 40).

Fifth mechanisms the evidence supports. (1) The nose as attack surface: whoever knows what the gifted person reacts to can feed her or freeze her (ch. 10, 27). (2) Holding back as the active choice: three allies in a Hummer, each withholding; her silence makes her part of the lie (ch. 20). For a James who mostly receives, deciding what to pass on is the action. (3) The hero's own old post as the tripwire (ch. 41). (4) The reward as a trap: they pay her to be quiet; she gives the money away and keeps the file (ch. 43).

sections.title: 5. Transfer to SDF
sections.html: Already on the page, so not proposed: the reverse canary (v6 "Leiden": the corrector uses a style-guide phrase, Noor spots it); the forum turning into people (v6 "The gorilla mask": the forum man who found the house from a photograph); the edited persona and its eleven readers ("The gorilla mask"); the forum password ("The sheets").

items.title: 5.1 The invented book bites back through Beard Man
items.html: Chapters: "On land" → a Sunday market beat in "The gorilla mask" (placement PLACEHOLDER). Change: the book James invented at the pub comes back as a request: a polite man has asked Beard Man for that exact title. James does: goes back to the market, tells Beard Man the book doesn't exist because he made it up, and explains what a phone call to a polite man does, as he did in "Groningen"; Beard Man decides for himself. Cost: his lie has put a real person in the dealer's position, and he must admit it to the one man he has never told anything; Beard Man, offended that a book he's never heard of is in demand, builds a theory about it. Already on the page? Partly. The trap is in the v8.2 plan for "On land" (not in v6 "On land," which has only the Deventer slip) and is cashed only as an accusation in "The dinner." Gibson adds the bill through a third person (Judy, ch. 23).

items.title: 5.2 Kalder baits the nose
items.html: Chapters: "The corporate day" or the round in "Enjoy it while it lasts," paid off in "On land." Change: Kalder mentions, in passing, an (invented) book whose two printings "say different things." James does: buys both printings, spends a Saturday, lies to Ana about the price, and finds an ordinary corrected impression with the paperwork intact; he enters the negative result in the Record. At the pub he answers bait with bait: that is why he invents a book. Cost: money, a second lie to Ana, and the knowledge that someone knows exactly what makes him stop and look. Already on the page? No for the bait; partly for the idea (v6 "The gorilla mask": Kalder finishes James's private lab-coat line). It also gives Part Two the costly negative result 00 SYNTHESIS Rule 2 asked for. Gibson: Bibendum (ch. 10), Mama Anarchia (ch. 27, 38).

items.title: 5.3 Noor's gate: say the deleted question
items.html: Chapter: "Leiden." Change: before Noor tells him anything, she tests whether he is the man behind the handle and why he's asking: what did you type and delete in the spring? James does: says it out loud in her kitchen ("Has anyone here had an NDE…"), the question he was too ashamed to post in "Reading with a pen." Cost: the shame Santi set up ("flinch when it's your turn to be seen believing"), paid in person; and when the same question turns up restored, with four hundred replies, in "The gorilla mask," it hurts twice, because he finally said it to one person. Already on the page? Partly. v6 "Leiden": Noor messages "Who are you?" and talks without a test; the v8.2 password ("The sheets") is the professor's phrasing, not James's. Gibson adds the test of belonging that costs shame (Taki and Anne of Green Gables, ch. 17; "a ticket. And a lie," ch. 11).

items.title: 5.4 He holds back from Pieter, on the record
items.html: Chapters: "The drill," "The money," paid off in "The sheets." Change: in a one-to-one Pieter asks whether anything in the contracts needs flagging. James does: with the annex and Pieter's three dependants on his screen, says "nothing's expired": he does to Pieter what Pieter did to him in "Leave it." Cost: it is in the one-to-one notes, a system the counting job could read; and in "The sheets" Pieter says, "You knew in October," and James has to answer for it before Pieter asks "What do I do?" Already on the page? No. v7 "The money" shows the annex only to Ana; v7 "The drill" gives Pieter the unsaid sentence, not James. Gibson: the Hummer (ch. 20–21).

items.title: 5.5 His own old post as an object, and maybe the tripwire
items.html:
Chapters: "The gorilla mask," "Twenty minutes," "What was on the phone." Change: James finds an untouched copy of his own old thread (a reply that quoted him whole, or his own export of his posts; nothing not his). James does: prints old and new side by side and puts both on the tablecloth in "Twenty minutes." Cost: PLACEHOLDER, Santi's call: on Kalder's phone ("What was on the phone"), the handle's first note is dated years before the funeral, against an old did-you-know with one guess too many. Ana learns the hobby she found sweet was noticed long before the grief. Already on the page? Partly. The edits and eleven readers are in "The gorilla mask"; v8 "Leave it" already says the invoice stepped up the week he "typed a question into a forum," which conflicts with v8.2 and v7 "The money" (the ticket week). Gibson adds the archive as a thing he holds (ch. 13) and the reread post that was the trigger (ch. 33, 36, 41). Keep "The payload" intact: the bank list still shows him first as asked (job).

Rejected: Baranov-style buying of surveillance (hacking by proxy); Boone tailing and copying a laptop; Dorotea's drugging as the opponent's move.

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• The violent third act. Gun, drugging, kidnapping, a private prison (ch. 29, 38–40). SDF's organization discredits and kills rarely; the one drugging in the book is Ana's.
  • Outsourced intrusion. Rice decrypts, Baranov sells sig-int, Boone trails and copies (ch. 17, 25, 29–31). If a helper hacks for James, James has hacked.
  • The deflated conspiracy. Gibson's top turns out small and protective, an uncle shielding nieces (ch. 41). SDF's is large and real. Take "we are most often the merest of cogs" for the helpers, not for the old man.

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
• "Though the truth, Damien would say, is closer to allergy, a morbid and sometimes violent reactivity to the semiotics of the marketplace." (ch. 1) The gift defined by its cost.
  • "it felt like a friend's living room, but it was a sort of text-based broadcast" (ch. 7) The forum as home and fishbowl.
  • "An airport," she says, … "a ticket. And a lie." (ch. 11) The clue's price, stated plainly.
  • "Paranoia, he said, was fundamentally egocentric, and every conspiracy theory served in some way to aggrandize the believer." (ch. 13) The nose's built-in check.
  • "But now, in some way she can't quite grasp, the universe of F:F:F is everting." (ch. 23) The forum turns into people.
  • "To make you sufficiently uncomfortable that you would leave London." (ch. 24) The opponent wants her gone, not stopped.
  • "Who started the thread that gave Completism its first formal basis?" (ch. 40) Forum trivia as a password.
  • "when you suggested in a post that the maker might be a Russian mafia type" (ch. 41) The old post as tripwire.

notes.title: section 01 (chapters 1–11, "The Website of Dreadful Night" to "Boone Chu")
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 1–11 (about 31,900 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 01; no edition data in the file (OCR noise and "Contents - Prev / Next" links throughout).

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What she finds What it costs her Why she cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 1–6) Do one logo job, sleep off jet lag, watch new fragment #135 cleanly Her jacket burned at lunch (ch. 2); in the flat, a porn site in the browser history, a roll of tape standing upright, and a redial that reaches Dorotea's Italian voicemail (ch. 5) Her one irreplaceable garment; the flat's safety; a Saturday spent barricading and rekeying (ch. 6) She is under contract, and Dorotea will be at Monday's meeting Dinner with Bigend, the client she cannot refuse
2 (ch. 7–9) To be left alone with the footage Bigend reads her forum posts and wants her to find the maker (ch. 7); Parkaboy's letter: #78 may carry a hidden watermark number (ch. 8); Magda is paid by Blue Ant's Trans to talk up the footage in bars (ch. 9) Her refuge is a fishbowl, and the man she distrusts works inside it CNN has aired #135 (ch. 8); someone else may find the maker first She asks Voytek about watermarks (ch. 9)
3 (ch. 10–11) Sign off, fly home, be free of Bigend Dorotea shows her the Michelin Man, her worst trigger, then hangs a felt one on the flat's door (ch. 10). Boone's friend at Rice finds "something encrypted" in every segment (ch. 11) A panic attack in a client meeting; her enemy knows her secret Two separate sources (Tokyo forum rumour, Boone's mathematician) point at the same hidden number, and only she holds the Tokyo half A trip to Tokyo and a lie: the invented Keiko now needs a real person to turn up

Why it grips

  • The gift is the weak spot. Cayce's "nose" is set up in ch. 2 as a yes/no instrument with no reasons attached ("She has no way of knowing how she knows"; the carpet is "either blue or it's not"). Gibson spends the same pages on its price: the Tommy Hilfiger collapse in Harvey Nichols (ch. 3), the duck mantra (ch. 4). So when Dorotea pulls Bibendum out of the envelope (ch. 10), the reader already knows exactly how much damage it does. The scene is built for that payoff: a fake "wrong envelope", Stonestreet unable to see the board, and Cayce saying "It works" to make it stop. Her enemy gets the verdict out of her through her nose.
  • Small physical anomalies do the threatening. No intruder is seen. The menace is one browser-history line above the forum's, a roll of tape on its end, one redial (ch. 5). She tests each against memory (new keys, the only set), and the checking builds the dread.
  • Refusal as the engine. She says no to Bigend three times (ch. 7, ch. 10). Each time he lets the no stand ("You need to sleep on it") and changes what she knows instead: CNN, Trans, Boone. She is never pushed; the world shifts until no stops being worth saying.
  • Funny next to the dread. Teaching Bigend to wear his Stetson (ch. 7), "be French" (ch. 9), Kevin Bacon's dog (ch. 10), Parkaboy's voice (ch. 8).

How the conspiracy moves the story here

Two hidden things, and the section stitches them together. The maker is a pure question that blocks nothing and asks nothing of Cayce; the forum is where she puts her worry (ch. 6, "Psychological prophylaxis"). Then come the people who want to know. Bigend turns the question into a job; Magda's bar story (ch. 9) makes it worse: Blue Ant is already seeding the footage and debriefing its agents "for responses". The secret worth fearing is now the hunters', and they are inside her refuge.

Dorotea is a separate threat with no proven motive (Bigend offers jealousy, ch. 7). Her attacks are deniable: a burn, a browser line, a doll. Her old trade, Bigend says, was "black PR". She wrecks Cayce's footing without stopping her, and Bigend uses the moment to bring in Boone, the man with the tools.

The driving question narrows into an object, from "who makes it" to "what is the number in #78". A number can be fetched, at the cost of a lie told in person.

How the lore gets in

  • Forum factions (ch. 6), about 700 words, narration (Progressives, Completists, Garage Kubrick). Read behind a table jammed against the door, so it runs over live pressure; it ends with her posting as referee and the phone ringing. No stall.
  • The Curta (ch. 4), about 200 words, an object plus a lecture. Ngemi puts the "grenade" in her hand, then explains it. It also plants Hobbs (ex-NSA, ch. 9) long before he is needed.
  • Parkaboy's letter (ch. 8), about 900 words, a document. The biggest piece of lore, in a funny, vain voice, ending on a question ("So what to do?") that turns lore into a decision.
  • Bigend's theory (ch. 6–7), about 1,000 words over two scenes, conversation. Every lecture is part of a pitch, so we watch him work on her.
  • Watermarking and rendering farms (ch. 9 and ch. 11), each about 250–350 words, Q&A. Voytek answers in broken English; Boone argues over noodles and Cayce wins with feeling ("Lonely?").

Mechanism notes

  • B (canary), run twice, by both sides. Parkaboy and Musashi invent Keiko, a person who does not exist, and watch who bites. Taki does, and offers the number (ch. 8). Blue Ant runs the corporate version: Trans plants a mention, then debriefs for responses (ch. 9). Maurice asks if the Vatican story is a hoax (ch. 9): the forum tests too. For SDF the useful part is the bill. The invented persona pays off only if a real person turns up and plays it (ch. 11, "And a lie"). If James plants something through his old forum persona, collecting on it should mean being that persona, in person, at a cost.
  • The watched forum. Bigend knows CayceP is Cayce from her posts (ch. 7). He never breaks in; he reads, and seeds. That is close to SDF's edited posts, and it suggests the edits should come with a reader who quotes James back to himself.
  • D (lock and key). Cayce secures the flat properly (new locks, hair and powder, ch. 6–7). The perimeter holds, and the enemy hangs the doll on the outside of the door (ch. 10). Locks do not stop someone who knows what frightens you. Taki's number is a key he will hand only to someone he wants to meet.
  • C (front). Trans under Blue Ant; Dorotea's intelligence-run consultancy (ch. 7). Weak here.
  • A (gate). Self-set and soft: "If it's real, and you can get it" (ch. 11). She must confirm the number exists before the partnership means anything.
  • Fifth: the nose as attack surface. Whoever knows what the gifted person reacts to can steer or break her. Someone who knows what makes James pause could feed him exactly what he will chase, or what will freeze him: he pays for his talent with no hacking or force.

Quotes

  • "Though the truth, Damien would say, is closer to allergy, a morbid and sometimes violent reactivity to the semiotics of the marketplace." (ch. 1): the gift defined by what it costs.
  • "it felt like a friend's living room, but it was a sort of text-based broadcast" (ch. 7): the forum as a home and a fishbowl.
  • "Then why are they trying to do it with bloody video clips from the Internet? This couple kissing in a doorway?" (ch. 9): the reveal comes from a stranger's complaint in a pub.
  • "An airport," she says, having to admit to herself now that she's already worked it out, already gone there, "a ticket. And a lie." (ch. 11): the clue's price, stated plainly.

Flags

  • Real brands as triggers (Michelin/Bibendum, Tommy Hilfiger) and a real person in passing (Kevin Bacon's dog, ch. 10); none is complicit in anything. Curt Herzstark and the Curta are real history, told straight (ch. 4).
  • The Vatican "footage" statement (ch. 9) is a rumour, and the forum itself doubts it.
  • Post-9/11 background (a missing-person flyer for a Cantor Fitzgerald employee, ch. 3). No invented edits on real books.

notes.title: section 02 (chapters 12–26)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 12 ("Apophenia") to 26 ("S I G I N T"), about 30,000 words, read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 02; no edition data in the file (some OCR noise).

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 12–17) The watermark number from Taki, a Tokyo otaku Twelve digits in felt tip on her napkin map, which she copies onto her palm in a bar toilet Bigend's card, catfishing a sad man until he cries, an assault in the alley She took Bigend's money, and the number is the first hard object ever pulled from the footage Boone Chu, who has been tailing her, wants her laptop
2 (ch. 18–21) To know what the number is for, and who the "Italians" are Taki's next gift, a T-shaped map holding 135 numbers. Hers is one of them (ch. 19) She starts withholding; Boone lies to Bigend and makes her complicit (ch. 20–21) The match means the footage has a geography. The maker is building something on purpose Boone sends map and number to his friend at Rice
3 (ch. 22–26) Sleep, then to find out why Bigend has summoned her Dorotea, newly hired by Bigend, confesses: a Russian from Cyprus paid her to drive Cayce out of London and gave her Cayce's therapist's notes Her therapy file read; trust in Boone tested Somebody paid to make her quit, so quitting gives "them" what they paid for Boone flies to Sigil Technologies in Columbus. Hobbs Baranov, who "sells sig-int", is planted at dinner (ch. 26)

Why it grips

  • Each object is handed on and copied, and every copy is a risk. The number goes from Taki's Palm to the napkin (the ink is already spreading), to her palm, to a hotel notepad (ch. 17–19), then to Boone and Rice. The map goes from Mystic to Taki, to "Keiko" (really Parkaboy), to Cayce, to Boone. Holding a copy becomes the plot: the muggers go for her bag, and Boone's first question is "Is it in the laptop?" (ch. 17).
  • The nose gets checked, not trusted. When Billy Prion turns up on her flight (ch. 13), she runs her father's rule on paranoia over the hunch, and a TV ad shows he had an ordinary reason to be there (ch. 14). Then her nose misses the real threat: she clocks the RAF roundel on a scooter rider's parka (ch. 16) without linking him to the visor in Kabukicho. Boone, who has a method, spotted the tail. Her gift reads surfaces, not people working against her.
  • The suspense is in what allies keep from each other. Chapter 20 puts three people in a Hummer, each holding something back. Boone leaves out the head-butt and the map, and Cayce realises her silence makes her part of the lie. The scene that does the most work is the meeting room in ch. 24. The man with the taped nose has just run past her at the door (ch. 23), and the enemy sits at the table as a new hire. Bigend's "you are talking about loyalty, not honesty" turns the conspiracy into an employment deal.
  • Still funny throughout: the "dickhead" phone call (ch. 23), Ngemi buying "Stephen King's Wang" (ch. 26).

How the conspiracy moves the story here

Gibson runs the two hidden things on separate tracks.

Who makes the footage moves only through objects and the people who give them up: a number, a map pulled from a white flash, a watermarking firm. Cayce cracks nothing: Mystic decrypts, Taki hands over, Parkaboy forwards, Rice confirms segment 78 (ch. 25). What Cayce brings is access and judgement, and the access costs her shame.

Who wants to know moves through pressure on her body and her privacy: the alley (ch. 17), then the therapist's notes (ch. 24). Its stated aim is to drive her away, not to stop her. That is very close to SDF's organisation, which discredits rather than prevents. Gibson's turn: the opponent is bought, not beaten. Bigend hires Dorotea, so the front-line agent becomes a source, and the pressure moves up a level, to "an organization of some kind" behind the man from Cyprus (ch. 25), and the threat grows with it: Boone says they could turn Dorotea back with a threat to her life (ch. 25).

How the lore gets in

  • Win's 9/11 disappearance (ch. 15), about 1,000 words, memory. A deliberate stall between the jet-lag night and the Taki errand, held up by one small object: a dead rose petal falling in a shop window.
  • Parkaboy's emails (ch. 14, 16, 19), 300–600 words each, documents. Each has a joke and ends in an instruction or a new object. No stall.
  • Cynthia's EVP email (ch. 21), about 400 words, a document. It gives four numbered "files" of what her dead father supposedly says. Funny and painful, it repeats the plot's idea of a message hidden in noise, like the map pulled from the whiteout. A 700-word memory follows; Damien at the stairs ends it.
  • Dorotea's confession (ch. 24), about 900 words, a hostile conversation. Cayce keeps interrupting, Dorotea needles her, and every exchange lands a fact. No stall: the reader waits to see whether Cayce walks out (she sits with her legs out from under the table).
  • Hobbs Baranov (ch. 26), about 600 words, dinner gossip. The next helper is planted as a tipsy sibling squabble, before he is needed.

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate), small and social. Before he gives up the number, Taki tests whether "Keiko" is real by asking if she likes Anne of Green Gables (ch. 17). The invented persona nearly fails. Cayce then sets her own gate on Boone: she will keep working with him only if he keeps her informed (ch. 25). Both test belonging, not a theory.
  • B (canary), already central, and it bites back. Keiko is an invented person planted to see who believes in her, and Taki believes. Chapter 23 sends the bill: Judy, the real model, finds out, takes Taki's side and threatens to go to a journalist. Boone runs a quieter one in the car (ch. 20–21): he leaves the map out to see if Bigend already knows. For SDF: let the canary bite back through a real person.
  • C (front), layered. Franco works for Dorotea, Dorotea for a Russian "if indeed he was from Cyprus", and he for "them" (ch. 24). Each exposed layer opens onto another; Boone even suspects Blue Ant (ch. 18).
  • D (lock and key). Literal first: Damien's new German keys, and whom to trust with them (ch. 12). Then the number unlocks the map, and the map points to the next lock, Sigil.
  • Fifth: the forum becomes a place with a past. On the plane Cayce searches a CD of every F:F:F post and finds her own first one, from before she added the P (ch. 13). For James, whose posts get edited, this is the model: the forum archive is an object, and what the forum made up can turn up as a person.
  • Division of labour. Nose (Cayce), method (Boone, ch. 25), reach (the forum): the heroine never hacks. SDF can copy this if James pays each helper in shame, trust or money.

Quotes

  • "Paranoia, he said, was fundamentally egocentric, and every conspiracy theory served in some way to aggrandize the believer." (ch. 13): the nose comes with a built-in check.
  • "No, she knows that Taki is for real. Taki is too sad not to be real." (ch. 20): judging the person stands in for checking the evidence.
  • "To make you sufficiently uncomfortable that you would leave London." (ch. 24): the opponent wants her gone, not stopped.
  • "But now, in some way she can't quite grasp, the universe of F:F:F is everting." (ch. 23): the forum turns into people.

Flags

  • Real institutions brushed against: Cynthia believes the CIA had an office near the WTC (ch. 15). The fictional Hobbs draws an NSA pension (ch. 26), but the agency is not shown as complicit.
  • Real event: a fictional man vanishes on 9/11 (ch. 15, 21).
  • No invented edits on real books in this section.

notes.title: section 03 (chapters 27–43, the end)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapter 27 ("The Shape of the Enthusiast") to chapter 43 ("Mail") plus the Author's Note (about 37,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: Viking/Penguin 2003 per the copyright page; a converted scan, chunk file 03.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What she finds What it costs her Why she cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 27–31) The address behind the watermark code Mama Anarchia, writing to Ivy, knows Cayce is in Tokyo, which she can't know; Margot finds a clean rectangle in the dust where the mail lay. Baranov can get the address, for a price A gun to her forehead (rusted, useless); £4,500 of Bigend's money, which ties her to him They are already in her flat and her keystrokes, so waiting isn't safe; she has paid An email address on a curry-house card, and nothing to do with it
2 (ch. 32–37) To know who the maker is Her letter sends itself; Stella replies; the maker is Nora, and the T-map is the shape of the mine fragment in her brain She lies to Boone and breaks with Bigend in her head She has seen Nora work and promised to protect her from the man paying her She refuses to name her source
3 (ch. 38–43) To get home quietly Dorotea, the apparat, a private prison; then the full explanation and a file on her father Drugged, kidnapped, miles of polluted waste, the skin off her feet They want Baranov's name; she won't give it. Her father's file is the payment Win's legal death, the cash given away, Paris

Why it grips

  • The clue turns out to be the answer, in physical form. The T-shaped "map" has been an abstract puzzle since Part One. In ch. 33 Parkaboy's shape-matching bot returns a fact with no meaning attached: 75% of the T matches part of a Claymore mine's arming mechanism. Gibson holds back the meaning for four chapters. In ch. 35 Stella mentions a bomb in a tree and "The last fragment" that can't be removed. Only in ch. 37, watching Nora work, does Cayce see it: the city in the footage is the shape of the wound. The puzzle everyone was decoding was shrapnel. It works because the object was planted as plain data long before it was given any feeling.
  • The reveal is a disappointment that then becomes something greater. Every forum theory was too big; the truth is one wounded woman, her sister, and a rich uncle. Then the three silent hours of watching Nora edit (ch. 37) make it bigger again. Gibson shows one edit, not an explanation: a zoom on the corner of a mouth changes the frame.
  • The way in is a letter that was never meant to be sent (ch. 32). Following her therapist's exercise, she writes to the maker as if to the dead, types the address, and "watches as it sends." No clever move gets her there. Her grief does, and the reply comes within half an hour.
  • Cost and comedy stay together. After the gun, Ngemi says "People don't have guns." (ch. 29). When she asks Parkaboy his real name he gives a joke one first (ch. 34), and he arrives to rescue her with a card that reads MIDDLE-AGED WHITE GUY (ch. 40).

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The hidden order is a security apparatus split into two halves that don't trust each other: the ex-KGB "traditionalists" and Sergei's web people (ch. 41). It moves the plot twice. First, it watched the forum, and that is how it found her. Paid graduate students lurked on F:F:F, and one of them broke the rule against posting. Cayce's throwaway post guessing at a Russian mafia patron touched a nerve. From her ISP they got her name, from her name her father's dossier, and from there the break-in, the bugs and the copied therapist's notes. She rereads that post twice (ch. 33, 36) before she learns it was the tripwire. Second, it puts Dorotea in the room, and Dorotea's need to know the source of the address leads to the drugging and the prison. Then the conspiracy deflates. Its secret was protective (an uncle shielding his nieces), and its last act is to pay her, with cash and a file on her father.

How the lore gets in

  • Ngemi on Baranov and Echelon (ch. 30), about 600 words, conversation on a train. It explains why she has to buy the calculator rather than pay cash, so the lore justifies the price. The email arrives within the chapter.
  • Stella's story (ch. 35), about 1,500 words, conversation in a café. It doesn't stall because the reader has wanted it all book, because Cayce keeps losing her nerve and grabbing at "next question", and because it ends with drivers in leather coats and a blue light.
  • Parkaboy's prison briefing (ch. 40), about 700 words, in helicopter headsets. Told in flight; ends on landing.
  • The dinner explanation (ch. 41), about 2,000 words. The longest lecture, placed after the climax. It works as a rereading: each item explains a weirdness already shown (the dust rectangle, the therapist's notes, the man from Cyprus). Wiktor pressing her for the source, and hinting her father is alive, keeps it tense.
  • Win's last morning (ch. 42), three blue sheets. She reads it three times before it makes sense. The book's private wound is closed by a document, and in ch. 43 her mother's lawyers confirm "every last thing" in it.

Mechanism notes

  • The forum as tripwire. Her old post is what put her on their list (ch. 41), and she can search it up herself (ch. 33). For SDF: James's old forum persona could be how the organisation first noticed him, years before the book, so that his edited posts read as surveillance he walked into.
  • B (canary), in reverse. Mama gives herself away by knowing one fact she shouldn't: Tokyo (ch. 27). Nobody planted it, but the logic is the canary's, and it takes a friend (Ivy) to notice and report. Mama is also a fake poster written for Dorotea by a hired "puppenkopf" (ch. 38). A ghost-written organisation persona on James's forum fits SDF's rules.
  • D (lock and key), with a price. Baranov won't take money. He trades the address for the one object he hates paying for himself (ch. 29–31). The key is bought on someone else's credit, and the tie to the employer comes due later. Parkaboy proves who he is with forum trivia (ch. 40), so a forum fact works as a password.
  • A (gate), weak. Nothing has to be proved before she may act. The cost of being wrong comes as Dorotea (ch. 38), and Cayce gets out because she refuses to give up her source.
  • Fifth: the reward as a trap. The antagonist pays to make her quiet (the cash, the file). She gives the money away (ch. 43) and keeps the file.
  • The nose. Her allergy becomes the alarm: the hallucinated Michelin Man comes with her father's warning, "She's drugged the water. Scream." (ch. 38). Afterwards the allergy is gone (ch. 43). Win's rule against seeing patterns everywhere (ch. 36) is the book's check on its own heroine.

Quotes

  • "when you suggested in a post that the maker might be a Russian mafia type" (ch. 41): the forum post that set everything off.
  • "Who started the thread that gave Completism its first formal basis?" (ch. 40): forum trivia used as a password.
  • "Only the wound, speaking wordlessly in the dark." (ch. 37): the reveal comes from watching, not from an explanation.
  • "the actual conspiracy is not so often about us; we are most often the merest of cogs in larger plans." (ch. 41): the conspiracy is smaller than feared.

Flags

  • Real programmes and institutions are named but given no invented crimes: Echelon (ch. 30), the CIA, Putin named only as a type, "ex-KGB" (ch. 41).
  • Real history of the Curta and Herzstark (ch. 28, 31); no invented edits on real books.

books.qa:
Answers point to the section notes in this folder: 01 = 01-chapters-1-to-11.md, 02 = 02-chapters-12-to-26.md, 03 = 03-chapters-27-to-43.md. SDF chapters are named by their v8.2 title. Everything is a proposal; Santi's decisions are PLACEHOLDER. 11 Nov 2026.

The nose

1. What exactly is Cayce's "nose," and how is it different from James's? It is a yes/no reaction to brands with no reasons attached ("either blue or it's not," ch. 2), and it is close to an allergy (ch. 1). James's nose, in "The good life," is a hunter's instinct for things that don't fit, with a checking habit behind it. Cayce's is a bodily reaction that can be set off on purpose; James's isn't, yet. See 01, "Why it grips."

2. How does Gibson keep a gifted heroine from being always right? He gives the gift a blind spot and a check. It reads surfaces, not people working against her: she sees the RAF roundel on the scooter rider and doesn't connect him to the man who tails her (ch. 16). And her father's rule on paranoia is run over every hunch (ch. 13). See 02, "Why it grips."

3. Does the nose ever get checked and come back negative? Yes. When Billy Prion turns up on her flight, she runs her father's rule, and a TV ad shows he had an ordinary reason to be there (ch. 13–14). That is the shape 00 SYNTHESIS Rule 2 asks for, but it costs Cayce nothing. Proposal 5.2 in 00-map.md adds a cost. See 02.

4. How do enemies use the nose against her? Dorotea shows her Bibendum in a client meeting and gets "It works" out of her to make it stop, then hangs a felt one on her door (ch. 10). Later Dorotea's forum persona, Mama Anarchia, is written for her by a hired writer (ch. 38). Whoever knows the trigger can steer her. See 01 "Mechanism notes" (fifth mechanism) and 03.

5. Can that "nose as attack surface" work for James without breaking SDF's rules? Yes, if the bait is information, not force. Kalder mentions an invented book whose printings differ, and James spends money and a lie to Ana chasing a clean negative (proposal 5.2, in "The corporate day" or "Enjoy it while it lasts"). No threat, no break-in. See 01 and 03.

6. Does the nose pay off at the end? Twice. The allergy becomes the alarm: a hallucinated Michelin Man with her father's warning, "She's drugged the water. Scream." (ch. 38). Then the allergy is gone (ch. 43), closed with her father's case. See 03, "Mechanism notes."

7. Who does the work the nose can't do? Boone has the method, the forum has the reach, and specialists do the decrypting (Rice, ch. 11 and 25; Mystic, per 02). Cayce brings access and judgment and pays for it in shame. SDF can copy the division of labor only if no helper hacks for James. See 02, "Mechanism notes."

The forum

8. How is F:F:F made to feel like a real place? It is her refuge and a home ("a friend's living room," ch. 7), it has factions with names (ch. 6), and its people have voices in long, funny emails (Parkaboy, ch. 8, 14, 16, 19). Then it "everts": the people turn up in the flesh (ch. 23). See 01 and 02.

9. Who watches the forum in the book? Bigend reads her posts and knows CayceP is Cayce (ch. 7). Blue Ant's Trans seeds the footage and debriefs agents (ch. 9). And a Russian apparatus pays graduate students to lurk; one broke the no-posting rule (ch. 41). See 01 and 03.

10. What is the "old post as tripwire"? Cayce's throwaway post guessing at a Russian mafia patron is what put her on the apparatus's list: from her ISP to her name, to her father's dossier, to the break-in (ch. 41). She rereads the post twice (ch. 33, 36) before she learns that. See 03, "How the conspiracy moves the story here."

11. Is that already in SDF? Partly. "The gorilla mask" has James's twelve-year-old persona edited (v8.2; v6 draft has the eleven readers). v8 "Leave it" says the invoice stepped up the week he typed a question into a forum, which conflicts with v8.2 and v7 "The money" (the ticket week). What Gibson adds is the old post as the first cause, found by rereading. See proposal 5.5 and 03.

12. Does Cayce search her own forum history? Yes. On the plane she searches a CD of every F:F:F post and finds her first one, from before she added the P to her handle (ch. 13). The archive is an object she holds. For James: a copy of his own thread before the edits, printed and put on the tablecloth in "Twenty minutes." See 02, "Mechanism notes."

13. Do forum facts work as passwords? Yes. Parkaboy proves who he is with forum trivia, "Who started the thread that gave Completism its first formal basis?" (ch. 40). SDF already plans a password for "The sheets" (the deleted phrasing). Gibson's version tests belonging to a place, not knowledge of a document. See 03.

14. How did Noor-style contact happen in Gibson? Not by a forum message. The closest is Ivy, a forum friend, noticing that Mama Anarchia knows Cayce is in Tokyo, which she can't know, and reporting it (ch. 27). That is already the shape of v6 "Leiden": Noor spots a style-guide phrase in the reply to James. Don't propose it again. See 03.

15. What is the forum's canary in Gibson, and does it cost anything? Parkaboy and Musashi invent "Keiko" to see who bites; Taki does and offers the number (ch. 8). The bill comes in ch. 23: Judy, the real model, finds out, takes Taki's side, and threatens a journalist. See 01 and 02.

Clues as objects

16. How does Gibson turn an abstract mystery into an object? He narrows "who makes the footage" to "what is the number in #78" (ch. 11), then the number to twelve digits on a napkin (ch. 17), then a T-shaped map (ch. 19). Each step is a thing that can be carried, copied, or stolen. See 01 "How the conspiracy moves the story here" and 02.

17. Why does copying matter? Every copy is a risk and becomes plot: napkin to palm to hotel notepad to Boone (ch. 17–19); the muggers go for her bag, and Boone's first question is "Is it in the laptop?" (ch. 17). SDF's equivalent: James photographing the annex because he no longer trusts systems to keep things overnight (v7 "The money"). See 02.

18. How does the final reveal arrive? As a shape match with no meaning (75% of the T matches part of a Claymore mine, ch. 33), then a hint in Stella's story (ch. 35), then the meaning by watching Nora edit for three hours (ch. 37). Data first, feeling later. SDF's 02:14 does the same across "Leave it" and "The night he stops being afraid." See 03.

19. Does any big reveal come as a document? Yes: Win's last morning, three blue sheets she reads three times (ch. 42), confirmed by lawyers (ch. 43). It closes the private wound, not the plot. See 03, "How the lore gets in."

Lore and pacing

20. Where does the book stall? Win's 9/11 disappearance (ch. 15), about 1,000 words of memory between two errands, held up by one rose petal. Nothing in it changes what Cayce does next. See 02, "How the lore gets in."

21. How does a 2,000-word explanation not stall at the end? It comes after the climax and works as a rereading: each item explains a weirdness already shown (the dust rectangle, the therapist's notes, the man from Cyprus). Wiktor pressing her for the source keeps it tense (ch. 41). Compare "The final conversation," which also comes after the win. See 03.

22. How are Bigend's theory speeches kept moving? Every lecture is part of a pitch, so the reader watches him work on her (ch. 6–7). The old man in "The reading room, continued" can work the same way: his method speech is a pitch for five seats. See 01.

23. What makes Dorotea's confession work as lore? It is hostile: Cayce interrupts, Dorotea needles, every exchange lands a fact, and the reader waits to see if Cayce walks out (ch. 24). A lore scene holds if someone in it wants something from the listener now. See 02.

24. How long are the forum documents? Parkaboy's letter about 900 words (ch. 8); later emails 300–600 (ch. 14, 16, 19); Cynthia's EVP email about 400 (ch. 21). Each has a joke and ends on a question, an instruction, or a new object. See 01 and 02.

The engine and the opponent

25. Why can't Cayce stop? Early: competition (CNN airs #135, ch. 8) and a contract. From ch. 24: somebody paid Dorotea to make her leave London, so quitting gives them what they paid for. See 00-map.md section 2 and 02.

26. Does anyone threaten her to keep her going? No. She refuses Bigend three times and he lets each no stand, changing what she knows instead (ch. 7, 10). Pressure comes from the opponent, aimed at making her leave. That fits SDF's rule that doors open only when a person chooses. See 01, "Why it grips."

27. How close is Gibson's opponent to SDF's organization? On aim, close: it wants her gone, not stopped ("To make you sufficiently uncomfortable that you would leave London," ch. 24). On scale and violence, not: it ends small and protective, and it uses a gun, drugs, and a private prison (ch. 29, 38–41). See 02 and 03.

28. Is there a front (mechanism C)? Yes, layered: Franco works for Dorotea, Dorotea for a Russian "if indeed he was from Cyprus," and he for "them" (ch. 24). Bigend then hires Dorotea, so the agent becomes a source (ch. 24). See 02, "Mechanism notes."

29. Is there a gate (mechanism A)? Weak. Taki tests "Keiko" with Anne of Green Gables (ch. 17); Cayce makes Boone keep her informed (ch. 25). Nothing must be proved before she acts (03). For SDF, proposal 5.3 uses the social test as Noor's gate in "Leiden." See 02 and 03.

30. Is there a lock and key (mechanism D)? Yes, with a price: Baranov won't take money and trades the address for a Curta bought on Bigend's money, which ties her to Bigend (ch. 29–31). See 03. Don't copy the sig-int; copy the idea that the key is paid for with someone else's credit, which comes due.

31. What does "holding back" look like as action? Chapter 20: three people in a Hummer, each keeping something back; Boone lies to Bigend and Cayce's silence makes her complicit. Later she lies to Boone and refuses to name her source (ch. 32–41). Proposal 5.4 gives James the same choice with Pieter in "The money." See 02 and 03.

32. How is the payoff used as a trap? The apparatus pays her: cash and a file on her father. She gives the money away and keeps the file (ch. 43). In SDF the deal in "Monday" and "The final conversation" is a payment for silence; James asks only for the book he may publish. See 03.

Transfer and limits

33. Which proposal is cheapest to write? 5.4 (Pieter's one-to-one): one exchange in "The money," one line back in "The sheets." 5.1 (Beard Man and the invented book) is one market scene. See 00-map.md section 5.

34. Which SDF chapters do the proposals touch? "The corporate day" or "Enjoy it while it lasts" (bait), "On land" (trap), "The gorilla mask" (Beard Man beat; the archive), "Leiden" (Noor's test), "The money" and "The sheets" (Pieter), "Twenty minutes" and "What was on the phone" (the old post). Placement of the market beat is PLACEHOLDER.

35. What should never come over? The violent third act (gun, drugs, kidnapping, prison), outsourced intrusion (Rice, Baranov, Boone trailing her and copying the laptop), and the deflated conspiracy. Also the real brands as triggers. See 00-map.md section 6.

36. Anything in Gibson that breaks SDF's reality rule? No invented edits on real books. Real brands are triggers but not complicit; Echelon, the CIA, and "ex-KGB" are background (01, 02, 03 "Flags"). The 9/11 thread is real history with a fictional victim. Keep SDF's real interludes to documented facts only.

37. Is there an inconsistency in SDF the Gibson reading exposed? Two. Santi's "Reading with a pen" says James lurked for years and "never" spoke on forums, while v6 "Leiden" and "The gorilla mask" give him twelve years of did-you-know posts. And v8 "Leave it" ties the invoice step to a forum question, where v8.2 and v7 "The money" tie it to the ticket. Both are Santi's to settle (PLACEHOLDER).

books.author: King
books.readfor: A: the gate; the past pushing back
books.intro: Coverage: Scribner first hardcover, November 2011 (eBook ISBN 978-1-4516-2730-5) per note 01; the other notes used a converted text with no edition data. English. Read in full through eight section notes (01–08, about 273,000 words), 11 Nov 2026. Anything from outside the notes is marked [from memory, not from the text]. Brief: mechanism A, the gate. What Jake must know before he may act, how long King holds the gate, what fills the wait, and how "the past pushes back" works as an antagonist with no face. Standing-rule note: real people are named as complicit or suspect (de Mohrenschildt, Ruby, Marcello, Hosty, Hoover, Angleton; 03, 05–08). A real local paper is printed in altered versions (01). Jake bugs a house, buys a key, forges a degree, poses as the CIA, holds a gun on a witness and blackmails a woman (03, 04, 06). Take the shapes, none of that.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
Jake Epping, a Maine English teacher, is shown a pantry that opens onto 9 September 1958, and every trip resets. His dying friend Al gives him a mission (stop Oswald) and a rule (not until you know Oswald acted alone). Jake rehearses on a family murder in Derry, then lives five years in Texas under a false name. He falls in love with Sadie and watches the Oswalds while he waits for a test date, the Walker shooting of 10 April 1963. Missing the test costs him, and so does a beating. He saves Kennedy, Sadie dies, the future he made is a ruin, and he resets everything and gives her up.

What makes it work: the reader always knows the date, so the suspense comes from what Jake is not allowed to do before it. And every success is billed to someone he loves, usually through a channel he opened himself.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
• Rabbit-hole rules (ch. 1–2, 01): the trip first, then about 1,500 words of rules, each answering a question the reader already has.
  • Al's pitch (ch. 3, about 4,500 words, 01): a lecture at a deathbed, broken by coughing fits, ending on an object.
  • Al's notebook (03–07): the bulk of the history sits in an object studied off the page; on the page, a line or two, then action. Its gap (no rooming house) forces the plan (ch. 27).
  • Overheard talk (the Cuba speech, ch. 19, 05; the Easter bug, ch. 23, 06): long, but Jake listens for one name, and the gap in the tape is the event.
  • Lore as obstacle (Turcotte's sister, ch. 8, 02): told at bayonet point while the clock runs.
  • Where it stalls: the Hargis–Walker broadcast (ch. 20, 05), which Jake ends by switching the set off, and the Final Notes diary (08), which stalls on purpose. The working rule: violence or a decision comes within about two pages of any lore (03).

sections.title: 4. The mechanism we came for: the gate
sections.html:
Setup (ch. 3, 01). Al gives a number (ninety-five percent isn't a hundred), a deciding event (Oswald firing at Walker), a date before which the gate cannot open, and a price for opening it wrongly: Kennedy dies anyway and five years of a finite life are gone.

The rule (ch. 7, 02). Derry adds the other half: knowledge loses its value once you use it. A warning throws away a known time and place. So the gate controls when he may act, not only what he must know.

First use. A rehearsal gate Jake sets himself (ch. 4): see a big change play out first. He passes it; the bill arrives by phone (ch. 9).

Escalation (03–05). Three locks hold together: a doubt, the rule that any approach changes Oswald's course, and a calendar. The doubt alone wouldn't hold, because the reader would ask why he doesn't just look. The calendar is what makes waiting forced. Then the question narrows to one named man and one dated stand-in test, and King admits it can never be fully passed (ch. 21). Every attempt to pass it early makes things worse.

The wait is filled with equipment (getting ready to listen) and a life (what listening will cost). King checks the Oswald clock at moments of happiness (03, 04). Measured by the notes' word counts, the gate holds from chapter 3 to chapter 25, about seven tenths of the book.

Cost rarely comes from the enemy. Sadie leaves because Jake won't explain, and a school clerk exposes him (04). An unrelated man's jealousy steals the test, and the beating comes through the betting that paid for the wait (06). Waiting until the 22nd puts Sadie on the stairs (07).

Payoff (07–08). Certainty arrives after the act. Being right about the target made nothing safe. A second gate follows (warn Sadie?), and he cannot pass it.

The past pushes back only through ordinary, deniable causes (tires, a jammed door, flu, amnesia), in proportion to the change, harder on repeat, each delivered by a small agent with his own motive (01, 03, 06, 07). It also rhymes, and the rhymes carry information: JIMLA turns out to be a billboard that tells Jake what to buy next (04). It gets a face only at the end, a worn-out guard who can only warn and beg (08).

Against A–D. A: supported, with two additions (the gate governs timing; passing it doesn't make the act safe). B: small (Al's carved tree, 01; Frati sent to test Jake, 02). C: weak (the Derry paper, 03; Ruby inside the clearing clipping, 06; the FBI's cover story, 07). D: steady (the children, the Cullums, the Depository co-worker, private facts as keys, 02–08). Fifth mechanisms: the page that changed because of the hero's harmless act (01); a witness's record right in its claim and wrong in a detail (Harry's essay, 02); the cost landing on the side channel that kept the wait going (06); echo as a clue-giver (03, 04); the investigator becoming the theory (08).

sections.title: 5. Transfer to SDF
sections.html: Already on the page, so not proposed: the hero's harmless act changing the record (The payload; The money's step the week of his ticket); the investigator turned into the theory (The gorilla mask); echo (02:14, eleven); the threshold as a number (Leiden, "until we're a hundred per cent"); the cost of keeping the secret (The math; The schedule); "ask the one who knows" (the thin book's Ask). The gap is a gate and a cost of being wrong.

items.title: 1. The eighth address as the Walker test
items.html:
The other ten → The reading room, continued.

  • Change: the eighth address, dated nine days off, becomes the test James must witness before anyone gets a sheet. If someone comes, the schedule is real, and so is his own line on it.
  • James does: on the date he sits in his car on a public street with Buddy. He chooses between knocking to warn them, which tells the organisation he holds the schedule (King ch. 7), and watching. He watches. Nobody comes.
  • Cost: the test fails because he was there, and a week later the address goes quiet anyway (PLACEHOLDER: quiet, moved, or dead). The old man turns it on him.
  • On the page? Partly. v7 The other ten holds the dates back; v7 The reading room, continued has only the margin note "I was there. Nobody came. Why." and the old man's "nobody came because you'd gone." The v8.2 plan has neither.

items.title: 2. The schedule is right about the visit and wrong about the date, and James moved the date
items.html:
The schedule, A car park, A street, night, The vet.

  • Change: James trusts the printed date the way Jake trusts Harry's essay. The visit comes early because the review moved when he stopped asking out loud.
  • James does: he books Buddy into Frank's flat for the printed week and writes it in his diary.
  • Cost: Buddy is poisoned before that week (PLACEHOLDER: how many days). In The vet James sees that the verb that moved the date was his.
  • On the page? Partly. v8.2 has the eleven days, a date moved by a verb (A car park), and Ana leaving "knowing a house with one old dog in it is a target." James never plans around the date, so its moving costs him nothing he chose.

items.title: 3. The friendship is the side channel, and it carries the bill
items.html:
On land, The gorilla mask, A street, night.

  • Change: after the invented-book trap James keeps the friendship going deliberately, as his way of watching, the way Jake's bets pay for the wait.
  • James does: he agrees to the barbecue for a reason he keeps from Ana: to see what Buddy does with Kalder in the house. He gets his answer (four hours in the doorway).
  • Cost: the barbecue is where Kalder learns the back lane, the fourth gate and the water bowl.
  • On the page? Partly. In v8.2 Ana insists on the barbecue; On land says only that the friendship "continues." A street, night uses the layout but never says where Kalder learned it.

items.title: 4. A written gate with a skeptic as its keeper
items.html:
Leiden, Frank, loose, The sheets.

  • Change: after Noor gives him the professor's rule, James writes his own smaller one, as Jake does after Poulin: no sheet to anyone until Frank has tried to explain one piece of paper and failed.
  • James does: he holds the sheets back until Frank, loose, while the ninth date approaches. Frank's "I believe the invoice" opens the gate.
  • Cost: the ninth date passes while he waits (PLACEHOLDER: what happens there).
  • On the page? Partly. v7 Frank, loose has James decide Frank "needed to see one thing he couldn't argue with." Nothing states the condition in advance, and nothing is lost while he waits.

items.title: 5. The cost lands on the person who opened the door
items.html:
The money, Enjoy it while it lasts.

  • Change: the annex role Saskia granted "with a sigh" turns up in the bank's quarterly access review, the same kind of routine paperwork as the immunization record that exposes Jake (ch. 17).
  • James does: he writes his own justification on the review form for Pieter to sign. He gives the true, dull reason and leaves the annex out.
  • Cost: Saskia loses the right to grant roles and is moved; James's access narrows.
  • On the page? No. In v7 The money the role is added and nothing follows. The v8.2 Enjoy it while it lasts narrows his access with no person paying.

items.title: 6. The price of a visit, from a person
items.html:
The vet, Leiden, Friday, The other ten.

  • Change: James learns what his Leiden visit cost Noor as Jake learns about Harry: by phone.
  • James does: he rings her workshop. A colleague says she has stopped taking private clients and "said you'd call." From then on he stops visiting helpers in person and works on paper, which is The sheets' method.
  • Cost: Noor's livelihood, and James knowing his visit caused it.
  • On the page? Partly. v8.2 The vet ends "Then nothing"; Leiden, Friday shows the cost to the reader, never to James.

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• Jake's methods (bugs, bought keys, forged papers, posing as the CIA, the gun, blackmail; 04, 06). In King the gate opens at gunpoint; in SDF someone must choose to open it.
  • The body count and register (a child killed on the page, a kneecapping, a murder left unpunished; 02, 03, 06).
  • Real people as suspects, and the altered real newspaper (01, 05–08).

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
1. "Because being ninety-five percent sure isn’t a hundred." (ch. 3) The gate as a number.
  2. "You also put Carolyn Poulin back in a wheelchair." (ch. 3) The reveal turned on the hero.
  3. "Something doesn’t want it to be changed, I’m pretty sure of that. But it can be." (ch. 3) The antagonist named by what it does.
  4. "As it was, I knew where and when. If I warned him, all bets were off." (ch. 7) The gate as a rule about when.
  5. "By committing suicide, Al had taken away the scholar’s greatest weakness: calling hesitation research." (ch. 12) The deadline against the gate.
  6. "GOOD ENOUGH TO TAKE THE SON OF A BITCH OUT." (ch. 17) A threshold, not certainty.
  7. "I’d gotten the heart-to-heart, but it made things worse instead of better." (ch. 19) Passing early raises the doubt.
  8. "Savior, or part of the plot? People held actual conventions to discuss it" (ch. 31) The investigator becomes the theory.

notes.title: front matter to chapter 4 (prologue, Part 1 chapters 1–4)
notes.html:
Coverage: front matter, unnumbered prologue, Part 1 "Watershed Moment" chapters 1–4 (about 32,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: Scribner, first hardcover edition November 2011 (eBook ISBN 978-1-4516-2730-5).

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 1–2) To find out why Al closed the diner overnight and sounds like he is dying Al has aged four years in a day; the pantry steps lead to 11:58 a.m., 9 September 1958; every trip resets Nothing visible yet (a root beer) Al is dying, the diner is demolished on 1 July, and Jake already wants to go back (ch. 2 §8) The night visit to Al's house
2 (ch. 3) To learn what Al wants The Kennedy mission; the rule that Oswald must first be proved the Walker shooter; a past that resists; the Poulin printout His first harmless trip undid Al's rescue and put a girl back in a wheelchair He is responsible without having chosen, and Al may be dead by morning (he hands over the diner key) Decide overnight
3 (ch. 4) To know what changing a watershed does before he touches Dallas Harry Dunning's theme dates the hammer murders to Halloween 1958, within reach Years in the past under a name off a gravestone (George Amberson) He sets his own gate: Poulin was a poor test, he needs a better one Down the steps, bound for Derry

Why it grips

King gives the experience before the explanation. Al refuses to explain the pantry (ch. 1 §4), so Jake and the reader go through with no rules; the rules come afterwards (ch. 2 §7) as answers to questions the reader already holds. Each lecture is earned by a scene.

Al's body is the clock. Every long speech in ch. 3 is broken by coughing fits, bloody napkins and a box of maxi pads, and each fit reminds the reader the speaker may not finish. The lore is long but the scene is a deathbed, so it never sits still.

The best-built scene ends ch. 3. Al tells the Poulin rescue as a success, asks "happily ever after?", Jake agrees; Al points to an object he planted in advance (a printout in the notebook's back cover); Jake reads it and works out the twist himself before Al confirms. The reversal lands on the hero, not the world.

The prologue promises that "every terrible thing" flowed from Jake's tears over Harry's theme; Harry is parked for three chapters and returns in ch. 4 as the next mission. The comedy never drops (catburger rumours, Al's baffled answer to the grandfather paradox, a gnome's Texas flag that turns out to be a clue).

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The conspiracy's job is to be the thing that must be ruled out. Jake asks what happens if he stops Oswald and someone shoots from the knoll (ch. 3 §4). Al is "close to positive" it was Oswald alone and explains why theories exist (Manchester's scale: the waif does not weigh enough against the president), but close is not enough. He gives a threshold in numbers (he wanted ninety-eight percent), a deciding event (seeing Oswald fire at General Walker, April 1963), and the price of error: kill Oswald, Kennedy dies anyway, and a man in his sixties may not get another five years to retry.

So the possibility of a conspiracy blocks action. Al stood within choking distance of Oswald in Fort Worth and did nothing (wife and baby present, prison, doubt). It also fills the waiting: the gate cannot open before April 1963, so the hero must live in the past until then. The energy here is not whodunit; it is that acting before you are sure wastes years you cannot get back.

Jake then copies the logic at smaller scale: no Kennedy until he has seen a bigger change play out (ch. 4 §6). The gate is stacked: test case, then Walker, then Dallas.

How the lore gets in

  • Rabbit-hole rules (ch. 1 §4–ch. 2 §7): first instructions without reasons (hand over your phone, take old money, give the wino half a rock), then the trip as scene (about 4,000 words), then about 1,500 words of rules in dialogue. No stall: each rule answers something just seen.
  • Watershed lecture and Kennedy pitch (ch. 3 §3–4, about 4,500 words): argument, Jake objecting. It holds because Jake guesses the target before Al names it, the Oswald meeting is told as a remembered scene with dialogue, and the coughing marks time.
  • Poulin test case (ch. 3 §6, about 2,800 words): a story within the story with its own obstacles, ending on an object.
  • The Oswald Book (ch. 3 §4): a notebook holding the timeline and evidence. King hands the bulk of the lore over as an object to "cram" off-page and puts none of it here.
  • The tin box (ch. 4 §7): cash, ID, typed credit cards, a sports-results sheet; each object carries one rule of 1958 in a line of dialogue.

Mechanism notes

  • A, the gate. The clearest version on the reading list so far. It has a threshold, a deciding event, a date before which it cannot open, and a cost of opening it wrongly (years of a finite life, since a do-over restarts in 1958 and every reset erases the good with the bad). For SDF: James's gate could be one named event he must witness or one named document he must hold that rules out the bigger explanation, and being wrong costs a resource he cannot get back (PROPOSAL; the map writer names the v8.2 chapter).
  • The past pushes back. A faceless antagonist working through ordinary failures (two flat tyres, a bridge down, a tree across the road) that escalate on repeat (a thrown rod the second time, ch. 3 §6). Every obstacle has a mundane explanation and can be denied, which fits SDF's rule that the organisation discredits rather than prevents. Al's image: a nylon stocking that gives, snaps back, and can be torn. His phrase "Something doesn't want it to be changed" is close to the SDF title.
  • B, a canary in miniature. Before trusting the hole, Al carves his name and "2007" into a tree in 1958, then drives to Sebago to see whether it survived (ch. 3 §6). He plants a mark and checks it.
  • A fifth mechanism: the page that changed, and you changed it. The Poulin printout is two printings of one newspaper page, wheelchair in one and not the other, and the difference is the hero's own fault. That is SDF's premise turned on James: an innocent act of his (a library request, a query at work) triggers a re-edit. It gives Part Two a cost of being wrong with no break-in and no pressure on anyone (PROPOSAL).
  • D, lock and key. Absent.

Quotes

  1. "Because being ninety-five percent sure isn’t a hundred." (ch. 3 §4) — the gate as a number.
  2. "I knew I might not get another chance to make it right if I killed Oswald and someone else shot the president anyway." (ch. 3 §4) — the cost of opening it wrongly.
  3. "Something doesn’t want it to be changed, I’m pretty sure of that. But it can be." (ch. 3 §6) — the faceless antagonist, named by what it does.
  4. "That’s right, buddy. You bought yourself a dime root beer this afternoon. You also put Carolyn Poulin back in a wheelchair." (ch. 3 §6) — the reveal turned on the hero.

Flags

  • Real people: Oswald as killer and Walker as target are on the historical record; Al dismisses theories blaming the Mafia, KGB, Castro or Johnson. No real person is made complicit beyond the record, and SDF must not do so either.
  • An altered real publication: King invents changed versions of the Lisbon Weekly Enterprise (a real local paper [from memory, not from the text]). Under SDF's rule (no invented edit on a real book), the printout device transfers only to an invented book or paper.
  • Frank Anicetti, a real shopkeeper [from memory, not from the text], appears as a character. SDF invents its people.

notes.title: Part 2, "The Janitor's Father" (chapters 5–8)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 5–8 (about 42,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk 02-part-2-to-chapter-8.txt; the file carries no edition data.

This section is the rehearsal, not the Oswald case. Jake goes to Derry in 1958 to stop Frank Dunning killing his family on Halloween, because the trip exists to find out what saving the janitor's family does to the future (ch. 7). So the gate appears here in small: a test case Jake must run before he may try the big one. Oswald's own gate gets one line: Jake remembers Al's lingering doubt that Oswald acted alone (ch. 7).

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 6) The address of the right Dunning family 96 Dunnings in the phone book; the 1950 census was moved to City Hall and lost in a flood, and nobody knows who ordered the move; two children give him Kossuth Street only after he warns them He has said "Dunning" aloud to strangers outside a bar, and one of them starts watching him He has now seen Ellen and Harry alive; they are people, not names in an essay Seven weeks of waiting until the fixed date
2 (ch. 7) A way to stop Frank before Halloween His own list (police, anonymous call, frame, disable, kill), and each fails: police won't believe an outsider; a warning wastes his only advantage; disabling only delays; letting it happen once to learn details defeats the test Weeks of shadowing; a gun bought in the open, seen by the same man; a "friendly" informant planted on him Any early move spends his knowledge of where and when One shot, on the night, from a hiding place behind the house
3 (ch. 8) To be behind the hedge at 8 pm A watcher he never suspected (Turcotte) holds him at bayonet point, demands his purpose, then decides to let the murders happen Flu on the day, a scalp wound, Tugga dead anyway, Turcotte's heart attack, the car abandoned The clock is fixed; waiting means losing Back through the rabbit-hole to see what he changed in 2011

Why it grips

  • The reader knows the date and the method from the start. Harry's essay (Part 1) is the script, and every Derry scene is measured against it. The suspense is watching where the script holds and where it slips: the orange card instead of the yellow one (ch. 5), a sledgehammer where the essay had a hammer, Doris saying different words from the ones Harry remembered (ch. 8).
  • The waiting has jobs to do. Shadowing, the notebook, the fake property tours look like dead time, but each plants something that pays off on the night: the Rec and Wyemore Lane give him a hiding place, the TV Guide gives him a clock (Ellery Queen at 8), and Frati's gossip turns out to be Turcotte's probe.
  • Ch. 8 §§8–10 carries the most weight. Jake is trapped behind a garage with the target house in view, a gun he no longer holds, and a watch he keeps checking. Turcotte's backstory (his sister and her baby, missing since 1938) is told while the clock runs, so the lore itself is the obstacle; Jake admits he let the story distract him when he could have grabbed the gun. The reversal: the one person who knows Frank is a killer chooses to let it happen.
  • A late retrospective line pulls the floor away (ch. 8 §1): the narrator tells us that a scene we read as warm (Frati at the bar, ch. 7) had been arranged.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

No conspiracy behind Oswald appears in this section. What it has is a small-town hidden order in three layers, each changing what Jake does:

  1. The town's "veil" (ch. 6). People go quiet when asked questions, records vanish, posters warn against strangers. It blocks the ordinary routes (paper records, talking to children) and leaves only people who choose to talk.
  2. A private watcher with his own case. Turcotte has suspected Dunning of murder for twenty years. He shadows Jake, sends Frati to sound him out, and on the night stands between Jake and the target: a second investigator whose aim is the opposite of the hero's.
  3. "The past pushes back," an antagonist with no face. Its tools are small and deniable: the flooded records, the match the fan blows out, the flu, the dropped gun, the sandbox, air gone "syrupy" as he runs. King keeps it unprovable, so the reader can never pin a will on it, which is why it scares. The irony: the flu meant to stop Jake also brings on Turcotte's heart attack, and Turcotte is the one who kills Dunning.

How the lore gets in

  • The Derry murders (ch. 6 §3): bartender's gossip over a beer, about 1,500 words. It runs into a child killed by his stepfather with a hammer, an echo of Jake's case, so it does not stall.
  • Frank's history (ch. 7 §8): Frati at the bar, about 1,200 words, while Jake watches Frank in the mirror.
  • Derry's wrongness (ch. 8 §2): a catalogue of omens ending at the pipe in the old ironworks, about 700 words. The one place the story goes still; King keeps it short.
  • Turcotte's sister (ch. 8 §§8–9): a confession at knifepoint, about 2,000 words, broken by watch checks. It cannot stall the story because it is what is in the way.

Mechanism notes

  • A, the gate. Here the gate is not "rule out the bigger explanation" but knowledge loses its value once you use it. Jake may not act early, because any warning throws away a known time and place (ch. 7 §5). The gate governs when he may act, not what he must prove. For SDF: James's findings could be worth something only while the organisation doesn't know he has them, so every use costs him.
  • B, the canary, turned on the hero. Turcotte uses Frati as a canary on Jake: feed him gossip, watch the reaction (ch. 7–8). For SDF: the friendly colleague who hands James a document is testing him.
  • D, lock and key, twice. The children hold back the address until Jake gives them a truth, a warning that Tugga is in danger (ch. 6). Turcotte demands the same, and Jake tells him the version he already believes, minus the time travel (ch. 8 §9). The cost: the right key opens the wrong door. Turcotte believes him and chooses to wait.
  • A fifth: the witness's record is wrong in the details. The essay is true in outline and false in detail (sledgehammer, different words), and trusting it costs Tugga's life. For SDF: a document James relies on is right in its claim and wrong in a detail that matters.
  • Paying for being wrong (the SDF gap). Jake misreads Frati, trusts the essay's hammer, and trusts the flu to deal with Turcotte. Each mistake costs blood, and the partial win (he promises Doris he will do better next time) sets up a second try.

Quotes

  1. "As it was, I knew where and when. If I warned him, all bets were off." (ch. 7) The gate as a rule about when.
  2. "no one seems to know why they were or who authorized it." (ch. 6) The missing record, with no one to blame.
  3. "The past does not want to be changed. The past is obdurate." (ch. 8) The antagonist's refrain, during the flu.
  4. "Certainly I had no idea that a man named Bill Turcotte had put Frati up to it." (ch. 8) The late line that reveals an arranged scene.

Flags

  • Real people: Oswald named as the future target, no one else called complicit; Muskie and Eisenhower appear as background only. No real books edited.
  • Period slurs (anti-Jewish, racial) in dialogue and narration (ch. 7–8). Do not carry over.
  • Richie, Beverly, the clown and the Barrens cross over from King's earlier Derry novel [from memory, not from the text].
  • Ch. 8 kills a child on the page, far darker than SDF's register. Take the structure, not the gore.

notes.title: Part 3, chapters 9–13
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 9–13 (about 41,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, no edition data in the file (chunk 03-part-3-to-chapter-13.txt).

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch 9) To confirm that saving the Dunnings worked, then sleep A changed photo on Al's wall; Ellen says Harry died at Khe Sanh; Al has killed himself Guilt: his rescue bought Harry a different death Going back resets 1958, so Tugga must be saved again; the diner will be padlocked by morning He goes back the same night and starts over
2 (ch 10–11) To repeat the Derry rescue without changing anything until the moment comes The past fights back in proportion to what is at stake: migraine, snapped banister, dead car, cracked spare, a gravel truck through a red, a door that locks itself He becomes a murderer, killing Dunning before he has harmed this family If he turns back, the new reset makes him complicit: "participated in murdering them" (ch 10 §10) Carolyn Poulin, then Florida, then Texas
3 (ch 12–13) To stop Oswald Al's "window of uncertainty"; Oswald in Russia until June 1962; any early approach wastes his foreknowledge Florida house firebombed after a big bet; years of waiting; a life in Jodie he will have to risk He may not act until he is sure, and he cannot leave because Kennedy will die He settles, teaches, meets Sadie; the Yellow Card Man's "Jimla" returns as a football chant

Why it grips

Oswald is off the page for most of this section. The suspense comes from three other sources. First, the rules get tested before the big job. The Derry redo (ch 10) rehearses Dallas: Jake states a theory, resistance proportional to consequence (ch 9 §5), then pays for it item by item in ordinary bad luck that piles up past coincidence. He has prepared (a mechanic paid $20 the day before), so it is his foresight against the past's inventiveness. The headache lifting in the cemetery ("on the other side") shows resistance has a limit.

Second, every success costs something. Chapter 9's best scene: Jake phones Ellen Dunning to confirm his triumph and learns Harry died in Vietnam. Ellen reads his voice (“You sound like you’re no more than thirty-five”) and turns his false identity against him. It is funny until it isn't, and it ends on "Where were you then, you son of a bitch?" Al's suicide follows within a page and closes off the option of quitting.

Third, the waiting becomes the stakes. Chapters 12–13 fill the gate with a life: fake diploma, substitute teaching, Of Mice and Men, Mimi, Sadie. King checks the Oswald clock at moments of happiness. At the curtain call Jake thinks of the newlyweds in Minsk (ch 13 §4). When Mimi offers a contract he works out the Oswalds' arrival date before he says yes (§5).

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The conspiracy question decides when Jake may act, not whether he will. Al's notes keep "a small but statistically significant possibility" that Oswald was not alone (ch 12 §8). Jake adds the patsy scenario: scare Oswald off and Kennedy may still die by "some crazy Mafia or CIA plot,", costing him five more years (§9). So: watch, do not interfere, and close the window on Al's date, April 10, 1963.

What Jake has to know before he may act is that Oswald is the only shooter. The section never says how he will prove it, only that he must wait and watch.

The gate is held by three locks working together: (1) the conspiracy doubt, (2) the butterfly rule, under which any approach changes Oswald's course and wastes the foreknowledge, and (3) the calendar, since Oswald is out of the country. Lock 3 does the real holding. Locks 1 and 2 explain why he does not shoot Oswald on arrival.

King also adds pressure in the other direction. Al's suicide removes "calling hesitation research" (ch 12 §2). The gate stops Jake from acting early, and the deadline stops him from investigating forever.

The conspiracy also puts people in the room. The bookie Gutierrez is linked by gossip to the New Orleans Mob, which Jake connects to Oswald's uncle (ch 12 §3). His fear of Gutierrez drives him out of Florida early.

How the lore gets in

  • Rules of time travel (ch 9 §4–5): dialogue in a moving car, about a page. Al asks "Could you give it to me in English?" and Jake answers with a concrete comparison (the Poulin girl against the Dunnings). A nurse interrupts a few lines later. No stall.
  • Derry's cover story (ch 9 §7): two newspaper archives, read as objects. Jake knows the official version is false because he was there (bayonet, not hunting knife). About a page. Echoed by "In Derry, we keep ourselves to ourselves" (ch 10 §13).
  • Al's Oswald notes (ch 12 §2, §8–9): an object Jake carries, quoted in fragments ("Red dress, white slippers"; "Open auditorium, no bullet-pr’f podium").
