The longest block, two pages of reasoning outside the Depository, sits inside a scene of menace: the sixth-floor window whispers an invitation ("Come on in"). Within two sections a man shoots a girl and then himself on Greenville Avenue.
  • Dallas as a place (ch 12 §9): a page and a half of billboards, then the shooting. Lore is followed by violence within about two pages, every time.
  • The Oswald family (ch 12 §19): no exposition at all. Jake watches Marguerite chase Robert down the street. Character delivered as surveillance.

Mechanism notes

  • A, gate. King builds the gate from a doubt plus a date. The doubt alone would not hold, because a reader would ask why he doesn't just look. What makes it work is that the doubt cannot be checked yet. Transfer: James's gate needs an event he cannot inspect before a known date (a reprint run, an archive release, an AGM), so that waiting is forced rather than chosen. Then fill the wait with a life he comes to value, as Jodie does for Jake. PROPOSAL.
  • The faceless antagonist. The past acts only through deniable, ordinary causes: corroded plugs, a gravel truck, kids "who were out drinking and carousing," blamed for a firebombed house (ch 12 §7). Only the pattern is hostile. This fits SDF's rule that the organisation discredits rather than prevents: the harm is always explainable.
  • Cost of being wrong. Ellen's call (ch 9 §8) is the model SDF lacks: a correct action produces a fresh casualty, and he learns it by phone, from a person.
  • B, canary (reversed). Jake's bets use knowledge he should not have, and that marks him. Gutierrez's "my Yanqui," and then "Stupid me" after Faith Financial (ch 12 §17–18). Using what you know makes you visible.
  • C, front. The Derry paper's tidy hero story (ch 9 §7) is a front read by the one man who was there.
  • D, lock and key. The Cullums (ch 11): no coercion, just an odd offer, and the wife decides. "God sent me an answer, but not the whole answer." The door opens because a person chooses.
  • Fifth: echo. The past rhymes: a nurse named Doris, a second Al's Diner in Jodie, "JIMLA." Cheap dread that is also funny. An SDF version would be a word from the edited passage turning up in James's ordinary day.

Quotes

  1. "I had come back to Derry to knock Frank Dunning’s house of cards down, but until then I had to protect it." (ch 10)
  2. "By committing suicide, Al had taken away the scholar’s greatest weakness: calling hesitation research." (ch 12)
  3. "Sure as he was about his lone gunman theory, Al had held onto a small but statistically significant possibility that he was wrong." (ch 12)
  4. "But I would watch out for the past, because it senses change-agents, and it has teeth." (ch 12)

Flags

  • Real people tied to crime: Carlos Marcello and "Dutz" Murret are named as Mob figures (ch 12 §3). SDF must not name real people as complicit.
  • The hero kills a man in cold blood and is not punished for it (ch 10). Under SDF's rules killing is rare and a failure.
  • Jake forges a reference and buys a mail-order degree (ch 12 §4, §16). Check against James's rules.
  • A landlord's racist speech (ch 12 §10). Do not quote it.

notes.title: Part 4 "Sadie and the General" (chapters 14–17)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 14–17 (about 34,400 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, reading chunk 04 (the file gives no edition data).

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 14–15, Oct–Dec 1961) To be in position to overhear Oswald before Oswald exists in Texas Silent Mike's lamp bugs; 2703 Mercedes Street, rented by Ivy Templeton; the house opposite has a clear view in $180 plus $200 to Ivy; his first lie to Sadie ("research for your book") the day after they become lovers The meeting that decides everything (Oswald and de Mohrenschildt) will happen in that living room, and he has to hear it A duplicate key, a bugged lamp planted on New Year's Day (ch. 16 §2), and the plan to rent 2706
2 (ch. 15–17 §1, winter to May 1962) To keep Sadie and the mission both The secrecy shows: night talk ("Derry is Dallas"), anachronisms ("Honky Tonk Women", "excellent, dude"), faked references; Sadie's full name reads DORIS DUN under his thumbs Sadie ends it (ch. 16 §11); the school exposes him over a missing immunization record (ch. 17 §1) Telling her means pulling her into "the shark's mouth", and the test that would end the secrecy is a year away He leaves Jodie and rents the shack across from Oswald's future house
3 (ch. 17 §2–14, June–July 1962) To see Oswald and get a usable ear on him Oswald at Love Field, cruel and tender inside a minute; the planted bug can only be wired up by going near the house Isolation on Mercedes Street; he watches Sadie fly to Reno from the same terminal and does not follow De Mohrenschildt is the open question, and the bug is too risky to use The "Jimla" billboard and Coach's complaint point him to a long-range microphone; he goes back to Silent Mike (ch. 17 §14)

Why it grips

The reader is waiting for the shooting, and King makes the wait the subject. The gate is stated only near the end (ch. 17 §8); everything before it is the life Jake builds while waiting, and that life is the stake. Each step into Jodie (the dance, the Candlewood, the Jamboree) raises what leaving will cost.

The withheld item is Jake's secret, kept from Sadie. The reader knows it, so the tension is how it leaks: small, funny slips, a Rolling Stones lyric in the car, future slang at the checkout. The blow-up (ch. 16 §11) is built as Sadie's list of every slip she has saved, each one recognised by the reader. Then King flips it: mid-fight Jake thumbs two parts of her name on a job application and reads DORIS DUN. She is exposing him, and suddenly he sees she is in danger; he looks maddest just when he is most right.

Pressure falls on the people around him: Vince dies, Bobbi Jill is scarred, Ivy's husband is crushed. Jake fears he caused it (ch. 15 §14); the book never answers.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

Here the gate is stated outright (ch. 17 §8): Jake may kill Oswald only once he knows whether de Mohrenschildt took part in the Walker shooting (10 April 1963). If Oswald acted alone then, Al's notes put a second gunman in November near zero.

It demands surveillance, and every practical step aims at one future conversation: bugs, key, rental, night-watchman cover, binoculars, microphone. It blocks a normal life: no contract, no play at first, no truth for Sadie, because the test is a year off and he must be free and unknown when it comes. It costs Sadie, his job and his name (he comes to hate "George"). It puts in the room Ivy (sells the key), Silent Mike (sells the tools), Ellie and Deke (cover for him, then gently expose him).

The past pushing back has no face, and here it works mostly as harmony. Ivy shares Al's surname; Sadie's name echoes Doris Dunning, making her husband a likely Frank Dunning; the Derry skip-rope chant turns up on Mercedes Street. The "Jimla" haunts Jake's dream and a child's nightmare, then turns out to be a billboard for Jim LaDue that tells him what to buy next. The echoes warn and hand him the next tool. The actual obstruction is ordinary: a state immunization clause, slashed tyres, a bug he cannot safely wire up.

How the lore gets in

  • Al's rule for the gate (ch. 17 §8): about 450 words, a dream conversation with dead Al, then a paragraph on de Mohrenschildt and two lines from Al's notes. Within half a page there is something to watch (the skip-rope girls); binoculars are bought next day. No stall: the lecture is an argument (Jake asks if Al believes it; Al says no) and ends on a decision rule.
  • Sadie's marriage, the broom (ch. 15 §11): about 1,300 words of confession in the dark. A nightmare and Vince's death follow at once. No stall: every detail (alphabetised books, hand-washing) later becomes evidence that Clayton is dangerous.
  • Spy-gear lore (ch. 14 §2, ch. 15 §6, ch. 17 §12–14) comes as shopping and grumbling (Silent Mike's pitch, Coach's anger at the sideline mic): comedy, and objects Jake can buy.
  • The Jamboree's minstrel history (ch. 16 §5): texture.
  • Identity evidence as objects: Ivy's duplicate key, the Harrah's application, the Tiger Tails yearbook page 89 (lent by Ellie, with forceps marks at Clayton's temples), the Time cover of Jackie Kennedy that keeps Jake in his seat at the airport.

Mechanism notes

  • A, gate. King's gate has four parts SDF can copy. (1) One named question: was de Mohrenschildt involved. (2) A dated test in the future that can be observed: the Walker shooting. (3) A "good enough" threshold written by someone else: a rule, not certainty. (4) A long hold of about ten months in story time, filled with preparation that costs something. The waiting holds two things: equipment (getting ready to listen) and a life (what listening will cost). For James: a stated rule from someone he trusts ("if X made the edit alone, you may go public"), a date when it can be checked, and a life he must hide meanwhile.
  • The cost of being wrong comes from keeping the secret, not from the enemy. Sadie leaves because Jake will not explain; Ellie exposes him through routine paperwork. The organisation never has to act. This is the cost SDF's Part Two lacks, and it needs no villain.
  • D, lock and key, partly. Each helper wants one particular thing: Ivy wants money, Mike wants to be admired as a craftsman, Ellie wants an explanation. Ellie and Deke open doors (the Candlewood, the yearbook) because they choose to, which fits SDF's rule.
  • A fifth idea, the echo as clue-giver. The faceless force rhymes events, and the rhyme carries information (DORIS DUN; JIMLA to microphone): uncanny and funny at once.

Quotes

  • "the only thing keeping me from killing Oswald as soon as he moved in across the street." (ch. 17 §8). The gate stated as the only barrier.
  • "GOOD ENOUGH TO TAKE THE SON OF A BITCH OUT." (ch. 17 §8). A threshold, not certainty.
  • "The past might be obdurate but the future was delicate, a house of cards" (ch. 16 §10). The double constraint on acting early.
  • "“It’s too early,” I said." (ch. 17 §10). The gate's timetable overrides the love story.

Flags

  • Real people are named as possible conspirators (de Mohrenschildt, Walker, Oswald). SDF's rule is that people and companies are invented, so copy the shape, not the naming.
  • Jake threatens to tell Ivy's husband about the money if she forgets to call (ch. 14 §3) and pays for the key. That is pressure and buying access, and SDF forbids James both.
  • Jake plants a bug in a rented house (ch. 16 §2). SDF does not allow breaking in or covert entry.

notes.title: section 5 (chapters 18–21)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 18–21 (about 32,600 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: plain-text conversion, no edition details in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 18–19) To hear Oswald and de Mohrenschildt alone, so he can rule de Mohrenschildt out A bugged lamp that nearly falls and breaks; a de Mohrenschildt who names Walker, tears his shirt open and points at Jake's window Months away from Sadie; nearly caught; has to watch Marina beaten and do nothing The listening made things worse. De Mohrenschildt now looks able to aim Oswald, so killing Oswald alone might change nothing Moves below the Oswalds' future flat on Neely Street and plants a second bug
2 (ch. 19–20) To keep Sadie alive through the Cuban crisis Clayton's Hiroshima photos; Sadie overdosed on Nembutal and Scotch Spends future knowledge to calm her; is bound to her again The gate date has not come, and now he has something to lose Two lives: Jodie at weekends, surveillance in Dallas
3 (ch. 20–21) To learn whether the Walker shooting is a one-man job De Mohrenschildt says killing Walker would do society a favour; the bug dies mid-reply; Oswald scouts the alley; a stranger talks to him at the bus stop Buys a gun, hides Al's notes in a deposit box, tells Sadie his real name and proposes, knowing he may have to run His own rule: no act until he has seen Oswald alone on April 10 Wednesday night in the alley (next section)

Why it grips

The reader always knows the date. Al's notes give a hard deadline (April 10, then November 22), so eight months of waiting read as a countdown, not a drift. The waiting is filled with scenes where looking is itself dangerous: the lamp toppling as Jake plants the bug (ch. 18 §11), de Mohrenschildt jabbing a finger at the house across the street, which is Jake's (ch. 19 §2), Oswald walking straight toward him on Oak Lawn (ch. 21 §7).

The scene that does the most work is the bug failing (ch. 21 §5). It tightens step by step: Haiti, then Walker's ambitions, then de Mohrenschildt's line that killing Walker would be a public service. Oswald begins "If you really believe—" and the line goes dead. The one sentence that would open the gate is the one the reader never hears.

The pressure also comes from his passivity. An old woman on a walker orders him to stop Oswald beating Marina and calls him a coward (ch. 20 §5); he cannot even suggest the police, in case that changes the future. Each new fact raises the price of acting: Marina is pregnant (ch. 20 §9), so the target is now a father of two.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The possibility of a conspiracy is the only thing stopping Jake. He says he could simply wait for the Walker attempt and kill Oswald afterwards; he is bugging the flat only because de Mohrenschildt might be more than he looks (ch. 18 §11). That suspicion decides where he lives, what he buys and whom he follows (de Mohrenschildt, finding nothing, ch. 19 §6).

The gate is stated exactly in ch. 20 §9 and ch. 21 §7: he must see Oswald alone at the Walker shooting. He admits it is a stand-in. Acting alone once does not prove acting alone twice, but it is the best test he has. So the gate is a smaller, earlier crime used to test the big one, and King says openly that it can never be fully passed: the man at the bus stop might be a co-conspirator, and there is no way to know.

The conspiracy also brings people into the room. De Mohrenschildt's arrival is staged as an entrance, and every Oswald scene after it carries the question of whether this charmer is steering him.

How the lore gets in

  • Al's notes (document): one or two laconic lines at a time; action resumes at once. The notes now visibly go wrong (the Y, where the rifle will be hidden), so the guidebook becomes a risk. No stall.
  • De Mohrenschildt's Cuba speech (conversation overheard on the bug, about 2,000 words, ch. 19 §2). Long but never still: Jake is listening for one name, Walker, and the speech ends in a shirt-ripping show aimed at his window.
  • Kennedy's quarantine speech (TV in a bar, about a page, ch. 19 §7). Within a paragraph Jake is phoning Sadie, getting no answer, and driving to Jodie.
  • Two flyers (objects): Hands Off Cuba, bought from a waitress for five dollars (ch. 19 §6); the Hidell flyer in his mailbox, given complete with misspellings (ch. 20 §8). They come through ordinary channels.
  • Hargis–Walker broadcast (TV, about 1,200 words, ch. 20 §8). The nearest thing to a stall; it shows the target, and Jake ends it by switching the set off.

Mechanism notes

  • A, gate. The clearest case in the reading list. Jake must know one thing before he may act: that Oswald is alone on April 10. The gate has a fixed date, a stand-in test (Walker for Kennedy) and an admitted weakness. Every attempt to pass it early fails or backfires: the overheard talk makes things worse, following de Mohrenschildt shows nothing, the bug dies at the key moment. For SDF: give James one dated, observable stand-in event he must witness before he may act, and let what he learns beforehand raise his doubt instead of settling it.
  • The past pushes back, with no face. It works through equipment (the lamp, the bug's buzz, the car throwing a rod), wrong notes, near-meetings, and "harmonics": a white-over-red Fury three times, the same Colt, a banker who looks like the Lisbon Falls banker. Jake even wonders whether Sadie is a trap the past has laid (ch. 21 §9). The opponent is how the world is built, and it wins by making the hero hesitate. That fits an organisation that discredits rather than prevents.
  • B, canary (reversed). Jake gives Sadie predictions she can check (Scali, Stevenson at the UN) to earn her belief. A true fact planted to test trust.
  • C, front. De Mohrenschildt sees fronts everywhere (the NAACP, the segregationists), and Jake's question is whether de Mohrenschildt is one himself, the tempter who makes the offer and stands aside (ch. 21 §10).
  • D, lock and key. Sadie offers trust instead of demanding answers (ch. 20 §1), and gets one true thing, his name, Jake, before she agrees to marry him (ch. 21 §10).
  • Fifth: the certain paranoid as foil. Clayton writes that statistical analysis does not lie; Jake answers that there is always a window of uncertainty (ch. 19 §9). The investigator is defined by not being sure. SDF could give James a conspiracy-minded figure who is certain, so James's doubt shows by contrast.

Quotes

  1. "You’re here because if George de Mohrenschildt is more than he appears, then maybe Oswald wasn’t the one." (ch. 18)
  2. "I’d gotten the heart-to-heart, but it made things worse instead of better." (ch. 19)
  3. "Even that wouldn’t be enough to put all my doubts to rest, but it would be enough to proceed on." (ch. 21)
  4. "My ear in the Oswald apartment had gone deaf." (ch. 21)

Flags

  • Real people are suspected of complicity: de Mohrenschildt as possible handler, the bus-stop stranger as possible accomplice. King never confirms either; the gate exists because of that doubt. Under SDF's rules, suspicion like this may fall only on invented people.
  • De Mohrenschildt makes defamatory claims about Billy James Hargis and repeats talk of CIA plots against Castro. This is a character talking, not something the novel establishes. Do not borrow it.
  • Oswald's beatings of Marina are shown in detail and watched by a passive hero. The tone is far from SDF's comedy; take the structure (a witness who judges the hero's inaction), not the material.

notes.title: section 6 (chapters 22–25)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 22–25 (about 35,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text as in the scratch file; Part 5 ("11/22/63") opens at chapter 23.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch 22–23) To watch the Walker shooting on 10 April and see whether Oswald fires alone. This is his planned test. Clayton's phone call. Sadie is held at knifepoint three hours away. He drives to Jodie. He misses the test. Sadie's face is cut open. Clayton dies. Jake's cover is now on file with the police. The one observation that would have cleared Oswald or implicated someone else is gone. He has a gun and the chance, but he still doesn't know whether killing Oswald changes anything. Bugging the Easter visit ("how'd you miss him", a half-heard phrase) leaves him with more doubt, not less.
2 (ch 23 §7 – ch 24 §8) To decide whether to kill Oswald before he leaves for New Orleans. His own reasoning: de Mohrenschildt may be a CIA cutout, even the shooter. The evidence is circumstantial, and a murder would expose the fake Amberson. He lets Lee board the bus, puts the mission on hold for Sadie, and gambles to pay her bills. Killing the wrong man would waste the whole loop and force a reset that erases Sadie. Three months of waiting, then one plain idea: ask the man who knows.
3 (ch 24 §8 – ch 25) To learn whether de Mohrenschildt was with Oswald at the Walker shooting. De Mohrenschildt hands over a newspaper clipping. It puts him at the Carousel Club that night, and its host is Jack Ruby. The gate opens and he means to kill Oswald in October. Then the bet that paid for the waiting brings Roth's men, who beat him nearly to death. He no longer wants to stop. The past stops him instead, through a channel he opened himself. Hospital, injuries, and the October window now at risk ("Ozzie wins").

Why it grips

  • The test is stolen as it arrives. Ch 22 times the stakeout to the minute (3:30, 3:33, 3:39). Marina's knock delays Jake just long enough for the call to catch him. Had he left on time, it would have rung in an empty apartment.
  • The hero admits the ugly thought. In ch 22 §5 Jake briefly weighs Sadie's life against learning whether Oswald was alone. The gate becomes a moral cost before any action.
  • Two clippings side by side (ch 23 §1): Walker on page 1, Sadie on page 7. The investigation and its price share a newspaper, with no comment.
  • The waiting is a love story with a clock inside it. The Jamboree, surgeries and Candlewood weekend fill about two thirds of the section, each with a dated history event in its margin (Lee on the New Orleans dock, the test-ban promise).
  • A verifiable prediction carries the suspense. Jake stakes his sanity with Sadie on a fight result (ch 24 §10). The fight runs at full length and Case goes down twelve seconds in. Belief, money and Al's notes ride on one outcome.
  • The reversal comes from off-stage. Once the gate opens, the beating arrives from the bookie subplot that paid for the waiting, while the reader was watching the CIA thread.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The possible conspiracy is the only thing between Jake and the trigger. What he has to know is one specific fact: was anyone else in the alley with Oswald on 10 April, especially de Mohrenschildt? Al's notes call this the "window of uncertainty". The text gives three reasons it blocks action. A pointless kill would mean a reset (ch 23 §7). He refuses to kill without having "seen", as he did with Dunning (ch 23 §7). And Sadie makes him promise "never by mistake" (ch 24 §11), which turns the gate into a vow to someone he loves. The gate holds from 10 April to 5 August, about four months of story time and roughly 25,000 of the section's 35,000 words. It opens through a person who chooses to answer, holding a document. Once it opens, Jake files the Ruby clipping as "just another harmonic".

How the lore gets in

  • Two newspaper clippings (ch 23 §1, about 400 words). Documents. No stall: the reader gets the news as Jake does.
  • The Easter bug (ch 23 §6, about 1,000 words). An overheard scene with a gap in the tape. No stall: the gap is the event.
  • The Dealey Plaza bench (ch 23 §7, about 900 words). The big CIA theory as inner monologue. It risks a stall, but King ties it to a yes/no decision (kill Lee before the 24th?) and treats the theory as a list of costs.
  • The Around Town clipping (ch 25 §4, about 100 words of quoted newsprint). An object handed to the hero by a suspect. It closes one question and quietly brings in a new name.
  • The hillside explanation to Sadie (ch 25 §8, about 1,200 words). Why not tip off the police. It doesn't stall, because Sadie pushes back and her questions test the rule out loud.

Mechanism notes

  • A, the gate. This is the clearest instance in the book so far. The gate is precise (one fact about one night). It has a deadline (Oswald back on 3 October). It's enforced by cost (a reset that erases Sadie) and by a promise to another person. Test one fails by bad luck, test two by a gap in the tape, and test three works only when he stops observing and asks. For SDF: one checkable fact, with a first try that fails for an unrelated human reason.
  • The past pushes back with no face. Every blow comes from an ordinary agent with a small motive of his own (Clayton's jealousy, Gutierrez's syphilis, Roth's pride), none linked to Kennedy. The rule is stated once (ch 25 §8). The strongest lesson: the cost lands on the side-channel the hero opened to keep the wait going (the bets that paid for Sadie and the rent), not on the investigation.
  • C, the front. The document that closes the gate contains the next layer: Jack Ruby raising a glass. The hero dismisses it. The reader [from memory, not from the text] knows Ruby's later role, so the irony works. Good shape for SDF, with an invented name.
  • D, lock and key. Sadie will believe only after one verified prediction (the Case–Tiger round). Her belief, and her promise "never by mistake", become a second gate.
  • A fifth shape: the borrowed authority. Jake gets past de Mohrenschildt by repeating things only a watcher could know (the stuffed rabbit, the "how did you miss" joke). The other man fills in "The Company" on his own. The truth is real, the frame is false, and the suspect builds the frame himself.

Quotes

  • "If I killed Oswald and Kennedy died anyway, it would all be for nothing." (ch 23)
  • "De Mohrenschildt knew, so I would ask him." (ch 24)
  • "I felt I had closed Al Templeton’s window of uncertainty to the merest draft." (ch 25)
  • "Because the past doesn’t want to be changed. It fights back when you try. And the bigger the potential change, the harder it fights." (ch 25)

Flags

  • Real people named as possibly complicit: George de Mohrenschildt (speculated CIA cutout and possible shooter, ch 23 §7), Jack Ruby (ch 25 §4), Carlos Marcello as the mob boss above the bookies (ch 24 §13, ch 25 §15). SDF can't copy this. Its edits, people and companies stay invented.
  • Jake's methods break James's rules: impersonating the CIA and holding a gun on de Mohrenschildt (ch 25 §2–4), and blackmailing Jessica Caltrop (ch 25 §6). Only the shape transfers: a person chooses to produce a clearing document.
  • Violence level (Sadie's disfigurement, Clayton's suicide, the kneecapping) is far above SDF's "killing is rare and a failure".

notes.title: Section 07 (chapters 26–29)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 26–29 (about 37,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk 07 of the split; the file does not name the edition. Ends with Part 6 opening (chapter 29, "The Green Card Man").

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 26–27 §7) The assassin's name and the place he will shoot from After the beating his memory is walled off; a church sign with missing letters ("THE WORD OF AL") leads him to the notebook, which is in a safe deposit box he can open with a key already on his ring Eleven weeks, his spleen, 47 pounds, and a habit of lying to Sadie about what he remembers Kennedy arrives in days; Sadie and Deke cannot help without a name; Deke reports that the police already pass every tip to the FBI, which ignores them The notebook, which turns out to cover almost nothing about the last weeks
2 (ch. 27 §10 – ch. 28 §13) To stop Oswald and stay free for Sadie The notes give the day itself but not the rooming house; the rifle in the Paine garage is uncertain (Al was wrong before); the house has four children; at work he would be caught He chooses the last possible moment, cuts Sadie out with a letter, and then the day attacks: wheel snaps, bus is hit, a car is stolen at knifepoint, the door is locked Every earlier option ends in jail or in hurting children, so the only moment left is the window itself The run up six flights; the shot; Sadie killed
3 (ch. 29) Get out, and go back to undo Sadie's death The police and FBI accuse him of being Oswald's co-conspirator; Hosty instead offers a cover story and an exit Sadie; his name; any public life Kennedy is saved, but Sadie can only be restored by a full reset through the rabbit-hole Bus north toward Maine; a tornado erases the two Mercedes Street houses behind him

Why it grips

The reader knows the date, the hour and the window, so King cannot get suspense from "who" or "where". He gets it from two withholdings.

First, in chapter 26 the hero's own memory is the locked room. Amnesia is the antagonist's weapon, so every recovery is a small fight: pushing too hard brings on sudden sleep. The answer comes through a found object, a church sign with letters missing, which Jake reads the way he once read a name half-covered by a hand. That is the scene that does the most work: a broken sign gives him the notebook, then the key, the checkbook, the address, and only then the face in the photo (ch. 27 §6).

Second, in chapter 28 King sets a clock (a time every few pages, 8:15 to 12:28) and lets the world fail one ordinary piece at a time: a wheel, a dump truck, a jammed door, a locked lobby. Jake predicts it ("Look ahead, because that’s where the next trouble will come from") and is still caught. The reversal is that Sadie, the person he lied to and left behind for her safety, is the one who gets him there: she finds his hiding place, cuts the car thief, buys the crutch, and is killed by the bullet meant for him.

The jokes never stop (the beggar haggling over one crutch), which keeps the losses from going numb.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The "bigger plot" question closes here in an odd order: Jake acts before he is certain. Only after Oswald is dead does he say he now knows Oswald was alone, and he counts that as a gain for the next attempt: next time he will not have to wait. The gate did not open because he proved something; the clock ran out and he went through it anyway. The certainty arrives afterwards, bought with Sadie's death, and it lowers the price of the second run (ch. 29 §8).

Then the conspiracy turns on the hero. Fritz and Hosty's first theory is that Jake and Sadie were in on it and lost their nerve (ch. 29 §5); Jake's private comment is that every home should have a conspiracy theory. Hosty later decides he is a planted agent: CIA, the Russians, Angleton (§9). Being suspected of a conspiracy is what gets him out. The FBI has its own secret to protect (its handling of Oswald, the note Hosty destroyed), so it does not lock Jake up. It writes him a cover story, "The Modest Hero", hands him a disguise, a service-elevator key and cash, and sends him away. Jake keeps his freedom by threatening lies about the Bureau it could not disprove.

How the lore gets in

  • Al's notebook, last page (ch. 27 §10). A document read in Jake's hands: about 250 words of dated entries. Its gap matters more than its content: the rooming house is missing. He acts at once (Kenopensky, the gun). No stall.
  • The rule of the past (ch. 26, repeated through ch. 28). Delivered in a dream conversation with Al (about 400 words) and in one-line statements during action ("When you try to change the past, it bites"). Slight stall, ended by a nightmare image.
  • The memory flood (ch. 27 §7). A list of fragments, about 150 words, triggered by a photo. It works as the payoff to a chapter of not remembering.
  • Hosty's offer (ch. 29 §9–10). A conversation of about 2,500 words, with objects laid on the coffee table (glasses, hairnet, key, cash, kitchen whites). It holds because it is a negotiation: each side has something on the other.

Mechanism notes

  • A, the gate. What shows here is the gate's price. Jake waits until the 22nd because acting earlier means prison (ch. 27 §13), and waiting is what puts Sadie on the stairs. The certainty he paid for (lone gunman) only becomes useful after the act. For SDF: a gate that is still partly shut when the deadline arrives, so James acts on incomplete proof and pays for being wrong in a way he cannot undo, would supply the missing cost.
  • "The past pushes back" without a face. It works through the hero's body (amnesia, sudden sleep, the knee), through ordinary objects (a wheel, a door handle), and through bystanders who don't listen (police hanging up on Deke, Bonnie Ray laughing). The Yellow Card Man only appears in dreams. Steady, impersonal, expected.
  • D, lock and key. The locked Depository door opens only when Jake recalls a co-worker's name from Al's margin notes, and the man chooses to let them in (ch. 28 §12). A helper who needs one specific truth, and a door that opens only because a person decides to open it, fits SDF's rules exactly.
  • C, front. Hosty's "Modest Hero" story is a front made in real time to cover the Bureau's failure. The organisation discredits and redirects rather than kills ("We don’t kill people").
  • Reveals as objects. Key stamped FC 775, checkbook, notebook photo, phone bug, Hosty's two notes: every step forward in chapters 27 and 29 is something Jake holds.

Quotes

  1. "But the past is obdurate and protects itself against change." (ch. 26)
  2. "Now he’s walling off those memories—the vital ones—because he knows it’s his last hope of stopping you." (ch. 26, Al in a dream)
  3. "now that I knew Lee really had been the lone gunman, I wouldn’t have to wait so long to dispatch his sorry ass." (ch. 29 §8)
  4. "No one wants to kill you, Amberson. And no one wants to poke holes in your story." (ch. 29 §9)

Flags

  • Real people are shown as complicit or negligent: Agent James Hosty (handling of Oswald, destroying his note "as per Mr. Hoover’s orders"), Hoover, and Angleton named as a possible handler; Dallas police hanging up on tips. SDF cannot copy this; its organisation and its people must be invented.
  • Jake invents testimony about real people to the police (de Mohrenschildt, Oswald). SDF lacks that licence.
  • No invented edits on real books.

notes.title: section 08 (chapters 30–31, Final Notes, "Citizen of the Century", Afterword)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapter 30 to the end of the book, including Final Notes, the 2012 coda and King's Afterword (about 19,400 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 08; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 30.1–6) Rest, then reset and get Sadie back An LA earthquake that never happened in his history; the Green Card Man says every trip leaves residue and saving Kennedy was the biggest change The win he spent five years on caused a disaster The only way back to Sadie runs through 2011, and Lang tells him to go and see what he has done He walks into the future he made
2 (ch. 30.7 to 31.4) Check the damage fast and get back Ruined Lisbon Falls; Harry Dunning in a wheelchair tells fifty years of history over whisky His good deed made things worse. Harry half-recognises him and asks if he killed his father The world is coming apart, and one reset fixes it and brings Sadie back He returns to 1958 and runs from the Card Man
3 (Final Notes, coda) A quiet life with Sadie; at least a warning postcard to Deke That any act is a change ("Only each child is a wave."); Clayton is the unknown he cannot settle He burns the postcard, gives up Sadie, and lives on not knowing if she survived The Card Man's rule, "Close the circle", and what he saw in 2011 The last reset; a newspaper archive shows she lived; one dance in Texas

Why it grips

  • The win is the reversal. The reader has waited all book for Dallas to come out right, and chapter 30 takes it apart within a few pages. The doubt comes before any explanation: the cab driver's earthquake (30.3), with Jake sure Kennedy is dead before she says what happened. King then takes Jake back to a childhood guilt he never settled (did he shut the gate on his dog Rags?), so the news hits as guilt before the reader has any facts.
  • Withholding to the end. Whether Jake will save Sadie stays open until the coda. The dated diary entries (Final Notes) circle the question, "I don’t know, I don’t know" comes back like a chorus, and each entry ends in a small act. The scene that does the most work is the burned postcard (10/7/58): one object holding one sentence of warning, and destroying it is how he gives her up.
  • Proof by private knowledge. Both recognition scenes (Harry's family photo, 31.4; Sadie and the chaperone question, coda 8) are built alike: Jake says one small true thing only an insider could know, and the other person's face changes. No plot machinery.
  • Still funny in the apocalypse. "Charlie Fucking Chaplin" (30.7), the plaster Jesus edging off the mantelpiece (31.2), Hillary as president.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The Oswald question was the gate, and here it has closed without comment: stopping one man was enough, so Al's lone-gunman bet was right. King's Afterword then says it outright: "ninety-eight percent, maybe even ninety-nine." What the gate was worth shows in what it did not protect against. Being sure of the target guaranteed nothing about what would follow. Jake picked the right man and still wrecked the world.

Two moves matter. First, the conspiracy changes hands: in the new 2011, George Amberson is the mystery, "Savior, or part of the plot?" (31.3), with conventions of theorists. The man who investigated the conspiracy becomes the thing people theorise about. Second, the hidden order finally gets a face, and it is a pitiable one. The Card Men are men who "watch. Sometimes we warn." (30.5). Holding many strings wears out their minds, and Zack Lang ends up on his knees begging (31.6). They cannot stop Jake, only tell him and plead. So with no one to beat, the last obstacle is Jake's own choice.

How the lore gets in

  • Zack Lang's explanation (30.5), about 1,800 words, a conversation. Every rule (bubble, strings, residue, harmonics) is tied to a gauge you can see: the card in his hat flickers from green to yellow as he talks, and he smokes something medicinal to bring it back. He uses Jake's own past as evidence (the same meat bought over and over; Kyle, the Yellow Card Man). Within a page Jake is walking through the hole. No stall, because the lecture ends in an order: "go back and see".
  • Harry's alternate history (31.2–3), about 1,500 words. Jake declines to give it in full ("forget about it"). It comes in compressed paragraphs, broken up by a tremor, a ripping sound overhead and Harry's own losses. The family photo scene follows straight after.
  • Final Notes, about 2,600 words, a diary. The rules come back as a guitar-string metaphor, and Jake argues with them. The diary is an object (legal pads in a buried lockbox, "Maybe it will be you"). It stalls on purpose, to show his indecision.
  • The Dallas Morning News article (coda 2), about 250 words, a document. The biggest reveal of the ending (Sadie lived) is an archive page in the hero's hands, with no one explaining it.
  • Afterword, about 2,500 words, outside the story. Real-world lore (Karen Carlin, Ruby, the sweater) puts the assassination down to chance.

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate), the payoff. When the gate opens, being sure of the target does not make acting safe. King sets up a second gate at once, and this one Jake cannot pass: to save Sadie (the postcard) he would need to know the consequences, which he never can, so he does not act (10/7/58). The first gate's success costs the world; the second gate costs Sadie. For SDF: a gate gets its weight from a cost that comes after it is passed. James ruling out the bigger explanation should not make his act safe. It should only make the act his own.
  • The faceless antagonist gets a face late. "The past pushes back" turns out to be self-protection (the turtle-shell line; "Want has nothing to do with it", 31.6). After 29 chapters with no face, it gets one: a suffering employee who can only warn. That is very close to SDF's organisation, which discredits rather than prevents.
  • D (lock and key). Harry (31.4) and Sadie (coda 8) each open up because of one specific private truth (Ellen as a carrot-top, the 1961 chaperone). No force is used, which fits SDF's rule that a door opens only when a person chooses to open it.
  • C (front), weakly. Each answer opens a deeper layer: the obduracy is protection, the hole is one bubble among a few, the guards are men from some unnamed time.
  • Fifth: the investigator becomes the theory. Amberson becomes a conspiracy figure in the world he changed (31.3). Useful if James's own traces become the next thing someone finds.

Quotes

  • "Savior, or part of the plot? People held actual conventions to discuss it" (ch. 31.3): the hero turns into the conspiracy.
  • "Want has nothing to do with it. You have to go back one last time." (ch. 31.6): the antagonist's whole case, with no threat.
  • "The past is obdurate for the same reason a turtle’s shell is obdurate: because the living flesh inside is tender and defenseless." (Final Notes): the rule is explained only once it costs him.
  • "The Sadie Hawkins dance, back in 1961. Who did you get to chaperone with you when Coach Borman’s mother broke her hip?" (coda 8): a private fact used as a key.

Flags

  • Real people named as complicit in the alternate history (31.3): Hoover is said to have ordered Martin Luther King's assassination, Arthur Bremer kills Wallace, Curtis LeMay runs the Hanoi strike. In the Afterword, King asks where de Mohrenschildt was on 10 April 1963. SDF must not do this.
  • No invented edits on real books in this section.

books.qa:
Answers point to the section notes in this folder (01–08) and, where relevant, to a v8.2 chapter by title. The map is 00-map.md. Everything about SDF here is a PROPOSAL; Santi's decisions are PLACEHOLDER.

The gate

1. What exactly must Jake know before he may act? At the start (ch. 3), that Oswald was the Walker shooter, with Al's bar set at ninety-eight percent rather than ninety-five (01-front-matter-to-chapter-4.md). By ch. 17 it narrows to one named question: was de Mohrenschildt involved in the Walker shooting on 10 April 1963? If Oswald acted alone then, Al's notes put a second gunman in November near zero (04-chapters-14-to-17.md). By ch. 20–21 it is stated as an act of seeing: Jake must watch Oswald fire alone (05-chapters-18-to-21.md).

2. How long does King hold the gate, and what fills the wait? From ch. 3 to ch. 25, about seven tenths of the book by the notes' word counts, and nearly five years of story time. Two things fill it: equipment (bugs, a key, rentals, a microphone) and a life (Jodie, the school, Sadie), and the life is what the gate will cost (03-chapters-9-to-13.md, 04-chapters-14-to-17.md). The stretch from 10 April to 5 August alone is roughly 25,000 of the 35,000 words in 06-chapters-22-to-25.md.

3. Why doesn't the reader ask why Jake doesn't just check? Because the doubt cannot be checked yet. Oswald is in Russia until June 1962, so the calendar does the real holding, while the conspiracy doubt and the butterfly rule only explain why he doesn't shoot Oswald on arrival (03-chapters-9-to-13.md). A gate made only of doubt would read as dithering. Add a date and the wait is forced.

4. What stops the gate from becoming an excuse to investigate forever? A deadline pressing the other way. Al's suicide removes "calling hesitation research" (ch. 12), and the 22 November date is fixed (03-chapters-9-to-13.md). The gate stops Jake acting early, and the deadline stops him dawdling. SDF has the equivalent pieces (the review date, the schedule's dates, 2 December) but nothing yet stops James acting early. See map proposal 4.

5. How does the gate finally open? Not by observation. The Walker test is stolen by Clayton's call (ch. 22), and the Easter bug leaves a gap (ch. 23). Jake then simply asks de Mohrenschildt, who hands him a clipping that places him elsewhere that night (ch. 25, 06-chapters-22-to-25.md). But Jake gets that answer at gunpoint while posing as the CIA, so in SDF terms the door was forced. Take the shape ("ask the one who knows") and not the method.

6. Is the gate ever really passed? No. King says outright that acting alone once does not prove acting alone twice, and a stranger at the bus stop might be a co-conspirator (05-chapters-18-to-21.md). Note 07-chapters-26-to-29.md says Jake acts before he is certain and learns Oswald was alone only afterward. The Afterword gives King's own estimate (08-chapters-30-to-31.md).

7. What does Derry add to the gate? Timing. Knowledge loses its value once you use it, and any warning wastes a known time and place (ch. 7, 02-chapters-5-to-8.md). So the gate controls when Jake may act as well as what he must know. In SDF, James's knowledge of the schedule is worth something only while the organisation doesn't know he has it. Map proposal 1 builds on that.

8. What does the gate cost once it opens? Everything after it. The certainty is bought with Sadie's death and becomes useful only for a second run (07-chapters-26-to-29.md). Then the future he made is a ruin: he was right about the man and still wrecked the world (08-chapters-30-to-31.md). Lesson for SDF: ruling out the bigger explanation should not make James's act safe, only make it his own.

9. Is there a second gate? Yes, and Jake cannot pass it. To save Sadie he would have to know what a warning postcard would do, and he never can, so he burns it (Final Notes, 08-chapters-30-to-31.md). In this book a gate that can't be passed ends in a refusal to act, which costs as much as acting.

10. Does the gate need someone else's rule? It helps. Al writes the threshold in his notes ("GOOD ENOUGH TO TAKE THE SON OF A BITCH OUT"), so Jake works to a rule rather than to certainty (04-chapters-14-to-17.md). Sadie's "never by mistake" turns it into a promise to someone he loves (06-chapters-22-to-25.md). SDF already has the professor's rule in Leiden ("until we're a hundred per cent"). What it lacks is James setting his own smaller version and paying for keeping it.

The past pushes back

11. How does a faceless antagonist work on the page? Through ordinary failures that can each be explained away: flat tires, a bridge down, flu, a jammed door, amnesia (01, 02, 03, 07). Only the pattern is hostile. It pushes in proportion to the size of the change and harder on repeat (a thrown rod the second time, 01-front-matter-to-chapter-4.md; the rule stated in ch. 9 and ch. 25).

12. Does it fit SDF's organisation, which discredits rather than prevents? Closely. Every harm has a plausible cause, which is exactly what the review's "each ending plausible" already is. The difference: King's force mostly makes Jake hesitate (05-chapters-18-to-21.md). SDF's organisation should do the same thing to James: make him doubt the paper, rather than block him from it.

13. Who delivers the blows? Small agents with motives of their own and no link to Kennedy: Clayton's jealousy, Gutierrez, Roth's pride (06-chapters-22-to-25.md). In SDF the equivalents are already ordinary people (Pieter, Saskia, the Groningen dealer). A routine process can hurt James with no handler behind it. See map proposal 5.

14. When does it get a face, and what is it like? Only at the end. The Card Men "watch. Sometimes we warn"; the strain wears out their minds, and Zack Lang ends up on his knees begging (08-chapters-30-to-31.md). That is close to SDF's old man defeated and talking in The final conversation, and to Bram. Don't give the organisation a face any earlier than v8.2 already does.

15. What are the "harmonics" and are they worth copying? Rhymes: a second Doris, a second Al's Diner, a white-over-red Fury three times, "JIMLA" (03, 05). They work best when they carry information. JIMLA turns out to be a billboard that tells Jake to buy a long-range microphone, and Sadie's name read under his thumbs as DORIS DUN warns him about her husband (04-chapters-14-to-17.md). SDF already rhymes (02:14, eleven). Make at least one echo tell James what to do next.

Cost of being wrong

16. How could James's Part Two have a cost of being wrong without violence? Copy King's three non-violent costs. A secret kept costs a relationship (Sadie leaves, 04). Routine paperwork exposes him (the immunization record, 04). A dated test fails because of his own presence (06, and map proposal 1). Map proposals 1, 4 and 5 are the non-violent ones. Only proposal 2 involves harm, and it is harm v8.2 already has (Buddy poisoned).

17. What is the Poulin printout, and is it already in SDF? Two printings of one page: in one a girl is in a wheelchair, in the other she isn't, and Jake's root-beer trip caused the change (01-front-matter-to-chapter-4.md). SDF already has James's harmless act changing a record (The payload, "asked (job)"; The money, the step the week of his ticket; The gorilla mask, his forum account edited). What SDF lacks is the harm landing on someone else. See map proposal 6 (Noor).

18. What's the best single scene of a cost arriving? Ellen's phone call (ch. 9): Jake rings to confirm his triumph and learns Harry died in Vietnam. She hears his voice is too young and ends with "Where were you then, you son of a bitch?" (03-chapters-9-to-13.md). The cost comes by phone, from a person, and is aimed at him. Map proposal 6 puts this shape into The vet / Leiden, Friday.

19. Where does King put the cost so the reader doesn't see it coming? On the side channel. The bets that paid for the wait bring Roth's men, while the reader watches the CIA thread (06-chapters-22-to-25.md). In SDF, the channel James keeps open to watch is the friendship with Kalder, and the dog is the bill. See map proposal 3.

20. Does Jake ever choose to let something bad happen to learn more? He considers it in Derry (let it happen once to learn details) and rejects it because it defeats the test (02-chapters-5-to-8.md). In Dallas he watches Marina beaten and won't even call the police, and an old woman calls him a coward (05-chapters-18-to-21.md). That witness is the model for map proposal 1: James watches the eighth address rather than warning it, and has to live with the choice.

Lore

21. How does King deliver a big lecture without the story stopping? He sets it at a deathbed (Al coughing blood, 01), at bayonet point (Turcotte, 02), or in a negotiation where each side holds something (Hosty, 07). He ends it on an order or an object. Violence or a decision follows within about two pages (03). For The reading room, continued, the old man's method talk already has an offer at the end. Keep his speeches broken by objects on the table.

22. Where does the bulk of King's lore live? In an object: Al's Oswald notebook, studied off the page and quoted a line at a time (01, 03, 05). The notebook goes wrong partway through and becomes a risk (05), and its gap forces the climax (07). SDF's thin book and the List already work this way. The transferable bit is letting the document's gap or error force an action.

23. Where does King stall? On the Hargis–Walker broadcast (ch. 20, 05), on Derry's catalogue of omens (ch. 8, 02, kept short), and on the Final Notes diary (08), deliberately. Treat TV and catalogue lore as the risk. In SDF, the hearings on the bar TV in The reading room, continued should stay a single paragraph.

Specific SDF chapters

24. Which King move fits The money? Routine paperwork as the antagonist (the school immunization record, 04-chapters-14-to-17.md). The role Saskia grants James can come back through the bank's access review, and the cost falls on her. See map proposal 5. The "number wrong by a clean multiple" is already on the page there, so don't re-propose it.

25. Which King move fits The other ten? The Walker test (05, 06) and the Derry rule about when (02). The eighth address, with a future date, becomes the test James must witness, and he has to choose between warning and watching. v7 The reading room, continued already holds the trace ("I was there. Nobody came. Why."). See map proposal 1.

26. Which King move fits The schedule and A street, night? Harry's essay, which is true in outline and wrong in a detail that kills (02-chapters-5-to-8.md). The schedule is right about the visit and wrong about the date, and the date moved because of James's own verb (A car park). See map proposal 2.

27. Which King move fits On land and The gorilla mask? The cost landing on the side channel (06) and Turcotte's use of Frati to test Jake (02). Kalder testing James "in small clever ways" after the pub is already the Frati move. What's new is James keeping the friendship going on purpose and paying for it. See map proposal 3.

28. Which King move fits Frank, loose? A gate opened by a person who chooses to answer (06), and the certain paranoid as a foil (Clayton, 05). Frank is the reverse: the doubter whose failure to explain is the threshold. Make it a rule James states in Leiden and keeps until Frank, loose. See map proposal 4.

29. Which King move fits The reading room, continued? The suspect who builds the frame himself (de Mohrenschildt fills in "The Company", 06) and the clearing document that carries the next name (Ruby in the clipping, 06). The old man explaining away the eighth address ("nobody came because you'd gone") is the stolen test used against the hero. Proposal 1 sets that up.

30. Which King move fits Twenty minutes? Sadie believes only after a prediction comes true (the Case fight, 06), and Harry and Sadie open up to one private fact (08). v8.2 already does it differently and better for its tone: Ana counts six "I don't know"s and believes him. Don't add a prediction there.

31. Is "the investigator becomes the theory" worth using? It's already in The gorilla mask (his forum account edited with bloodlines). King's version is larger: Amberson becomes a conspiracy figure with conventions (08). If anything, use it in Leave it: the book James may publish could be filed among the cranks, which v8.2 already implies ("filed as fiction").

Rules and risks

32. What in King breaks SDF's rules? Bugging a rented house, paying Ivy for a key and threatening her (04); a forged reference and a mail-order degree (03); posing as the CIA, the gun on de Mohrenschildt, blackmailing Jessica Caltrop (06); invented testimony about real people (07). Real people named as complicit run through 03, 05–08. None of it transfers.

33. Is there a King move that fits "doors open only when a person chooses"? Several: the Cullums' wife deciding on an odd offer (03), Ellie and Deke lending the yearbook (04), the Depository co-worker opening the door once Jake recalls his name (07), and Harry and Sadie opening up to one private fact (08). The children give the address only after Jake gives them a true warning (02).

34. What's the tone risk? King's violence and period slurs are far from SDF's register (02, 03, 05, 06). But his comedy never stops, even at the worst moments (the beggar haggling over a crutch, 07; "Charlie Fucking Chaplin", 08). That matches SDF's rule to stay funny to the end.

35. Did the notes find a fifth mechanism beyond A–D? Five. The page that changed because of the hero's act (01). The witness's record that is wrong in one detail (02). The cost landing on the side channel (06). Echo as a clue-giver (03, 04). The investigator becoming the theory (08). Also, from 05, the certain paranoid as foil: Clayton's "statistical analysis does not lie" against Jake's window of uncertainty.

36. Where do the notes disagree with each other? 06 says the gate opens with the clipping in ch. 25; 07 says Jake acts before he is certain and learns afterward. Both are true if the post-beating amnesia and the gaps in the notebook reopen it. 01 gives the gate's question as seeing Oswald fire at Walker, 04 as de Mohrenschildt's involvement. The question narrows as the book goes on. 06 calls de Mohrenschildt's answer a person choosing to answer, but its own flags show it came at gunpoint.

books.author: Orwell
books.readfor: rewriting records; the forbidden book as the state's trap
books.intro: Coverage: Penguin edition, English, read in full via four section notes, 11 Nov 2026: 01-part-one-a.md (I.i–vii), 02-section-two.md (I.viii–II.viii), 03-section-three.md (II.ix–III.iii), 04-section-four.md (III.iv–vi, Appendix). Cites are Part.chapter. Brief: Winston's job rewriting records, against SDF's editing machine; the forbidden book as the state's own trap, against "we leave them findable." Standing-rule note: the classics "translated" and the originals destroyed (I.v, Appendix) and Ampleforth's Kipling (III.i) are invented edits on real books. Room 101 and the dial are torture. Martin is described in racial terms (II.viii). Take none of it; take the structure.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
Winston Smith forges records at the Ministry of Truth and keeps a forbidden diary. He finds Julia and a room above a junk shop with no telescreen. O'Brien, an Inner Party man, invites him into the Brotherhood, and a stranger hands him Goldstein's banned book. The room was bugged all along; the shopkeeper is Thought Police; O'Brien helped write the book. In the cells O'Brien takes him apart, and Room 101 makes him betray Julia. He ends at a café table, loving Big Brother. A dry appendix on Newspeak follows "THE END."

Every way forward Winston finds was put there by the other side, so the reader's hope and the trap are one thing until it shuts. The conspiracy never has to stop him; it lets him want something, hands it to him, and writes down what he does.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:
Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (I.i–ii) One true thought on paper The diary brings back O'Brien's glance; a knock is only a neighbor's sink He decides he is already dead The thought is the crime; tearing out the page undoes nothing He lives like a suspect; a grain of dust on the diary
2 (I.iii–v) To prove the Party lies His own job makes lies true: he invents Comrade Ogilvy and enjoys it He is good at what he hates He seems the only one who remembers last week He looks outward: the girl, the proles, O'Brien
3 (I.vi–vii) To understand why The one proof he ever held, a photo; he put it down the memory hole himself No evidence, and nowhere to publish it He knows how, not why, and doubts his sanity He writes the diary as a letter to O'Brien
4 (I.viii) A living witness An old man who remembers only top hats; a shop with a room and no telescreen The girl sees him leave; he thinks of killing her He thinks he's already seen, so caution buys nothing He resolves to go back
5 (II.i–v) Julia, then a place to be alone The note, the wood, Charrington's room, let without a question Every meeting risks death; Syme vanishes Julia's dodging isn't enough; he wants an organization He tells Julia about O'Brien
6 (II.vi–viii) To get inside A coded mention of Syme, an address, "the Brotherhood is real" He swears to murder; refuses one thing, to leave Julia, and O'Brien records it He has confessed all to an Inner Party man in that man's flat He waits for a misprint and a brief-case
7 (II.ix) To read the book Goldstein describes the forgery he has just spent ninety hours doing Nothing; it feels like safety It breaks off just before the why He reads on aloud, sleeps sure he is sane
8 (II.x) To keep the room and the hope A telescreen behind the picture; Charrington is Thought Police Julia, the room, freedom No choices left The cells
9 (III.i–iii) To survive, keep one true thing O'Brien co-wrote the book: true as description, "nonsense" as program Body, the photo (shown, then burned), certainty Each answer becomes the next question; wrong ones cost pain Room 101 ahead
10 (III.iv) Hide his hatred until the bullet Seven years of watching; the dust on the diary put back; he cries out for Julia in a dream The held-back feeling is out Giving in with the mind isn't enough; the test is feeling "Room 101"
11 (III.v) Escape the rats The only way out is someone else in the cage He betrays Julia and means it Instinct decides, not courage Release
12 (III.vi, Appendix) Gin, warmth, his table Julia changed; a victory bulletin The last private feeling A scrap of doubt survives until the bulletin The end; then the Appendix, from a later time

Read the fifth column down. Rows 1–7: something in him won't let him stop. Rows 8–12: there's no choice left. In rows 5–7 every advance is a delivery, but each needs a risk he takes himself: her table, the room, O'Brien's bell (02). James in Part Two receives and risks nothing; he could stop on any page.

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
Goldstein's book (II.ix), two extracts, about 5,300 and 5,500 words. Carried by its setup: handed over mid-riot, carried unopened for six days, opened in the one safe room. "War is Peace," read silently, does not stall: it explains the switch we just watched him forge for, and the reading itself is the event. "Ignorance is Strength," read aloud to Julia, slows. Orwell pays three ways: she falls asleep (a joke on the book), it cuts off at "This motive really consists…", and about two pages later the iron voice speaks from behind the picture (II.x). (03)

O'Brien's explanations. In the flat (II.viii, about 900 words) a clock holds it: the telescreen is off for half an hour at most, and the lecture mostly withholds. In the cells (III.ii–iii, about 11,600 words) every rule is tested on Winston as it is said; he argues back and loses, so it plays as a fight. In III.v each paragraph about Room 101 comes with the cage moving closer. (02, 03, 04)

The Appendix (about 4,000 words, after "THE END"). The story stops on purpose. It works because the voice is past tense and outside the regime, so it can explain the machine calmly. (04)

Stalls: I.vii, the proles plus a copied textbook, about 1,800 words of essay. Paid for by the photograph story the telescreen cut off four chapters earlier (I.iii). (01) Doesn't: I.iv, the Records Department, about 3,500 words, the longest block in Part One. Winston has a task with a result: four slips, a rival across the hall, a finished forgery he's proud of. The lore is the job. (01)

sections.title: 4. The mechanism we came for
sections.html:
Setup (I.i, I.v). The Party is the only source of news about its enemy. Goldstein is on screen daily; his book is "the book"; his speech uses more Newspeak than any Party member. The café where the purged drank is not forbidden, only "ill-omened." The way in is open and in plain sight.

Rule. The bait is true. O'Brien calls the book accurate as description, "nonsense" as program (III.iii). Winston trusts it because it tells him "what you know already" (II.ix). The trap needs no lie, only his relief at being confirmed, and it sorts people: whoever reads and acts has picked himself out.

First use (II.vi–viii). O'Brien mentions the unperson Syme, a planted thoughtcrime that watches who takes it as a signal; writes his address in view of a telescreen; runs a catechism that is easy to pass and really collects the one refusal ("It is necessary for us to know everything"). The summons is a deliberate misprint in Winston's work queue.

Escalation and cost (II.ix–III.iii). A handover so casual it feels like luck; then the bugged room, and his oath played back as evidence. Every door that opened was opened from the other side.

Payoff (III.iii, III.vi). "I wrote it." Then what SDF most needs: the state keeps its heresy alive to discredit it daily, and once Winston is broken it lets him go: a sinecure, a reserved table, nobody sitting near him. The broken man in public is the proof.

Against A–D:

  • A (gate): contradicts, then adds. Winston never tests O'Brien: "there was no way of doing so" (I.i). The catechism records rather than blocks. The dial (III.ii) is the real gate: someone who knows more asks, and a wrong answer costs. Take the shape, not the pain; a wrong answer should close a door, a name, a copy.
  • B (canary): supports, run on the hero. The book is invented to see who believes it. Winston's own canary, the dust, is noticed and put back (III.iv): the defense against a canary is to restore it.
  • C (front): supports. The Brotherhood fronts for the Party; the book fronts for its motive; the bottom layer stays unanswered (III.ii).
  • D (lock and key): partly. The rhyme as countersign (II.iv); Room 101 cut from his own dream (forbidden to SDF, but the craft point stands: the key comes from material the reader has already seen).
  • Fifth: true bait (accurate material left findable so the reader identifies himself); the restored tell; the broken man left in public as proof. The fourth candidate, the error-language cover (edits filed as "misprints," I.iv; a misprint as summons, II.viii), is real but already all over SDF (section 6).

items.title: 1. James does the forgery's homework. The drill, The money
items.html:
• Change: the continuity program gives James a task with a result: reconcile Annex C against HR records before the drill and sign it off.
  • James does: the job, well. He finds Pieter's "dependants per allocation: 3" against two children, corrects it, and initials the reconciliation (Ogilvy, I.iv; "anxious… that the forgery should be perfect," II.ix).
  • Cost: his initials are on the machine's own paperwork; he is a helper by his own hand. The old man can thank him for the cleanest annex in years (The reading room, continued); James's own name belongs among The sheets.
  • Already on the page? No. V7 The money: Saskia says "See if anything's expired" and he reads. V7 The drill: five idle hours. Nothing he produces carries his name.

items.title: 2. "Why could I find it?" The money
items.html:
• Change: the role that opens the annex was granted before he asked.
  • James does: before opening Annex C he asks Saskia who approved it. "It came through already ticked," dated the week of his ticket. He opens it anyway.
  • Cost: next night's payload has a new line against his number: read (annex). He counts himself, knowingly: the book sorting its reader (II.ix, 03) with SDF's own machine.
  • Already on the page? Partly. The opening has "We leave them findable" (plan, The reading room); v7 The money has the role added "with a sigh, because I'd asked," and James never asks why it was easy.

items.title: 3. The one refusal is recorded. On land, The schedule
items.html:
• Change: like the catechism (II.viii), the "companion" note comes from one thing James refuses in front of Kalder.
  • James does: at the pub Kalder offers a weekend at his club, two rounds and a hotel, "no dogs, sorry." James declines because of Buddy, as a joke. In The schedule he reads companion and knows which sentence put it there.
  • Cost: the threat to Buddy traces to James's own mouth, so A street, night has a cause he can feel guilty for. The "I told them what I loved" beat moves from the end of v7 The reading room, continued, where nothing follows from it, to where it costs.
  • Already on the page? Partly. V7 The corporate day ("Bring the old boy"); plan A car park ("near enough to know what he loves").

items.title: 4. The restored tell. The gorilla mask, The vet, Frank, loose
items.html:
• Change: James sets a tell on the thin book; the other side puts it back (III.iv). They don't take the book; they make it useless.
  • James does: after the barbecue (perhaps the plan's unnamed "building something at four in the morning," PLACEHOLDER) he lays one of Buddy's gray hairs across the thin book. Home from the vet at six, the hair is exactly in place; he tells Ana nothing was touched and doesn't copy the book. In Frank, loose he orders a library copy of one of the forty-one titles to show Frank, and it is "withdrawn for conservation." So is the next.
  • Cost: the book was photographed, and his two-copy method has lost its second copies. Frank gets the invoice, not the edit. Discredit, not prevent: nothing stolen.
  • Already on the page? No. Canon conflict: plan The vet says "the thin book gone"; the v8 brief says it "is not stolen"; v7 The reading room, continued puts it on the old man's tray. This follows the brief. PLACEHOLDER.

items.title: 5. The broken man at his table. The other ten
items.html:
• Change: one of the four "quiet" addresses becomes a person: alive, cheerful, politely avoided (III.vi), the organization's best outcome.
  • James does: goes to the sports club whose newsletter dropped its treasurer and has a coffee with him. The man insists nothing ever happened and returns to his garden every time.
  • Cost: James meets his likeliest ending, which is not a canal; Ana's "that's a Tuesday" gets harder to answer. "Quiet" in Aylin's visitor book (The night before) becomes someone the reader has met.
  • Already on the page? Partly. V7 The other ten has the quiet four as records only; the widow is the only person he meets.

items.title: 6. True bait, James's. The sheets, The leak
items.html:
(PLACEHOLDER) James gives the brewery man his sheet last, knowing he'll report it. Cost: the man at Pieter's door is partly James's doing. Already? Partly (plan The sheets: "we know he'll report it," not chosen). Risk: James as manipulator.

Rejected: any key cut from James's fears (torture, pressure); the oath played back as leverage (pressure); James writing to the organization like Winston's diary-letter (the plan already spends that as the professor's mistake in Deventer, March).

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• The error-language cover as news. SDF has it: typos left in (The sentence), "diagnostic artefact" (Leave it), the duplicate ticket (The week it vanished), When a Reader Notices (The math), Julian K.'s eleven-minute fix (Enjoy it while it lasts), "No impact observed" (v8 Leave it).
  • A broadcast Goldstein. The organization feeding its own opposition is already the thermostat (The band) and the farmed forum (The gorilla mask).
  • Total control of memory. SDF's organization can't edit memory, which is why it must count and visit. Keep it that weak.

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
• "always the reference was to slips, errors, misprints or misquotations which it was necessary to put right in the interests of accuracy." (I.iv): edits filed as corrections.
  • "Winston had never made the smallest effort to verify this guess: indeed, there was no way of doing so." (I.i): no gate.
  • "it would never be possible for me to prove it, even when I did the falsification myself." (II.v): the editor can't prove his own edit.
  • "one of the messages among your morning’s work will contain a misprinted word, and you will have to ask for a repeat." (II.viii): the error as summons.
  • "Excuse me, I think you’ve dropped your brief-case." (II.ix): the trap handed over as an accident.
  • "The best books, he perceived, are those that tell you what you know already." (II.ix): why true bait works.
  • "I wrote it. That is to say, I collaborated in writing it." (III.iii): the forbidden book as the state's work.
  • "Even the speck of whitish dust on the cover of his diary they had carefully replaced." (III.iv): the watcher restores the tell.

notes.title: section 01 (Part One, chapters I–VII)
notes.html:
Coverage: Part One, chapters I–VII (about 26,800 words of novel), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: Penguin, with Thomas Pynchon's introduction (skimmed, not cited); converted text, chunk file 01. Part One, chapter VIII is not in this section.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. I–II) To put his thoughts on paper, in a diary bought at a junk shop The first entry brings back O'Brien's glance during the Two Minutes Hate; then a knock, which is only Mrs Parsons and her sink He decides he is already a dead man: the thought is the crime Stopping changes nothing. Tearing out the pages would not undo the thought He lives like a suspect: scrubs the ink off, puts a grain of dust on the diary cover
2 (ch. III–V) To remember the world before the Party and prove one lie His own job makes lies true. He invents Comrade Ogilvy and enjoys it; the chocolate ration is announced as raised to the figure it was cut to the day before He is good at the thing he hates, and everyone around him swallows the lie He seems to be the only one who remembers last week He looks outward: the dark-haired girl (whom he fears), the proles, O'Brien
3 (ch. VI–VII) To confess, then to understand The one proof he ever held: a 1973 photo of Jones, Aaronson and Rutherford in New York on the day they confessed to being in Siberia. He put it in the memory hole himself His only evidence is gone, and the charges have since been rewritten so often that it would prove nothing now He knows how the lie is made but not why, and is not sure he is sane He writes the diary as a letter to O'Brien

Why it grips

  • Crime first, punishment certain. Chapter I opens with the decisive act, and Winston decides within pages he will be caught. The question is only when and through whom, so every later scene reads as a possible capture.
  • False alarms. The knock ending ch. I is a blocked sink (ch. II); the watcher at the next canteen table is the dark-haired girl (ch. V). Each alarm goes quiet, so the reader cannot tell which will be real.
  • The best story is interrupted. In ch. III Winston starts to tell the one time he held proof, and the telescreen instructor shouts his number. The story is held for four chapters and told in ch. VII. Surveillance cuts off the lore at its best moment, and the lore becomes a debt the book owes the reader.
  • The scene that does most: Ogilvy (ch. IV). A clerk invents a dead hero, worries about cross-referencing, and is sure his version will beat Tillotson's across the hall. The whole lie of the state is shown as an office job with a rival. Funny and horrible at once.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

Two conspiracies, and only one acts. The Party acts on every page, but through paperwork, not people: telescreen, memory hole, slips in the pneumatic tube. It takes his memory and gives him his job. The Brotherhood does nothing. It exists only as the Party's own broadcast (ch. I): Goldstein on screen daily, his theories knocked down a thousand times a day, his book known only as the book. The Party is the only source of news about its enemy.

That is the trap, laid before anyone springs it. The Hate keeps Goldstein and the rumour of the book alive, and Winston's hope feeds on what the Party puts on display. Details are planted: Goldstein's speech uses more Newspeak than any Party member does (ch. I), so it sounds Party-written; the café where the purged leaders drank is not forbidden, only ominous (ch. V, VII). The way in is open and in plain sight. [from memory, not from the text: O'Brien later hands Winston the book and says he helped write it.]

What it puts in the room: O'Brien, through one look (ch. I) and a voice in a dream (ch. II). Winston never tests either. Here the conspiracy moves the story by giving the hero someone to hope for, not by blocking him.

How the lore gets in

  • Oceania and the ministries (ch. I), about 1,200 words. A man at a window, intercut with gin and an itching ulcer. No stall.
  • Goldstein and the book (ch. I), about 900 words. Inside the Hate, while the crowd screams and the girl throws a dictionary at the screen. Lore as noise. No stall.
  • Doublethink (ch. III), about 1,200 words. Thought during morning exercises, broken off when the instructor singles him out.
  • The Records Department (ch. IV), about 3,500 words. Delivered as work: four slips, a procedure, a rival, a finished forgery. The longest block, and it does not stall because Winston has a task with a result.
  • Newspeak (ch. V), about 1,000 words. Syme lectures over stew, between hanging talk and Parsons's spy-daughter story. Slight stall.
  • The proles and the textbook (ch. VII), about 1,800 words. Essay plus a copied document. The one real stall, paid for by the photograph story that follows.

Mechanism notes

  • The editing machine (ch. IV). The orders never mention forgery; every change is called a correction of a misprint. SDF's machine leaves typos in so nobody checks; Orwell's labels its edits as typo fixes so no one has to admit what they are doing. Both use the language of error as cover. A possible object for James: an errata slip that calls the change a misprint. Also ch. IV: a dozen people may write rival versions and an unseen senior picks one, so two printings that differ in different ways could be competing drafts.
  • Proof without an audience (ch. VII). The photo could destroy the Party only if published, and there is nowhere to publish, so he burns it. Later it would not even be proof. This is discredit rather than prevent in pure form: no need to seize the evidence, only to move the context until it means nothing.
  • A (gate), in negative. Winston has no gate. He trusts O'Brien on one look and never tests it (ch. I, VII). A hero who acts on hope walks straight into we leave the seats findable; a gate is his only defence.
  • B (canary). Ogilvy is an invented person who becomes record (ch. IV), the canary's tool in the enemy's hand. Winston's grain of dust on the diary (ch. II) is a home-made canary for whoever handles his book; James could do exactly that with a library copy.
  • C (front). Weak here: the Records hall is one cell in a branch in a ministry, run by anonymous directing brains (ch. IV).
  • Fifth: the state advertises its enemy. Goldstein's influence never fades because the Party shows him daily (ch. I). The rumour of resistance is the recruiting tool.

Quotes

  • "always the reference was to slips, errors, misprints or misquotations which it was necessary to put right in the interests of accuracy." (Part One, ch. IV): edits disguised as corrections.
  • "Winston had never made the smallest effort to verify this guess: indeed, there was no way of doing so." (Part One, ch. I): the missing gate.
  • "There was no law, not even an unwritten law, against frequenting the Chestnut Tree Café, yet the place was somehow ill-omened." (Part One, ch. V): the seat left findable.
  • "It was enough to blow the Party to atoms, if in some way it could have been published to the world" (Part One, ch. VII): proof with no venue.

Flags

  • Syme says Chaucer, Shakespeare, Milton and Byron will exist only in Newspeak versions (ch. V): invented edits on real books. SDF must not do this.
  • No real people named as complicit in the novel text. Pynchon's introduction (Stalin, Trotsky, Burnham) is not Orwell and is not used.

notes.title: section 02 (Part 1, ch. 8 to Part 2, ch. 8)
notes.html:
Coverage: Part 1, ch. 8 (prole walk, pub, Charrington's shop) to Part 2, ch. 8 (O'Brien's flat), about 32,900 words, read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: Penguin (per brief); chunk file 02, no edition data in it.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (P1 ch. 8) A living witness to life before the Revolution The old man remembers only top hats and pints; the junk shop gives him the paperweight and a room with no telescreen The dark-haired girl sees him leaving the shop. He is sure she is spying and thinks about killing her He believes he is already seen, so caution buys nothing He resolves to go back to the shop; the girl's next move comes to him
2 (P2 ch. 1–5) The girl, then a place to be alone The note, Julia, the hide-outs, Charrington's room let without a question Every meeting is a risk ("suicidal folly", ch. 4); Syme disappears (ch. 5) The room has made him well (ch. 5), and Julia's dodging is not enough for him: he wants evidence and an organisation, which she refuses to believe in He tells Julia about O'Brien; the next contact again comes to him
3 (P2 ch. 6–8) To get inside the conspiracy A coded mention of the vanished Syme, an address, then the Brotherhood "is real" He swears to murder and to throw acid in a child's face. He refuses one thing, to separate from Julia, and O'Brien notes it: "It is necessary for us to know everything."
