  • Philby's border survey in 1948 ("Operation Spyglass", ch. 13) is the cover for a balloon that lures djinn. Burgess visiting Turkey puts him at the wire. [from memory: both events are on the record.]

The conspiracy also makes paper that will come back later. Theodora's cover story for Hale includes a crime that "can’t be disproved" because the illegal "kept no records", and in 1948 he gave Hale the name of a real Soviet agent while telling him the agent was invented (ch. 13). That 1948 forgery drives 1963: it makes Hale a fugitive whom Mammalian trusts and then doubts, which threatens Hale's revenge. It also turns Elena against him. The CIA men show surveillance as record-matching: IATA tickets against bylines (ch. 11).

How the lore gets in

  • Philby's confession to Elena (ch. 11), about 4,000 words, a conversation under threat. The birds circle closer every page or so, so the danger grows while he talks.
  • The djinn lecture, about 150 words, delivered twice (toy phone in ch. 11, Hale's mouth in ch. 12). The repeat turns the rule into a plot event.
  • Hale's debrief (ch. 12), about 1,500 words, to a wire recorder. Mammalian's answer sets the cost straight away: the stone will be destroyed.
  • The Wabar flashback (ch. 12), about 9,000 words, dramatized. The theory is tested in the field, its source a real book read against its author ("This is the work of God, not man" becomes "angels, not man"). Within a page the danger arrives.
  • Theodora's briefing (ch. 13), about 1,500 words, while walking. Broken up by the Kurd anecdote.
  • The Khan's amomon lore (ch. 13), about 800 words, over dinner. The proof is objects: the honey, Balaklava, the jacket, the stone talisman. The torches cut him off mid-gift.

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate): Elena names it outright: no exfiltration until she is convinced he will tell everything (ch. 11). The Wabar trip is a gate of proof. A hostile witness (the king) confirms the stone has killed. In 1963 the full account costs him the stone.
  • B (canary): the SIS feeds "barium meal" information to Philby so that a leak can be traced to him (ch. 11). The CIA drop "Charles Garner" and the fox to watch how he reacts. The Philby record supplies B ready-made.
  • C (front): this is the strongest showing in the section. Each documented fact covers the next fact down (radiator, Spyglass, the Armenians). For SDF, each anomaly James solves could come with a dull, true explanation that is also the organisation's cover.
  • D (lock and key): Elena opens Philby with one private quotation from Maly's own lips (ch. 11). The Khan's wife's jacket opens Hale.
  • Fifth: telling has a cost. Each disclosure in the present changes the plan. When James tells someone what he found, the telling should change what the organisation does next.

Quotes

  • "bash his head again, against the radiator, to conceal from his wife the fact that he had been shot" (ch. 11): a documented accident turned into the cover for a hidden act.
  • "He was beginning to relax—this story was verifiably true" (ch. 11): a spy, and the author, relax on documented ground.
  • "the illegal kept no records, so it can’t be disproved" (ch. 13): a fabricated record built to be unfalsifiable.
  • "Don’t hint, say." (ch. 11): the interrogator forces the lore out as payment.

Flags

  • Real people made complicit in the supernatural plot: Kim Philby, Guy Burgess, Theodore Maly, St. John Philby, T. E. Lawrence (said to have destroyed translations), Konstantin Volkov, Nicholas Elliott, Peter Lunn, Flora Solomon. SDF must not do this.
  • A real book used as an occult source: St. John Philby's The Empty Quarter is reread for the occult and not altered. Whether its Wabar dream passage is in the real book cannot be checked from the text; Lawrence's lost files are invented. Rereading a real book fits SDF's rules; adding to one does not.
  • [from memory, not from the text: the real large Wabar iron was found on site in 1965. Powers' removal of it in 1948 may strain his own rule of never contradicting the record.]

notes.title: section 05 (chapters 14–16)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 14–16 (about 33,200 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 05; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 14, Ararat 1948) Blow up the djinn with the Shihab stone A Soviet ambush. To survive the djinn he joins their rhythm and shares in eating his men. Then a poker hand with Philby: Elena against a dead GRU man's envelope on how not to die. The burned balloon rope in Philby's jeep points to Philby as the Soviet driver His men, Elena ("cannibale"), and his career: C sends him back to Oxford The suspicion about Philby is never tested and the hand is never finished. The chapter ends by saying he did not see Theodora again until 1963 The 1963 strand, where both debts fall due
2 (ch. 15, Elena, Beirut 1963, flashbacks to 1942 and 1948) Decide whether to fly Philby out or kill him In memory: how the Rabkrin made her, her defection, her 1948 suicide attempt that Philby talked her out of before sleeping with her, and her vow to light a candle at St Basil's in 1964 If Philby defects alive, that night goes into his recorded biography and ends her career Her failed sniper shot proved his offer to defect is genuine. Then Hale appears on the terrace Hale and Elena in one city, both carrying 1948
3 (ch. 16, Beirut 1963) Get his Declare briefing without losing his cover He gets arrested on purpose. In the jail Hartsik tells him the 1948 maths was wrong, that Philby is his half-brother, and that a pellet in Philby will kill the Soviet angel when she eats his body Two punches and scalding coffee, so he matches his double. One phrase in the double's transcript nearly makes Mammalian abort If the mission is aborted Mammalian will "verify" him, meaning kill him, and Philby has to be forced up the mountain Philby chooses to live. Hale leaves his watch on the correct local time

Why it grips

  • A past strand leaves a question that the present scene answers. The poker hand in chapter 14 stops before anyone declares, because the shelter is thrown over. Two chapters later Philby's stammered "Declare?—low on the l-list of likelihoods" settles it in front of Mammalian (ch. 16).
  • The hero's mistake comes back as a fact. Chapter 14's disaster turns out to be a technical error: Hale had the mould when he needed what comes out of it. The guilt the reader has been carrying becomes information, and the new plan is built on top of it.
  • A second viewpoint changes how the first one reads. Chapter 15 shows the same night through Elena: "Nous cannibales", and the jeep that drove past her unlocked door. Hale's departure in chapter 14 hurts after the fact, and she gets a 1963 motive (she would prefer Philby dead) that Hale does not know about.
  • The lore gets in through slapstick and pain. Farid interrupts Hartsik's briefing three times: he hits the double too hard, then hits Hale again, then brings in coffee. The longest lecture is also the funniest scene.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

Declare works by making records for the enemy to read. Hale's 1948 confession to the Rabkrin was bait ("all that math was bad"; it will "enhance the look of the old math"). A double takes the beating and a script makes him "Charles Garner". A clerk the Soviets pay is called in on his day off, so that Mammalian hears from an eyewitness that nothing was said. Hale has to match those records, down to the bruise and the coffee stain. The danger is wherever the record does not fit him. The double's line about a dog that wouldn't hunt was not "the sort of thing he would say", and that is the line Mammalian picks on.

The documented record is the engine. Powers takes each known Philby fact as fixed and invents only its cause. Then he uses that cause to force the next scene. The death of Jackie the fox explains Philby's reluctance, his request to The Observer for leave and his feelers to France. His defection becomes Declare's order ("cross at the Aras River"). The end of the USSR becomes the delayed effect of a pellet in his corpse. Burgess's father dying in bed gets a djinn at the window. The reader knows the ending and reads on for what forces it. [From memory, not from the text: Philby reached Moscow in January 1963 and died there in 1988; the USSR ended in 1991; the fox and Burgess's father are in the biographies.]

How the lore gets in

  • Philby's envelope (ch. 14), about 500 words of dialogue. The envelope is an object (bloodied, signed "Maly") and it is the stake in the card game. Philby explains the GRU purge, the telegraph rhythm and the cure for death while the cards are dealt, so the story does not stall.
  • Elena's backstory (ch. 15), about 9,000 words of flashback framed by a single morning at a window. The Machikha Nash lore is one summary paragraph, delivered while she is drunk and being conditioned. Each part of the flashback ends in a violent act, and it returns to the present with Hale at a terrace table.
  • Hartsik in the jail (ch. 16), about 4,000 words. The biggest dump in the section: death-shapes, Solomon's "sword", the half-brother, the fox, Burgess, the pellet plan. It is anchored to objects (lead balls rolled across the desk, a clockwise-rifled derringer) and interrupted by Farid. Philby is waiting in the hall when it ends.
  • Survey photos (ch. 16), about 300 words. American wartime films, the 1959 Turkish Geodetic survey and NSA drone photos are given as sources: real archives lend the lore provenance. The "real Ark" is a formation about twenty miles from Ararat, exposed by the 1948 earthquake. [From memory: this is the real Durupınar formation.] Powers keeps a real anomaly real and supplies the explanation.

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate): In 1948 Hale acted before he understood the mould and the bullets, and men died. In 1963 he is given the answer, so the gate is passed by a briefing handed to him, which is SDF's trap. The real engine is the cost of being wrong, paid fifteen years later.
  • B (canary): The strongest lesson here. Declare plants false maths and a staged arrest, then watches what Mammalian believes. One phrase that sounds wrong almost gives the plant away, which is the risk a canary carries. Proposal for SDF: James's invented detail reaches the organisation in a document he did not write, and they test him on the one phrase that is not in his voice.
  • C (front): Each cover hides another. Hale's defection covers his Declare work, "Garner" covers Hale, and Philby's 1952 doubling covers his Soviet loyalty, which covers his Rabkrin role.
  • D (lock and key): Philby turns on one specific truth, the old challenge "O Fish, are you constant to the old covenant?", and on his own fear: he would rather live as a prole than die as an aristocrat. The door opens because Philby chooses, though Declare's death threat stands behind that choice.

Quotes

  • "Seven-card stud—high-low—declare, not cards-speak." (ch. 14): the title word is planted inside a card-game rule.
  • "You mistook the mold for the bullets." (ch. 16): the old failure is answered with one fact.
  • "I can’t imagine the U.S.S.R. surviving Philby by more than three or four years." (ch. 16): a documented outcome gets a hidden cause.
  • "In Philby’s hesitant speech Hale had caught the phrase, I declare low." (ch. 16): the past strand settles the present scene.

Flags

  • Invented edit on a real book: Hartsik says copyists changed a word in 1 Kings 3 to "sword" (ch. 16). That is an invented variant of a real text, which SDF forbids.
  • Real people named as complicit: Philby, Burgess, St John Philby, Menzies, Cumming, Marty, Beria and Macmillan are written into the occult plot. The Ukrainian famine is recast as a sacrifice. SDF must not do this.

notes.title: section 06 (Book Three: chapters 17–18, Epilogue, Afterword, Author's Note)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapter 17 to the end, including the Epilogue ("Declare", Moscow 1964), the one-paragraph Afterword and the Author's Note with its footnotes (about 38,000 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 06, no edition data. The Author's Note is read as Powers's statement of method, not as story.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 17) Reach the Ark, kill the djinn, put Shihab shot in Philby's back unnoticed Mammalian reveals that he and Philby are both St. John Philby's sons, and the sacrament needs them together. Over a crevasse he is tempted to unclip and drop His identity (the brothers would merge into one mind), nearly his life He is roped into a Spetsnaz line. The mission works only at the Ark. Theodora will "verify" him either way The approach to the Ark beside Philby
2 (ch. 18) Fire the derringer, get off the mountain Elena's helicopter veers away when she sees him. Mammalian turns on the Spetsnaz. The angel nearly wins him over He kills two commandos and shoots his brother Philby tries to shoot the second rope and strand Mammalian A walk out to Siamand Khan's village and a year in hiding
3 (Epilogue) Come home alive, and be at St. Basil's at noon on Elena's fortieth birthday Theodora still means to kill him. Philby holds the rafiq diamond and knows about the vow He gives up immortality (three amomon roots) and the diamond he needs to fly Theodora's kill order is lifted only while Hale is useful, and the date is fixed The unfinished 1948 card game: "Declare"

Why it grips

  • The record runs the clock. Chapter 17 opens in Philby's head and walks through documented Beirut, January 1963: Elliott's confrontation, the typed partial confession, Lunn taking over, the dinner at the Balfour-Pauls'. Powers hangs the invented departure on that real night. Philby phones home, his son Harry answers, and Mammalian presses down the plunger. The next day would have been the wedding anniversary. The real calendar makes the invented scene hurt.
  • A lore lecture that ends in a bombshell. Mammalian's tent briefing (Hippolytus, Bishop Jacob, drogue stones) looks like exposition until "The brothers are divided" is answered: the two sons are Philby and Hale. The scene turns from information to injury.
  • Cross-cut. Elena's section ends with the rockets armed ("Montrez-moi"). Chapter 18 pays it off from the ground, then from her cabin: she knows his posture and veers.
  • The title is a bet. The 1948 hand of seven-card stud, "high-low declare", is finished in a Moscow park. The cards hardly matter. All that counts is which way each man declares: high wins Elena, low wins immortality. Philby goes low and Hale goes high. Philby's prize is a fraud: the root will die on the shot in his back.
  • Still funny. Philby: "t-two middle-aged Englishmen k-killed ten spit-spit—fucking—Spetsnaz". Theodora's 1918 plan to parade Lenin in his underwear. "The Beetles".

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The hidden order (Theodora's SOE remnant, Declare) is what stops Hale from just going home. Once the djinn are dead, Hale knows that a Prime Minister authorised a "sorcerous" strike on the USSR, so in Theodora's logic he has to be killed: "we’ve killed bigger heroes, famous ones". Nobody tries to stop him knowing. Instead he is scheduled for a quiet death and an "enduring disgrace" of his last cover.

Hale beats this with a document. He has written the story down as a book, Declare, and left it with a Belgian solicitor, who sends it to the press if Hale's yearly Christmas card (with a photo dated by a newspaper) fails to arrive. Then he offers the conspiracy what it needs, the only man who can kill Philby, inside a cover story Whitehall will accept (a journalist investigating Burobin). The secret goes from being the thing that will kill him to his ticket into Moscow.

The second hidden order, Machikha Nash, gets a community: the Gray People, defectors who learn whom they serve only "when we’ve surrendered our passports".

How the lore gets in

  • Mammalian's briefing (ch. 17), about 1,300 words, conversation. Legend is mixed with climbing drill ("recite the multiplication tables") and it ends in an order ("Up"). The brothers reveal lands mid-lecture, so it does not stall.
  • Elena's catch-up (ch. 17), about 1,500 words, backstory. It is told in the past perfect from inside a helicopter heading for the target. The countdown in the present-tense frame ("Une dizaine minutes") keeps it moving.
  • Moscow travelogue, about 1,500 words. This is the one slow stretch. Powers keeps it going with a deadline (noon on the 22nd) and two errands Hale keeps putting off.
  • Afterword and Author's Note, about 1,900 words plus 19 footnotes. The Afterword gives documented facts: Philby died in 1988 and was buried, and the USSR fell in 1991. That closes the chain the Epilogue set up, where cremation would melt the shot and burial lets the ghula take it in. A public fact becomes the last plot beat. The Note then lists the real "wobbles" with sources: the fox mourned like a father, the coat lined with red fox fur, the "lost" Lawrence files, the Ararat photograph, feet bruised from a walk, The Birds.

Mechanism notes

  • The method. Powers treats documented facts as fixed points and invents only their cause, like astronomers who infer a planet from wobbles in other orbits. He quotes real books (Seven Pillars, The Empty Quarter, My Silent War) accurately and reads them as cover stories, never inventing a passage. That is the SDF rule: the real anomaly stays real, and the explanation is the invention.
  • Ending on a checkable fact. The plot's last event, the burial, is something the reader can check. [Inference] For SDF, the final proof could be an odd real fact anyone can look up, which only the invented organisation explains.
  • A (gate) as leverage. Hale may not come home until he holds something that makes killing him cost more than letting him live. He gets past the gate with an object, not force.
  • B (canary), reversed. Hale sells Philby a value he knows is false, and Philby's belief settles the bet.
  • C (front). The layers are stacked: the Burobin journalism covers the plan to kill Philby, and that plan covers Hale's real errand (Elena). Theodora builds his own deniability into it: "I’ll be as shocked as anyone else".
  • D (lock and key). Doors open on private phrases. The Arabian Nights line about the fish and the old covenant [from memory, not from the text: its source] opens the Gray Person. "Segne mich" (the GRU code for trust me) and "I did not kill Cassagnac" open Elena. She had already decided on the helicopter, so the key only confirms her own choice.
  • Fifth: the hero writes the leak. Hale's insurance is the novel itself. For SDF, this could be James's manuscript held in escrow, which the organisation would rather discredit than suppress.

Quotes

  • "I could not change or disregard any of the recorded facts, nor rearrange any days of the calendar" (Author's Note): the whole method.
  • "then I tried to figure out what momentous but unrecorded fact could explain them all." (Author's Note): invent the cause, never the fact.
  • "Into his silence I’ve presumed to fit the admittedly extravagant—but, I think, consistent—premise of this story." (Author's Note): the invention goes in the gaps of the record.
  • "Whatever the outcome, I declared high." (Epilogue): the title paid off as a moral choice.

Flags

  • Real people are made complicit: Philby betrays SAS men and serves the djinn, and Burgess relays MiG photos. A legend in chapter 17 says Declare "dealt with" Turing, T. E. Lawrence and Kitchener. The Note hints at the black car at Lawrence's crash. SDF must not do this.
  • No invented edits on real books. Powers quotes real texts accurately and only reinterprets them, which is the model SDF should copy.

books.qa:
Answers point to the section notes in this folder (01-prologue-to-chapter-4.md, 02-chapters-5-to-7.md, 03-chapters-8-to-10.md, 04-chapters-11-to-13.md, 05-chapters-14-to-16.md, 06-book-three-to-afterword.md) and, where it matters, to a v8.2 chapter by title. The map is 00-map.md. Everything about SDF here is a PROPOSAL. Santi's decisions are marked PLACEHOLDER.

The method (secret history that never contradicts the record)

1. What exactly is Powers's rule? He lists the odd details in the documented record and keeps every one of them, with every date. Then he asks what single unrecorded fact would explain them all. The Author's Note says so outright ("I could not change or disregard any of the recorded facts, nor rearrange any days of the calendar"), and compares the method to inferring a planet from the wobbles it causes in other orbits (06).

2. How is that different from SDF's rule? SDF keeps real anomalies real and invents edits, people and companies, which is the same discipline. The difference is where the invented cause goes. Powers puts it inside a real event and a real person: Philby's head injury becomes a hidden gunshot (04), and Cowgill's real loss of his section gets a supernatural reason (03). SDF may only put an invented person beside a real event and leave the cause unsaid, as Urfa, 1994 does ("The book never says he found it").

3. Does SDF already use the method anywhere? Yes, in the real interludes. Down House, 1860; Croton, 530 BC; Washington, 1953; Urfa, 1994; and Mexico City, 1994 keep the real record, and the invented plot runs next to them (Tresidder walking east in 1929; the invented Utrecht physicist). Powers adds one more lesson: put an invented scene on a real night so that the calendar does the hurting. Chapter 17 times the departure to the documented Beirut dinner, the night before the wedding anniversary (06). SDF can do this only with invented characters on real dates.

4. Does Powers ever break his own rule? Two notes suspect it. Note 04 flags that the real Wabar iron was found on site in 1965, so having it removed in 1948 may strain the record [from memory, not from the text]. Note 05 flags Hartsik's claim that copyists changed a word in 1 Kings 3, which is an invented variant of a real text. It is a character's claim, though, not the narration's, so in SDF terms it is the old man's licence in The final conversation and nobody else's.

5. Can SDF reread a real book the way Powers does? Yes, provided nothing is added to it. Powers quotes The Empty Quarter, Seven Pillars and My Silent War accurately and reads them as cover stories (04, 06). Elena's point that "Declare" appears in the Protestant Job but not in the Douay is a real difference between real editions (02). That is the legal version of SDF's "given/arose", which SDF keeps for its invented 1926 book.

The engine

6. Why can't Hale stop? Every step closes the door behind him. "Raincoat" means he can't go home (ch. 1). The frame for murder means he can't ask anyone to confirm his orders (ch. 3). Refusing the djinn's orders "confirms" him, and there is no way back (ch. 8). An abort in 1963 means he will be killed (ch. 16). See the map, section 2, and 01, 03, 05.

7. When does the reason become something Hale did himself, the switch Addendum 05 asks for? In chapter 3, when he keeps the "Bueno Año" slips from Theodora (01). It is his first break with the service, and from then on a private reason (Elena) runs beside every order. SDF has the same shape in The math, where James lies to Ana about where he was, but there the private reason costs only her trust.

8. Who is the antagonist that pushes back? The paperwork, more than the Soviets. Declare's forged records (ch. 3, 13) make Hale a fugitive whom the Soviets trust and then doubt, and they turn Elena against him (04). That is SDF's organisation exactly: it discredits rather than prevents. Powers simply aims it at the hero.

9. What is the cost of being wrong, which SDF's Part Two lacks? The 1948 raid fails because Hale "mistook the mold for the bullets". Men die, and fifteen years later the error returns as a single fact that the new plan is built on (ch. 14, 16, 05). This supports King map proposal 2 (The schedule: the date James trusted was moved by his own verb). It doesn't add a new one.

The timelines

10. How do the two strands force each other? The present quotes the past before the past shows it ("Kiss the bride quick, Andrew", ch. 8, then the wedding, ch. 10). Chapter 7 hands over a list of results (five dead men, Cassagnac shot "yesterday") that the past then has to explain. And a phrase left open in one strand is settled in the other: the covenant phrase (03), the poker hand (05). See 02 and 03.

11. Does that help SDF's frame (the opening reading room, then "Eight months earlier")? Yes. It argues for letting the opening say one line that Part Two later explains. The ledger at page 118 already works this way. Powers would add a spoken line as well. On PLACEHOLDER #7, that favors planting the old man's "some of us remember" once in the opening, as a joke.

12. Should SDF's villain-alone chapters be cut against the James chapters more tightly? Possibly. Powers's past strand answers the question the present has just raised (01). SDF's Leiden, nine years ago answers who Kalder is, but it comes before The vet asks. Moving it later is a structure call, PLACEHOLDER. Nothing in Declare forces it.

Lore

13. What is the largest lore dump, and why does it not stall? Hartsik in the Beirut jail (ch. 16, about 4,000 words, 05). It is tied to objects (lead balls rolled across the desk, a derringer), it is interrupted three times by Farid's slapstick, and Philby is waiting in the hall. For SDF's Leiden or The reading room, continued: keep one object moving and one person interrupting.

14. Where does Declare stall? In the archive montage (ch. 9, 03) and the Moscow travelogue (Epilogue, 06). Powers keeps the montage short and funny, gives Hale a duty (sign off the files honestly), and ends on a chain of words instead of an explanation. He keeps the travelogue moving with a fixed noon deadline.

15. What does the Number 10 briefing teach, given SDF bans crimes? Run lore beside a task in the hero's hands. In Declare the task is bugging a table (ch. 3, 01). In SDF it would be a real job task: the reconciliation in The money (Orwell proposal 1), the drill in The drill.

16. Does lore ever arrive as payment? Yes, all the time. In ch. 11 Philby pays Elena in disclosures for his escape. In ch. 12–13 Hale trades his history for a place in the operation, and the telling costs him the stone (04). SDF has this already: in v7 The reading room, continued, James realizes he has told the system what he is watching for.

The mechanisms

17. What is "records made for the enemy to read"? Declare writes papers so that the enemy will read them: Hale's Kuwait crimes and Registry file (ch. 3), a 1948 crime that "can't be disproved" (ch. 13), a double's beating and transcript (ch. 16). Hale then has to match those papers in person. The danger is wherever the record doesn't fit him, and here that is one phrase in the double's transcript (05). Map proposal 5.1 gives James this move.

18. What is the forged heartbeat (map 5.1), in one paragraph? After Noor says a loud reader is manageable (v6 Leiden), James schedules harmless forum posts so that he will look loud. Bram (A room with a long table) reads the timer as a performance, and the source of the advice as Noor. In What was on the phone James sees his posts marked performed, source Leiden. It needs the twelve-years-of-posts canon (Addendum 05 d, PLACEHOLDER).

19. Why not put the forged record after The night he stops being afraid instead? That works too. James could keep posting frightened questions to stay in the left column, and Kalder could read that the jokes about dying have stopped. But The long table, again already has "he said soul to the dog", so it would be a second tell in one scene. The Leiden placement gives the cost to Noor and to the passive stretch of Part Two the diagnosis names.

20. How does Declare's front (C) become something the hero does? Hale wears fronts, "Charles Garner", the defector and the Burobin journalist, and has to live up to them physically (ch. 16, Epilogue, 05, 06). That contradicts Addendum 05's finding that in Tier 1 the hero only learns the front. Map 5.3 has James send the sheets under the continuity programme's own format, true facts in his real role.

21. Isn't 5.3 impersonation? It is not, if he uses only his real role and invents no task. He is on the continuity programme (Leave it: "Continuity want you"), and a sheet really is a reconciliation of the recipient's records. If Santi reads it as misusing the bank's systems, drop it (PLACEHOLDER).

22. What is "they write him onto the list" (map 5.2)? After James refuses the five seats, the bank's annex is revised to include him, which discredits him by improving his record (ch. 3: "you never left the force"). He prints it on every sheet with "added the week after I said no", initialled. The cost: the brewery man, and at least one other, use it against him.

23. What does Declare add to the gate (A)? Three ways through it. You can pass it by refusing (ch. 8: "no SOE infiltrator would have perversely refused my orders"), by an embarrassing honest report to the person who hired you ("Magic, that is, sir", ch. 10), or with leverage (the solicitor, Epilogue). And there is an inverted gate: a hateful order proves itself genuine (ch. 7). See 02, 03, 06.

24. And to the canary (B)? It runs in both directions. Ishmael trusts Hale more after catching him in a vain lie (ch. 7). Philby mutters a phrase to see who flinches (ch. 9). Declare plants false maths and then watches what Mammalian believes (ch. 16). See 02, 03, 05. For On land, it is a reminder that Kalder's "Oh, that one. Yes" may itself be a canary aimed at James. The v8.2 plan already allows that reading.

25. Lock and key (D)? Present and ordinary: "Bless me", "Segne mich", "I did not kill Cassagnac", the covenant phrase (01, 03, 06). Elena had already decided before the key was used. That matches SDF's rule that a door opens only when a person chooses.

SDF fit and limits

26. Can SDF use Hale's solicitor? Not as leverage. A dead-man's switch is a threat, and SDF bans threats. Monday already gives James the same protection without one ("You made yourself too expensive. I don't think you planned it."). That is the better line for him (06; v8 Monday).

27. Then what of "the hero writes the leak himself"? It is already SDF's ending. Leave it is the book he is allowed to publish, and The final conversation has "If anyone asks, it's a novel" and "Nobody reads the middle". Map 5.4 adds only Powers's Author's Note: a back page of real, checkable oddities, because nobody reads the middle.

28. Is ending on a checkable fact useful to SDF? Yes, if the fact is real and its cause is left unstated. Declare's last beat is that Philby was buried, which any reader can check (Afterword, 06). SDF's last pages are invented (page 212 gone, the invoice stepping down). A real anomaly could close the book's back matter (map 5.4), never the narration's claims.

29. Which real people does Declare make complicit, so that nobody copies the pattern? Kim Philby, Guy Burgess, St John Philby, Macmillan, Dick White, Menzies, Cumming, Cowgill, Footman, Marty, Lenin, Stalin, Beria, Yezhov, Dzerzhinsky, Volkov, Elliott, Lunn, Flora Solomon. Lawrence, Turing and Kitchener are hinted to have been murdered, and Simex is recast as a hermetic front. See the Flags sections of 01–06.

30. Does the organisation in Declare kill like SDF's? It kills more and more casually ("we've killed bigger heroes, famous ones", 06), and Theodora plans a quiet death and an "enduring disgrace" for Hale. SDF's organisation kills rarely, and when it does it has failed. Take only the disgrace, which is the discrediting half (map 5.2).

31. Is Declare funny, as SDF must be? Yes, at the worst moments: Philby coughing gin out of his nose while the CIA quote Matthew at him (ch. 11), Farid hitting the wrong man (ch. 16), "two middle-aged Englishmen killed ten Spetsnaz" (ch. 18). See 04–06. Its longest lecture is also its funniest scene, which is the model for SDF's Leiden and The reading room, continued.

32. Is there a dog? A fox. Philby's fox Jackie, whose death explains his reluctance and his feelers to France, is a documented detail that Powers turns into the hidden reason (ch. 16, 05; Author's Note, 06). It is the nearest thing in Declare to Buddy: an animal whose loss moves the plot.

33. What should an agent check before proposing anything from Declare? Three things. First, whether a real person would be given an invented act or motive: if so, drop it. Second, whether v8.2 or a v7/v8 draft already does it: The final conversation, Monday and the visitor book's Pending already cover a lot. Third, whether the King, Orwell, Eco, Gibson or Borges maps, or Addendum 05, have already proposed it.

books.author: Pynchon
books.title: The Crying of Lot 49
books.readfor: signs left findable; played, or mad?
books.intro: Coverage: Perennial Fiction Library edition (1986, reissued 1990), English, converted text. Read in full through one section note (01-whole-novel.md, chapters 1–6, about 46,900 words), 11 Nov 2026; map written 12 Nov 2026. The file has no heading "4"; chapter 4 starts at "though she saw Mike Fallopian again". By that boundary "Kirby sent me" and "Shall I project a world?" are chapter 4, not 3 as the note has them. Brief: signs left findable, and whether the heroine is being played or going mad. Read against SDF's "we leave them findable" and the clown beside every real question. Standing-rule note: the invented Tristero is grafted onto the real Thurn and Taxis and real US postal history. Oedipa finds "an ambiguous footnote" in Motley's real Rise of the Dutch Republic: an invented claim about a real book, which SDF bans. Her small lies for reactions ("Kirby sent me", ch. 4; "an agent of Thurn and Taxis", ch. 5) would be impersonation in SDF. Take the shapes, none of that.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
Oedipa Maas, a California housewife, is named co-executor of her dead ex-lover Pierce Inverarity's estate. In San Narciso, his town, she keeps meeting a muted post horn and the word Trystero: on a latrine wall, in a Jacobean revenge play, in forged stamps in the estate's own collection. The trail suggests an underground mail system centuries old. Everyone who could confirm it or rule it out leaves her: her lover elopes, her shrink goes mad, her husband dissolves on LSD, the director drowns himself. She ends in an auction room, waiting for a hidden bidder to surface for lot 49, the forgeries. The book stops before he does.

What makes it work: a legal duty makes her look, so every clue is also an asset she must inventory, and stopping would mean failing the job. And every reading (real, hoax, madness) has evidence and a weak spot and leaves a cheap physical test, so she keeps acting without ever settling it.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:
Step What Oedipa wants right now What she finds What it costs her Why she cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 1) To know why Pierce named her A codicil, a list of legal duties A sleepless night It is a job, and the lawyer adds "In what you might find out" San Narciso
2 (ch. 2–3) To do the job and resist Metzger Every TV advert is Pierce's; bones in cigarette filters Her marriage, in effect Everything she sees is an asset she must list; she may have been "set up or sensitized" (ch. 3) A night at The Scope
3 (ch. 3) A drink W.A.S.T.E. and the horn on a latrine wall Nothing; she copies it into her memo book Writing it down is free, and now the book holds a question The bones are tied to a play
4 (ch. 3–4) To check the bones parallel "Trystero" spoken once; Driblette sends her to "another copy" at Zapf's Metzger's scorn She went to ask about bones and left talking about Trystero, and wonders "how accidental it had been" The paperback: "Cf. variant, 1687 ed."
5 (ch. 4) To bring order to the estate Koteks's doodle, a Wells Fargo marker, Cohen's planted-error stamps in Pierce's collection Koteks and Cohen back off Sources that look independent agree, inside what she must legally appraise Berkeley, for the source edition
6 (ch. 5) To make it go away: drift and "watch nothing happen" The hardcover lacks the line; within an hour a horn on a lapel; then a night of horns Her self-command Her test to disprove it came back positive She posts the sailor's letter, follows a carrier
7 (ch. 5) For her shrink to call her mad Hilarius shooting at "Israelis"; Mucho on LSD; "Cherish it!" Shrink and husband The people who could rule her mad have gone mad Back south, "a fugitive"
8 (ch. 6) The truth about Trystero Driblette's suicide; the Vatican variant; the history; Zapf's, the theater and the college all belong to the estate Every man around her; her health Four readings, one test left: the hidden bidder The auction room; the end

Read the "cannot stop" column down: steps 1–5 are the duty; at step 6 she tries to quit and quitting produces evidence; from step 7 nobody is left who could stop her.

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
• Peter Pinguid and the lake bones (ch. 3), about 600 words each, bar talk and a roof. Each ends on an event (the mail call; a remark about a play), so one piece of history hands her to the next.
  • The Courier's Tragedy (ch. 3), about 3,500 words, a play summarized for laughs. Where it doesn't stall: she and the reader are waiting for the bones, which come in Act IV, and the act ends on the one word. A long lecture holds if the reader is waiting for one item inside it.
  • Inamorati Anonymous (ch. 5), about 1,000 words, a drunk stranger's story. Farce that ends on an object: gasoline lifts a stamp's ink and the horn shows in the watermark.
  • The Tristero's origins (ch. 6), about 1,500 words in Bortz's costume-drama voice. Where it stalls, on purpose: she has stopped checking. The Zapf's sticker on the catalogue addendum restarts it, and Bortz turns the last document into an order: "Why don't you?"

sections.title: 4. The mechanism we came for: signs left findable, and the trail that runs home
sections.html:
Setup (ch. 3–5). The signs are public and cheap: a latrine wall, chalk, a laundromat card that anyone can find and only the already sensitized can read (quote 1). That is your opening's "we leave them findable": the seats are in the open, and only a man who has already asked will read them.

The rule (ch. 4). Cohen's forgeries each carry a planted error "like a taunt", a signature for checkers. SDF's typos do the reverse job (left in so nobody checks). The same device reads two ways, depending on who sees it.

First use (ch. 5). The disproof test: she drives away from the estate to "watch nothing happen," and the horn finds her within an hour. SDF already has this in The control case, so it is confirmation.

Escalation (ch. 5–6). Everyone who could rule on her sanity goes. The organization never blocks, threatens or speaks to her; it decides who stays in the room. The one possible killing can't be read (quote 6): your "a body is a fingerprint" with the print smudged.

The turn (ch. 6). "Every access route to the Tristero could be traced also back to the Inverarity estate." The findable trail becomes the evidence it was laid. She names "Those symmetrical four": the Tristero is real; she is imagining it; Pierce set it up; she is mad. The point for SDF: the old man's "we leave them findable" puts James in that room. If he believes the trail, he is counted. If he thinks it was laid for him, he doubts, and the final conversation tells you what doubt is worth to them ("we need you unsure"). The opening line works on James whichever way he reads it.

The clown. The Tristero hides among cranks (Pinguid's society, Nefastis, Inamorati Anonymous), and a crank club is its cover. The twist: the chief clown, Fallopian, gives the sanest advice in the book, the two-column gate, and she hates him for it. SDF has both halves already: Beard Man's bucket turns out right, and Frank keeps the two columns in Frank's kitchen.

Cost and payoff. The cost is people, not danger; the proof stays locked in a room with her at the end. Part Two can hold the four readings open until What was on the phone closes them.

Against A–D. A: stated by a clown and refused; the refusal drives ch. 6. It supports ADDENDUM 05's Frank as keeper. B: small, run on lies SDF can't use. C: fronts four deep (Pinguid covers W.A.S.T.E., W.A.S.T.E. covers Tristero, Tristero may be Pierce's), and still something learned, never done. ADDENDUM 05's verdict stands. D: doors open by choice (the lapel man, ch. 5; Driblette; the sailor). Confirmed.

New, checked against ADDENDUM 05's list:

  • Evidence put up for sale. The estate lists the forgeries as lot 49, so the hidden party has to come, through an agent, and pay. When his agent asks to examine the lot in advance, the house says no (ch. 6). Legal and public: the opponent surfaces because the hero followed the rules of a sale.
  • The hero as carrier. Oedipa posts a crying sailor's letter through the underground (ch. 5): a one-errand helper, out of pity, before she knows what she carries. Orwell's "homework" is the same family, but Oedipa is kind, not proud, which suits James better.
  • Duty as the engine confirms ADDENDUM 05's first change. Receiving paper grips when the job obliges looking and stopping is a breach, which is what the Orwell fix for The money gives James.

sections.title: 5. Transfer to SDF
sections.html: Already on the page, so not proposed: the clown with the sane method (Frank's kitchen; Beard Man's bucket); the disproof test (The control case); the left-in error (The sentence); the people who could confirm going quiet (The vet; Leiden, Friday). The professor's books going to the market as a whole lot is your lot 49 already (Deventer, March: "the one mistake").

items.title: 5.1 The errand that signs him in
items.html:
The drill → The sheets.

  • Change: Pieter, who doesn't go upstairs, asks James to carry the drill's sealed returns envelope to the archive desk, and Aylin chooses to buzz him through.
  • James does: he carries it out of pity for Pieter, signs for it in the big bound book on her desk, and sees the shelfmark format on her card index.
  • Cost: his name is in the visitor book in his own hand months before he asks for anything; in The sheets it shows twice (the drill; December, Pending), and Pieter has to say "I sent you up there."
  • Already on the page? No: v7 The drill has the glass door, a silent badge, Aylin's back. Already proposed? No. Eco 5.5 also uses Pieter at the drill: pick one, or the errand first and the question on the stairs. With Borges 1 the book would hold three James entries; keep two at most. It can also be the one place the format arrives (ADDENDUM 05, d).

items.title: 5.2 Every route runs home
items.html:
Twenty minutes → The other ten.

  • Change: beside each object on the tablecloth James writes who put it in his hands, and since Leave it nearly every route runs through the continuity programme or Julian.
  • James does: he says the hoax reading out loud before Ana can ("or they handed me all of it"), then goes looking for one thing that didn't come through them. That is why he searches the public records himself in The other ten, and why the widow's flask matters.
  • Cost: the widow becomes his one independent source, so he takes her husband's flask out of her house and makes her a witness. And the strongest things on the cloth are the organization's own paper, which the old man uses ("what they are in a room is nothing").
  • Already on the page? Partly: v6 Twenty minutes doubts one object ("I don't know whether that was an accident"); v7 The other ten checks records with no question it must answer. Already proposed? Partly: ADDENDUM 05's "why could I find it?" asks it of one annex. This asks it of the whole table and gives The other ten a gate. It fits King 1.

items.title: 5.3 The lot
items.html:
A Sunday market beat (in The other ten or before The band; PLACEHOLDER) → The reading room, continued.

  • Change: James asks Beard Man to put one of the professor's own books back on his stall, priced, with a card naming the house it came from. Canon gives the motive: the visitor came back for the furniture and found the books gone, and The List's method rule is "correct → ridicule → buy → vanish."
  • James does: he chooses the book and gives it up. Beard Man agrees because he enjoys the theory. A polite man pays without haggling and asks for "more from the same house." Beard Man can't give James's name, because they have never exchanged names, only "the man with the old dog."
  • Cost: the book is gone (which: PLACEHOLDER; never the first impression or the thin book), Beard Man has been seen, and Buddy has been described. In The reading room, continued it lies on the old man's tray with Beard Man's pencil price on the flyleaf: the Zapf's sticker, the readout as an object.
  • Already on the page? No. Already proposed? Not this. Eco 5.1 and Gibson 5.1 use a dealer to read out the invented title. This is the true-object version, with no lie and so no "invention that can't be taken back." Part Two has room for one dealer readout. Rule check: a legal sale, Beard Man's choice. If the title is real, it carries no edit.

items.title: 5.4 The clown's evening
items.html:
The band → The reading room, continued.

  • Change: once the accounts show which years paid for nonsense, James goes to one public event a grant paid for (a screening with Q&A, or the retreat's open evening) and asks his real question from the floor.
  • James does: he asks the question he typed and deleted in Reading with a pen. The room laughs, the speaker answers with the Sphinx, and one woman at the back doesn't laugh and writes something down.
  • Cost: he is in the event's photographs asking it, beside the tinfoil crowd. That is the organization's preferred weapon (discredit, not prevent), and it makes the old man's "in a forum by Thursday next to the bloodlines" (v7) literal. The woman becomes one of the quiet ones in The sheets (PLACEHOLDER: who).
  • Already on the page? No: v6 The band is paper at three in the morning; the retreat appears only in the forum man's monologue. Already proposed? No. ADDENDUM 05 puts Eco 5.4's negative in The band; take one, or move this after Frank, loose.

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• The open ending. The proof stays locked in a room. SDF's reveals are objects, and James publishes. Hold the four readings open in Part Two only.
  • Oedipa's methods. Small lies for reactions, and her plan to make a scene at the auction "to bring the cops into it." In SDF a person has to choose to open the door.
  • The real-world graft. An invented footnote in a real history book, and real postal history recast as a cover-up.

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
1. "If you know what this means, the note said, you know where to find out more." (ch. 5) Findable by anyone, readable by the sensitized.
  2. "Each one has an error like this, laboriously worked into the design, like a taunt." (ch. 4) The planted mistake as a signature.
  3. "Shall I project a world?" (ch. 4) She writes her own risk under the symbol.
  4. "She had only to drift tonight, at random, and watch nothing happen" (ch. 5) The disproof test, stated before it fails.
  5. "they are stripping away, one by one, my men." (ch. 6) The organization decides who stays in the room.
  6. "Changing the script had no clearer motive than his suicide." (ch. 6) A death that can't be read.
  7. "Write down what you can't deny. Your hard intelligence. But then write down what you've only speculated, assumed. See what you've got." (ch. 6) The gate, said by a clown.
  8. "Every access route to the Tristero could be traced also back to the Inverarity estate." (ch. 6) The findable trail as evidence of a hoax.

notes.title: whole novel (chapters 1–6)
notes.html:
Coverage: chapters 1–6, the whole novel (about 46,900 words), read in full, 11 Nov 2026. Edition: Perennial Fiction Library (1986, reissued 1990), converted text. The heading "4" is missing from the file; chapter 4 starts at "though she saw Mike Fallopian again".

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What she finds What it costs her Why she cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (ch. 1) To know why her dead ex-lover named her executor A codicil; a list of legal duties A sleepless night It is a legal job; Roseman adds "In what you might find out" She goes to San Narciso
2 (ch. 2) To do the job, and resist Metzger Every TV advert is "Inverarity's"; bones in cigarette filters Her marriage (Metzger) Everything she sees is an asset she must inventory She is "sensitised"
3 (ch. 3) A night out "potsmaster" on an envelope; W.A.S.T.E. and the muted horn on a latrine wall Nothing; she copies it into her memo book Writing it down is free, and now the book holds a question The Paranoids tie the lake bones to a Jacobean play
4 (ch. 3) To check the bones parallel "Trystero" spoken once; Driblette points her to "another copy" at Zapf's Metzger's scorn She asked about bones and left talking about Trystero, and wonders "how accidental it had been" The paperback, with "Cf. variant, 1687 ed."
5 (ch. 4) To bring order to the estate Koteks's doodle, the Wells Fargo marker, Mr Thoth's ring, Cohen's watermark in the estate's own stamps Koteks and Cohen back away Independent-seeming sources agree, inside what she must legally appraise Berkeley, for the source edition
6 (ch. 5) To make it go away: drift and "watch nothing happen" The hardcover lacks the line; within an hour, a horn on a lapel; then a night of horns Her self-command Her disproof test came back positive She posts the sailor's letter and follows a carrier in a circle back to Nefastis
7 (ch. 5) For Hilarius to call her mad Hilarius shooting at "Israelis"; Mucho on LSD Shrink and husband ("Cherish it!") The people who could rule her mad are mad Back south, "a fugitive"
8 (ch. 6) The truth about Trystero Driblette's suicide; the Vatican variant; the history; Zapf's, the theatre and the college all belong to the estate Every man around her; her health Four bad explanations, one test left: the hidden bidder The auction; the book ends before he is named

Why it grips

  • A duty pushes her. Oedipa never chooses to investigate. She is an executor, and the conspiracy sits inside the estate (stamp albums, theatre, bookshop). It is SDF's Part Two setup, documents arriving through a job, but the job obliges her to look, so receiving becomes compulsion.
  • The disproof test (ch. 5). She goes to San Francisco to prove nothing is there, and in an hour the horn finds her. A test meant to free her that traps her gives the night a stake that "another clue" never could.
  • Guides removed, one per chapter. Metzger elopes, Hilarius goes mad, Mucho dissolves, Driblette walks into the sea, Fallopian turns on her, the inamorato says "It's too late". Nothing blocks her; everyone who could confirm or deny goes. She says it herself: "they are stripping away, one by one, my men."
  • Comedy carries the dread. Strip Botticelli, the flying hairspray can, Mucho calling her "Edna Mosh" on air. The lore reads as more of the same high spirits rather than a pause.
  • The scene that does most: the sailor (ch. 5). A crying old man hands her a letter to post. For one errand she is a helper who knows one small task. It is the only time she touches the system from inside, and she does it out of pity, not detection.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The Tristero never blocks, threatens or speaks to Oedipa. It decides who stays in the room: everyone on the trail falls silent or leaves the book. The one possible killing is unreadable. Driblette changed the script one night and then drowned: "Changing the script had no clearer motive than his suicide." That is SDF's "a body is a fingerprint", but here no one can read the print.

All three readings stay open because each has evidence and a weak spot:

  • Real: too big and old to fake (a 1904 horn cancellation, the sailor's tattoo "in old ink", bins and carriers she follows).
  • Hoax: every route runs back to the estate (quote 4); the catalogue addendum carries a Zapf's sticker.
  • Mad: she is drunk at most finds, and admits she may not have seen it "as often as she later was to remember".

In ch. 6 she names the options herself, "Those symmetrical four", so the reader cannot settle them ahead of her. She still acts because every reading leaves a cheap physical test: Zapf's, Berkeley, following the carrier, calling Schrift, sitting in the auction room. The proof is locked in a room with her when the book ends.

Findable signs among clowns. The latrine notice, chalk marks, the laundromat card ("you know where to find out more"), the paperback: all public. The Tristero hides among cranks: Peter Pinguid, Nefastis, AC-DC, Inamorati Anonymous. That is SDF's clown beside every real question, with one twist worth copying: the chief clown, Fallopian, gives the sanest advice (quote 3), and she hates him for it.

How the lore gets in

  • Peter Pinguid (ch. 3), about 600 words, told by the narrator in a bar conversation. It ends in a spit-take and the mail call, the first sight of the system. No stall.
  • Lago di Pieta bones (ch. 3), about 650 words, on a roof. Cut short by a remark about a play and by pursuers. One piece of history passes the reader to the next.
  • The Courier's Tragedy (ch. 3), about 3,500 words, a staged play summarised for laughs. Long, but she is waiting for the bones; they pay off in Act IV, and the act ends on the one word.
  • Maxwell's Demon (chs. 3, 5), about 900 words. It ends in a test at the machine that fails, and an escape.
  • Inamorati Anonymous (ch. 5), about 1,000 words, a drunk stranger's story. Farce that ends on an object: gasoline dissolves a stamp's ink and the horn shows through the watermark.
  • Tristero origins (ch. 6), about 1,500 words, built from Blobb and others, told in Bortz's "costume dramas" voice. Here the book stalls on purpose: Oedipa has stopped checking (no follow-up with Cohen's Committee or the publisher; she refuses D'Amico). The Zapf's sticker restarts it, and Bortz turns the last document into an order: "Why don't you?"

The variant as lore. One couplet exists in four states: missing from the Folio, "lusts of Angelo" in the 1687 Quarto, a corrupt pun in "Whitechapel", and "Trystero" in a Vatican obscene version made by Puritans to damn the play. It reaches her through a pirated, unsigned, misprinted paperback from a shop the estate owns, and Driblette spoke it one night only. A variant proves someone bothered to suppress or restore a name, and who did it is never answered. This is the same shape as SDF's "given" to "arose": the cheap edition carries the edit, and the scholarly edition denies it.

Mechanism notes

  • A (gate). Fallopian states the gate (quote 3); Oedipa refusing it drives ch. 6. The ch. 5 disproof test is the stronger form: trying to rule out the bigger explanation produces evidence. Proposal (The drill or The money): James sets one test meant to clear the organisation, expecting to be wrong. The cost is that his own result is evidence he cannot unsee.
  • B (canary). Small lies as probes: "Kirby sent me" (ch. 3), "an agent of Thurn and Taxis" (ch. 5); each gets a reaction. Cohen's planted-error stamps (quote 2) are the organisation's own canaries.
  • C (front). The Pinguid Society's fake mail covers W.A.S.T.E., W.A.S.T.E. covers Tristero, Tristero may be Inverarity's front, and the estate turns out to be "America".
  • D (lock and key). Doors open by choice: the lapel man after she "told him everything", Driblette over texts, the sailor with his letter.
  • Fifth: evidence put up for sale. The estate lists the forgeries as lot 49 in a public catalogue, so the hidden party has to come in person to buy them. Legal, public, no pressure. Proposal (The other ten): something of the dead man's goes up for proper sale or donation, and the organisation has to surface to collect it.
  • Sixth: the hero as carrier. Posting the sailor's letter makes Oedipa a one-errand helper. SDF's helpers could recruit James the same way, through a request made out of pity, before he knows what he carries.

Quotes

  • "Shall I project a world?" (ch. 3): she writes her own risk under the symbol.
  • "Each one has an error like this, laboriously worked into the design, like a taunt." (ch. 4): planted mistakes as a signature for checkers.
  • "Write down what you can't deny. Your hard intelligence. But then write down what you've only speculated, assumed. See what you've got." (ch. 6): the gate, said by a clown.
  • "Every access route to the Tristero could be traced also back to the Inverarity estate." (ch. 6): the findable trail becomes evidence of a hoax.

Flags

  • The invented Tristero is grafted onto the real Thurn and Taxis and the real US postal reforms. Characters speculate that the federal government hired the 1853 marauders, and that Tristero staged the French Revolution. These are speculations about institutions, with no living person named.
  • Oedipa finds "an ambiguous footnote" in Motley's real Rise of the Dutch Republic. That is an invented claim about a real book, close to SDF's ban. Wharfinger, his editions and his publishers are invented. K. da Chingado [from memory, not from the text: Spanish slang for "screwed"].
  • Real US stamp issues appear as forgeries with altered details: forgeries of real objects, not claims that the real issues differ.

books.qa:
Answers point at the section note 01-whole-novel.md (the whole novel, ch. 1–6) and the map 00-map.md. Chapter cites follow the boundary in the map's coverage line (chapter 4 starts at "though she saw Mike Fallopian again"). Everything about SDF is a PROPOSAL; Santi's decisions are PLACEHOLDER. 12 Nov 2026.

1. Why read this book for SDF at all? Because its heroine receives evidence through a job, which is James's situation in Part Two. Oedipa is an executor, and the conspiracy sits inside the estate she must inventory. The book shows how receiving can still grip: the duty makes looking compulsory. 01 (Why it grips), map §1.

2. Does Oedipa ever choose to investigate? Not at first. The codicil and the lawyer's "In what you might find out" push her (ch. 1), and every clue is also an estate asset (stamps, theater, bookshop). Her first free choice is the San Francisco night in ch. 5, and she makes it to stop. 01 rows 1–6.

3. What is the single most useful structural move? The disproof test (ch. 5). She goes away from the estate to "watch nothing happen," and within an hour the horn finds her. A test meant to free her traps her, and that gives the night a stake another clue wouldn't. SDF already has the shape in The control case, so the map treats it as confirmation. 01 row 6, map §4.

4. Is she being played, or mad? The book never says. She names four options herself in ch. 6 ("Those symmetrical four"): real, imagined, Pierce's hoax, madness. Each has evidence and a weak spot: the horn in old ink and a 1904 cancellation (real); every route leading back to the estate (hoax); drink and her own admission that she may not have seen it "as often as she later was to remember" (mad). 01 (How the conspiracy moves the story).

5. How does she keep acting if she can't settle it? Every reading leaves a cheap physical test: Zapf's, Berkeley, following a carrier, calling Schrift, sitting in the auction room. The proof is always one errand away. For SDF that means doubt should produce an errand, never a sit-down. 01, map §4.

6. What does "we leave them findable" gain from this book? Two things. Pynchon's findable signs are public but readable only by the already sensitized (the laundromat card, quote 1). And once she sees every route leads to the estate, the findable trail itself becomes evidence of a hoax. The old man's line in The reading room (the opening) works the same way: if James believes the trail he is counted; if he suspects it was laid for him, he doubts, which is what they want. Map §4 "The turn".

7. Should James ever say the hoax reading out loud? The map proposes he does, in Twenty minutes, before Ana can: "or they handed me all of it." Then he looks for one thing that didn't come through the bank, which gives The other ten its reason. Map 5.2.

8. What does "every access route" mean concretely for SDF? Since Leave it, almost everything James holds reached him through the continuity programme or Julian: the role, the invoice, the annex, the lanyard on the sign, Julian K.'s email tip. Only a few things came another way: Els's folder, Noor, the widow's flask. Map 5.2 asks James to write that column down. PLACEHOLDER: whether the column appears on the page or only in his head.

9. How does the clown work here? The Tristero hides among cranks (Pinguid's society, Nefastis's machine, Inamorati Anonymous), and a crank society's fake mail is its cover. The chief clown, Fallopian, gives the sanest advice in the book (the two-column gate), and she hates him for it. 01 (Findable signs among clowns), map §4.

10. Is the clown-with-the-sane-method already in SDF? Yes, twice: Frank's two columns in Frank's kitchen, and Beard Man's bucket theory, which turns out right. Don't add a third. Map §5 opening.

11. Is there a way to make the clown beside the real question into something James does? The map proposes The clown's evening (5.4). After The band shows which years paid for nonsense, James attends one funded event and asks his deleted question from the floor. The room laughs, he is photographed beside the tinfoil crowd, and one woman doesn't laugh. The cost is being discredited, which is the organization's preferred weapon.

12. What is "evidence put up for sale," and is it new? New to the pipeline. The estate lists the forgeries as lot 49 in a public catalogue, so the hidden party must come through an agent and pay; when the agent asks to examine the lot in advance, the house refuses (ch. 6). It is legal and public, and it forces the opponent to surface. 01 (Mechanism notes, Fifth), map §4.

13. How would the lot work in SDF without breaking rules? James asks Beard Man to put one of the professor's books back on his stall with a card naming the house it came from. A polite buyer pays without haggling and asks for "more from the same house," and the book turns up on the old man's tray in The reading room, continued with Beard Man's pencil price inside. A legal sale, Beard Man's choice, no lie. Map 5.3; placement PLACEHOLDER.

14. Why would the organization buy rather than ignore it? Canon gives two reasons. In Deventer, March, the visitor returned for the furniture and found the books gone, which is "the one mistake," so they want the lot. And The List's method rule is "correct → ridicule → buy → vanish." Buying is their second-cheapest move. Map 5.3.

15. Doesn't 5.3 duplicate the other dealer readouts? It shares a channel with Eco 5.1 (Groningen) and Gibson 5.1 (Beard Man), which both read out the invented title from On land. 5.3 uses a true object, so there is no lie to be caught in. Part Two has room for one dealer readout; choose. Map 5.3.

16. What does Beard Man risk? He has been seen, and he can describe Buddy. He can't name James, because canon says they never exchanged names (v8 brief). That is the one canon detail the lot pays off.

17. What is "the hero as carrier"? In ch. 5 a crying sailor asks Oedipa to post a letter through the underground. For one errand she is a helper, out of pity, before she knows what she carries. It is the only time she touches the system from inside. 01 (Why it grips), map §4.

18. Where does the carrier go in SDF? The drill (map 5.1). Pieter, who doesn't go upstairs, asks James to carry the drill returns to the archive desk. Aylin chooses to buzz him through, and he signs her visitor book, so in The sheets his name is there twice. Pieter has to own "I sent you up there."

19. Does 5.1 conflict with the opening, where Aylin says "Not today, but we were expecting you"? No, it sharpens it: she has seen his face and his signature. Check that the v7 Reading room, continued line "Same time Thursday?" still reads right. PLACEHOLDER: whether the reader sees the signing in The drill or learns of it only from the book in The sheets.

20. How does 5.1 sit with Eco 5.5 and Borges 1? Eco 5.5 also uses Pieter at the drill (the "recall" question); pick one, or run the errand first and the question on the stairs. Borges 1 puts a request in James's name in the register in Part One; with both, the book holds three James entries, so keep two at most. Map 5.1.

21. What does this book say about the Part Two diagnosis (James receives paper)? That receiving isn't the problem if the job obliges him. Oedipa's duty makes stopping a breach. That supports ADDENDUM 05's first change (The money: James reconciles and signs the annex). Map §4 "Duty as the engine".

22. How does the organization act on Oedipa? It never blocks, threatens or speaks. It decides who stays in the room: Metzger elopes, Hilarius goes mad, Mucho dissolves, Driblette drowns, the inamorato says "It's too late." 01 (How the conspiracy moves the story). SDF's version is already on the page (Noor goes quiet in The vet; Leiden, Friday).

23. Is Driblette's death a model for SDF's killings? As a warning. "Changing the script had no clearer motive than his suicide": the one possible killing can't be read. SDF's bodies are meant to be fingerprints the reader can read (A pension visit, Zwolle), so take only the idea that a death can be ambiguous to James while the reader knows. 01, quote bank 6.

24. Where does the lore stall, and why? The Tristero origins in ch. 6, about 1,500 words in Bortz's costume-drama voice. It stalls on purpose: Oedipa has stopped checking. A Zapf's sticker on the catalogue addendum restarts it, and Bortz turns the last document into an order: "Why don't you?" 01 (How the lore gets in).

25. Where doesn't it stall, even though it's long? The Courier's Tragedy, about 3,500 words. She and the reader are waiting for the bones, which arrive in Act IV, and the act ends on the one word. The lesson for Leiden or The reading room, continued: a long explanation holds if the reader is waiting for one item inside it. 01, map §3.

26. What about the variant (the couplet in four states)? It is SDF's given-to-arose shape: the cheap pirated paperback carries the name, the scholarly edition lacks it, and someone bothered to suppress or restore a single word. Already on the page in The sentence, so nothing to take. 01 (The variant as lore).

27. Do the four mechanisms (A–D) hold up here? A: the gate is said by a clown and refused, which supports Frank as the keeper. B: small, and run on lies. C: fronts four deep, but learned, never done, so ADDENDUM 05's verdict stands. D: doors open by choice. Map §4.

28. Does this book help mechanism C (the front)? No more than Tier 1 did. Pinguid covers W.A.S.T.E., W.A.S.T.E. covers Tristero, Tristero may be Pierce's front, and the estate is finally "America", but Oedipa only ever learns it. Leave C to Illuminatus!. 01 (Mechanism notes).

29. Are there Pynchon-style planted errors SDF could use? Cohen's forgeries each carry an error "like a taunt," a signature meant for checkers. SDF's typos do the reverse (left in so nobody checks). Don't add taunting errors to the edits; it would break the "nobody checks" rule. The contrast is useful to know, not to copy. Map §4 "The rule".

30. Does Oedipa use small lies as probes? Can James? She does ("Kirby sent me", ch. 4; "an agent of Thurn and Taxis", ch. 5), and each gets a reaction. James can't: posing as someone is impersonation. His canary must be an invented book, as in On land, not an invented self. Map §6.

31. What in the book breaks SDF's real-world rule? An invented "ambiguous footnote" in Motley's real Rise of the Dutch Republic, the Tristero grafted onto real Thurn and Taxis and real US postal history, and real stamp issues recast as forgeries. 01 (Flags), map standing-rule note.

32. How does comedy work against the dread? The comedy carries it: Strip Botticelli, the flying hairspray can, Mucho calling her "Edna Mosh" on air. The lore reads as more of the same high spirits, not a pause. That supports SDF's "funny to the end" and Ana's put-downs in Twenty minutes. 01 (Why it grips).

33. Should SDF copy the open ending? No. The proof is locked in a room as the book ends. SDF's reveals are objects in James's hands, and James publishes. You can borrow the open question for Part Two (are the seats bait or proof?) and close it in What was on the phone. Map §6.

34. Which three proposals would I take first? 5.1 (the errand, The drill) because it is cheap and gives the visitor book a payoff. 5.3 (the lot) because it makes the organization surface by a legal act and returns as an object on the tray. 5.2 (every route runs home) because it gives The other ten a reason. 5.4 competes with Eco 5.4 for The band.

35. Which quote best states the book's method for an SDF agent? "Every access route to the Tristero could be traced also back to the Inverarity estate." (ch. 6). The findable trail turns into evidence of a hoax, which is the double edge of SDF's "we leave them findable." Map §7, quote 8.

books.author: Pérez-Reverte
books.title: The Club Dumas
books.readfor: comparing copies as a whole plot (read in the Spanish original)
books.intro: Coverage: the Spanish original, from a converted text with no edition data; chapters have titles and epigraphs but no numbers, so cites are by chapter title. Read in full through four section notes (01–04, about 113,000 words, cut by word count, not at chapter breaks), 15 Nov 2026. Anything from outside the notes is marked [from memory, not from the text]. Brief: a plot made of comparing copies of one invented book, run by a hunter with no authority. What the routine is, why the pattern needs a third copy, what each owner wants, what each look costs, how the second plot works as a front, and how the invented book is kept apart from real history. Standing-rule note: Corso hires a theft (02), gets an owner out of the room by showing her a photograph of her past (03), and beats two men (04). Real figures are made to vouch for the invented book (Bruno, Bacon, popes, Himmler's circle; 01, 03), real people sit on the club's guest list (04), and a real novel is given an invented manuscript find (04). Take the shapes, none of that.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
Lucas Corso finds rare books for clients who pay. He takes two jobs at once: checking a manuscript chapter of The Three Musketeers whose seller has just hanged himself, and comparing a collector's copy of a 1666 book of nine engravings, The Nine Doors, with the only two other copies, in Sintra and Paris. Each time he compares, the owner dies and the copy burns. People dressed as Dumas characters follow and rob him. At the end the Dumas chase turns out to be a literary society's game, unconnected, and the killer is his own client, who wanted the plates for a ritual that fails because one plate is a forgery.

What makes it work: the evidence is a table Corso rules himself, so every reveal is something the reader watched him write down. And the loud plot is the wrong one, so the reader makes the same reading error he does and is corrected with him.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:
Step What Corso wants right now What he finds What it costs Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 ("El vino de Anjou", "La mano del muerto", 01) A fee for authenticating the Dumas chapter The seller hanged a week ago; the widow denies any sale and asks who the buyer is; anonymous calls Nothing yet A paid job now has a dead seller and people asking after it He keeps it as a side errand and takes the bigger job
2 ("Gente de toga y gente de espada", 01) To be paid without becoming Borja's instrument Borja says his own copy is false, will not say how he knows, will pay anything for a true one He walks out, comes back, takes the book and dossier, leaves the check The book is in his bag and he has seen the client afraid He examines copy One
3 ("El hombre de la cicatriz", "Remember", 01) To know if One is genuine and who tried to run him down A bibliography says this copy lacks plate nine; it has it. An imprint no authority could have granted. A scarred man A crushed hand The first mismatch is on his desk and someone knows his route The binders
4 ("Sobre apócrifos e infiltrados", 02) To know whether One can be faulted His flat entered; two binders find nothing wrong and explain how a missing leaf is faked A bottle at his throat (the widow) Experts cannot fault one copy alone; any answer needs a second Sintra
5 ("El número Uno y el número Dos", 02) To set One beside Two Five plates differ, and so do the engraver's credits An afternoon with a ruined collector; he orders the copy stolen The differences are in no bibliography, and two copies cannot say which is the rule Paris, for Three
6 ("Postuma necat", 02) To get Two Fargas drowned, Two burned, its plates removed first A third of the evidence; barred from Portugal; he cannot tell whether his own order caused it Someone is destroying the set and one copy is left Paris, with the girl
7 ("El librero de la Rue Bonaparte", 02–03) To settle the Dumas pages They are genuine; the dealer watches the street Nothing The manuscript holds no puzzle, and he is still followed The baroness
8 ("El número Tres", "Los muelles del Sena", 03) To read Three against his table Three more differences; every plate that differs also differs in its credit He uses the photograph; beaten on the quay He holds the whole pattern and a man waits outside The hotel
9 ("Buckingham y Milady", "Se complica la trama", 03–04) To make La Ponte and the widow explain La Ponte told her where he was; the bag with One, the manuscript and his notes is taken; the baroness burns with Three Every copy and his own table; police in his room Only the Dumas script still points anywhere Meung
10 ("Los sótanos de Meung", "Corso y Richelieu", 04) The bag and the manuscript The bag under a bed; Balkan explains the club and says the two stories never touched A staged walk at gunpoint; he hurts the actor badly If the chase was a game, the deaths belong to someone else, and one name is left Toledo
11 ("Un recurso de novela gótica", close, 04) His pay, and who killed Borja on the floor with the plates torn from all three copies; the ritual fails The fee Nothing left to collect He leaves and works out that the ninth plate was forged

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
• Borja's library ("Gente de toga", about 2,000 words, 01): talk over objects; Corso keeps asking for proof, and it ends on his walk to the door.
  • The binders' lecture ("Sobre apócrifos", about 3,500 words, 02): how to fake a leaf, with tools, ending on a plot fact (two plates credit a second hand). It does not stall, because two chapters later Corso uses its vocabulary at a table. The method is taught before it is needed.
  • The plate list and the two comparison tables (about 800, 1,000 and 1,200 words, 01–03): his own notes. The reveal is a document he makes.
  • The baroness ("El número Tres", about 7,000 words, 03): the longest lore in the book. It holds because Corso is hiding what he sees on the page in front of him while she explains what it means.
  • Balkan's account ("Corso y Richelieu", about 5,500 words, 04): told on a walk through a castle to a man who is losing his theory as he listens.
  • Where it stalls: the Dumas bibliography ("El hombre de la cicatriz", about 900 words, 01), a screen of titles nobody in the room can lose by, and Fargas's family history (about 4,500 words, 02), which the notes call the slowest stretch. Addendum 05's rule holds: lore runs when someone present can lose by it.

sections.title: 4. Comparing copies as a plot
sections.html:
Setup. One client, one claim Corso cannot check (the copy is false), and the copy itself lent to him as a guarantee, so he carries half of every pair (01).

The routine. First, one copy against its descriptions: he listens to the paper, types the collation and one line per plate into a file, and writes the first discrepancy as a margin note (01). Then, at each owner's table, he rules a sheet into strips, one per copy, and goes page by page noting anything, however small. He records what is the same before what differs: the gatherings, where each plate sits, a shared erratum and a shared broken letter. That proves the two were printed together, so any difference left is deliberate and not wear. Only then the plates, line by line under a lens, and a list of five plain words, one per difference (02). A second strip tracks the engraver's credit on each plate, a detail the binders mentioned in passing.

Why the third. Two copies give a list. It reads as "one of these is the fake," which is what the client said. The third does three things. No plate varies the same way twice, so nobody is correcting anything. Crossing the two strips shows that every plate that differs also carries the second credit, so the differences are signed. And the count closes: eight such plates across three copies, where the book has nine (03). That missing one is the ending, and it was planted in part one as a bibliographer's error about plate nine (01, 04). Two is a difference. Three is a total you can be short on.

What each owner wants. Borja wants a man with no cause, paid in advance. Fargas will not sell and turns suspicious at the mention of money; what moves him is seeing the two copies side by side, and nothing leaves his house (02). The baroness wants a pupil and will not leave him alone with the book, and here Corso uses the photograph, the one key in the book that is a threat (03). Balkan and, at the end, Borja open their own doors because they want an audience (04). Money never opens a door in this book. A second copy does.

What each look costs. After every comparison the copy is destroyed and the owner dies, and the part that differed is taken before the fire (02, 03). So Corso's table becomes the only record of each copy, and then the table is stolen too. He also cannot rule out his own side: he ordered a theft the night Two burned (02).

The front. The Dumas plot carries everything that looks like plot: the suicide, the widow, the scarred man, the cigar ends, a note in Richelieu's hand. The real job sits in libraries. Corso joins the two himself, and Balkan's defense is that nobody ever told him they were joined (04). It meets Addendum 05's four conditions for C: he acts on the layer (he goes to Meung), it breaks on a person and an object, the club is real at its own rank, and there is a floor (the client).

Real and invented. The invented book is described by invented reference works, which can be wrong, and the first clue is that one is. It sits on tables beside real books, and the method Corso uses is a real bibliographer's (01, 02). Where it breaks your rule is in the dating: real thinkers are made to quote it (01, 03).

Against A–D. A: nearly absent. The only gate is step 4 (one copy cannot be faulted alone). B: absent. C: supported, with an addition: a front nobody built for him, a real, unrelated story with its own cause. D: supported, and it sharpens Libra's limit: a key gets Corso a look, never a copy. New mechanisms: (1) the hunter's own table as the only surviving record; (2) the cost he may have caused himself.
