The removal of only the differing part belongs under Addendum 05's "make it useless."

sections.title: 5. Transfer to SDF
sections.html:
Where you already are. The sentence is this book's routine, done well: two copies, a ruler, a finger on each line, sameness first (typos, blemish, line breaks), then the middle, then the Record with a field nothing fits. The control case buys a third copy, but of the same impression: it proves the run and adds no new kind of evidence. After that James never compares a printing again. In Part Two he compares paper about people (v7 The other ten: schedule dates against death notices; The band: accounts against years), all in the third movement. The stretch REVIEW 02 calls passive (The math to Enjoy it while it lasts) has no comparison in it at all. Checked: v8 The sentence; v6 The control case, The math, Leiden; v7 The other ten, The reading room, continued, The sheets.

Also already there, so not proposed: the front. The seats are your Dumas plot (plot-shaped, left findable, said on page three, deflated in The final conversation). In v7 The reading room, continued James spends the professor's appointment laying down six findings about the bank and none about the books, which is Corso at Meung. Leave that as it is; 5.5 uses it.

REVIEW 02 says build little. Take two of these at most. Everything is a PROPOSAL.

items.title: 5.1 The wrong key first: James offers Els money
items.html:
The math.

  • Change: Els's refusal gets a cause James supplied.
  • James does: he tells her he got her father's forty books for almost nothing and offers to pay what they were worth. To her that is the polite man with the van again. She shows him the door. The line he says on the way out (PLACEHOLDER 5) is the second key, and it has to work a week later without him.
  • Instead of pressure: he offers money, the thing Fargas refuses, and then nothing.
  • Cost: the door stays shut longer than "a week later" (REVIEW 02 5.3), and he knows he sounded like them.
  • On the page? Partly. v8.2 has the refusal ("everyone who comes about her father is polite"); in v6 he arrives with a cover story about a letter, not an offer.
  • Already proposed? No. Illuminatus! 5.1 (the neighbor) gives the refusal another cause; take one.

items.title: 5.2 The reply laid beside page three
items.html:
The math → Leiden.

  • Change: Els's folder is your binders' lecture, the other side's method on paper. James uses it once, on purpose.
  • James does: having read When a Reader Notices, he posts the dull, true page-118 question with photographs, his first real question in twelve years, to see whether the answer follows paragraph one. It does. He lays the reply beside the photocopy, finger on each line. Then he stops.
  • Instead of pressure: he risks himself, knowingly: he has read paragraphs two to four.
  • Cost: he has started the sequence that ends in The gorilla mask (the edited account is paragraph four). Noor writes to him because of that reply, so her first breach of the professor's rule is his doing, and Leiden, Friday is its bill.
  • On the page? Partly. v6 Leiden has the post and the correction, but in July, before the folder, as backstory. v8.2 has "the polite correction he received" with no cause.
  • Already proposed? No. Declare 5.1 (loud on a timer) and Eco 5.3 (a second bait) differ: this invents nothing and predicts the answer. It conflicts with "he withdraws from everyone" unless the post comes first. PLACEHOLDER.

items.title: 5.3 Look, don't copy
items.html:
Leiden → Twenty minutes.

  • Change: entry 26 becomes James's second comparison, at an owner's table, under her rule.
  • James does: he puts the thin book in Noor's gloved hands before he asks for anything. Then he asks to read the two versions of the Utrecht paper himself. She agrees on Fargas's terms: no photograph, no note, nothing leaves the kitchen. He collates them his way and goes home with no entry for the Record.
  • Instead of pressure: he shows his half of the pair first and accepts her condition.
  • Cost: in Twenty minutes it is one of the six "I don't know"s. After Leiden, Friday the pair is out of reach and his memory is the only record of it.
  • On the page? Partly. v6 Leiden: the gloves, and Noor tells him what the two versions say ("I scanned it"). He compares nothing.
  • Already proposed? No. Gibson 5.3 gives Noor a different gate; take one. Borges 4 (dropped by REVIEW 02) showed Els's papers to Noor; this shows nobody's.

items.title: 5.4 A watch on three copies
items.html:
The gorilla mask → The schedule → Twenty minutes.

  • Change: the thing he builds at four in the morning is a nightly check of public library catalogs for three first printings from the thin book (invented titles, unnamed libraries).
  • James does: he picks three and only three, because each query is a question and questions are counted. Weeks later one status changes to withdrawn for conservation. When the schedule arrives, he reads its "records moved for conservation" column against his own log. Then he switches the check off for the other two.
  • Instead of pressure: public catalogs, his own name.
  • Cost: the public has lost a copy and, like Corso after Sintra, he cannot tell whether his looking did it. Ana hears that in Twenty minutes. He is blind on the other two by choice.
  • On the page? No. The build is undescribed; the schedule's records column is in v8.2 and unused; The List's entry 17 has the phrase, dated 1994.
  • Already proposed? Partly. REVIEW 02 5.2 proposes the monitor, pointed at the eleven addresses. Borges 1 has a copy already withdrawn before he asks. One build, one feed: choose addresses or copies.

items.title: 5.5 The third copy is on the tray
items.html:
The reading room, continued.

  • Change: the 1931 ledger is read as copy Three. Two printings are a variant anyone would shrug at, as The sentence says. The struck line and the line written beside it are the order: "the yes," in a hand.
  • James does: he takes both impressions out of his bag, opens them at 118 on either side of the ledger, and collates the three, before the offer. The old man refuses every specific. The page does not.
  • Instead of pressure: nothing is asked of anyone. He brings his only first impression into their building. Reading-room rules allow pencil.
  • Cost: a transcription in his own handwriting, which is worth nothing outside the room. He has now seen it and can show no one, which is the condition the five seats are offered to. To make room, one of the six findings goes (PLACEHOLDER: which).
  • On the page? Partly. The ledger is on the tray in v8.2 and v7; James looks at it and never sets a copy beside it.
  • Already proposed? No. The request slip (Addendum 05, Rose 5.4, Libra 5.1) can stay; decide with your decision 1 what the tray shows and what the slip fetches.

Rejected: any look James gets by paying for access or by using an owner's past; any copy that burns.

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• Corso's means: the hired theft, the photograph, the fists (02, 03, 04). In SDF an owner chooses, or James goes home.
  • Real names holding up the invention: thinkers quoting the invented book, a real novel's manuscript "found," real guests at the club (01, 03, 04).
  • The body per comparison. Your organization discredits and kills rarely; a copy withdrawn or an owner made quiet does the same work.

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
1. "Investigue Las Nueve Puertas como si de un crimen se tratara." ("Gente de toga y gente de espada") Investigate The Nine Doors as if it were a crime. The book becomes the case.
  2. "En realidad no hay dos iguales, porque ya el nacimiento los distingue con detalles." ("Gente de toga y gente de espada") No two are alike; birth already marks them. A difference alone proves nothing.
  3. "El truco consiste en localizar un gemelo." ("Sobre apócrifos e infiltrados") The trick is to locate a twin. Faking and checking start from the same thing.
  4. "Página tras página, empezó a anotar cualquier diferencia entre el Uno y el Dos, por mínima que fuese" ("El número Uno y el número Dos") Page by page he noted every difference between One and Two, however small. The routine.
  5. "nadie se ocupó nunca de concretar en qué mano sostenía las llaves" ("Postuma necat") Nobody ever bothered to say which hand held the keys. The detail that differs is the one no record keeps.
  6. "Un tercio del misterio, exactamente el 33,33 por ciento -periódica pura- había volado." ("Postuma necat") A third of the mystery, exactly 33.33 percent, had gone. The cost of a look, as arithmetic.
  7. "Se llevaron los grabados. Los nueve" ("El número Tres") They took the engravings. All nine. What the other side removes is the part that differed.
  8. "Nadie le dijo en ningún momento que las cosas ocurriesen como usted creía." ("Corso y Richelieu") Nobody ever told you things happened as you believed. The front he built himself.

notes.title: part one (opening scene; "El vino de Anjou" to the start of "Remember")
notes.html:
Coverage: the unnumbered opening scene (the hanged man), then "El vino de Anjou", "La mano del muerto", "Gente de toga y gente de espada", "El hombre de la cicatriz", and "Remember" up to Corso asking Balkan about Aristide Torchia (about 28,400 words), read in full, 15 Nov 2026. Edition: converted Spanish text, chunk file 01; chapters have titles and epigraphs but no numbers.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 ("El vino de Anjou", "La mano del muerto") To authenticate a Dumas chapter for La Ponte's buyer, for a fee The seller, the publisher Taillefer, has hanged himself a week ago; his widow denies any plan to sell and asks the buyer's name; La Ponte has had two anonymous calls about the manuscript He tells La Ponte nothing about his later trouble A dead seller, a widow who delays and unexplained callers turn a fee into a case He keeps the Dumas job as a side errand and takes the bigger commission
2 ("Gente de toga y gente de espada") To be paid for checking Las Nueve Puertas without becoming Varo Borja's instrument Borja says his copy is false "con absoluta certeza", will not say how he knows, and will pay anything if another copy proves authentic He walks out, comes back, takes book and dossier but not the cheque A book in his bag that he can test, and a client's fear he has just seen He starts examining Borja's copy
3 ("El hombre de la cicatriz", "Remember") To learn whether the book is genuine and who tried to run him down Mateu's 1929 bibliography says the Coy copy lacks plate 9; Corso's copy has it. The imprint "con privilegio y licencia de los superiores" cannot name any real authority. A scarred man trails him A crushed hand, and the end of his habit of standing outside events The first mismatch is on his desk and someone knows his route He turns to Balkan and asks about Torchia

Why it grips

  • The opening scene points at the book, not the body. A policeman remarks on a page marked in red pencil; the reader's first clue is a printed page.
  • A hero who sells his time and gives nothing away. Corso invents a Swiss client to close a sale (ch. 3), waits until the widow's nails drum (ch. 2), and lies about where an old sword came from. Every scene is a bargain in which both sides hold something back, so the reader reads the gap between what is said and what is wanted.
  • The turn is built on a refusal. In "Gente de toga" Corso walks toward the door; Borja speaks after three paces and the tone changes. That is the scene that does the most work: the client's fear is the first evidence that the book matters.
  • Comedy between beats. 5,775 palindromic tram tickets, Makarova's bar and La Ponte's cowardice keep the pressure bearable.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

Nothing here is yet a conspiracy. What moves the hero is a commission with a hidden aim: Borja says his copy is false and refuses to say why, so Corso must test a claim he cannot check. The Dumas manuscript adds a dead seller and phone calls. The pursuit shows that someone else wants the book or the hero gone. It does not say who or why, and it makes the client a suspect too, since Borja promises to have an authentic copy "como sea".

How the lore gets in

  • Borja's library (ch. 3), about 2,000 words, conversation with objects. Corso holds the real copy while Borja recites the Delomelanicon, Bruno and Torchia. Corso interrupts, doubts and asks for proof, so the talk keeps moving.
  • The dossier at the terrace table (ch. 3 end), about 1,500 words, a document. It ends when a car engine sounds off stage.
  • The typed plate list (ch. 4), about 800 words, Corso's own file. Nine captions, one figure each. This is the material to compare later.
  • The Dumas bibliography (ch. 4), about 900 words. A screen of titles; the story stalls here.
  • Balkan's café talk (ch. 5), about 2,500 words, a lecture on d'Artagnan and Rochefort, ended by Corso's question about Torchia.

Mechanism notes

  • How he compares. In this part, one copy against its descriptions. He thumbs the page edges to hear the paper, looks at each plate, sets his copy beside a photocopied bibliography entry and writes "verify" in the margin. Then he types the title page, collation (160 pages, nine plates numbered 1 to VIIII, last page blank, no colophon, 299 x 215 mm) and one line per plate into a computer file. The first discrepancy is recorded as a margin note: Mateu says the Coy copy lacks plate 9; this copy has it. The odd numerals IIII and VIIII are typed in so they can be checked.
  • D (lock and key). Borja's lock is a keypad door and a vitrine key on a gold chain. His key is Corso: a man with no cause, paid in advance. Corso's counter-key is the book itself, which Borja lets him carry as "garantía", the one thing he needs to compare. The other two owners are only named (a private collection, a public foundation); Corso does not yet know what either wants.
  • C (front). The Dumas chapter and the Torchia book are set side by side from the first page: a Porthos line in a dead man's open book, then the dead seller, the widow and the phone calls on the Dumas side, the real work on the Torchia side. Corso himself calls both "puntas de iceberg" (opening of "Remember"). The Dumas strand carries the plot-like events (death, calls, widow); the real task sits in a library.
  • Who follows and why. A scarred man appears three times (Makarova's bar, a chauffeur's cap outside Liana's house, a car at the Toledo cloister wall). Corso cannot say who he is, and fits him to Rochefort, then finds the image came from a film. The false pattern is his own reading of threat through literature. First cost: a crushed hand.
  • Real and invented kept apart. The real Aldine Hypnerotomachia (1545) sits on Borja's table beside the invented book, and real figures (Bruno, Bacon, Innocent VI) date the invention. [From memory, not from the text: the Delomelanicon, Torchia, Terral-Coy and Mateu's entry are invented; Bruno's "nine secret doors" and the papyrus citations are not real.]

Quotes

  • "Investigue Las Nueve Puertas como si de un crimen se tratara." (Borja, "Gente de toga"): the book becomes a case. (Investigate The Nine Doors as if it were a crime.)
  • "En realidad no hay dos iguales, porque ya el nacimiento los distingue con detalles." (Corso, "Gente de toga"): differences are not proof of forgery. (In fact no two are alike, because birth already marks them with details.)
  • "Falto de lámina 9. Aquello era incorrecto, comprobó Corso." ("Gente de toga"): the first recorded discrepancy. (Lacking plate 9. That was wrong, Corso checked.)
  • "Con privilegio y licencia de los superiores. Aquello era imposible." ("El hombre de la cicatriz"): a detail in the copy that does not fit history. (With the privilege and licence of the superiors. That was impossible.)

Flags

  • The invented book is given false support from real figures: Bruno is made to quote it, Bacon and Innocent VI are tied to it, and real texts (Corpus Hermeticum, papyri) are cited. SDF must not do this; its invented edits sit in invented printings only.
  • Real names appear as texture (Dumas, Maquet, Courtilz). No real person is complicit.

notes.title: part two (end of "Remember" to the opening of "El librero de la Rue Bonaparte")
notes.html:
Coverage: the rest of "Remember" (Balkan's café talk, the searched flat), "Sobre apócrifos e infiltrados", "El número Uno y el número Dos", "Postuma necat", and the start of "El librero de la Rue Bonaparte" up to Corso and the girl walking to Replinger's shop (about 28,400 words), read in full, 15 Nov 2026. Edition: converted Spanish text, chunk file 02; chapters have titles but no numbers.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (end of "Remember"; "Sobre apócrifos e infiltrados") To know whether his copy of the book can be faked, and whether the Dumas pages belong to the same story His flat was entered (the computer shows use at 19.35 while he was at the café); a Montecristo cigar butt is left on his table and another in La Ponte's bed; two bookbinders judge his copy genuine and explain how a missing leaf is faked; Liana comes for the manuscript A slap and a broken bottle at his throat The experts cannot find a fault in his copy, so any answer must come from a second copy He leaves for Sintra
2 ("El número Uno y el número Dos") To compare Borja's copy with Fargas's Five of nine plates differ, and the engraver credit on one plate differs A long scene with a ruined collector; Borja's nod to a theft The differences are in no bibliography He must see copy Three in Paris
3 ("Postuma necat"; start of "El librero...") To keep copy Two without trouble, then to learn who is ahead of him Fargas drowned; copy Two burned in the grate; the girl "Irene Adler" knew before he did A third of the evidence; Pinto tells him not to return to Portugal; he takes fragments and cigarette ends from a death scene Only Three is left, and someone is destroying the set Paris, Replinger's shop, the girl at his side

Why it grips

  • The method comes before its use. The Ceniza brothers lecture on how a missing leaf is faked, step by step, with the tools. Two chapters later Corso uses their vocabulary ("gemelos", worn type) at a table. The lecture is paid off in a scene.
  • The discovery is a seven-errors puzzle. Corso sets two plates side by side and feels "infantil", as when he played at spotting seven errors. The answer comes in a sentence ("Entonces lo vio"), then the detail (a hand), then a pause at the window.
  • Pressure follows the puzzle at once. A tail on the road, then a death and a fire, come right after the table.
  • Comedy with a body count. Pinto's measles-stricken children and La Ponte's betrayals keep the book light while a man dies.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The pursuers do not stop Corso; they leave signs and remove evidence. The cigar butt in two flats is a literary signature. The cost lands on others: Fargas dies, copy Two burns, La Ponte gets silent night calls, Liana's anger ends in violence. The girl who shadows him never says who sends her; she says only that she looks after him. Corso's own order to Pinto to steal copy Two means he cannot be sure whether the fire came from his side. So the hidden side moves him by clearing the field, not by threatening him.

How the lore gets in

  • The Ceniza lecture (about 3,500 words, a conversation). It ends on a plot fact: seven plates credit A. TORCH. as inventor and engraver, two only as engraver, with the inventor given as "L. F.". Plot inside a trade lecture, so no stall.
  • Fargas's monologue (about 4,500 words, a scene). The family's collapse and his ritual of selling one book at a time. The cognac, the violin and the painted Abraham keep it a scene, but it is the slowest stretch.
  • The comparison table (about 1,000 words, Corso's own notes). The reveal comes from a document he makes, not one he is handed.
  • The burned book (about 800 words, a physical scene). He works out from the ash how long it burned; again an object gives the news.

Mechanism notes

  • How he compares. He brings his copy (Uno) to the other (Dos), is lent a side room, and rules three strips on a sheet, each headed by a number and a name. Page by page he notes any difference, then checks each plate line by line with a 7x lens. He records: gatherings (twenty of eight), plate positions identical (I between pp. 16 and 17, through IX between 144 and 145), the same erratum on p. 72 and the same broken s on p. 87. That means the pair was printed at once under one press, "gemelos" in the Cenizas' word. Then the five differences: the hermit's keys in the left hand or the right (plate II), a labyrinth with or without an exit (III), the hourglass empty above or full above (V), chess squares white or black (VII), a halo on the executioner or none (VIII). He also records the engraver marks. Later he sets them out as a collation table and a list of five words (hand, exit, sand, board, aura). He reads the pattern as a plan by the printer, not as a fake.
  • D (lock and key). Fargas will not sell: he sells one book to one buyer, a "compatriota", twice a year. His lock is a ritual. Corso's key is shared recognition (a toast, "hermano de culto"), and only the pair on the table moves him: seeing both copies together excites him, so he lets Corso study them. Nothing leaves the house. When Corso offers money from Borja, Fargas becomes suspicious and the offer is dropped. This owner wanted a witness to a rare event, not money.
  • C (front). The Dumas strand supplies the danger: Liana's attack, the cigar butts, the calls. Corso reads each as a Dumas scene (Milady, Rochefort, Montecristo). The Ceniza lecture and the plate table point the other way: the puzzle is in the book. The Dumas strand keeps drawing attention to people, the book to the copies.
  • Who follows and why. The scarred man with the Montecristo cigar reappears on the Sintra road and asks for a light. The girl is new: she walks into the train and the hotel, and she is in Fargas's garden before Corso. Neither says why.
  • What each discovery costs. The comparison costs Fargas his life, or at least coincides with it. Corso loses copy Two. His table is now the only record of copy Two.
  • Real and invented kept apart. Fargas's shelves hold real books (Vasari, Agricola, Kircher); only the Torchia copies are invented. Corso borrows a real method, Eco's collation tables on the Hanau Pantheon [from memory, not from the text: Eco's Hanau study is real].

Quotes

  • "El truco consiste en localizar un gemelo." (Pedro Ceniza, "Sobre apócrifos e infiltrados"): faking and comparing both start from a second copy. (The trick is to locate a twin.)
  • "Página tras página, empezó a anotar cualquier diferencia entre el Uno y el Dos, por mínima que fuese" ("El número Uno y el número Dos"): comparison as routine. (Page by page, he noted every difference between One and Two, however small.)
  • "nadie se ocupó nunca de concretar en qué mano sostenía las llaves" ("Postuma necat"): bibliographies never recorded the detail that differs. (nobody ever bothered to say in which hand he held the keys)
  • "Un tercio del misterio, exactamente el 33,33 por ciento -periódica pura- había volado." ("Postuma necat"): the cost of the discovery. (A third of the mystery, exactly 33.33 percent, had gone.)

Flags

  • Real figures appear only as references (Dumas, Eco, Doyle's characters). No real person is complicit.
  • The hero orders a theft (Corso to Pinto, "Postuma necat"). SDF's hero cannot hire crime or break in.

notes.title: part three (Replinger's shop to the taxi after the Crillon)
notes.html:
Coverage: the rest of "El librero de la Rue Bonaparte" (Replinger authenticates the manuscript), "El número Tres", "Los muelles del Sena", "Buckingham y Milady", and the start of "Se complica la trama" up to the taxi ride back to Ungern's foundation (about 28,400 words), read in full, 15 Nov 2026. Edition: converted Spanish text, chunk file 03; chapters have titles but no numbers.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (end of "El librero..."; "El número Tres") To have the Dumas pages checked and to reach copy Three Replinger confirms the manuscript from his own files (blue paper from Lille, Maquet's white sheets) but looks nervously at the street; the concierge gets a name for the girl ("Irene Adler", 221b); Liana and La Ponte are seen in a Paris taxi Nothing physical The Dumas question is settled and the chase still unexplained He visits the Ungern foundation
2 ("El número Tres"; "Los muelles del Sena") To read copy Three beside what he knows of One and Two Baroness Ungern owns it and explains the plates; copy Three differs on plates I, III and VI; the plate differences line up with the engraver credits He has to show her a Nazi-era photograph to get her out of the room He now holds the whole pattern, and a man waits outside Beaten on the river steps, rescued, ends the night with Irene
3 ("Buckingham y Milady"; "Se complica la trama") To make La Ponte and Liana explain themselves La Ponte has slept with Liana and told her where Corso was; Liana was waiting for Rochefort A second blow; the bag with copy One, the manuscript and his notes is gone Only copy Three is left Back to Ungern's, with La Ponte

Why it grips

  • One more copy, and the differences turn into a scheme. Two copies gave five differences; a third gives three more, and no plate varies the same way twice. The reader gets "a pattern with a purpose" in one paragraph ("Los muelles del Sena").
  • A task and a chase alternate. In the library Corso studies, bluffs and hides what he sees; outside, a BMW waits. Each scene sets what he knows against what he must conceal.
  • The scene that does the most work is the plate-by-plate reading with the baroness. She gives a confident symbolic reading of each plate; at each one Corso silently checks a physical difference on the copy in front of him. The narration lets the reader see both readings at once.
  • Humiliation carries the pace. A failed night with Irene, a nosebleed, the punch to La Ponte, and La Ponte's defence that all he did was go to bed with her.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The hidden side now acts openly, but through a theatre of literature. Rochefort attacks twice, each time with a punch behind the right ear. Liana plays Milady, and a note in Richelieu's hand is left under a cigar butt. Each blow takes something: the first nearly took the bag, the second takes it. The staging keeps Corso reading people instead of copies. The cost to him is steady: bruises, the lost bag, and the end of the idea that La Ponte is an ally. The plate pattern, the thing that matters, stays in his head.

How the lore gets in

  • Replinger (about 2,500 words, conversation). He authenticates by a trade method: a filed sample of the same hand and paper. The one useful fact is the paper's colour. It slows the story on purpose.
  • Ungern's talk (about 7,000 words, interview with objects). Demonology, Torchia's years in Prague, the plate captions and a hidden-verse card. It stays alive because Corso hides what he sees, and it ends in a trade (the photograph).
  • Corso's table (about 1,200 words, his own notes). The reveal (8 differences, 19 plates altered, 8 by "L. F.") comes as his own conclusion over a drink in a bar, then he doubts it.

Mechanism notes

  • How he compares. In the baroness's library he lays copy Three on the table and reads it plate by plate while she talks: three towers on the city instead of four (I), an arrow in the archer's quiver where the others are empty (III), the hanged man hung by the right foot instead of the left (VI). Left alone he fills in "los cuadros comparativos iniciados con el número Uno", and adds a second table for the engraver marks A.T. and L.F. Crossing the two tables he finds that every plate that differs also differs in its inventor credit: of 27 plates, 19 are credited to the printer as designer and 8 to L.F. (two in One, three in Two, three in Three). He concludes the printer did not forge; he scattered one book across three. He had also matched 16 fragments of burnt copy Two to pages of One, and found that every recovered fragment is text, none a plate or the title page: the part that differed was taken before the fire.
  • D (lock and key). The baroness lets him in on the strength of a phone call, then treats him like a promising pupil. She will not leave him alone with the book. Her key is her past: Corso's counter-key is a 1943 German magazine page showing her as an astrologer's assistant beside Himmler. He gives it to her, and she tears it up. This is blackmail, the one place in the book where a key is a threat. Replinger's lock is only mistrust; Corso offers to pay costs and gets his answer.
  • C (front). Replinger shows the Dumas pages are genuine, so the manuscript is no puzzle. The pursuers still use the Dumas script (Liana as Milady, the Richelieu safe-conduct, Montecristo cigars). Corso reads it as a staged plot, too elaborate to be a joke. A second front sits inside the book: Ungern says the plates are a formula for summoning the devil, and also that the book is false.
  • Who follows and why. Rochefort waits outside the foundation, jumps Corso on the Quai steps, takes the bag at the Crillon. Irene follows, kicks Rochefort, and sleeps with him. Neither says why. La Ponte says Liana knew Rochefort and let him in.
  • What each discovery costs. The plate pattern costs him the bag and notes; the loss of Two's plates shows the other side wants the differences gone, not the books.
  • Real and invented kept apart. Ungern backs the invented book with real figures (Bacon, Dee, Bruno, popes, an astrology circle round Himmler). [From memory, not from the text: the Delomelanicon, Torchia and Ungern are invented; Cazotte's Le Diable amoureux is real.]

Quotes

  • "Aristide Torchia había confesado la verdad a sus verdugos; pero no completa." ("Los muelles del Sena"): the printer's confession read as the sum of three copies. (Aristide Torchia had told his executioners the truth, but not all of it.)
  • "Se llevaron los grabados. Los nueve" ("El número Tres"): the theft shows what the other side wants gone. (They took the engravings. All nine.)
  • "Trabajo mejor a solas." ("Los muelles del Sena"): the request the owner will not grant without a lever. (I work better alone.)
  • "Es por orden mía y para bien del Estado por lo que el portador de la presente hizo lo que hizo." ("Se complica la trama"): the staged literary front. (It is by my order and for the good of the State that the bearer did what he did.)

Flags

  • Corso gets the baroness's consent by showing her a photograph that exposes her past. SDF's hero cannot threaten or pressure.
  • Real persons support an invented book: Himmler's circle, popes, Bruno, Bacon, Cazotte, Nerval linked to the book's provenance. SDF must not do this.

notes.title: part four (end of "Se complica la trama" to the close)
notes.html:
Coverage: the rest of "Se complica la trama" (the burned flat, the police, the girl's hint), "Los sótanos de Meung", "Corso y Richelieu", "Un recurso de novela gótica", and the dated close (about 28,200 words), read in full, 15 Nov 2026. Edition: converted Spanish text, chunk file 04; chapters have titles but no numbers.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (end of "Se complica la trama") To reach copy Three before the others The baroness's flat burned at 3 a.m. with her in it; copy Three is gone; police are in his hotel room; the girl tells him to reread chapter one, line one of the Dumas novel The last copy; his hotel; La Ponte, who is dragged along Only the Dumas script still points anywhere Meung-sur-Loire, on the night before the first Monday of April
2 ("Los sótanos de Meung"; "Corso y Richelieu") To catch Liana and Rochefort and get the manuscript and his bag back Under the bed he finds his bag with the Toledo copy; Balkan, in a cardinal's red jacket, explains the Club Dumas and the whole Dumas strand A staged gunpoint walk through a castle cellar; he hurts Rochefort badly Balkan says the two stories are unconnected, and Corso cannot accept that He drives to Toledo with the girl
3 ("Un recurso de novela gótica"; close) To be paid, and to know who killed Fargas and Ungern Varo Borja is conducting a ritual with the plates torn out of every copy; Corso burns plate I and breaks the mirror; Borja screams No pay, no cheque book in the house The contract is the only thing left to collect He leaves; reads the forged plate as the flaw

Why it grips

  • The reversal is a reading error. Corso confronts the "mastermind" in a castle and learns that half his theory (Rochefort, Milady, Richelieu) was a game played at him. In "Corso y Richelieu" the villain says he never lied; Corso filled in the gaps. The reader has done the same for three parts.
  • The second reversal is the real culprit, a client. Borja turns up for the last scene, undramatic: the door opens on the fifth knock, he is unshaven and wants to be left alone. The scene that does the most work is the ritual room, where every plate difference from parts 2 and 3 lies on the floor, so the reader sees the comparison material used for the opposite purpose.
  • The ending turns on one detail from the first part. Plate IX was the only plate identical in all three copies, and Mateu had claimed one copy lacked it. Corso's last thought, "Ceniza sculpsit", pays off both.
  • Comedy to the end. La Ponte bangs his head on the window and Corso asks whether there is any gin.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The conspiracy is sorted into two plots. The Dumas plot is a society, a game and a feud that Balkan ran for fun and spite; its cost was a hanged man and some bruises. The Torchia plot is one rich collector with a ritual, and its cost was two murders and Corso's use as scapegoat (Corso works out that Borja hired him to confirm the three-copy theory and to carry the police attention). Because the Dumas plot was a false pattern, it sat in front of the real one and ate Corso's attention. The reveal costs Corso his client, his pay and the idea of himself as a reader who got it right.

How the lore gets in

  • Balkan's exposition (about 5,500 words, a walk and a terrace talk). The Club Dumas has 67 members, each holding one chapter of the manuscript as a share, voted in by a board Balkan chairs. Taillefer broke the rule by selling chapter 42; Liana holds chapter 37. It is delivered mid-action (a lit corridor, a drinks table), then Corso's counter-account takes one paragraph.
  • Borja's ritual (about 4,500 words, a scene). Magic square, nine plates, nine words, drugged drink. The lore is done with props and with Corso's refusal ("quiero mi dinero"), so it never stalls.
  • The car conversation with Irene (about 2,500 words). She explains that she is the devil (a fallen angel, alone). Slow, but it carries the book's emotional close.

Mechanism notes

  • How the copies are finally used. Borja has torn the plates from the copies of Fargas and Ungern and from his own, and sets plates on the floor in a pattern. Corso sees them there: plate VI with the hanged man by the right foot, two plates VII (white board and black board), plate I with three towers. He reads the nine words Borja wrote on the back of plate I, then burns that plate and breaks the mirror. So the differences recorded across three copies were not for authentication; they were the inputs to a procedure, and the proof of that is physical.
  • The last comparison. Corso concludes the final plate is a forgery by the Ceniza brothers, made to fill the missing plate Mateu mentions. That is why Borja's sums fail. It is a result reached by thinking back over the table, not by new inspection.
  • D (lock and key). Borja's door has no lock to defeat: it opens after the bell and two knocks, and Borja lets Corso in because he brings the book. Corso refuses to step into the circle until the end. Balkan's door (the castle) opens because he wants an audience.
  • C (front). The strongest case in the book. Balkan's Club Dumas supplied the cigars, the safe-conduct note in Richelieu's hand (Balkan wrote it) and the quotation game. Balkan insists he told no lies and Corso built the false plot himself. The reader sees a pattern that invites reading while the real crime sits behind it.
  • Who follows and why. Rochefort (an actor called Laszlo Nicolavic) and Liana wanted the chapter back for the club; Irene guards the book; Borja, the one who kills, never follows. Corso concludes there are two "authors".
  • What each discovery costs. Learning the real culprit costs him the fee. Every earlier discovery cost another person: the plate differences cost Fargas and Ungern their lives.
  • Real and invented kept apart. Balkan claims to have bought the whole real manuscript of Les Trois Mousquetaires from Le Siècle's papers [from memory, not from the text: no such manuscript is known]. Its provenance is invented around a real book and real people (Maquet, Baudry).

Quotes

  • "Esta historia tiene dos autores" (Corso, "Corso y Richelieu"): the front is named. (This story has two authors.)
  • "Nadie le dijo en ningún momento que las cosas ocurriesen como usted creía." (Balkan, "Corso y Richelieu"): the front was left for him to fill. (Nobody ever told you things happened as you believed.)
  • "Alquilé sus servicios sin confiarle mis razones, ni mis planes" (Borja, "Un recurso de novela gótica"): the client hired him blind. (I hired your services without telling you my reasons or my plans.)
  • "en los tres ejemplares, la última lámina era falsa. Ceniza sculpsit." (close): the comparison's real result. (in all three copies, the last plate was false. Ceniza engraved it.)

Flags

  • Real figures in the Club Dumas guest list: the Duchess of Alba, a Spanish Interior Minister, a former Argentine president, the Moroccan crown prince, a Nobel winner. SDF must not name real people at a real conspiracy table.
  • Balkan's claim to have found the real Dumas manuscript is an invented provenance for a real book. SDF must not invent a find for a real book.
  • Corso beats Rochefort down a stair and Borja; SDF's hero cannot use force or pressure.

books.qa:
Answers point to the section notes in this folder (01-part-one.md to 04-part-four.md) and, where relevant, to a v8.2 chapter by title. The map is 00-map.md. The novel's chapters have titles and no numbers. Everything about SDF here is a PROPOSAL; Santi's decisions are PLACEHOLDER.

The comparison

1. What exactly does Corso do when he compares two copies? He brings his copy to the other one and is lent a side room. He rules a sheet into strips, one per copy, and goes page by page writing down anything that differs. He checks the plates last, line by line, with a lens, and ends with a collation table and a list of five plain words, one per difference (02-part-two.md, "El número Uno y el número Dos"). The reveal is a sentence in his own notes, not something an expert tells him.

2. What does he record before he looks for differences? What is the same: the number of gatherings, the position of every plate, one erratum and one broken letter that both copies share (02-part-two.md). That proves the copies came off one press together. Without it a difference could be wear, a repair or a later state. The sentence already does this (same typos, same blemish on 118, same line breaks) before it shows the changed middle.

3. What does he do with one copy before he has a second? He checks it against its descriptions. He types the title page, the collation and one line per plate into a file, sets the book beside a photocopied bibliography entry, and writes the first mismatch in the margin: the bibliography says this copy lacks plate nine and it has it (01-part-one.md). So the first clue is a disagreement between a book and a record of it.

4. Why does the pattern need a third copy? Two copies give five differences, which can be read as "one of these is a fake," the client's own claim. The third adds three more, and no plate varies the same way twice, so nothing is being corrected. Crossing the differences with the engraver's credits shows every differing plate carries the second credit, and the total comes to eight across three copies where the book has nine plates (03-part-three.md). Two gives a list; three gives a rule and a count.

5. Where was the crossing detail planted? At the end of the binders' lecture, as a trade remark: seven plates credit the printer as designer and two credit someone else (02-part-two.md, "Sobre apócrifos e infiltrados"). It reads as texture until Corso gives it its own table in Paris. A detail noted before anyone knows it matters is the cheapest way to make a later crossing feel fair.

6. How is the last twist prepared? In part one a bibliography claims one copy lacks plate nine (01-part-one.md). In part four plate nine is the only plate identical in all three copies, and Corso concludes it is a modern forgery by the binders who taught him the method (04-part-four.md). He reaches it by thinking back over his table, with no new inspection. See question 31 for a wrinkle in the notes.

7. Does Corso ever get a comparison wrong? Not on the plates. His errors are about people: he fits the scarred man to a Dumas character and later finds the image came from a film (01-part-one.md), and he joins the two plots (04-part-four.md). The book keeps the bench work reliable and puts all the error in the reading of motives. SDF does the same: James is right about page 118 and wrong about what the seats are for.

8. How long are the comparison passages, and do they stall? About 1,000 words for the first table and 1,200 for the second (02-part-two.md, 03-part-three.md). They hold because pressure follows at once: a tail on the road and a death after the first, a beating on the quay after the second. In SDF terms: a table scene is safe if the next page costs something.

The owners

9. What does each owner want before Corso may look? Borja wants an agent with no cause of his own, paid in advance (01-part-one.md). Fargas wants a fellow believer and a witness to the two copies lying together; he will not sell and nothing leaves his house (02-part-two.md). The Paris dealer wants his costs paid; the baroness wants a pupil and will not leave him alone with the book (03-part-three.md). Balkan and, at the end, Borja want an audience (04-part-four.md).

10. What actually opens a door in this book? Carrying the other copy. Fargas is moved by seeing the pair, and Borja lets Corso in at the end because he brings the book (02-part-two.md, 04-part-four.md). Money does the opposite: when Corso mentions the client's money Fargas turns suspicious and the offer is dropped. Map proposal 5.1 uses that for Els in The math.

11. Which of Corso's ways in can James not use? The hired theft of copy Two (02-part-two.md), the 1943 photograph he shows the baroness to get her out of the room (03-part-three.md), and force (04-part-four.md). The invented Swiss client he uses to close a sale (01-part-one.md) is a lie for gain and is out too. Each map proposal says what James offers or risks instead: money that is refused, a question asked where it is counted, his half of the pair shown first, public catalogs, his only first impression carried into their building.

12. Does a key ever get Corso the copy itself? No. Every key gets him a look. Fargas lets him study and keeps the book; the baroness lets him read under her eye. This agrees with the limit Addendum 05 takes from Libra: a key opens talk, it does not decide for the owner.

13. Who in SDF is an owner in this sense? Els (the folder), Noor (the two versions of the Utrecht paper, v6 Leiden), the Groningen dealer (his ledger and the receipt), the widow in Zwolle (the flask), Aylin (the visitor book), and the old man (the 1931 ledger on the tray). All but one already choose to show James something. The gap is that James rarely collates what he is shown with his own hands; see map 5.3 and 5.5.

What a look costs

14. What does each comparison cost? The owner and the copy. Fargas drowns and copy Two burns the night after the Sintra table (02-part-two.md); the baroness burns with copy Three (04-part-four.md). Corso himself pays in bruises, a ban from Portugal, the bag with copy One and his notes (03-part-three.md), and finally the fee (04-part-four.md).

15. What is removed, the books or the differences? The differences. Every fragment Corso recovers from the grate is text; the plates and the title page were taken before the fire (03-part-three.md). The other side has no interest in the copies as copies. Addendum 05 already has "make it useless, don't take it"; this is the same idea aimed at the one part that matters.

16. What happens to Corso's table? After Sintra it is the only record of copy Two. In Paris the bag with his notes is stolen, and the pattern survives only in his head (03-part-three.md). SDF has the same shape in The vet (the thin book gone) and Twenty minutes ("photographs where the thin book should be"). Map 5.3 and 5.5 add looks that leave James with nothing he can show.

17. Can Corso tell whether he caused a loss himself? No. He had told a Portuguese contact to steal copy Two, so when it burns he cannot be sure the fire did not come from his side (02-part-two.md, "Postuma necat"). SDF cannot use the theft. Map 5.4 gets the same doubt lawfully: a catalog status changes after James starts watching it, and he cannot rule himself out.

18. How does SDF's version of the cost stay inside "kills rarely"? By using the organization's own paperwork. v8.2's schedule already has a column for records "moved for conservation" beside the visits, and Leiden, Friday already shows an owner made quiet with a clipboard. A withdrawn copy or a quiet owner removes evidence as completely as a fire. REVIEW 02 5.1 notes the plan already has two acts that cost someone (The schedule, The vet).

The front

19. How does the Dumas plot work as a front? It carries every event that looks like plot: a hanged man, a widow, anonymous calls, a pursuer, cigar ends left in two flats, a note in a cardinal's hand (01-part-one.md to 03-part-three.md). The real task happens at tables. Corso reads each event through a Dumas character, which keeps him looking at people while the answer is in the copies.

20. Who built the front? Nobody built it for him. The club is a real society with a real feud over a sold chapter, and Balkan insists no one ever said the two stories were connected; Corso filled the gap (04-part-four.md, "Corso y Richelieu"). That is the map's one addition to mechanism C: a front that is an unrelated true story.

21. Does it meet Addendum 05's four conditions for C? Yes. Corso acts on the layer as if it were the bottom (he goes to Meung). It breaks from outside him, on a person explaining and on his bag under a bed. The club is true at its own rank. There is a floor: the client, undramatic, opening his door on the fifth knock (04-part-four.md).

22. Does SDF already have this? Yes, and the map proposes no new front. The seats are plot-shaped, left findable, announced on page three and deflated in The final conversation ("the bunkers are fuel"). In v7 The reading room, continued James lays six findings about the bank in front of the old man and none about the books, on the day the professor's book list sent him there. Map 5.5 has him put his two printings beside the ledger in that scene.

23. Is there a second front inside the main plot? A small one. The baroness gives a confident symbolic reading of each plate while Corso silently checks a physical difference on the same plate (03-part-three.md). The meaning of the pictures sits in front of the fact that they differ. For SDF: the old man talking about method while a struck line lies on the tray.

Lore

24. Which long lore scene works best and why? The baroness, about 7,000 words (03-part-three.md, "El número Tres"). Corso is hiding what he sees on the page while she lectures, he needs her out of the room, and a man waits in the street. Compare the Dumas bibliography in part one, about 900 words of titles with nobody at risk (01-part-one.md), which stalls.

25. How does the book teach a method without stalling? It gives the lecture to tradesmen with tools on the bench and ends it on a plot fact, then has the hero use the vocabulary two chapters later (02-part-two.md). Els's folder in The math is SDF's version: the other side's method on three photocopied pages. Map 5.2 has James use it once, on purpose, in the same chapter.

26. How is the final explanation delivered? Twice, by two different people. Balkan's is a walk and a terrace talk of about 5,500 words; Borja's is a ritual with props, about 4,500 words, during which Corso keeps asking for his money (04-part-four.md). The first is an explanation that removes a theory, the second a scene. SDF's The final conversation is closer to Balkan's; the v8 brief's rule that a speech over about 150 words gets broken applies.

Real and invented

27. How is the invented book kept apart from real history? It has invented reference works that describe it (a 1929 bibliography, a dossier), and those can be wrong. It sits on tables and shelves beside real books, which stay unaltered (01-part-one.md, 02-part-two.md). The method Corso borrows is credited to a real bibliographer [from memory, not from the text: the study he cites is real].

28. Where does it break SDF's rule? Real thinkers are made to quote or own the invented book, and real papyri are cited for it (01-part-one.md, 03-part-three.md). Balkan claims to hold the real manuscript of a real novel, with an invented provenance (04-part-four.md). Real people are listed as club members (04-part-four.md). SDF's rule: invented edits live in invented printings; real works appear only as the old man's claims.

29. Is there a safe version of "a detail that does not fit history"? Yes: put the impossible detail inside the invented object. The imprint on the invented book names an authority that could not have licensed it (01-part-one.md). SDF already does this with the second impression that still says "first edition" and kept its typos (The sentence).

The notes

30. Do the notes disagree about the plate numbers? Yes. 02-part-two.md gives the labyrinth as plate III; 03-part-three.md gives plate III as an archer and says copy Three differs on I, III and VI, while also saying no plate varies the same way twice. Both cannot be right. [From memory, not from the text: the labyrinth is the fourth plate, which removes the clash.] The map avoids plate numbers for that reason.

31. Do the notes disagree about the count and the forged plate? Partly. 03-part-three.md says in one place "19 plates altered, 8 by L.F." and in another that 19 of 27 plates credit the printer and 8 credit L.F.; the second is the consistent one (two, three and three across the copies). 04-part-four.md says the forgery fills the plate one copy lacked, but its verified quote says the last plate was false in all three copies. Check the text before building on which copies carried the forgery.

Transfer

32. What does SDF already do with comparing copies? The sentence is the full routine on two impressions. The control case adds a third copy of the same impression (proving the whole run) and nine controls that show nothing. The thin book is forty-one comparisons done by other hands. In v7 The other ten and The band James compares documents about people and money. Between The control case and The reading room, continued he never sets one printing beside another.

33. Does the third copy in The control case do what Corso's third copy does? No. It is a second copy of the second impression, so it confirms and adds no new kind of evidence. The thing in SDF that plays copy Three is the 1931 ledger with the struck line: two printings are a variant, the ledger is the order. It is on the tray in the opening and in The reading room, continued, and no draft has James read it against his copies. Map 5.5.

34. Which proposals sit in the stretch REVIEW 02 calls passive? 5.1 and 5.2, both in The math. 5.1 makes Els's refusal the result of James offering money. 5.2 has him post the true page-118 question after reading When a Reader Notices and lay the courteous reply beside the photocopy. Take one if The math is already too long; 5.2 is the one with a price.

35. Does anything here answer REVIEW 02 finding 5.2 (James never uses his trade)? 5.4. The four-in-the-morning build in The gorilla mask becomes a nightly check of public catalogs for three first printings, and The schedule's "records moved for conservation" column is read against his own log. REVIEW 02 already proposes the monitor for the eleven addresses; this is the same build with a different feed, so choose one.

36. Does any proposal add another signature to the organization's paper? No. REVIEW 02 2.1 says keep two (the annex, the request slip). 5.5 costs James a pencil transcription in his own hand and nothing in their register. 5.2 adds a counted question, which the plan's machine already does to anyone who asks.

37. Which proposals collide with others already on the table? 5.1 with Illuminatus! 5.1 (both give Els's refusal a cause). 5.3 with Gibson 5.3 (both put a condition on Noor's kitchen). 5.4 with REVIEW 02 5.2 and Borges 1 (a monitor; a withdrawn copy). 5.2 needs the order in The math settled against "he withdraws from everyone." 5.5 has to be decided with Santi's decision 1 and the request slip.

38. Does this book change Addendum 05's open question on Borges's checks? It supports Borges 5 (a fossil in the apparatus) in principle, because Corso proves twinship from shared flaws before he trusts a difference. It offers an alternative to Borges 1: a copy that vanishes after the look is more plot than a copy already missing. It gives no support to adding visitor-book entries.

39. What should an agent not import by accident? A death per comparison, a hero who lies to close a deal, and real names vouching for the invention (map section 6). Also the supernatural floor: the girl who says she is a fallen angel (04-part-four.md) closes the book's emotion and is not part of the mechanism.

books.author: Shea & Wilson
books.title: Illuminatus!
books.readfor: C: the front; comedy under escalation
books.intro: Coverage: the English text of the trilogy in one volume (converted HTML; no edition data in the files). Read in full through nine section notes (01–09, about 283,000 words, appendices included), 12 Nov 2026. Cited as "Trip N" or by appendix. Anything from outside the notes is marked [from memory, not from the text]. Brief: mechanism C, the front: each solved layer is cover for the next. This is the deciding book for C, which ADDENDUM 05 ruled out as a Part Two engine and as something James does (since qualified by the Name of the Rose, Libra and Declare maps). Also: how the comedy survives escalation, how the reader stays oriented, and the "diagnosis." Standing-rule note (strict): real people and organizations are named as complicit on almost every page (Oswald, Hunt, Hoover, Nixon, FDR, Hitler, Rothschild, Hegel, Washington, the Federal Reserve, the Pentagon, the AMA; 01–09, Flags). Real books get invented secret meanings or uses (Moby-Dick, the Tarot "deliberately reversed," Derleth "persuaded" to deny the Necronomicon, Crowley's Book of Lies as a working spell; 02, 03, 08, 09). The Holocaust is used as conspiracy evidence (03). Every proposal below uses invented people, invented documents and SDF's own foundation. None of the above transfers.

sections.title: 1. What it is
sections.html:
A New York magazine is bombed and its editor, Joe Malik, is missing. Detective Saul Goodman reads Joe's box of memos on the Illuminati, each contradicting the last. George Dorn, a reporter, is jailed in Texas and rescued by Hagbard Celine, an anarchist with a golden submarine. Every explanation (assassins, a hoax, communists, Satanists, Atlantis, five rival lodges) is overturned by the next. The strands meet at a rock festival in Ingolstadt, where the Illuminati's leaders turn out to be a rock band and Hagbard turns out to be the fifth. Joe bombed his own office. Fourteen appendices keep the joke going after the plot.

What makes it work: every layer is offered as the whole answer and broken a scene later by someone with one more fact, so the reader always holds two versions. And every escalation comes with a joke beside it, never instead of it.

sections.title: 2. The engine
sections.html:
No single hero. Each row says whose step it is.

Step Wants right now Finds Costs Why he cannot stop here Forces next
1. Saul (Trip 1, 01) Who bombed the magazine A box of Illuminati memos Hides it from the FBI; outside the law The memos tie the bombing to the assassinations Malik's flat
2. Saul (Trips 1–2, 01) True from false Dogs heard, no bowls; a dead letter-writer His theory; "He was also wrong" His logic says their goal is unmet The ninth memo
3. George (Trips 1–2, 01) A story on assassins A chapel in the jail; a rescue; Hagbard Arrest, terror, his self-image Offered money to go ashore, he stays: best story of his life Atlantis; the reader learns the rescue was allowed
4. Joe (Trip 3, 02) Something not corrupt 23s, a black mass, Dillinger alive His liberal faith His own tests all came back positive The JAMs, bottom rank
5. Saul (Trip 4, 02) Their real aim Fascists, Satanists, the Eschaton Kidnapped, drugged, told he is "Muldoon" The diagnosis attacks who he is He catches the doctor out: it's Joe
6. George (Trips 4–5, 02–03) To stop being a coward 1776 was a lie told to him; Atlantis Four porpoises die for him Hagbard gives him a job at once Drake's study
7. Joe (Trip 5, 03) To be "illuminized" Iggy: "most of… bullshit" Trusts no one, his side included His doubt is rewarded: "your next promotion" Checking his own side
8. Drake (Trip 6, 04) To own the Mafia A layer behind it Four tails vanish No deal holds until the hidden layer answers, so he provokes it The Grand Master's card
9. George (Trip 6, 04) To reach Saul Drake dead; "several Illuminati" Nearly dies That question must go to Hagbard "I've got to start telling you the truth"
10. Danny, police (Trip 8, 06) A lead on Marsh A kind counter-history: the Illuminati as persecuted reason Four bourbons; recruited to defend them It fits all he holds and says he's in danger A clearance line breaks it, for the reader
11. Joe (Trip 9, 07) "A straight answer this time" Hagbard knows Joe bombed his office His secret Each answer opens a bigger one A pistol, a silver bullet
12. Joe (Trip 9, 07) To stop Hagbard The band is four Primi; the fifth is Hagbard No sacrament but his own Only one Primus left Fires, then hands back the gun
13. Joe (Trip 10, 08) The answer Cartwright's yarn was planted for him He was "programmed" More surprises promised The Tarot, Leviathan
14. George (Trip 10, 08) Are Stella and Mavis real? The god behind the symbols is a single cell Both women as he knew them Nothing left to find The appendices

Where someone acts on a layer (rows 3, 8, 10, 11–12), C is an engine. Where Saul only reads (rows 1–2), it turns pages but doesn't move him.

sections.title: 3. How the lore gets in
sections.html:
• The memos (Trips 1–4, about 7,500 words, documents). Two or three at a time, broken by argument or a call. They never stall, because each contradicts the last, so each is a plot event (01, 02).
  • Tellers who undo themselves. Iggy breaks his own lecture on a timer set by the acid; Maldonado and Dillinger each open by calling the last layer "bullshit" (03, 04).
  • A counter-history paced by drink. Mama Sutra, about 5,000 words. Danny goes from "Can't drink on duty" to "May I have more?" (06).
  • Where it stalls: Malaclypse to Joe (Trip 6, about 3,000 words, 04), rescued only by Joe pushing his arm through Malaclypse's side and by an order. Where it doesn't: Pat's memos, for the reason above.
  • The rule: no layer comes from a neutral voice. Each teller wants something from the listener, so every lecture is also a move.

sections.title: 4. The mechanism we came for: the front
sections.html:
Setup and escalation. Six layers in Trip 1 alone, each broken a different way ("Saul was convinced. He was also wrong," 01). Later they run at three scales at once (memos, deductions, cast, 02), the register flipping at each step (04). Often the reader learns the break before the hero, which makes dread without anyone acting (01, 07).

Rule. "Behind the mask is a man and behind the man is another mask" (Trip 3). Two refinements. Every front is partly true and does real work: the front law firm keeps up appearances by doing real legal work (07). And each layer is true for the rank of whoever hears it. Flanagan is "only a Fourth-degree Illuminatus," George will "become a deacon," and Hagbard says "the human mind can only accept a little of the truth at a time" (03).

How a layer breaks (01–08). It breaks on an object, a second person with one more fact, the teller's admission, a clearance detail ("Mama isn't cleared"), or a promotion. The hero's theories are always wrong. He can catch a flaw in an object (Saul's missing mole, 02), but he never deduces the next layer.

The planted resting place. "I sent Jim Cartwright to you with that yarn" (08). The middle layer was built so the investigator would have somewhere to stop.

Payoff (08, 09). Trip 10 strips the layers and lands on a method said plainly (the power to say No; fear of death as the lever) while the documents stay incomplete. The appendices show the danger: Gimmel stacks fronts down to a joke, and the reader stops caring which is true. C needs a floor. SDF's is what happens when we die, reached in The night he stops being afraid.

Verdict (a): C works as an engine under four conditions. (1) Someone acts on a layer as if it were the bottom, and the act costs him: George stays aboard, Drake provokes the hidden layer through the visible one, Danny defends the conspiracy, Joe bombs his own office. (2) The break comes from outside the hero, which matches SDF's "reveals are objects." (3) Each layer is true at its rank. (4) There is a floor.

A correction to the brief: Illuminatus's ladder is vertical (degrees, promotions). SDF's four helper words sit side by side; they are compartments, not rungs. SDF's ladder is James's own climb: asker, program staff (the badge sounds "one note up," v7 The drill), annex role, schedule, the offer of a seat. Each promotion hands him the next layer, so C is already running in Part Two. What's missing is condition (1): a layer he acts on and pays for. ADDENDUM 05 was right about Tier 1. Illuminatus shows what turns C into an engine: an act on the wrong layer.

Verdict (b): James can wear a front, within the rules. Declare 5.3 and Libra 5.4 have proposed two. Illuminatus adds the cheapest kind, a true front the organization has already written for him (5.2), and names one he already uses without saying so (5.3). The limits: no impersonation, no invented task, no staged ordeal. Chips gives the reason a true front is enough: "They won't believe it, but they'll think you believe it. That's good enough" (08).

Against A–D. A weak (02). B aimed at recruits (02) and once at the reader ("Joe Malik's mysterious dogs," 09). C confirmed, with conditions. D inverted: Joe gets every key and declines the act (07).

New, checked against ADDENDUM 05. The diagnosis: the answer to an investigator is a file saying he is ill (Saul as Muldoon, 02; Marsh's "suicide during drug psychosis," 03; leaks filed as madness, 04). It discredits without killing and reads his cleverness as a symptom. The kind counter-history: a credible person already holds your evidence and frames it the other way. Mama Sutra asks whether the memos were unfavorable before Danny describes them (06).

Comedy under escalation. Every horror gets a deflation in the same paragraph (07). The jokes are about institutions, never victims (04). Atrocity passages carry no jokes; the comedy stands on either side of them (03). Evil is a dull office (07). Mavis states the rule (quote 8).

Orientation. The reader always knows when, even when not who: every jump carries a date, a clock, or "while" plus a known event; refrains work as hinges; each voice has a fixed idiom (01–08). It fails only when the point of view slips mid-scene (01).

sections.title: 5. Transfer to SDF
sections.html: Already on the page, so not proposed: the resting place ("we leave them findable"; "You found the seats and thought they were the point. They all do," v8 The final conversation); the clown run by the organization (the thermostat; the polite forum correction); a cover that does real work (disaster recovery, "true, and that was the genius of it," v7 What was on the phone); declining the act (the lower door). Already proposed elsewhere: the door that was allowed (Libra 5.2, Pynchon 5.1); James's own sheet (ADDENDUM 05 c.1); the program's format as cover (Declare 5.3).

items.title: 5.1 The neighbor's kind version
items.html:
The math (or the end of The week it vanished; PLACEHOLDER).

  • Change: before the curtain shop, James walks past the professor's house in Deventer, and the neighbor asks him in and gives him the kind counter-history (Mama Sutra, Trip 8): Hendrik was unwell at the end, stopped sleeping, wrote to people about printers; the foundation that once funded him was the only one that visited, paid for the van, put up with forum cranks. Before he has said why he came, she asks: "Did he write to you about the printings too?"
  • James does: he carries her version into the shop. He tells Els he's sorry about her father's illness and asks about the last months, and Els refuses him ("everyone who comes about my father is polite"). When the folder comes, When a reader notices says agreement, then reclassification, and the layer breaks on a document, not on his deduction.
  • Cost: Els's first door is shut by words he borrowed. And the neighbor telephones (conservation's one task), so the count learns of the visit.
  • Already on the page? Partly. v7 What was on the phone lists "a woman in Deventer who turned out to be the professor's neighbour" under Conservation; v6 The week it vanished has "he'd stopped sleeping at the end"; v6 A car park's voice knows of "a visit to the daughter." No scene introduces her, and v8.2 gives Els's refusal no cause. PLACEHOLDER #5, his line to Els, gains a job: undoing the borrowed sentence.
  • Already proposed? No.

items.title: 5.2 Reclassified, and he wears it
items.html:
The math → A car park → The sheets.

  • Change: the folder's last rule is used on James. At a one-to-one, Pieter kindly hands him an invented bank wellbeing referral, three sessions. Someone else has filled in the reason: recent bereavement in family; sleep disturbance; preoccupation with historical documents.
  • James does: he signs it and uses it as cover. He tells the counselor a true small story (the funeral, four a.m.), lets her read his jokes as deflection (the captors aim at Saul's jokes, Trip 4), and stops asking at work. He lets Ana find the appointment card and believe it explains four a.m., the way he let her think the notebook was about her grandmother.
  • Cost: the cover works on paper and fails with people. The counselor writes "settling." The handler reads faces: "stopped asking out loud, which is worse," and the review moves closer. The verb that moves the date comes from a front James chose. Later the referral is still in his file, and in The sheets Anneke asks about it first, so he has to answer the diagnosis before she will read the invoice (PLACEHOLDER: Anneke, or the old man in The reading room, continued).
  • Already on the page? Partly. "Reclassified" is in v8.2 The math (word for word in v6). "Stopped asking out loud" (A car park) has no cause James chose. No draft reclassifies him.
  • Already proposed? No. It fits before Declare 5.1 (quiet, punished, then told loud is safe). It competes with Pynchon 5.4; take one discredit (PLACEHOLDER).

items.title: 5.3 The brochure
items.html:
The sheets → The final conversation → Leave it.

  • Change: the sheets' strongest line, "Your name is not on this list. Please check" (v7), runs on the seats-as-lifeboat story, the layer printed for helpers ("That's what they're told," v8). James is using their front. Name it and let it cost.
  • James does: writing "Who is kept," he notes that he doesn't know what the seats are for ("it is not what you think," v7 The reading room, continued) and prints it anyway, because it's the version they'll read. When the old man starts on the seats, James gets there first: "I know. I used your brochure." In Leave it, Pieter asks whether he's still on the list, since the deal keeps the seats. James gives him the floor in one line: nobody's kept, the ones on it included.
  • Cost: the only thing he says outside the deal's silence goes to the one helper who was on the list, and Pieter has to work out what his three dependants were for. PLACEHOLDER: does Anneke hear of it?
  • Already on the page? Partly. v7 The sheets and v8 The final conversation each hold half, and nothing joins them. Pieter is absent from v8 Leave it.
  • Already proposed? No. Canon conflict: v7 The sheets keeps the brewer off every list, while v8.2 gives him five seats ("I'm in").

sections.title: 6. Do not take
sections.html:
• Real people or organizations as complicit, and invented secret meanings for real books, the Tarot or real films (01–09, Flags).
  • Hagbard's method: kidnap, drugs, staged ordeals, lies fed "a little at a time" (02, 03, 05). It makes the hero a handler. James labels what he can't prove (Twenty minutes).
  • The bottomless stack (Gimmel, 09). The old man's film claims in The final conversation stay his claims, set against James's floor, never confirmed by the narration.

sections.title: 7. Quote bank
sections.html:
1. "Saul was convinced. He was also wrong." (Trip 1) A layer held, then broken in five words.
  2. "Behind the mask is a man and behind the man is another mask." (Trip 3) The engine in one line.
  3. "I lied to you because the human mind can only accept a little of the truth at a time." (Trip 5) The ladder.
  4. "The homosexuality bit had been a false front (with its own reality, of course, like all false fronts)." (Trip 7) Every front is partly true.
  5. "be sure to ask for Miss Mao, not Mama Sutra. Mama isn't cleared for this." (Trip 8) A layer broken by a clearance detail.

notes.title: section 01 (Book One, First and Second Trips)
notes.html:
Coverage: Book One "Verwirrung", the First Trip (Kether) and the Second Trip (Chokmah) (about 31,800 words), read in full, 12 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 01; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Trip 1, Saul) To know who bombed Confrontation and where its editor Malik went A metal box of Illuminati research memos in the rubble. Malik's associate editor says Malik was reopening the King and Kennedy killings He hides the box from the FBI and transfers his suspected CIA plants. From here on he works outside the law The FBI is on its way, and the memos tie the bombing to the assassinations He breaks into Malik's flat to read the rest
2 (Trip 1, Saul) To sort true from false in the memos Washington portraits labelled G.W. and A.W.; dogs the neighbours heard, but no food and no bowls; the man who wrote to Playboy about the Illuminati, found dead Nothing yet. He builds a theory (the Illuminati are anarchists), and the narrator says at once that he is wrong His own logic says their goal is unmet, or they would not still be hiding The ninth memo (Trip 2)
3 (Trips 1–2, George) A story on a right-wing assassination ring in Mad Dog, Texas A sheriff who knew he had pot, a hired-assassin cellmate who is gutted and then vanishes, an Illuminati chapel inside the jail, a rescue, Hagbard Arrest, a near-rape at gunpoint, terror, his idea of himself as a radical He is held without a lawyer. Hagbard offers to put him ashore with money, and he stays because it is the best story he has ever found The voyage to Atlantis

Why it grips

  • Each layer works as the full answer for a while, then the reader is moved up a level (see Mechanism notes).
  • Dangling hooks. "George Dorn is screaming" cuts into Saul's scenes twice before the jail scene explains it. Flash-forwards are dropped and left: a general raising a pistol to Mocenigo's head; Mocenigo's next date being his last with a woman; a festival seven days ahead. The reader moves forward to reach things already promised.
  • Signal and noise side by side. The missing dogs (no food, no bowls, no tins) is honest detection. The CLARK KENT sticker Saul puts down to a magazine staffer is later shown, to the reader only, as a stray left by an obscene caller.
  • Orientation. The narrator admits the confusion on page one. Each jump carries a date or clock time, things happening at the same moment go in parentheses, refrains ("Rock Around the Clock") work as hinges, and sometimes the narrator just warns that a jump is coming. It fails three times: the point of view moves from Saul into Muldoon's "I" mid-scene; a nameless "I" after Cartwright's call turns out to be Atlanta Hope; George moves from third to first person mid-paragraph. Each time the reader loses about a page.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

It puts every person in the room. Hagbard intercepts two spy broadcasts and wires New York to activate Malik and prepare Dorn (Trip 2). So Malik's investigation, which Saul is reconstructing, was started by a rival conspiracy, and George's assignment was bait. Then Cartwright tells Atlanta Hope that the rescue was allowed. The investigators are steered by the conspiracy they chase and by the one fighting it. The real escalation is the reader learning that each discovery was set up.

How the lore gets in

  • Eight memos (Trip 1), about 2,500 words, documents in a found box. Two or three at a time, each batch broken by argument, a phone call or a break-in. The sources get worse on purpose, from encyclopedia to an underground paper saying Weishaupt replaced Washington. No stall: someone reacts within a page.
  • Rebecca on the phone, about 300 words. It is all a student hoax; one fact rides inside a flirtation.
  • Saul's analysis (Trip 1), about 1,200 words of reasoning. It stalls, and one line from the narrator ends it.
  • Atlanta Hope's confession (Trip 2), about 900 words. The cell structure arrives through her fear, and ends in an order to put protesters in hospital.

Mechanism notes

  • C (front), the core of this section. Six layers, each delivered and broken differently: 1. Right-wing assassins in Mad Dog (George's brief). Held for a Trip. Broken by the Sheriff dismissing him and by the Illuminati chapel inside the jail. 2. A student hoax (Rebecca). Held for one line. Broken by Saul's hunch. 3. The Illuminati are anarchists (Saul's deduction). Held for a paragraph. Broken by the narrator, with no evidence given. 4. The jail is communist (Mavis: the sheriff discredits America on purpose). Held for a few pages. Broken by an object, the eye-in-triangle tattoo on her chest. 5. Hagbard's people beat the Illuminati to George. Held for a chapter. Broken by a phone call the reader overhears and George does not. 6. The Order is the top layer (Atlanta). Broken from inside: she doubts the Five see the whole picture, and the banker Drake, who funds her, seems to know more than she does. The pattern to copy: a break is either seen by the hero (chapel, tattoo) or told only to the reader (the call, the narrator). The second kind puts the reader one layer ahead, which creates dread without the hero doing anything.

  • The clown is the method. Rebecca's hoax story is SDF's funding-nonsense rule exactly: students sending out press releases so that believers have something to point at. The memos put the Washington swap beside real Masonic history. Saul throws out the silly half first, and that is what makes him trust the rest.

  • A tiny edit with consequences (Trip 2). A Houston store sign gains "NO SPITTING"; rich customers take offence, and God's Lightning gains rich members. The Management did not put it up. The closest thing here to SDF's "given" to "arose": one change, no traceable author, and it moves people rather than informs them.
  • The Law of Fives as compartments. Atlanta's cells match SDF's one-task helpers; her fear shows the structure from inside.
  • A and D (gate, key). Simon gets nothing more until he makes the right move; the key is his dead father's sentence in a stranger's mouth. George must say "Hail Eris" himself.
  • Comedy that escalates with the danger. Over Fernando Poo, each power is sure the other has troops there, and Moscow plans to sneak troops in so it can be seen withdrawing them. The same paragraph about the leader runs three times, word for word, for Washington, Moscow and Peking. Each layer gets sillier as it gets more frightening (a nuclear ultimatum), so the book stays funny without lowering the stakes.
  • Proposal (PLACEHOLDER): borrow layer 5 for SDF. A door that a person chooses to open for James is later shown to have been allowed by the organisation, because his finding it suits them. The cost is that what he did with it served them. This keeps the rule that doors open only by choice and adds the missing cost of being wrong.

Quotes

  • "Saul was convinced. He was also wrong." (Trip 1): a layer held as the full answer, then broken in five words.
  • "The odd thing was that the Management had nothing at all to do with the sign." (Trip 2): a small edit with no author.
  • "each group a separate vector so that the most any infiltrator can learn is a small part of the design" (Trip 2): compartments explained from inside.
  • "We let Celine's crowd take Dorn, according to plan" (Trip 2): the rescue was part of the plan.

Flags

  • Real people named as complicit: the Kennedy shooting is given to Harry Coin, Oswald, Bernard Barker and a fourth man, with Howard Hunt at the Grassy Knoll; Nixon, Mayor Daley and William Buckley appear through the memos. SDF must not do this.
  • The memos hang invented claims on real books and magazines (Ellul, the Britannica, Playboy); [from memory, not from the text] some citations are real. Too close to SDF's ban on invented edits to real books: use invented sources only.

notes.title: section 02 (Third Trip, or Binah, and Book Two's Fourth Trip, or Chesed)
notes.html:
Coverage: Third Trip and Fourth Trip (about 46,000 words), read in full, 12 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 02; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
