1 (Trip 3, memos 9–14) Saul and Barney want to know what Malik knew and where he went Pat's memos, each naming a different "real" Illuminati (Robison's free-love anarchists, Webster's Prussians, Levi's false Zoroaster); Malik's pencil jottings (23, TARO = TORA) Nothing yet but their nerves; they start joking about werewolves Malik and Pat are missing and two buildings are bombed, so the papers can't be put down as a hoax They keep reading, and Saul starts a theory of why the evidence contradicts itself
2 (Trip 3, Joe's flashback, 1968–69) Joe wants something not corrupt after Chicago Simon's 23s, a black mass that summons something that looks like Billy Graham, then Dillinger alive in Los Angeles His liberal faith; he takes acid and is initiated He set his own tests (the tooth, Graham's whereabouts, Tlaloc) and they all came back positive He joins the JAMs at the bottom rank, and a flash-forward says he will later plan the bombing of his own magazine
3 (Trip 4, Saul) Saul wants the Illuminati's real aim Fascists, then Satanists inside the Church (Barney), then a plan to immanentize the Eschaton, with Fernando Poo as the false front He goes underground, is taken, drugged, shown faked pornography of his wife and told he is a Trenton patrolman called Muldoon If he is right the world ends, and the "diagnosis" goes after his sense of who he is He catches the "doctor" out: it is Joe Malik

Why it grips

  • Every answer arrives already cracked. The reader gets a theory and the next scene breaks it. Saul's long deduction (Trip 4) wins Barney's praise, then Barney produces a list of Catholic assassins and goes one better, and Saul tops that with Fernando Poo. Each detective is Holmes for a page, so the case speeds up though nobody leaves the flat.
  • The reader is shown the trick before the victim falls for it. Saul explains how the conspiracy recruits: it pretends to help, and it tells the target a story that fits his ideals (Trip 4). Twenty pages later Hagbard tells George that the right-wing version was "a test" and that a left-winger would have got the other one. So the friendly submarine feels dangerous.
  • The frame is a con, and that is the last thing we learn. Trip 4 opens with Hassan i Sabbah's severed head screaming from hell and closes with the head climbing out of a trapdoor, "undamaged". The founding miracle was staged, and the reader learns it only after George's hanged double has vanished through a ceiling with no trapdoor. One trick is explained, one left open.
  • The heaviest scene attacks the detective's method. The Playboy Club ordeal (Trip 4) wears down Saul's scepticism. Each fake slide has one flaw he catches (a missing mole), and the next slide fixes it. His jokes are his defence, and the captors aim straight at them.
  • Orientation in a book that jumps. Every memo is dated. A hymn line ("WE SHALL NOT BE MOVED") stands between strands like a chapter break. Smiling Jim's speech is a running clock; parentheses mark time jumps. Repeated objects (the Sacred Chao, the mermaid, 23) link strands that never say they connect.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The conspiracy works by handing out explanations, not by blocking anyone. Saul names its method himself: kill rarely, because the dead man may have hidden copies, and neutralize, ideally by recruiting. The section acts it out. George is recruited with a version of the story tailored to him. Joe is recruited through checks he set himself. Saul is offered a diagnosis that turns him into a mental patient. Each layer arrives through a person who wants something from the hero, and the investigator turns out to be inside it. Joe, whose papers drive the detectives' case, is the man who will bomb his own office.

How the lore gets in

  • Pat's memos (Trips 3–4), about 5,000 words in total, documents. They come in 150 to 700 words at a time, and each is followed by the detectives arguing or by a cut to another strand. They never stall, because each memo contradicts the last, so each is a plot event; Pat herself notices the contradictions look deliberate.
  • Simon's 23 rant and JAM history (Trip 3), about 1,500 words, talk. It is framed as Joe's experiment in believing for one evening, so the reader may doubt it, and Dillinger interrupts. The Daleville robbery is played as a scene in the present rather than told.
  • Father Muldoon on the phone (Trip 4), about 1,300 words, a lecture. Saul steers it with questions toward his own hypothesis (light-bringer, atomic light). It ends in a decision to go underground, then the capture.
  • Hagbard's 200-year history (Trip 4), about 1,500 words, talk. George asks for a sign, and the proof is a phone call George controls: he dials a number Hagbard can't see. He learns the office has been bombed and Joe is missing.

Mechanism notes

  • C (front), at full strength. The layers come at three scales. In the memos, each source's Illuminati is a mask for the next (Webster says the anarcho-communist utopia was only a mask). In the deduction, communist gives way to fascist, then Satanist, then Eschaton, and Saul then calls Fernando Poo itself a false front. In the cast, the JAMs and the LDD are fronts with absurd names. Each layer is held as the full answer for about one scene. What breaks it is always a second person with one more fact: Barney's slip of paper, the W.H. letter, Hagbard's admission. The hero never breaks a layer by thinking alone. Robison's lodge degrees (memo 12) state the front structure as lore, and Dillinger enacts it by telling Joe he is not cleared yet.
  • The clown is part of the plan. The W.H. letter is the organisation's best cover: a calm, helpful reply saying the whole thing is a campus joke. Hagbard says it outright: the yellow submarine and the silly name work because everyone already thinks Illuminati-hunters are crackpots. This is SDF's clown-beside-every-question with the clown run by the conspiracy itself.
  • A (gate), weakly. Joe won't commit until his own tests come back (Trip 3, the Tlaloc note). They are checks on objects (a tooth, a date), which James could legitimately run.
  • B (canary), reversed. Each recruit is told a different version and watched (Hagbard's test): the canary is aimed at the hero.
  • Fifth: the diagnosis. The organisation's reply to an investigator is a file saying he is ill and was never who he thinks he is. It discredits without killing, and it reads his cleverness as a symptom. For SDF: James's nightly-counted questions could come back to him as a document that reads him as the anomaly.

Quotes

  • "they keep creating masks so all sorts of scapegoat groups will get the blame for being the 'real' Illuminati" (Trip 3): the front stated outright.
  • "If you suspect either of these groups of being involved in something sinister, you have probably just fallen for one of their put-ons." (Trip 4): the clown as a document.
  • "We came on like right-wing paranoids, at first, to see how you'd react. It was a test." (Trip 4): the earlier layer revealed as bait.
  • "Behind the mask is a man and behind the man is another mask." (Trip 3): the engine in one line.

Flags

  • Real people named as complicit: Bernard Barker (CIA) on the grassy knoll; Stanton behind Lincoln's death; Wilson poisoned; Orwell killed; John McCone on Malik's list; Billy Graham's face on the summoned being. SDF must not do this.
  • Invented hidden meanings in real books (Moby-Dick as a Sabbah text, the Silmarillion as counter-propaganda). Not edits, but close to SDF's rule.
  • The racial and sexual shock material in Saul's ordeal is this book's tone, not SDF's.

notes.title: section 03 (Trip 5, "Geburah")
notes.html:
Coverage: the whole Fifth Trip, from the "Swift-Kick, Inc" epigraph to the Crowley epigraph that opens "The Golden Apple" (about 33,900 words), read in full, 12 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 03; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 George (Atlantis, Drake) To survive the sea battle and stop being a coward The Pyramid of the Eye: the Illuminati are 30,000 years old, and Hagbard lied about 1776 on purpose Four porpoises die for him, and he has to admit he kills by proxy Hagbard gives him a job straight away: four statues for the head of the Syndicate A negotiation where his only weapon is the truth, and a deal that depends on statues he can't promise
2 Joe (1969 initiation, 1972 doubt) To be "illuminized" and to know what is real Dr. Iggy's history, then Iggy saying most of it was bullshit; later Joe suspects Atlantis was a tabletop model He can trust no one, and his memory is "retroactive" Hagbard rewards the doubt with a card: understand it and you're ready for "your next promotion" His own side's story becomes something else he has to check
3 Saul (deprogramming) To know who he is George's night at Drake's ends with Mavis calling him "Saul"; she was one of the Five who run the US; the lloigor are "real" He sees his seventeen death sentences as sacrifices He sees the fnords; Vegas and Ingolstadt both need people The cast splits into the "one-two punch"

Why it grips

  • Every layer comes with its own doubt. Hagbard gives five reasons the Illuminati have not taken over the world, and George points out "Those reasons contradict each other". Iggy's lecture takes itself apart in the middle. Joe's special-effects suspicion is the strongest argument in the section, and nobody answers it. The reader always holds two versions.
  • Order of telling against order of events. Iggy's debunking (1969) comes after the Atlantis battle (1973–74), so the reader has already "seen" Atlantis when told the history was invented in 1776. Layers are undercut by placement, never refuted.
  • Keeping the reader oriented. Date tags in parentheses ("This was in '72"). Simon's dollar-bill lecture is picked up in three years, each named ("Simon asks in nineteen sixty-nine... Simon shouts in nineteen seventy"). One clock: "10:30 P.M., Ingolstadt time". A counting chant ("big rhinoceroses") runs across cuts until we learn it is Sherri's. Joe's "flash forwards" turn the structure into a symptom of the initiation.
  • The scene that does most work: Drake's study. A naive messenger, a parchment, an expert with a jeweler's glass who will "know if they are not" real, and a contract with "considerations of equal value yet to come" added. His only asset is the truth, which is that he has nothing more.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The conspiracy sets the jobs. Project Tethys (raising the temple) causes the sea battle, the battle produces the statues, the statues buy Drake. Flanagan's scene shows the enemy as an organisation with ranks and shortages. He is "only a Fourth-degree Illuminatus and not fully instructed in the history". Both sides keep their own people on partial layers; George will "become a deacon" after this mission. Hagbard gives the conspiracy's theory of itself: five leaders make 120 possible coalitions, and a random element is added on purpose. They recruited both ecology leaders and polluters "to create ambiguity", so anyone describing them sounds paranoid. That is the SDF clown principle, stated by a character.

How the lore gets in

  • Simon's 23/17 letter (about 3,000 words in five pieces). A document read in parts, each piece cut short by a Mothers March collector. The interruption both keeps the lore moving and deflates it.
  • The dollar-bill lecture (about 800 words). A prop in Joe's hand, cut into pieces of about 150 words between other scenes.
  • The Holocaust passages (about 1,200 words). Flat historical prose with no jokes in it. Then the "Bavarian Fire Drill": Simon empties a line of cars at a red light to show how obedience works. The prank is the proof.
  • Hagbard on Atlantis (about 1,500 words). Tied to things on screen (the pyramid, the eye) and ends on a mission.
  • Dr. Iggy (about 2,500 words). A monologue timed to the acid; the drug decides when he tells the truth ("Good: the acid is starting to work").
  • Marsh's book (about 600 words). A document in a detective's hands, page 123, delivered "in seventeen minutes". A discredited book confirms the deepest layer, and nobody explains it to him.

Mechanism notes

  • C (front), the core of this Trip. Six layers. (1) 1776 and the dollar bill (Simon, a lecture with a prop). (2) Atlantis, 30,000 years (Hagbard). An object too big for the old story breaks layer 1, and the teller admits he staged it for George's level. (3) Joe's special-effects doubt. It comes from the hero, is rewarded, and is left open. (4) Iggy: everything before 1776 is invented, "Or maybe we're just a front for the Illuminati". The teller breaks his own layer on a timer. (5) Mavis: the lloigor, a being kept "inside the Pentagon". Saul supplies it himself ("I've got it"), so it does not feel handed over. (6) Marsh's book, an outside discredited document, confirms layer 5. Layers hold from minutes (Iggy) to whole Trips (1776). They break in one of four ways: an artifact, the teller's admission, the hero's doubt, or a promotion. New for SDF: the front is a training ladder, and each version is true for that rank. Proposal: someone who gave James a document later says calmly that it is the version handed out at his level. The cost: James has already acted on it in front of someone. Check whether "The money" or "The drill" already does this. PLACEHOLDER.
  • Discredit, not prevent. Marsh is ridiculed until he disappears, and his file is closed as "suicide during drug psychosis". Emperor Norton's money circulated because he was mad, while Spooner's sane bank was suppressed.
  • Cases closed by category. Oedipuski's death goes uninvestigated because it is "connected with God's Lightning". The narrator says what nobody traced (the spiked KCUF punch). Close to SDF's nightly job: the system files it away and nobody decides anything.
  • Fifth: the book reviews itself. Wildeblood pans "this mishmash" without reading it and lists every fault a reader might find. It disarms the objection in advance.

Comedy under escalation. The Mothers March gags (Polio, Psoriasis, Hernia, Dandruff, then a whole dollar for Muzak) run under the numerology. Drake farts on the stairs after the deal. "Pajamas? Aisle seven" answers Simon's revelation. Waterhouse says "Just to fuck you up, man." The atrocity passages carry no jokes; the comedy stands either side of them, and the Fire Drill turns a joke into evidence. Mavis states the rule (Quotes).

Quotes

  • "I lied to you because the human mind can only accept a little of the truth at a time." (Trip 5, Hagbard): the front as a teaching method.
  • "First of all, most of what I've been telling you is bullshit." (Trip 5, Dr. Iggy): the teller breaks his own layer on cue.
  • "A conspiracy with one hundred and twenty vectors doesn't look like a conspiracy: it looks like chaos." (Trip 5, Hagbard): why the organisation can't be seen.
  • "It's not true unless it makes you laugh, but you don't understand until it makes you weep." (Trip 5, Mavis): the tone rule.

Flags

  • Real people named as complicit: Hitler joining the "Illuminated Lodge", with Haushofer; Washington as Weishaupt; the CIA and the President in Project Tethys; Oswald as a double agent; Derleth "persuaded" to deny the Necronomicon in every edition; Lovecraft's and Seabrook's deaths implied as murders. SDF must not do this.
  • The Derleth note is the nearest thing here to an edit inserted into real books. Strong model; SDF must use an invented book.
  • The Holocaust is used as conspiracy evidence; "Winifred" is an invented official set against real history. [From memory, not from the text: the real obstruction is usually tied to Breckinridge Long.]

notes.title: section 04 (Book Three opening, the Sixth Trip, Tipareth)
notes.html:
Coverage: Book Three's epigraph and the whole of the Sixth Trip, "The Man Who Murdered God" (about 24,000 words), read in full, 12 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 04; no edition data in the file.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Drake, 1936) To own the Mafia by proving he can read Dutch Schultz's last words The Mafia's secret has a layer behind it: the Illuminati. A novelist hints at a Master behind Hitler; Lovecraft calls the occultists absurd Four Mafia soldiers tailing him vanish; Lovecraft warns him to "remember their attitude toward servants" Any deal with the Mafia "is written on the wind" until the people behind them answer A janitor lays a prismatic eye-and-pyramid card on his desk
2 (Drake, 1936–47, then the night of April 25) Partnership with the people behind the Mafia The Grand Master is a Justice Department official with a typed plan (the 1947 Act, the Pentagon, the syndicate as a pretext) He owns the country and not himself; he switches to the Discordians, and the thing eats him that night Jung on power and Lovecraft's warning keep returning He sends George out in the Rolls and dies; twenty-seven gangland killings follow
3 (George, Joe, Saul, present) George: to reach Saul Goodman. Joe: test AUM. Saul: tell Rebecca Goodman's wife is scared; Drake is dead; a real 1972 book says several groups claim to be "the Illuminati" George nearly dies and says so; Hagbard's answer is a lecture "Several Illuminati?" is a question he must put to Hagbard Hagbard: "I've got to start telling you the truth, George"; the section ends there

Why it grips

  • One document, read again at every depth. Dutch Schultz's last words open the trip as phone threats (each quote a line "that would really sink us all"). Then they become thesis material, then the novelist's occult reading ("the Chinaman and Hitler's commander"), then the Illuminati formula to summon the lloigor. Last, in Drake's dream, Jung decodes them as acronyms and mocks the whole game ("Child's play! Glasspielen!"). The reader decodes alongside Drake, so Jung's mockery lands on the reader too.
  • The interrupted card. The janitor hands Drake the card ("The Grand Master of the Eastern United States is ready to talk to you"), and the scene breaks off for twenty-three years: Malaclypse in Chicago, Talbot's suicide, Drake's last dinner. Only then does it resume, with "And he turned the card over". The reveal is an object held in his hand for about 3,000 words.
  • Two deaths cut together. Drake's end is cut line by line against the Dutchman's hospital transcript. The document that started the hunt narrates the man who solved it being consumed.
  • How the reader stays oriented. Each cut opens with a date or an elapsed time ("April 25 began", "in 1936", "twenty-three years later", "In present time again"). Cuts happen on a repeated word ("Holy Cleopatra!" becomes "Kleopatra?"). Simultaneous action goes in parentheses. Refrains link the strands: "Camptown Races", "fun is fun", "unify the forces", Jung on power.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The conspiracy is the plot's engine in Drake's strand and the reason anyone moves in the present strand. Drake cannot do business with the visible layer (the Mafia) until the invisible one answers, so he provokes it: Lovecraft, the bank, "Will the All-Seeing Eye please look in my direction?" The conspiracy answers by recruiting him, which is the cost: he becomes its satrap. His defection to the Discordians kills him and puts George on the road. In the present, Drake's death and the April 25 killings send George back to Hagbard; Saul's disappearance pulls Rebecca to the hotel.

How the lore gets in

  • Phone calls (Drake to the Mafia), about 2,000 words. Lore as threats: each quoted line gets a reaction (cold sweat, a mass said, soldiers sent). No stall.
  • The novelist's lecture (Thule, Golden Dawn, Vril), about 1,500 words. His evasion is part of the scene, and cut-aways (Hitler screaming, Luciano's lawyer tracing Drake) keep it moving.
  • Lovecraft, about 1,200 words. A debate, not a lecture: two warnings exchanged. Four men vanish off-page at the end.
  • Malaclypse to Joe (Jesus, Melos, neophiles, transcendental illumination), about 3,000 words. This one stalls. It is rescued by a proof Joe performs with his own arm (through Malaclypse's side), by the joke that he might be "doing a two-thousand-year-old man routine", and by an order (test AUM).
  • Maldonado and Dillinger's counter-histories, about 1,000 words each, as dialogue. Each opens by declaring the last layer "bullshit".
  • The real Francis King book, one paragraph, a document. George opens it at random. One sentence of real history makes a new problem ("Several Illuminati?").

Mechanism notes

  • C (front), shown in its pure form. Each layer is delivered by a speaker who calls the one before it a front. Maldonado: "Adam just acted as her front"; the Haute Vente was so secret "Mazzini was a member all his life and never knew". Dillinger: "This Bavarian stuff is all bullshit… They're mostly Englishmen." Malaclypse: the Illuminati used "Plato's Academy as a front." Each layer lasts one conversation. What breaks a layer is always the next speaker's confidence, never evidence. The register also flips at each step: gangsters, then the occult, then a dull bureaucrat ("No mystical trappings"), then a monster in the Pentagon. For SDF (proposal): break each layer on a document rather than a speaker, and change register each time. The house style rule would read first as a publisher's quirk, then as a budget line, then as a continuity procedure.
  • Discredit, not prevent, stated four times. The pentagon shape: "They will be dismissed as superstitious cranks." Lovecraft is safe because his lore is "published as fiction". Maldonado files the leaks under madness: nuts "get it all scrambled". The FBI dismisses the widow's correct identification of Albert Stern as "a no-account junkie" who confessed falsely. Each dismissal is shown from the inside, which is why it works as plot.
  • The clown beside the real question. Canvera: a crank's phone line, mutating weekly, ends with an invitation priced at 5⁵ dollars and a shooting. The narrator then reveals the death "had nothing to do with the Illuminati": it was a sex grudge and a Mafia favour. The reader has been made the paranoid. Wildeblood reviews this very novel as "a fairy tale for paranoids", unread.
  • B (canary). Hagbard's gorillas: he claims they were men in suits to test whether Joe trusts his senses or an authority. Passing it means disbelieving the guide.
  • Comedy under escalation. Death camps, Hiroshima and the plague sit beside farce (the VSR marching song, a Vice President met through a personal ad) with no change of tone. The jokes are about the institutions, not the victims.

Quotes

  • "They're tuned in like gypsies. Telepathy, you know? But they get it all scrambled because they're nuts." (Trip 6): a real leak filed as madness.
  • "They will be dismissed as superstitious cranks." (Trip 6): discredit as policy, stated in the plan itself.
  • "Adam just acted as her front because people are used to taking orders from men." (Trip 6): each layer names the previous one a front.
  • "Actually, poor old Canvera's death had nothing to do with the Illuminati" (Trip 6): the narrator punctures the reader's conspiracy reading.

Flags

  • Real people and institutions named as complicit: Wilson "hoodwinked" into the Federal Reserve, the National Security Act of 1947 and the Pentagon as Illuminati designs, Cecil Rhodes, Luciano/Capone/Lepke, Hitler as a "medium". Real figures in invented scenes (Lovecraft, Jung, an unnamed Nobel novelist [Thomas Mann, from memory, not from the text]). SDF must not do this.
  • Lovecraft is said to have quoted Levi's formula "not in full" on purpose. That is an invented intention behind a real text, which comes close to SDF's ban on invented edits to real books.
  • Dutch Schultz's last words are a real document [from memory, not from the text] re-read as code. Allowed (read differently, not edited), but the exact edge.

notes.title: section 05 (Trip 7, "Netzach")
notes.html:
Coverage: the whole of the Seventh Trip, from the Hagbard Celine epigraph to FUCKUP's forecast for Ingolstadt (about 29,800 words), read in full, 12 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 05; no edition data in the file. The Trip has no numbered chapters, so cites name the strand (Midget, George, Vegas, Joe, Otto, FUCKUP).

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (George, Hagbard's stateroom) The "Truth" Hagbard promised A drugged lesson that ends with a loaded gun on the desk, then Harry Coin (whose death was faked) pushed through a panel His own account of the Mad Dog jail rape; Mavis says he is "no good to us" until he will kill Hagbard calls arriving "another starting place", then gives his guru role to a fifteen-year-old The submarine heads for Ingolstadt and George has no teacher
2 (Vegas: Despond, Knight, Filiarisus) The government wants the girl who carried Anthrax Leprosy Pi Two witness descriptions that agree only on "Female", because every witness lied Nearly a thousand men stopped on the roads, none of them Carmel Filiarisus's correct explanation ends with the carrier still loose Martial law; the narrator then names Filiarisus as Gracchus Gruad of the Illuminati
3 (Joe: fnords, plastic martini, Atlantis film) To learn what the eye-and-pyramid on a press release means A costumed board that shows him a film: the Illuminati come from Atlantis, not 1776 Drugged, used, left alone in the dark His teachers never mentioned this group, so what they taught him is incomplete FUCKUP names the three crises

Why it grips

  • Each answer is broken by the next scene. The Vegas strand is a run of solutions, each corrected within pages: the FBI theory (Mocenigo had two women), the blackboard chart of the two descriptions, the pimp's first-person panic, Filiarisus's computer account. The reader is a step ahead of the agents, having watched the Midget and Naismith invent their women, and laughs at an investigation built on lies told for small private reasons.
  • The right answer is the trap. Filiarisus gives the section's most honest speech: punishment makes witnesses lie, so a government cannot learn the truth. He uses it to argue for suspending the Bill of Rights, and only then does the narrator give his order name.
  • Orientation by hinge lines. The book jumps narrator, time and grammatical person (George becomes "I" partway through the Mavis scene; Joe's strand opens in first person and goes back to third). It stays readable because each jump is pinned to a time marker and an echo: "And, twenty-five hours earlier"; "And twenty-three hours later", with the Midget's exact words playing on Knight's earphones. The reader always knows when, even when not who.
  • The comedy is bodily and never stops. The apocalypse moves forward next to a coffee urn the Midget escapes in, an FBI bug under a CIA desk, a President on Demerol ("Tree that coon"), and Joe's bladder after the end of Atlantis ("Piss on Atlantis"). Every escalation has a pratfall next to it, and the pratfall never cancels the stakes.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

It puts people in rooms by using them. Each Vegas witness is drawn in because a planted plague passed through his body, and each self-protective lie pushes the investigation toward the Illuminati's goal. The conspiracy prevents nothing; punishment makes people lie, and lies make the government panic. For Joe it works the other way: the hidden board summons him and gives him lore, with a condition (he may only hint at it in Confrontation). For Otto it demands a killing; the Morituri "bomb nest" turns out to be an empty flat, a front that covers his shooting of Flanagan. FUCKUP's closing briefing then joins the strands into one plan: Fernando Poo was a feint to make heads of state jumpy, Vegas is the "ace in the hole", Ingolstadt the strike. The band poster Joe pinned up earlier shows four Illuminati Primi.

How the lore gets in

  • Hagbard and Mavis on the Robot (George), about 6,600 words, a stoned conversation. It moves because two physical acts break it up, each with a cost (the gun; Coin through the panel). Stretches stall (the property dialectic), and the book admits it: Mavis is "stoned, too; otherwise she'd be explaining it better".
  • The fnords and the saucer (Joe), about 1,400 words, first-person discovery. The lore arrives as an object he can test: the New York Times at breakfast, then a check of the advertisements (no fnords there). Holding a document and testing a hunch against it is the James move.
  • "When Atlantis Ruled the Earth", about 5,600 words, a film told in present-tense synopsis. The biggest dump in the section, interrupted once: Joe "sat up with a jolt" when Gruad, the first Illuminatus, turns out to love novelty, which contradicts what he was taught. It ends in the bathroom gag, and holds because the reader knows a costumed board staged it and chose to show it.
  • FUCKUP's forecast, about 1,000 words, a computer dialogue. Lore as a probability list ("fourteenth in order of probability"), cut off at "The end."

Mechanism notes

  • C (front) is the backbone. Six layers, each held as the full answer for a different time: 1. Mocenigo's sex life (FBI): about a page, broken by the chart. 2. Carmel the immune carrier (Filiarisus): three paragraphs, broken by the narrator naming him Gruad. A true answer used as cover for the move it justifies. 3. Illuminati founded in Bavaria, 1776: held since early in the book, broken by the film ("Ancient" means "a lot older than 1776"). 4. Saucers as a government hoax: one exchange. Hagbard's real saucer hides inside the debunk. 5. Fernando Poo as the crisis: broken by FUCKUP; it was a feint. 6. George's fear of homosexuality: seen as "a false front" over the fear of the Robot. The rule underneath: a layer breaks when someone shows the protagonist something (chart, film, saucer ride, gun), never by argument alone.

  • The clown beside the real question. Naismith sells a "vast Illiminati conspiracy" and the John Dillinger Died For You Society as cons, never suspecting they are true; Mavis then tells George, deadpan, that Dillinger is alive and shot Kennedy. The truth hides among frauds whose sellers disbelieve it. SDF's organisation funds exactly this.

  • The authoritative edit. The Midget changes one line on a store sign and nobody questions it, because it is signed by management. It is SDF's "given"/"arose" principle as a joke: the edit survives because of the authority of its frame, not because it is plausible.
  • Fifth: disclosure as recruitment. The board chooses to show Joe the film, then leaves him alone with the door unlocked. A door opened by choice, with a price attached. For James: someone hands him the next layer with a condition and walks out.

Quotes

  • "Nothing signed "THE MGT." would ever be challenged; the Midget could always pass himself off as the Management." (Trip 7, Midget): an edit protected by its frame.
  • "That there was an element of truth in these bizarre notions never crossed his mind." (Trip 7, Vegas, Naismith): the clown who carries the truth.
  • "is regarded by the government as a case of autosuggestion— since they know they didn't plant it themselves." (Trip 7, Joe, the saucer): the real thing hidden inside its debunk.
  • "The homosexuality bit had been a false front (with its own reality, of course, like all false fronts)." (Trip 7, George): mechanism C stated outright; each front is partly true.

Flags

  • Real people named as complicit: Hitler, Himmler and Bormann carry out an Illuminati-arranged mass sacrifice, and Bormann is called an Illuminati Primus (FUCKUP). Real novels (The Monk, Melmoth, Frankenstein, Otranto, de Sade) are put down to the psychic after-effect of Weishaupt's rites: a hidden cause behind real books, not an edit to them. SDF must copy neither.
  • No invented edits on real books; the Midget's edits are to invented signs and memos.

notes.title: section 06 (Book Four, "Beamtenherrschaft": the Eighth Trip, or Hod)
notes.html:
Coverage: Book Four from its epigraph to the "Leviathan" heading, i.e. the whole Eighth Trip (about 29,400 words), read in full, 12 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 06; no edition data in the file. Cited as "Trip 8" plus the scene.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Trip 8, Pricefixer and Mama Sutra) Danny wants any lead tying the bombing to the Marsh disappearance; the Commissioner wants progress today A psychic gives him a full counter-history: the Illuminati are the persecuted party of reason, the anti-Illuminati memos are propaganda, Hagbard is a Mafia front Four bourbons on duty, his faith, his safety ("seek the protection of the Illuminati") It fits everything he already holds (Marsh's notes, Golden Dawn, Malik's name) and says he is already in danger He ends drunk, asking "what can I do about it?", recruited to defend the conspiracy
2 (Trip 8, Tobias Knight's memoir) To know which of his four masters he really serves Each is cover for another: the Order runs the Black Power cult he "knew" about; the heroin pirates use the A:.A:. password; the psychic is spied on by her receptionist He loses track of his own loyalties; "Conspiracy was its own reward" Every message he carries shows a level he isn't cleared for He joins a fifth ring, the Discordians
3 (Trip 8, Hagbard at Peos) To keep his Demonstration (start from zero, never kill) intact FUCKUP's verdict that the spider ships were "under remote control" was wrong: twenty-four people were aboard The Demonstration has failed; he is a killer He and his crew are now committed "Salvage what I can": Ingolstadt, starting with George

Why it grips

  • The same facts told twice, with the values flipped. Stella tells Hagbard's Mohawk story (he refused the dam job, helped the evicted families move), and the narrator corrects her at once: he was their lawyer, too ashamed to say so. Thousands of words later Mama Sutra tells it back: a "much-needed dam", "unbalanced behavior in the courtroom", a Mafia-paid Harvard degree. The reader can compare both versions, so the lie entertains instead of confusing. This is the strongest scene for C.
  • One scene played twice, from different heads. Harry Coin's gun trial is first Harry's terror, then Hagbard's side: "variation #2 of the third basic tactic", with Hagbard half hoping Harry will shoot so he can dodge the Peos decision. Repeated lines ("Three days and three minutes are both too long", "Ready for destruction of enemy ships") mark where in the old scene the new layer sits.
  • A withheld name. Dillinger at Dealey Plaza sees the real killer's face ("Christ!" John said. "Him?") and the scene cuts away.
  • Orientation. The jumps are always stamped: "half a mile below and twelve hours earlier", "in present time", the present frame in parentheses while a flashback runs, one run-on sentence that pulls Chips, the Midget, Dillinger and Weishaupt through the same space-time "tug". Each voice has a fixed idiom (Chips's "Not High Church at all", Harry's "Ace", Knight's agency jargon), so you know who is talking before you get a name. Refrains ("Now look what you made me do", "No remission without blood") stitch the strands together.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

The weapon here is the counter-story, not force. Mama Sutra does not hide evidence from Danny; she gets ahead of it. Before he describes the memos she asks whether they "portrayed them in an unfavorable light?", having already said that every leak against the Illuminati is enemy propaganda. The reader has just seen Hagbard refuse to kill, so the inversion is visible to us and hidden from Danny. This is SDF's "discredit, don't prevent" working on the page: his findings are left alone and given a frame in which they point the other way.

The break is small and cheap: a clearance detail. Hassan i Sabbah X, handing Knight a password, adds that Mama isn't cleared, and Miss Mao turns out to spy on her for three masters. The grand account Danny took for the whole answer becomes one ring of five. Knight's memoir repeats the move: each recruitment story holds until the next superior laughs at it. Winifred's speech supplies the method SDF's helpers need: each is told a convincing local story fitted to their own loyalties.

How the lore gets in

  • The Dealy Lama's Eris myth (about 1,500 words, a parable). Five stoned Visions, each atrocity's author wearing Oliver Hardy's face and saying "Now look what you made me do". No stall: the Lama turns the Good/Evil frame upside down first, the listener stands on sore feet throughout, and he answers it all with "No".
  • Never Whistle While You're Pissing (about 900 words, a document read aloud). The Snafu Principle and the redundancy passage, cut into a stoned game of "who is the Martian".
  • Mama Sutra's lecture (about 5,000 words, a conversation). Bourbon is the gauge: she tells him to drink before each layer, and he goes from "Can't drink on duty" to "May I have more?" It sags in the Konan/Kukulan stretch (reported speech) but ends on Hagbard, which brings it back to the plot.
  • Telemachus Sneezed (about 1,800 words in two parts, a book summarised by a reader on a plane). Atlanta Hope's novel has its own front reveal (mad Captain Cork secretly runs guns for God's Lightning), and its doomed pilot shares a name with the real pilot of Simon's plane. The clown version and the real thread are literally on the same flight.
  • Knight's memoir (about 4,500 words, a confession). It keeps moving because each layer gets its own scene (banquet, riot, password).

Mechanism notes

  • C (front), at full strength. Three ways a layer breaks: a superior's offhand remark ("Nobody in the Order has ever told you the truth?"); a clearance or password detail; a fact the reader already holds (the Mohawk story told both ways). A layer holds for a scene (Mama Sutra) or for years (Knight). Each layer is delivered by someone who believes it.
  • Transfer for SDF (proposal). The organisation's best move against James may be a Mama Sutra: a kind, credible person who already has his evidence and gives him a full counter-history in which the organisation is the careful, persecuted party and the leakers are cranks. James acts on it once (say, warns a helper off) and pays for it, then finds the crack himself in a small administrative detail (a distribution list, a "not cleared" note), never through a confession. It obeys the rules: it comes to him as an object, nobody is forced, and being wrong costs him.
  • A (gate), inverted. Hagbard's own front is FUCKUP's "Assumption A", which lets him press the button and costs him the Demonstration it was meant to protect.
  • Comedy survives escalation because each revelation comes in a comic voice, not because the stakes drop: Chips in a Lovecraft church, Danny's drink count, narcs named Galley and Eichmann "only following orders", the fifth set of strings. Hiroshima and the camps sit inside the Laurel-and-Hardy frame without being softened by it.

Quotes

  • "There is no religion in the world— not one— that is not a front for the Cult of the Yellow Sign." (Trip 8, Mama Sutra): the front names a front.
  • "be sure to ask for Miss Mao, not Mama Sutra. Mama isn't cleared for this." (Trip 8, Hassan): a whole layer broken by a clearance detail.
  • "Most people in espionage don't know who they're working for" (Trip 8, Winifred): one local cover story per helper.
  • "I'm tired being a puppet on four sets of strings." (Actually, I know I just wanted a fifth set.) (Trip 8, Knight): escalation as a joke.

Flags

  • Real people named as complicit throughout: Hoover; a Secret Service double agent at Dallas; S. M. Holland's death hinted at; Lindbergh Sr. and the Federal Reserve; Reles's death ordered by Drake; Jefferson and Franklin as Illuminati; AMORC said to hold "a couple of plants". SDF must not do this.
  • No invented edits on real books (Weishaupt's book and Telemachus Sneezed are invented).
  • The slurs and sexual content belong to this book's era and voice; none of it carries over.

notes.title: section 07 (Trip 9, Yesod: Walpurgisnacht Rock)
notes.html:
Coverage: the whole of the Ninth Trip (about 33,700 words), read in full, 12 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 07; no edition data in the file. No numbered chapters; cites name the scene.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Confrontation office, earlier) Joe Malik wants to run his magazine and work out which side Hagbard is on Mal's goose riddle; Jim Cartwright's cranks plus Anthrax Tau; a manuscript about something other than its pitch Fear (he rewrites his editorial on germ war); Pat Walsh radios his mail to the enemy Both sides fill his in-tray, and the scariest item points at Hagbard He goes to Hagbard for straight answers
2 (Hagbard's stateroom) "a straight answer this time" A dull stock-loser shot Kennedy; Hagbard knows Joe bombed his own office; May first is fixed His secret is known; each answer opens a bigger question Hagbard says he is "helping" the Illuminati, and the Tarot card he draws says trickster He takes a pistol (with a silver bullet) to Ingolstadt
3 (Ingolstadt) To stop Hagbard after the battle The AMA are four of the five Illuminati Primi; Eris throws the apple; the bridge is sunk; the Primi die one by one He refuses the acid and has to "find your own Sacrament" Once the four are dead only one Primus is left, and it is Hagbard He shoots Hagbard (or imagines it), then hands him the gun: "I still trust you."

Why it grips

  • How the reader stays oriented. The Trip cuts between a dozen places, times and narrators, often mid-sentence. "While" clauses tie each cut to a date the reader already knows ("On April 25, while Carmel looted Maldonado's safe"). Parallel clocks place the cut-ins ("It was 6:45 P.M. just then in Ingolstadt"). Song lyrics in capitals work as section breaks. First-person narrators (Mary Lou, an unnamed "pentuple agent") are never labelled; their first sentence identifies them. The climax becomes a nursery-rhyme countdown, "And then there were four", down to none.
  • The gun is planted three times before it is used. In Joe's pocket outside the tent, when Hagbard catches him holding it ("like a little boy caught playing with himself"), and in Mary Lou's acid stream ("a silver bullet in it"). The reader waits for the shot through the whole battle; it comes after the battle is won.
  • The reversal is a refusal. Joe works out the hidden layer (Hagbard is the fifth Primus) and then declines to act on it. Hagbard's "genuine surprise" is the first time he has been out-thought all book.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

A front, layer on layer, each taken apart on the page:

  1. The lore the reader was given earlier was planted. Pat Walsh's research memos were "false leads" (her transmitter scene). Gruad hands out five alternate histories (Carcosa, Mu, the snake, Urantia, Atlantis) for agents to plant, and the Atlantis one has "certain changes" to make the Illuminati look worse. The lore the reader trusted becomes one of five plants.
  2. The great assassination has a dull answer. A stock-loser fired before "Oswald or Harry Coin or the Mafia gun". Held one page, then tied back: his stock was Blue Sky, Inc., client of the Illuminati's front law firm.
  3. The villains wear a cover identity. The world's biggest rock band is the four Primi: "We spent years building up our identity as the American Medical Association".
  4. The heroes are inside the enemy. Hagbard is the fifth Primus (Hastur, "the skeleton at the feast" at Agharti, who warns the other four).
  5. There is a layer below that. Mary Lou, tripping: "there's a secret society behind the secret society". A parenthesis also promises that a dolphin's discovery "would change everybody's conspiracies".

What breaks each layer is never deduction. It is a document arriving, a confession offered ("Ask me anything and you get the truth"), a drug, or an overheard scene. Each layer holds only until the next cut, and the reader usually learns before the characters do.

How the lore gets in

  • Cartwright's monologue (about 2,500 words, a visitor in the office). It mixes cranks (three Bavarian conspiracies run the TV networks; Rosebud) with the one claim that matters (Anthrax Tau). Joe can't tell them apart because Cartwright "knew so much about so many other things." It ends in an object, the manuscript with a false subject on its title page. No stall, because Joe's fear drives the next scene.
  • The Sea of Valusia tour (about 3,000 words, a scene). Lore seen through the sub's window (the peace symbol's "real" origin, Nessie, the sleeping army), punctured by Harry Coin suspecting "Rear projection".
  • Malaclypse on hair and serpents (about 1,200 words, table talk). Deliberate absurdity, broken up by George and by Mavis walking in.
  • The Drake book (about 600 words, a document arriving by post). Ends on a phone call and a coded promise of an emissary.
  • The Hierophant (about 700 words, three books on a shelf). Joe tries to settle his doubt by reading; the third book is by an enemy.

Mechanism notes

  • C (front), clear evidence. Every layer stays funny and partly true. The front law firm keeps changing its joke name ("Ruly, Kempt, Sheveled and Couth") yet "to keep up the front" does real legal work for Blue Sky. For SDF: a cover that does real work, and each new layer tied to a detail from the old one, so it feels found, not added.
  • Clown beside the truth, on purpose. Gruad's five planted histories, Pat Walsh's false memos, the peace-symbol gambit ("which to a small extent discredited the peace movement"). This is SDF's organisation exactly.
  • Leaks are shrugged off. Taffy explains a too-accurate novel: "A mind leak," something that "just happens sometimes". The organisation doesn't hunt the novelist. That is SDF's discredit-not-prevent attitude, played as office gossip.
  • D (lock and key), inverted. Joe gets every key, then refuses the act the keys were for: a door opens and he chooses not to walk through.
  • Comedy survives escalation by pairing. Every horror is matched with a deflation in the same paragraph: the White House burning / "TAKE A MIDGET TO LUNCH"; the Pentagon bombing / a man drawing a chalk line across the gap; the President shot / "Let's toast some marshmallows"; the eternal damnation of Wolfgang / "And then there was one." The SINK epigraph ("I sank it!") pays off as "I sank the George Washington Bridge!" Evil is a dull office: FDR, demoted, is "Monotony Monitor".
  • Fifth: every witness gets their own explanation of the miracle. Lady Velkor saw Isis, Fission Chips saw a drug, Joe (taken for a tree) saw "a master Magician" or "a master con man". The climax is its own cover: told so many ways that no account survives.

Quotes

  • "Each of you will be responsible for planting the evidence to make one ot these histories seem fairly credible." (Trip 9, Gruad): rival explanations planted on purpose.
  • "This lake thing is just to give us something we can understand, or almost understand." (Trip 9, Mary Lou): the visible threat as a cover.
  • "there's a secret society behind the secret society: The Illuminati we're fighting are puppets of another Illuminati and so are we." (Trip 9, Mary Lou): the next layer, announced while she is tripping.
  • "I read all the clues, just like you wanted me to. I know you're the fifth Illuminatus Primus" (Trip 9, Joe): the solver declines to do what the solution calls for.

Flags

  • Real people named as complicit: FDR as an Illuminati servant (Pearl Harbor implied); Hitler given power by the "Illuminated Lodge"; Bertrand Russell's circle manipulated; Cartwright's title page blames real assassinations (Malcolm X, JFK, King, RFK) on a conspiracy. SDF must not.
  • Real films (Gunga Din, Citizen Kane) and a real novel (The Manchurian Candidate, "A mind leak") are given hidden meanings. The texts themselves are not edited. No invented edits on real books here.

notes.title: section 08 (Book Five, Trip 10, Malkuth, and the Appendices note)
notes.html:
Coverage: Book Five "Grummet", the Tenth Trip (Malkuth) to the end of the narrative, plus the note that opens the Appendices (about 29,800 words), read in full, 12 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 08; no edition data in the file. No chapter numbers here; cites are Trip 10 plus the scene.

Movements

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (the Bugatti after the acid night) Joe wants the answer The Saures, Weishaupt, Hitler and Stalin only thought they were Illuminati; the real order (A∴A∴) has no name; Cartwright's three-conspiracies story was planted to steer Joe; the founder repented and spread his own bad press Joe learns Hagbard "programmed" him; bombing his own office was not his idea Hagbard promises more surprises; the fifth Illuminatus Primus is still unnamed The submarine, Stella's story, the Tarot
2 (the stateroom) George wants to know if Stella, Mavis and Miss Mao are real Stella was a Hollywood actress in the US top Five, turned by Hagbard, made into Eris by conditioning plus magic, then a faked suicide He loses both women as he knew them The fifth Primus is still unknown; Howard warns the Illuminati's god is at sea Leviathan
3 (the bridge; Portinari's beam to the Dealy Lama) Survival, then the last name The god behind the symbols is a three-billion-year-old single cell shaped like a pyramid; it wants the computer, not worship. Through it George learns Hagbard is the fifth Primus Hagbard admits his Demonstration failed; the California quake; the last eagle shot Nothing left to find; Hagbard names a starship and an immortality pill FUCKUP signs off; the earth cracks under Smiling Jim

Why it grips

  • Every answer arrives already doubted. The revelations land on two sceptics. Joe says he will not believe a word; at the Tarot both men wonder whether this is a final explanation or a new put-on. The reader is never asked to believe a layer, only to watch it hit someone who resists it, so the payoff moves without asking for trust the book has spent four volumes eroding.
  • A ticking clock under the philosophy. While the long talk goes on, two parenthetical threads count down: the Los Angeles seismograph climbs grade 2, 3, 4, 5 toward 6, and Smiling Jim climbs toward the last eagle's nest. The talk stays still; the clock does not. The book ends when both strike in the same sentence.
  • Orientation by signature. The section jumps between 1928 Boston, Ingolstadt, Las Vegas, Washington, Nairobi and the submarine, sometimes inside a paragraph. Each thread has a mark the reader knows at once: Mary Lou's monologues open with "NO—" and run unpunctuated; the street preacher is in capitals; the eagle and seismograph live in parentheses; the President asks everything "shrewdly"; the opening dawn panorama gives each city's clock time. A shared object often stitches the cut: a phone ringing, a book closing in Kenya as drums stop at Orabi.
  • The scene that does the most work is Mama Sutra's tarot reading for the young Drake (1928). A fraud who reads clues from the wrinkles in his suit makes a true reading, and Drake answers with the longest straight speech in the section (Château-Thierry, dominance). The villain's whole philosophy arrives as a scene with a two-dollar fee, cut against the preacher's capitals.

How the conspiracy moves the story here

Mostly by being cleaned up, and the cleanup is itself a front. Hagbard hands out envelopes. Danny gets a photo of Knight and Hirsch setting the bomb timer, a frame-up. Chips gets every BUGGER agent's name and bank account and is told his cover story need not be believed: "They won't believe it, but they'll think you believe it. That's good enough." Saul sells the President an international conspiracy and lies on television. Hitler goes into a Jewish cemetery on forged Israeli papers.

The official sceptic is part of the cover. Hauptmann, the German detective, dismisses conspiracy theories as unscientific while twenty-three dead Illuminati sit in the room. A reasonable man next to the real question does the same work as a clown.

How the lore gets in

  • Hagbard in the Bugatti (about 3,000 words, conversation). Broken by Drake heckling the preacher in 1928, the Dillinger quintuplets, the President and Mary Lou. Joe's objections keep it a duel. No stall: each claim meets a sharper one.
  • Stella's origin (about 2,500 words, flashback she narrates). Framed as a film romance, with George interrupting. Two servants in clown suits argue a different proposition every morning, so even the training is a joke.
  • Miss Portinari's Tarot (about 1,200 words, lecture). Its middle half-hour vanishes in one sentence; Joe later cites the skip as proof they are in a book. It stalls, and the authors admit it.
  • Gruad's confession (about 900 words, telepathic conversation). Given to Miss Portinari and the reader only.
  • Leviathan (about 1,500 words, scene). The deepest lore arrives as a talking sea monster, and Joe calls it camp.

Mechanism notes

  • C (front), the payoff. Trip 10 strips layers in order. (1) The Saures are frauds. (2) The single eternal Illuminati becomes many imitators, and Hagbard admits he planted the midway version: "I sent Jim Cartwright to you with that yarn about three conspiracies". The front was built as a resting place for the investigator. (3) Hagbard is the fifth Primus, the worm in the golden apple. (4) The devil-founder repented and wrote his own bad reputation. (5) Over the heroes' heads, for the reader only: the Dealy Lama, inventor of Operation Mindfuck, is Gruad, the Atlantean founder, who scattered false stories and hid. (6) The god behind the symbols is a lonely single cell. (7) The narrator is FUCKUP, and Joe says the real authors are outside the universe.
  • Reveal or refuse? Both. Each layer is revealed in full, then shown to be a story told by someone with a motive. The last content is a thesis: the power to say No, and the fear of death as the lever every government pulls. The documentary payoff is refused with a joke: "Eight of the appendices were removed due to the paper shortage." For SDF: James's bottom layer can be a method, not a person, said plainly, while the documents stay incomplete.
  • The defeated old head talks, twice. Hagbard, the active head, confesses failure (deception, carnival magic, murder) and waits for the bill. Gruad, the old cynic who never acted, laughs at his own youth: "The only thing to be said for me is that I happen to be right." SDF could use the pair: the defeated head explains; the one who never moved was right. Nobody is punished on the page; the bill arrives as an event (the quake).
  • Comedy survives escalation by sitting beside the serious material rather than breaking it. Drake's speech and Mary Lou's monologues are played straight and long; around them runs a low chorus (the poker game betting tons of flax, obscene phone calls cutting into Saul's TV lie). Every cosmic claim gets one deflating line within a sentence or two.
  • Fifth: the cost lands on a bystander. The last image is an anti-smut crusader shooting the last eagle and calling it immortality as the ground opens.

Quotes

  • "I sent Jim Cartwright to you with that yarn about three conspiracies" (Trip 10, the Bugatti): the cover layer built for the investigator.
  • "They won't believe it, but they'll think you believe it. That's good enough." (Trip 10, Chips): sincerity as cover story.
  • "The only thing to be said for me is that I happen to be right." (Trip 10, Gruad): the old head's last word.
  • "Eight of the appendices were removed due to the paper shortage." (Appendices note): refusing the final document as a joke.

Flags

  • Real people named as conspiracy members: Weishaupt, Hitler, Stalin, and (via Hauptmann) Goethe and Beethoven. Hitler dies on forged Israeli papers; Hauptmann voices an "elders of Zion" line. Eichmann and Calley appear as clown servants; Elijah Muhammad and W. D. Fard are set beside Hitler. SDF must not do this.
  • Near an invented edit on a real text: Miss Portinari claims the false Illuminati "deliberately reversed" the Tarot order. SDF forbids invented edits on real books.

notes.title: section 09 (the fourteen appendices, Aleph to Nun)
notes.html:
Coverage: Appendix Aleph (Washington's hemp) through Appendix Nun (additional information about the characters), all fourteen (about 24,400 words), read in full, 12 Nov 2026. Edition: converted text, chunk file 09; no edition data in the file.

Movements

There is no protagonist line here. The appendices are documents outside the story, and the plot is over. Two small scenes inside them move a character.

Step What the protagonist wants right now What he finds What it costs him Why he cannot stop here What it forces next
1 (Beth, Joe Malik, 1980) Proof that his Law of Fives is real A six-fingered baby: the Law holds only because a determined mind can always make evidence fit His evidence file is partly his own work; he is also facing indictment Contempt citation, grand jury, possible exile; the method he trusted is now the thing to doubt He has to read his own findings as findings about himself
2 (Lamed, Miss Portinari, aged almost fifteen) To stay a good Catholic and keep her meditations A stranger at a party corrects her lie about her favourite symbol: "The Sacred Heart." She walks out of her convent school and her family The second image he guessed keeps coming back every time she meditates She goes to find him; two years later he abdicates in her favour (Cheth)

Why it grips

  • The book keeps going after it ends. The appendices give minor characters futures (Aleph: Saul and Barney's agency; Nun: Pricefixer shot two years later, Markoff Chaney in 1984). Back matter carries plot, so every appendix must be read.
  • Every explanation is a trap. Kaph explains the "magic" roses as a gypsy switch, then leaves the three thieves dead in a ditch. Mem explains Mama Sutra's reading as scraps of Manhattan Melodrama, then notes it was the last film the man shot outside the Biograph saw. Each debunking hands the reader a new connection.
  • The narrators argue with themselves. Footnotes ask "Do you believe that?" (Gimmel, Yod), and a character reads the manuscript and says the authors made the evidence up (Tzaddi). The reader never settles which layer is the joke.
  • Withholding as a gag. Cheth is one sentence long. Mem's last question, "Where are the missing eight appendices?", is answered "Censored."

How the conspiracy moves the story here

There is no story left, so the conspiracy moves the reader. Lamed says the book is part of Operation Mindfuck and has programmed the reader, then tests it: "you have lost track of Joe Malik's mysterious dogs by now." A thread planted and dropped on purpose, checked at the end: a canary set in the reader. Yod makes OM a method: nobody knows who is in it, so an outsider must treat everything as part of it (paranoia) or nothing. Mem item 8 shows how a real connection survives: a historian's book records both the vanished eagle (p. 123) and the dead censor (p. 369), and "Neither he nor anyone else ever connected the two occurrences." The truth sits in the record, findable and never found.

How the lore gets in

  • Pseudo-scholarship with real citations (Aleph, Daleth, Vau, Zain), about 6,000 words. Real page numbers carry invented claims in. Each ends by cutting to a character (Simon's toilet paper, Rebecca's books), so no stretch goes long without a person.
  • The history-of-history (Gimmel), about 5,500 words, a mock treatise. The longest stall. It survives on the story at its centre (Weishaupt, drugged on a misread letter, finds a theory of history in a misprinted Necronomicon) and ends on a scene, George Dorn silencing his mother.
  • Hagbard's booklet (Teth), about 3,500 words. Pure argument; it stalls, and the authors joke in advance that Hagbard wanted all of it printed.
  • Operation Mindfuck (Yod), about 2,000 words, a field manual. The mock letter of appointment is reproduced whole: lore as an object a target would hold.
  • Q&A and dramatis personae (Mem, Nun), about 3,500 words. One-paragraph entries, each a joke or a fact. The fastest lore in the book.

Could SDF's List or interludes do this? The List already has the form (documents, no commentary). Illuminatus adds: back matter that carries plot (an entry that quietly finishes a minor character); explaining then re-mystifying (a mundane "after" with a marginal note that isn't); and a test of the reader, planted early and checked late. Proposal, PLACEHOLDER: one List entry whose margin note points back to a detail the reader was allowed to forget.

Mechanism notes

  • C, the front, laid out in full (Gimmel). Weishaupt keeps the Law of Fives secret and pushes Joachim's three ages through a "front man" (Hegel). Public theory (three stages) covers private theory (five), which comes from a drugged misreading of a misprint, which the authors doubt, which the A:.A:. call projection. The bottom layer is a joke. That is mechanism C's danger: if every layer is a front, the reader stops caring which is true. SDF needs a floor (what happens when we die) where the fronts stop.
  • B, the canary as method (Yod). Project Jake (one official gets absurd letters from dozens of real-sounding cabals), the honorary memberships, and Citizens Against Drug Abuse, which campaigns to ban catnip so the drug war looks absurd. SDF's thermostat with the owners swapped: rebels fund nonsense to discredit the state; SDF's Keepers fund it to discredit the question. It works when the target cannot tell "a conspiracy composed entirely of lunatics" from a public "much more imaginative and less stodgy" than he assumed (Yod). Nun gives the cleanest trick for a leak: pamphlets stamped both TOP SECRET and FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE, and no one can work out who stamped which.
  • A, the gate, by way of the investigator (Beth). "The harder I looked, the more things there were that fit." James's risk exactly: a gate that makes him rule out his own pattern-seeing would cost him real confidence in his nose.
  • D, lock and key (Lamed). Hagbard opens Miss Portinari with one private truth, her hidden symbol, and leaves her to come to him; she does, two weeks later. A person chooses.
  • Layered membership (Daleth). The Assassins' lower grades know only that a hidden meaning exists and that they must obey, like SDF's helpers with one task and the word "continuity". The order fell to outsiders it had never infiltrated: a weakness SDF could use (someone the count never reached).
  • Fifth: the misprint as engine (Gimmel). An error in one printing produces a whole doctrine: SDF's premise inverted, a corrupted edition creating belief. The book is fictional, so it is clean to borrow.

Quotes

  • "this relationship can always be demonstrated, given enough ingenuity on the part of the demonstrator." (Beth): the investigator's method turned on himself.
  • "the Joachimite theory would be revived and publicized to mislead others." (Gimmel): the front, stated as policy.
  • "the only safe assumption is that anything a Discordian does is somehow related to OM" (Yod): the double bind that makes discredit work.
  • "This book, being part of the only serious conspiracy it describes— that is, part of Operation Mindfuck— has programmed the reader" (Lamed): the book names itself the canary.

Flags

Real people and organisations named are everywhere. Strictly:

  • Named as Illuminati or complicit: Meyer Amschel Rothschild, de Sade and Sir Francis Dashwood as "the original Five" with Weishaupt and Kolmer (Gimmel; the Rothschild line repeats an antisemitic trope). Hegel as the Illuminati's "front man" (Gimmel). Joyce warned and blinded by the Illuminati (Gimmel). George Washington (the "Weishaupt impersonation theory", Aleph). The authors suggest "Adolf Hitler's link with the Illuminati was not invented" (Lamed footnote).
  • Real assassination figures: Kerry Thornley, named as a friend of Oswald's whom Garrison accused (Nun). The Warren Report called a "novel" (Nun); Capone and the FBI at the Biograph (Mem).
  • Other real people and organisations: Eldridge Cleaver (invented dialogue), Henry Ford and the Protocols, Nixon, Mayor Daley, Leary (Nun, Lamed); astrological lists of real people (Gimmel); ACLU employing the fictional detectives (Aleph), John Birch Society, AMA as a band name, Universal Life Church.
  • Real text reinterpreted: Crowley's Book of Lies, chapter 23, quoted in full as a working spell (Tzaddi). Nothing is edited, but a real book is given an invented secret use. SDF must not do this to a real book.
  • Misprint on a book: the scrambled Necronomicon passage (Gimmel) is a fictional book, so it is allowed.

books.qa:
Answers point to the section notes in this folder (01-trips-1-to-2.md … 09-appendices.md) and, where relevant, to a v8.2 chapter by title. The map is 00-map.md. Everything about SDF here is a PROPOSAL; Santi's decisions are PLACEHOLDER.

The verdict on C

1. Does C, the front, work as an engine or only as lore? Both, and the book shows the difference. When Saul sits in Malik's flat reading memos (Trips 1–4), each layer is broken by the next and the pages turn, but nothing he does is changed by it (01-trips-1-to-2.md, 02-trips-3-to-4.md). When someone acts on a layer as if it were the bottom, C becomes an engine: George stays on the submarine (01), Drake provokes the hidden layer (04-trip-6.md), Danny ends up defending the conspiracy (06-trip-8.md), Joe bombs his own office (07-trip-9.md). See map section 4, verdict (a).

2. So was ADDENDUM 05 wrong? Right about Tier 1, incomplete as a rule. In Tier 1 every front was something the hero learned. Illuminatus shows the missing ingredient: the hero acts on the wrong layer first and pays. Libra (the decoy layer) and Declare (the hero wears fronts) had already said C can be done; this book says what makes it move.

3. What breaks a layer? An object (the jail chapel, the tattoo, a film, a gun), a second person with one more fact, the teller's own admission, a clearance detail ("Mama isn't cleared for this"), or a promotion (01, 03-trip-5.md, 05-trip-7.md, 06-trip-8.md). The hero's theories are always wrong ("Saul was convinced. He was also wrong," Trip 1). He can catch a flaw in an object, as Saul spots the missing mole on a faked slide (02), but he doesn't deduce the next layer. That matches SDF's brief: insights happen to James, and reveals are objects.

4. The notes say "never by deduction." Is that strictly true? No. In Trip 9 Joe tells Hagbard "I read all the clues… I know you're the fifth Illuminatus Primus" (07-trip-9.md), and the Trip 5 note counts "the hero's doubt" as one way a layer breaks (03-trip-5.md). The pattern holds for the middle of the book. The one real deduction comes at the end, and the hero then refuses to act on it. For James, keep deduction for the reading-room offer, which he refuses, and let every earlier layer break on paper.

5. What does "true for the rank" mean, and does it match SDF's helper tiers? Each layer is what a person at that level is told, and it is true enough at that level: Flanagan is "only a Fourth-degree Illuminatus," George will "become a deacon," Hagbard lies "because the human mind can only accept a little of the truth at a time" (03-trip-5.md). That ladder is vertical. SDF's four helper words (honeypot, disaster recovery, conservation, heritage; v7 What was on the phone) sit side by side. They are compartments, not rungs. SDF's real ladder is James's own climb: asker, then program staff (The drill), then the annex role (The money), then the schedule (The schedule), then the offer of a seat (The reading room, continued).

6. What is the "planted resting place"? A middle layer built so the investigator has somewhere to stop. Hagbard confesses it: "I sent Jim Cartwright to you with that yarn about three conspiracies" (08-trip-10.md). Gruad hands out five rival histories for agents to plant (07). SDF already has it twice: "we leave them findable" (the opening) and "You found the seats and thought they were the point. They all do" (v8 The final conversation). Map 5.3 makes James's use of it cost something.

7. Why does a front need a floor? Because if every layer is a front, the reader stops caring which is true. The appendices show it happening: Gimmel stacks theory on theory down to a drugged misreading of a misprint, then a joke (09-appendices.md). Trip 10 avoids it by landing on a method said plainly (the power to say No; fear of death as the lever) while the documents stay incomplete (08). SDF's floor is what happens when we die, reached on the floor in The night he stops being afraid. The final conversation must keep the old man's film claims as his claims, set against that floor.

8. Can James wear a front himself? Yes, if it is made of true things and costs him. Declare 5.3 (the sheets in the program's format) and Libra 5.4 (a decoy ticket) are already proposed. This book adds the cheapest kind: a front the organization has already written for him, the wellbeing referral in map 5.2. It also points out one he already wears, the seats-as-lifeboat line on every sheet (map 5.3). Chips's rule is why a true front is enough: "They won't believe it, but they'll think you believe it. That's good enough" (08).

9. What fronts must James never wear? Anything that needs impersonation, an invented task, a staged ordeal or drugs. Hagbard's whole method (kidnap, a faked-porn ordeal, layered lies "for your own good"; 02, 05) makes the hero a handler. Ana's sleeping pills at The dinner are hers, improvised, and stay that way.

The new devices

10. What exactly is the "diagnosis"? The answer to an investigator is a file saying he is ill. Saul is drugged and told he is a Trenton patrolman called Muldoon, and his skepticism is treated as a symptom (02). Marsh is ridiculed until he disappears and his file is closed as "suicide during drug psychosis" (03). Leakers are filed as nuts who "get it all scrambled" (04-trip-6.md). It discredits without killing, which is SDF's rule for the organization.

11. Who runs the diagnosis in the book? Not only the enemy. Saul's "doctor" turns out to be Joe Malik (02), and the next Trip calls it deprogramming (03). So the diagnosis can also recruit: it breaks the old self so a new allegiance fits. Marsh's file is the hostile version. For SDF, use the hostile version only, and keep it kind on the surface.

12. Is the diagnosis already in SDF? As a rule, yes. Els's folder says a correct reader is "agreed with and then reclassified" (v8.2 The math; v6 The math word for word: "agreement, followed by reclassification"). Nothing on the page reclassifies anyone. Map 5.1 uses it on the dead professor (the neighbor's "he wasn't well") and 5.2 on James (the referral).

13. What is the "kind counter-history"? Mama Sutra (Trip 8, 06). She's kind and credible and already knows what Danny is carrying. She gives him a full history in which the Illuminati are the persecuted party of reason and every leak against them is propaganda. The tell: she asks whether his memos "portrayed them in an unfavorable light" before he has described them. His findings are left alone and given a frame that points the other way. Map 5.1 gives SDF one, the professor's neighbor, whom v7 What was on the phone already lists under Conservation.

14. How does the counter-history break? On a clearance detail, cheaply: "be sure to ask for Miss Mao, not Mama Sutra. Mama isn't cleared for this" (06). The grand account becomes one ring of five. In map 5.1 the break is a line on paper James already holds, When a reader notices.

15. What's the "clown run by the conspiracy itself," and does SDF need it? The W.H. letter, a calm reply saying the whole thing is a campus joke (02); Gruad's five planted histories (07); Naismith selling "Illuminati" cons he doesn't believe are true (05). SDF has it already in the thermostat (The band) and the polite forum correction (Leiden). Nothing to add.

16. What about the reasonable skeptic as cover? Hauptmann dismisses conspiracy theories as unscientific with twenty-three dead Illuminati in the room (08). A sensible man next to the real question does a clown's job. In SDF it is Pieter's "leave it" and the old man's "what they are in a room is nothing" (v7 The reading room, continued). Already there.

17. "The door that was allowed": should James learn a door he chose to walk through was opened for him? The book does it (the rescue "according to plan," 01; the film shown to Joe with the door left unlocked, 05). For SDF it's already proposed: Libra 5.2 (pulled versus handed), Pynchon 5.1 (the errand that signs him in). Don't add a third.

Comedy and orientation

18. How does the book stay funny while the stakes go up to nuclear war? Five habits. Every horror gets a deflation in the same paragraph ("the President shot / 'Let's toast some marshmallows'," 07). The jokes target institutions, never victims (04). The atrocity passages carry no jokes, and the comedy stands on either side of them (03). Revelations come in a comic voice without the stakes dropping (06). Each layer gets sillier as it gets more frightening: the same paragraph about Fernando Poo runs for Washington, Moscow and Peking (01).

19. What is the one-line tone rule? Mavis: "It's not true unless it makes you laugh, but you don't understand until it makes you weep" (03). It suits SDF's "funny to the end" with Buddy poisoned and the other ten. James's voice already does the first half, and the corridor and the vet do the second.

20. Which SDF chapters most need the pairing rule? The ones where the organization is at its worst and James isn't in the room: A street, night; Leiden, Friday; The leak; and Monday's "why they don't kill him." Illuminatus's version is evil as a dull office (FDR demoted to "Monotony Monitor," 07). SDF already speaks this language ("it's a budgeting thing," Utrecht, 1993; "a question of air," v7 The reading room, continued). Keep the jokes on the institution, never on Henk, Noor or the dog.

21. How does the reader stay oriented across so many jumps? Always when, not always who. Every cut carries a date, a clock, or "while" tied to an event the reader already knows ("On April 25, while Carmel looted Maldonado's safe," 07). Parallel clocks ("10:30 P.M., Ingolstadt time," 03). Parentheses hold the present frame during a flashback (06). Refrains and hymn lines work as section breaks (02). Each voice has a fixed idiom, so you know who is speaking before the name (06). A ticking clock runs under long talk: the seismograph climbing grade by grade (08).

22. Where does orientation fail? When the point of view slips mid-scene: Saul into Muldoon's "I," a nameless "I" who turns out to be Atlanta Hope, George moving from third to first person mid-paragraph. Each slip costs the reader about a page (01). SDF's single first person, with villain-alone chapters set apart, avoids most of this. Don't let a villain chapter open mid-thought without a time.

23. Can the fixed-idiom trick settle PLACEHOLDER #4 (the car park)? It gives a middle option. Keep the handler unnamed but give him one phrase the reader has heard from Julian (v6 A car park already has the flask: "he'd said he was a flask man"). The reader knows who he is and James doesn't, which is dread without anyone acting, as with Hagbard's call that George never hears (01). It isn't an action by James, so it isn't a map proposal.

24. How long can a lore dump run without stalling? The memos never stall at 150 to 700 words a piece, because each one contradicts the last (02). Mama Sutra holds for 5,000 words because the bourbon is a gauge and the account ends on Hagbard, back in the plot (06). Malaclypse stalls at 3,000 and is saved only by a physical proof and an order (04). The rule matches the v8 brief: any speech over about 150 words gets broken by the other person, a dog or a phone.

The proposals

25. Which map proposal would you take first? 5.2, reclassified. It cashes a rule SDF already prints (The math) and gives A car park's "stopped asking out loud" a cause James chose. It also answers verdict (b) with the cheapest legal front. It costs one scene with Pieter and a few lines with the counselor.

26. Does 5.1 (the neighbor) overload The math? It might. The math is about 2,800 words in v8.2 and already holds Els, the folder, the arithmetic and the breakfast. The alternative is the end of The week it vanished, after Beard Man's account of the death (PLACEHOLDER). Either way the scene should be short: a garden, one cup, one question she asks too early.

27. Does 5.1 decide Santi's line to Els (PLACEHOLDER #5)? No. It gives the line a job: James has walked in with the neighbor's word "illness" and has to undo it on his way out. What he says stays Santi's.

28. Are 5.2 and Declare 5.1 compatible? Yes, in sequence. Under the referral James goes quiet, and the handler punishes it ("out loud, which is worse," A car park). In Leiden, Noor says a loud reader is a story they can manage (v6 Leiden), and Declare 5.1 has him go loud on a timer. He tries both fronts and each is read. Pynchon 5.4 (photographed among cranks at a funded event) is a third discredit, and that's one too many. Pick one.

29. Does 5.3 break the deal in The final conversation? Only slightly, and on purpose. The deal is James's silence about the organization. Telling Pieter "nobody's kept, the ones on it included" repeats the old man's own claim to the one helper who was on the list. PLACEHOLDER: whether Anneke hears of it, and whether it costs James anything more than knowing he said it.

30. Should James ever run a ladder of lies the way Hagbard does? No. That's the first thing in Do not take. Twenty minutes is the counter-model: every object on the cloth, "I don't know" said six times. 5.3 lets James notice he used the organization's version once, and give the bottom layer plainly to one person.

31. Is there a canary to borrow? Only one, aimed at the reader: "you have lost track of Joe Malik's mysterious dogs by now" (Lamed, 09). A thread is planted in Trip 1 and checked at the very end. Section 09 suggests a List entry whose margin note points back at something the reader was allowed to forget. In SDF the dogs are never lost track of, so pick a different object (PLACEHOLDER).

32. Is there a misprint idea SDF can use? Gimmel's doctrine grows from one misprint in a fictional book (09): a corrupted edition creating belief, SDF's premise turned inside out. It's clean to borrow because the book is invented. Don't attach it to a real one.

Rules and risks

33. What exactly can't come over? Real people as complicit (Kennedy's killers named, Hoover, FDR, Hitler, Rothschild, Hegel; 01–09, Flags). Real organizations as fronts (the AMA, the Federal Reserve, the Pentagon, the John Birch Society). Invented secret meanings for real books, films or the Tarot (Moby-Dick, Gunga Din, The Manchurian Candidate as "a mind leak," Crowley chapter 23 as a spell). And the book's slurs and sexual shock material.

34. Is Dutch Schultz's last words (a real document read as code) allowed in SDF terms? At the edge (04).
